item.title: [SCMP] US scientist Elsa Reichmanis defends global collaboration amid scrutiny of science exchange
item.description:
American materials scientist Elsa Reichmanis, whose pioneering work helped lay part of the foundation for modern semiconductor manufacturing, said scientific collaboration should transcend rivalry after receiving one of China’s highest honours for foreign experts, describing science as “a universal language” that benefits all of society.

Reichmanis, a professor of chemical engineering in Lehigh University’s department of chemical and biomolecular engineering and the director of its Institute for Functional Materials and Devices, was one of nine recipients of the China International Science and Technology Cooperation Award in early July.

The award recognises exceptional contributions to scientific exchanges and collaboration with Chinese researchers.
item.content:encoded:
American materials scientist Elsa Reichmanis, whose pioneering work helped lay part of the foundation for modern semiconductor manufacturing, said scientific collaboration should transcend rivalry after receiving one of China’s highest honours for foreign experts, describing science as “a universal language” that benefits all of society.

Reichmanis, a professor of chemical engineering in Lehigh University’s department of chemical and biomolecular engineering and the director of its Institute for Functional Materials and Devices, was one of nine recipients of the China International Science and Technology Cooperation Award in early July.

The award recognises exceptional contributions to scientific exchanges and collaboration with Chinese researchers.

Reichmanis is best known for her groundbreaking work on chemically amplified photoresists – light-sensitive materials used to etch microscopic circuits onto silicon wafers. Her chemistry made it commercially viable to pack tens of millions of transistors – or more – onto a single silicon chip, laying the groundwork for the nanoscale semiconductor industry.

“I was shocked,” said the 72-year-old Reichmanis, an accomplished US chemistry and materials scientist, in an interview with the South China Morning Post.

China held the award ceremony on July 8 at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. Recipients came from eight countries: the US, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Russia, Australia, Belgium and Portugal, representing marine engineering, artificial intelligence (AI), photovoltaics and oncology, among other fields.

The award, established by the State Council – China’s cabinet – in 1994, honours those who collaborate with Chinese partners on significant scientific achievements, introduce advanced technologies, cultivate domestic scientific talent and promote international scientific exchange and cooperation.

This year’s award carries added significance as it comes at a fragile moment for US-China scientific exchange, which faces growing scrutiny amid intensifying technology competition and tightening research restrictions.

On the day of the award ceremony, the US National Science Foundation said in an open letter that it would bar its funded researchers from collaborating with restricted parties, particularly Chinese universities and technology firms, an escalation after years of mounting scrutiny of research ties with China.

Reichmanis said fundamental scientific research should remain distinct from technological competition.

In a sense, the development of technology can be independent from the science

Elsa Reichmanis

“Science is a universal language,” she said. “Scientific collaboration and communication, and having diversity of interactions … provides global society with a knowledge base that can benefit everyone.

“In a sense, the development of technology can be independent from the science”, she added, saying the discipline could be used to build pathways and understanding across borders to help further innovation globally.

Reichmanis’ own relationship with China developed gradually, beginning with early exchanges between the two countries’ chemical societies before expanding to collaborations with Chinese institutions.

A little over two decades ago, she began taking part in joint activities between the American Chemical Society (ACS) and the Chinese Chemical Society, helping organise academic exchanges and build ties with Chinese researchers.

Organisational exchanges gradually developed into a research partnership with Shanghai-based Donghua University. Since 2013, she has worked with the university’s State Key Laboratory of Advanced Fiber Materials to jointly train doctoral students, advance research collaboration and cultivate talent.

Reichmanis said decades working with China had given her a first-hand view of the country’s rise in research capabilities.

When she first visited Chinese laboratories in the early 2000s, state-of-the-art scientific instruments had begun to appear, she said, though some were still relatively underutilised.

But since then, she had observed sustained investment in research infrastructure, growing numbers of scientists and students, as well as steadily improving research quality.

As one of the executive editors of the ACS journal Chemistry of Materials, Reichmanis said she had seen a sharp increase in submissions from Chinese institutions.

“The number of manuscripts being accepted is increasing,” she said, calling it “a testament to the quality of the research that is being done”, adding that the research taking place in China was globally competitive.

Despite her long collaboration with Chinese institutions and early focus on chemically amplified photoresists, Reichmanis dismissed suggestions that she had helped China develop photoresist technology.

China has pushed to develop domestic photoresists to cut its reliance on foreign suppliers. It has made progress in entry-level materials, with a self-sufficiency rate of more than 20 per cent in older G-line and I-line photoresists used for power chips and LEDs, though the high-end market is still dominated by Japanese and US companies.

After Reichmanis received the science cooperation award, voices emerged online linking her pioneering work on chemically amplified photoresists to China’s drive to develop substitutes and localise chipmaking technology.

[Scientific] communication and networking … are going to continue. And it’s really at the essence of making the world a better place

Elsa Reichmanis

Reichmanis said that since her research in the field had been published openly in peer-reviewed journals decades ago, it now served as part of the broader scientific discoveries available worldwide.

“The research I do … is not application-specific. It’s in the realm of fundamental science,” she said, adding that “the research that I do now is very far removed from my early research.”

According to the Lehigh University website, Reichmanis’ work focuses on studying how to control materials at the sub-nanometre scale in “transistor devices, photovoltaics and high-capacity energy storage”.

An Australian emigrant who moved to the US, Reichmanis started her industry career at the AT&T Bell Laboratories, now known as Nokia Bell Labs, following a three-year postdoctoral fellowship at Syracuse University, where she earned her PhD in organic chemistry at age 22 in 1975.

At Bell Labs, Reichmanis and her team helped solve a critical bottleneck in modern semiconductor manufacturing by developing new “chemically amplified resists” for deep ultraviolet lithography, allowing chipmakers to print extremely small and precise circuit patterns that conventional optical photoresists could not achieve.

Her chemistry work made it commercially viable to pack tens of millions of transistors – or more – onto a single silicon chip, laying the groundwork for the nanoscale semiconductor industry.

Reichmanis credited the achievement to Bell Labs’ collaborative culture, emphasising that the breakthrough had been a team effort.

“I’m a very small piece of that really large effort,” she said, adding that advances in chipmaking had depended on contributions from chemists, physicists, engineers, materials scientists and equipment designers working together.

That collaborative philosophy at Bell Labs, she said, had shaped her entire career.

“Just about everything I’ve done in my career has been the result of very valuable collaborations.”

When asked about whether growing US-China tensions would threaten future scientific cooperation, Reichmanis remained optimistic.

“[Scientific] communication and networking … are going to continue,” she said, adding that technology would facilitate continued interactions with global support for multidisciplinary, fundamental research to underpin everything that scientists do.

“And it’s really at the essence of making the world a better place.”

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s Anwar seizes on haj fund report ahead of Negeri Sembilan election
item.description:
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has seized on the release of a long-delayed inquiry into the country’s Islamic pilgrimage fund to revive his anti-corruption message just days before the state of Negeri Sembilan holds an election.

The move is seen as a calculated bid by Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition to turn a governance issue against state rival Umno, although observers are divided on whether it would be damaging enough to hurt Malaysia’s oldest Malay nationalist party.

Anwar’s latest salvo further illustrates the fragility of uneasy political alliances in the country, where parties lock horns in state polls but govern together at the federal level. Umno has been a dominant force in government for more than six decades until 2018, when it lost the general election, and is now part of the federal unity government led by PH.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has seized on the release of a long-delayed inquiry into the country’s Islamic pilgrimage fund to revive his anti-corruption message just days before the state of Negeri Sembilan holds an election.

The move is seen as a calculated bid by Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition to turn a governance issue against state rival Umno, although observers are divided on whether it would be damaging enough to hurt Malaysia’s oldest Malay nationalist party.

Anwar’s latest salvo further illustrates the fragility of uneasy political alliances in the country, where parties lock horns in state polls but govern together at the federal level. Umno has been a dominant force in government for more than six decades until 2018, when it lost the general election, and is now part of the federal unity government led by PH.

Saturday’s Negeri Sembilan election follows PH’s drubbing earlier this month in the Johor election by the Barisan Nasional coalition, which is led by its founding party Umno.

In 2021, the Royal Commission of Inquiry (RCI) was established to examine the management and operations of Tabung Haji, the state-run haj pilgrims fund board, from 2014 to 2020 after independent reviews flagged governance concerns.

Tabung Haji was established in 1963 to help Muslims save and invest for the haj pilgrimage to Mecca. It is one of the country’s largest Islamic financial institutions, playing a central role in organising Malaysia’s annual haj pilgrimage.

Islam is the country’s largest religion, with over 63 per cent of Malaysia’s population, or 21.8 million of the current 34.4 million population, being Muslims.

The commission’s findings were submitted to the king in August 2022 but remained unreleased until they were declassified on Wednesday, putting the issue back in the political spotlight just days before the Negeri Sembilan polls.

Although the report did not directly implicate politicians, it raises questions over whether its release could sway the Malay-Muslim electorate.

Political analyst Azmi Hassan said the timing of the report’s release appeared “very fishy”, coming just days before the election, but questioned the furore surrounding it because the report did not find wrongdoing by politicians or members of Tabung Haji’s board and instead attributed mistakes to senior management staff.

“I don’t see whether Pakatan Harapan can gain any advantage by releasing the Tabung Haji RCI report, except that it gives a positive view of the Umno government at that particular time,” said Azmi, a senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research.

Prominent Umno leaders like former prime minister Ismail Sabri Yaakob, who approved the inquiry in the first place, were also among those who called for the release of the findings.

He said the report’s conclusions on issues such as high dividend payouts and haj subsidies were not new and would likely not be viewed negatively by Muslim voters, suggesting that the findings could instead reinforce positive perceptions of the previous Umno administration.

Despite this, Anwar used the report to reinforce his anti-corruption message on the campaign trail, calling for investigations into its findings during a rally in Nilai, a city in Negeri Sembilan, on Wednesday.

“I do not want to interfere. Let them investigate. Do not wait,” he said.

The political rivalry between PH and Umno has often been shaped by race-based narratives, particularly attacks targeting PH’s Chinese-majority component party, the Democratic Action Party (DAP). But Anwar argued that the Tabung Haji findings had nothing to do with race.

“People say this country is ruined by the Chinese, everything is Chinese. The Chinese are DAP Chinese,” he said. “This is Tabung Haji. This is a Malay issue, this is a Malay problem. It has nothing to do with the Chinese.”

Since losing power in 2018, the BN has seen some of its leaders, predominantly those from Umno, embroiled in a string of corruption scandals.

Investigations swept up former prime ministers, chief ministers and heads of government-linked organisations, with outcomes ranging from convictions and acquittals to withdrawal of charges.

The most prominent was former prime minister Najib Razak’s conviction for corruption charges over the sovereign wealth fund 1MDB scandal. Other cases saw Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, former Negeri Sembilan chief minister Mohd Isa Abdul Samad and former Tabung Haji chairman Abdul Azeez Abdul Rahim facing accusations of financial wrongdoings.

Abdul Azeez was given a full acquittal over three corruption and six money-laundering charges in December 2022.

Other analysts, however, said the release of the report, a long-delayed governance exercise, so close to the state election was clearly influenced by political timing and could resonate more strongly in the run-up to the next general election.

Wong Chin Huat, a political scientist at Sunway University, said the issue had shifted beyond questions of federal or state governance to “a normative choice between Malay unity and corruption”.

“Some voters may tolerate their predators from within for communal unity,” Wong said. “But it’s at least out in the public now. This may be too late for Negeri Sembilan, but expect it to grow in media attention in the 16th general election.”

Malaysia’s next general election is slated to be held on or before February 2028.

Ahmad Mohsein Azman, a senior analyst at BowerGroupAsia, said the timing of the report might not be intended to serve as an issue for debate for the Negeri Sembilan state election but rather as a broader move to push narratives in anticipation of the next general election.

“Pakatan Harapan’s intent to gain political mileage from the RCI’s release would only act as smoke and mirrors to plaster over faults in the current administration,” Ahmad Mohsein said.

He said the impact on voter perception ahead of the polls this weekend was slim, so long as the fundamentals of the pilgrimage management remain sound.

“Ensuring the continuity of Tabung Haji’s operations takes precedence over conducting a witch hunt to identify and penalise individuals responsible for the mismanagement and governance lapses.”

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s ‘shocking’ deal to return 5,000 Rohingya to Myanmar triggers refoulement fears
item.description:
Malaysia’s claim that Myanmar has agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya has raised hopes of easing pressure on its strained refugee system, but has also alarmed activists over the risks of returning members of the persecuted minority group to a country still engulfed by conflict.

Rights groups insist any movement of refugees into Myanmar – where the military is fighting multiple conflicts and most Rohingya are denied citizenship – must be voluntary and backed by guarantees of safety, legal status and freedom of movement.

Wednesday’s announcement covers only a fraction of the 126,144 Rohingya registered with the United Nations refugee agency in Malaysia, but experts say it would mark a rare attempt to return refugees from a persecuted minority to their country of origin.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia’s claim that Myanmar has agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya has raised hopes of easing pressure on its strained refugee system, but has also alarmed activists over the risks of returning members of the persecuted minority group to a country still engulfed by conflict.

Rights groups insist any movement of refugees into Myanmar – where the military is fighting multiple conflicts and most Rohingya are denied citizenship – must be voluntary and backed by guarantees of safety, legal status and freedom of movement.

Wednesday’s announcement covers only a fraction of the 126,144 Rohingya registered with the United Nations refugee agency in Malaysia, but experts say it would mark a rare attempt to return refugees from a persecuted minority to their country of origin.

As of the end of February, Malaysia had 215,600 registered refugees and asylum seekers, nearly 194,000 of whom were from Myanmar – including Rohingya.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced the agreement at a campaign event in Negeri Sembilan on Wednesday, presenting it as a product of bilateral ties.

“People ask why we do not simply send them back. Send them where? Myanmar had refused to accept them before,” Anwar was quoted as saying by local media.

“We have good relations with Myanmar. They have now agreed to take 5,000 Rohingya from Malaysia,” he said, without identifying who gave the undertaking, where the refugees would be sent or whether they had agreed to return.

Debbie Stothard, coordinator of the pro-democracy group Altsean-Burma, said any coerced removal would breach the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits sending people to a country where they face persecution or serious harm.

“It is absolutely shocking and incomprehensible that Malaysia is talking about, let alone thinking about, forcibly deporting asylum seekers from Burma,” she said. “This is essentially refoulement under international law.”

Stothard said returnees could face forced conscription, arbitrary detention, torture and forced labour, arguing that the violence that drove people from Myanmar had not abated.

There were 5,483 armed clashes and attacks on civilians, 1,625 civilian deaths and 1,416 air attacks in Myanmar during the first six months of 2026, according to figures compiled by Altsean-Burma from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project.

The UN said this month that more than 16 million people needed humanitarian help in Myanmar and nearly 3.8 million were displaced, as fighting, movement restrictions and blocked aid access deepened the crisis.

In Rakhine, the western state that most Rohingya fled, Myanmar’s military and the Arakan Army continue to fight for control of the territory.

Moe Thuzar, a senior fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and coordinator of its Myanmar studies programme, said the military government was seeking to expand its diplomatic room and establish itself as the country’s principal international representative.

“The regime in Naypyidaw is actively seeking to widen its diplomatic space to assert itself as the primary interlocutor for Myanmar,” she said.

Thuzar said the Association of Southeast Asian Nations had been monitoring the Rohingya repatriation issue and associated humanitarian conditions since before the 2021 military coup, but had made little, if any, progress towards securing their safe and voluntary return.

“As the ground and administrative control of Rakhine state remains contested, and the question of the status and treatment of the Rohingya is still pending, existing concerns will continue about what ‘safe and voluntary return’ means in actual implementation,” she said.

Charles Santiago, co-chairman of Asean Parliamentarians for Human Rights, said Malaysia should not present the proposed return as a diplomatic achievement without explaining what awaited the refugees.

“Malaysia cannot, in good conscience, celebrate the return of 5,000 Rohingya to Myanmar without first answering one fundamental question: return them to what?” he said. “If there are no credible guarantees of safety, dignity, citizenship and voluntary return, this is not a diplomatic achievement to shout about but a moral failure.”

Refuge under strain

Anwar’s announcement came two days after Malaysian authorities detained more than 100 Rohingya who had gathered outside the UNHCR office in Kuala Lumpur seeking help. The group said they had been evicted from homes in the northern state of Penang.

Police released 109 of them after confirming they held valid UNHCR documents, relocating the group to addresses linked to relatives or contacts in Kuala Lumpur, Selangor and Penang.

The episode followed weeks of worsening hostility towards Rohingya in Malaysia, where online misinformation and hate speech have been blamed for harassment and the closure of community-run schools serving refugee children barred from entering the public education system.

Malaysia is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and has no law formally recognising refugees, leaving UNHCR cardholders without the right to work or attend government schools, and vulnerable to arrest under immigration law.

The government last week asked UNHCR to suspend new registrations while it rolls out its own refugee registration document system.

Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan later said Malaysia should reconsider the UN agency’s presence unless it accepted stricter joint screening.

“We want cooperation and strict screening,” he was quoted as saying. “If they do not want to cooperate, in my opinion, it is time for us to reconsider the presence of UNHCR in the country so that we do not continue to be burdened.”

The agency said it remained committed to supporting Malaysia’s national asylum framework and had consistently maintained that Rohingya returns must result from each refugee’s free and informed choice, and take place safely and with dignity.

This Week in Asia has reached out to Mohamad Hasan for comments.

About 1.2 million Rohingya are based in Bangladesh, mainly in refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar. Conflict and dwindling aid continue to drive their dangerous journeys across the Andaman Sea.

The UN said this month that more than 500 people, mostly Rohingya, were feared dead after two boats that left Rakhine were reported missing or capsized.

Mariko Hall, UNHCR’s spokeswoman for Asia and the Pacific, told This Week in Asia that the agency was “concerned” about reports of Rohingya refugees returning from Malaysia to Myanmar, but had not been involved any such discussions.

“Given the ongoing conflict across Myanmar, current conditions do not support the safe and sustainable return of refugees from Myanmar,” Hall said.

“Any refugee return must be voluntary, based on an informed decision, and take place in conditions of safety and dignity. UNHCR stands ready to engage with relevant authorities on protection safeguards.”

item.title: [SCMP] East Timor’s Myanmar war crimes case puts Asean non-interference to the test
item.description:
East Timor has become the unlikely venue for a war crimes case against Myanmar’s military leadership, as proceedings advance in Dili’s courts and test Asean’s uneasy approach to the junta.

Brought by the Chin Human Rights Organisation (CHRO), the case is expected to shed light on whether a small nation with its own history of occupation and atrocity can use its courts to examine grave allegations against a fellow Asean member’s military rulers.

It lands at an awkward moment for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which has struggled to restrain Myanmar’s generals through diplomacy and non-interference even as parts of the bloc cautiously reopen channels with Naypyidaw.
item.content:encoded:
East Timor has become the unlikely venue for a war crimes case against Myanmar’s military leadership, as proceedings advance in Dili’s courts and test Asean’s uneasy approach to the junta.

Brought by the Chin Human Rights Organisation (CHRO), the case is expected to shed light on whether a small nation with its own history of occupation and atrocity can use its courts to examine grave allegations against a fellow Asean member’s military rulers.

It lands at an awkward moment for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which has struggled to restrain Myanmar’s generals through diplomacy and non-interference even as parts of the bloc cautiously reopen channels with Naypyidaw.

CHRO executive director Salai Za Uk Ling told This Week in Asia that the case had advanced to the judicial phase following the appointment of a senior prosecutor, adding that victim representatives had recently submitted questions of law for judicial determination and were now under the court’s consideration.

“As with any complex international criminal proceedings, progress is measured through legal procedure rather than political timelines,” he said.

“We respect the independence of the Timorese judiciary and remain encouraged by its continued engagement with the case.”

The rights group, which represents Myanmar’s Chin ethnic minority, launched legal proceedings against the country’s military administration, including its leader Min Aung Hlaing, alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Its complaint alleges abuses in Myanmar’s northwestern Chin state, including gang rape, the massacre of 10 people, deaths of Christian religious figures and air strikes on a hospital and religious buildings.

Dili accepted the CHRO complaint against senior members of Myanmar’s military on February 2 and appointed a senior prosecutor to examine the case.

Days later, on February 16, Myanmar’s military government ordered East Timor’s senior diplomat to leave the country – a rare move between Asean members.

East Timor’s President Jose Ramos-Horta had met CHRO members in mid-January. The case was formally submitted to the Court of First Instance in Dili for judicial review in May.

The case is being pursued under the principle of universal jurisdiction, which allows courts to investigate and potentially prosecute serious international crimes regardless of where they occurred or the nationality of those involved.

Za Uk said cases alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity were “inherently complex” and required careful judicial consideration, substantial review of evidence and close adherence to due process.

“Accountability is a long-term endeavour,” he said, adding that every procedural step mattered as it reinforced the principle that even the most serious crimes should be subjected to judicial scrutiny.

Za Uk recounted the words of Pu Joseph, the father of a 13-year-old boy allegedly killed by the military, who reportedly asked: “Will anyone outside Myanmar ever know what happened to my son? Will those responsible ever be held accountable?”

The complaint also mentions Cung Biak Hum, a 31-year-old pastor who was allegedly shot by Myanmar soldiers while trying to extinguish a fire blaze caused by artillery strikes, then summarily executed and his body mutilated.

“Universal jurisdiction … offers hope that justice is not confined by borders, that the voices of victims can be heard beyond Myanmar and that impunity is not inevitable simply because those responsible remain in power,” Za Uk said.

Chris Gunness, director of the CHRO’s Myanmar Accountability Project, said there was strong support for the case, particularly among Timorese civil society.

“This has strengthened because of the bullying tactics of Min Aung Hlaing, who had the most senior Timorese diplomat in Myanmar expelled when we filed our case,” he said.

East Timor gained independence in 2002 after a 24-year Indonesian occupation and a violent transition from foreign rule – a history that has made questions of atrocity, international justice and accountability politically resonant in the country.

Its entry into Asean last year has lent the case added regional significance, as the bloc continues to grapple with Myanmar’s civil war and the limits of its own diplomacy.

Ramos-Horta, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, has openly criticised Myanmar’s military rulers and regime, calling its civil war a “stain on Asean”.

Myanmar’s military administration first expelled East Timor’s charge d’affaires in August 2023 after Ramos-Horta met members of the shadow National Unity Government, formed by lawmakers ousted in the 2021 coup.

“East Timor sees the current military-backed government as being in the same autocratic, militaristic mould as Indonesia’s New Order government, which invaded the then Portuguese territory in 1975,” said Damien Kingsbury, a professor emeritus at Australia’s Deakin University who specialises in Southeast Asian politics.

International law superseded national boundaries, he added, particularly in cases involving war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Kingsbury said the CHRO’s charge was consistent with wider allegations of human rights abuses in Myanmar since the coup – including accusations of indiscriminate air strikes on civilian infrastructure, torture in detention facilities and the intentional blocking of humanitarian aid.

For Asean, long guided by non-interference, quiet diplomacy and consensus, the case marks an unusual first: one member state using its courts to examine alleged war crimes by another’s military rulers.

Joanne Lin, a senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and coordinator of its Asean Studies Centre, said the case introduced “a rare approach directly into Asean internal dynamics”, as issues were traditionally managed through “diplomacy, quiet engagement and non-interference”.

She said she expected the case to move slowly, given East Timor’s small size and the “resource-intensive” complexity of universal jurisdiction cases.

“Even if the case does not move quickly, it still matters politically,” she said. “It signals that as Asean member states re-engage the current Myanmar administration, accountability concerns have not disappeared.”

After five years of excluding Myanmar’s top leaders from high-level Asean meetings failed to force compliance with the bloc’s “five-point consensus” – a peace plan calling for dialogue and an end to violence among all parties – the bloc has in recent weeks shifted towards calibrated re-engagement with the military government.

This changing environment could put East Timor in a difficult position, according to Khoo Ying Hooi, an associate professor of international relations and human rights at the University of Malaya.

“As other regional governments rebuild working relations with Naypyidaw, there may be quiet diplomatic pressure on Dili to prevent the legal case from obstructing bilateral and Asean cooperation,” she said.

“The issue should not be reduced to a bilateral quarrel between Dili and Naypyidaw. The deeper question is whether victims of alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity can seek justice through a regional channel.”

item.title: [SCMP] China’s Politburo pledges policy support, spending to counteract sluggish growth
item.description:
Beijing has pledged to step up macro policy support and enhance the resilience of capital markets for the remainder of the year, sending signals to stablise growth amid a recent slowdown in economic activity and rising volatility in global markets.

After a meeting of the Communist Party’s 21-member Politburo – a major decision-making body led by President Xi Jinping – that ended on Thursday, the party’s upper echelon vowed to accelerate the pace of fiscal spending and speed up the transition from old to new growth drivers.

“[We need to] fully leverage the effectiveness of existing policies and roll out practical and effective incremental measures in a timely manner,” the Politburo said, according to a statement published by state news agency Xinhua.
item.content:encoded:
Beijing has pledged to step up macro policy support and enhance the resilience of capital markets for the remainder of the year, sending signals to stablise growth amid a recent slowdown in economic activity and rising volatility in global markets.

After a meeting of the Communist Party’s 21-member Politburo – a major decision-making body led by President Xi Jinping – that ended on Thursday, the party’s upper echelon vowed to accelerate the pace of fiscal spending and speed up the transition from old to new growth drivers.

“[We need to] fully leverage the effectiveness of existing policies and roll out practical and effective incremental measures in a timely manner,” the Politburo said, according to a statement published by state news agency Xinhua.

Amid growing concerns from Western politicians over China’s widening trade surplus, the leadership also urged the country to “expand the scope for mutually beneficial international economic and trade cooperation” and “promote more balanced trade development.”

The Politburo also said the fifth plenary session of the party’s powerful Central Committee would be held in October. This session carries particular importance, as it comes a year before the party’s next national congress, when a major leadership reshuffle is expected and Xi could be elected to a fourth term as general secretary.

Analysts said the meeting sent a more supportive signal to stabilise growth as the country’s economy faced “challenges and difficulties,” but stopped short of suggesting a large-scale stimulus package, instead pointing to more targeted measures.

The emphasis is on measures that are practical and effective – in other words, policies that deliver tangible results

Ding Shuang, Standard Chartered

“The focus remains on making better use of existing policies, while keeping additional measures in reserve,” said Ding Shuang, chief economist for Greater China and North Asia at Standard Chartered.

“It’s not simply a matter of spending more money,” Ding added. “The emphasis is on measures that are practical and effective – in other words, policies that deliver tangible results.”

The meeting was held in the wake of second-quarter figures that showed a slowdown in gross domestic product despite strong trade numbers, a dichotomy indicating a widening gap between surging exports and sluggish activity at home.

The elevated trade surplus has also fuelled pushback from the West, with politicians in the European Union and the United States threatening or taking action against China’s industrial overcapacity – a claim Beijing denies.

Su Yue, principal economist for China at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said the explicit reference to “trade balance” in the readout suggested Beijing was becoming more sensitive to international concerns over China’s trade surplus and sought to create greater room for external cooperation.

“Although this alone is unlikely to fundamentally ease trade tensions, it points to a more pragmatic tone that could provide a modestly more stable backdrop for US-China economic relations,” she added. “EU-China trade relations will remain under strain due to structural issues.”

Working teams from Beijing and Brussels have held more than 20 meetings in the past month, following an initial round of trade talks in Brussels between Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and his European counterpart Maros Sefcovic, commerce ministry spokesman He Yadong said on Thursday.

“China is ready … to explore practical, workable solutions to each side’s concerns in trade and economics,” He said.

Top policymakers have also been wary of heightened volatility in global capital markets, with hi-tech stocks facing a broad sell-off on concerns that an artificial intelligence-driven rally may have outpaced fundamentals.

Against this backdrop, the Politburo underscored the importance of deepening reforms to capital market investment and financing, while “enhancing the resilience and confidence of capital markets.”

Ding pointed to recent intervention by the “national team” – state-backed institutions that support domestic markets – and said stabilising the capital market can help improve household balance sheets and support domestic consumption.

China’s gross domestic product growth slowed to 4.3 per cent in the second quarter – the softest quarterly expansion since late 2022, down from 5 per cent in the first quarter. Growth for the first half stood at 4.7 per cent, remaining within the “4.5 to 5 per cent” target range set for the year.

The Politburo reiterated the importance of “effectively expanding domestic demand” and unlocking the potential of the services sector, and said Beijing would make comprehensive use of monetary policy tools and “adjust them as appropriate”, while improving co-ordination between fiscal and financial policies to boost domestic demand.

It also stressed the need to strengthen social welfare, protect the rights of flexible and gig workers, and ensure agricultural production.

Su Jian, an economics professor at Peking University, said the readout placed greater emphasis on boosting domestic demand, expanding service consumption and promoting trade in services.

“Strengthening social welfare can help reduce income inequality and ease consumers’ concerns about the future, thereby supporting consumption,” he said.

Meanwhile, analysts also pointed to infrastructure investment as an effective tool for boosting domestic demand and stabilising growth in the second half of the year, as the readout underscored the need to advance the construction of the “six networks” – a broad infrastructure initiative covering water, power, computing, next-generation telecommunications, underground utilities and logistics networks.

China’s contracting fixed-asset investment, coupled with a higher incidence of natural disasters this year, leaves policymakers ample room to ramp up infrastructure spending, Ding said.

Amid a rise in extreme weather events this year, the readout stressed the need to “resolutely prevent major accidents”, strengthen risk identification and mitigation, and step up flood control, emergency response and disaster relief efforts.

Other priorities outlined in the readout included continuing efforts to tackle “involution-style” competition, stabilising the property market and pressing ahead with the government’s debt-restructuring plan.

Separately, Xi held a symposium on Friday with representatives of the country’s non-communist political parties to hear their views on the current economic situation and priorities for the second half of the year, the People’s Daily reported on Thursday.

Xi said that China’s economy had “pressed ahead under pressure” and “showed strong resilience and vitality” in the first half of the year, while acknowledging “some difficulties and challenges”, as reported by the Communist Party’s official press organ.

The president emphasised the need to strengthen the effectiveness of macro policy in the second half of the year, prioritising the tapping of potential domestic demand, deepening the integration of technological and industrial innovation, improving people’s livelihoods and continuing to defuse risks in key sectors.

Additional reporting by Xiaofei Xu

item.title: [SCMP] China’s October plenum plan reveals focus on party discipline ahead of 2027 congress
item.description:
China’s top leadership has made party governance the focus of a coming key conclave, signalling the significance of a clean record in the selection process ahead of next year’s national congress.

The Politburo, China’s top decision-making body, announced on Thursday that the fifth plenary session of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee would be held in October, state news agency Xinhua reported.

The meeting is likely to be the party’s most important gathering ahead of its 21st national congress in autumn 2027, where key leadership reshuffles and the endorsement of a fourth term for Xi Jinping are likely to take centre stage.
item.content:encoded:
China’s top leadership has made party governance the focus of a coming key conclave, signalling the significance of a clean record in the selection process ahead of next year’s national congress.

The Politburo, China’s top decision-making body, announced on Thursday that the fifth plenary session of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee would be held in October, state news agency Xinhua reported.

The meeting is likely to be the party’s most important gathering ahead of its 21st national congress in autumn 2027, where key leadership reshuffles and the endorsement of a fourth term for Xi Jinping are likely to take centre stage.

According to Xinhua, the October plenum will focus on “consistently exercising full and rigorous governance over the party”.

For Beijing, the expression usually means three things: fighting corruption, tightening party discipline and shoring up political loyalty.

More than 370 full and alternate members of the Central Committee – the party’s top political and executive body – will take part in the fifth plenum.

Typically, seven plenary sessions are held during each five-year term of the Central Committee, a body elected at every party congress.

The selection process for the next committee is understood to have begun earlier this year, and the screening is expected to last until the final months before next year’s congress.

The party constitution stipulates that the Central Committee hold at least one plenum each year, and the sitting body has observed this rule since the new five-year cycle began in 2022.

Over the past three decades, the plenary session held in the year before the party congress has typically addressed issues relating to ideology and party-building matters.

However, it is running one plenum behind schedule because the third one was delayed, causing a shift in subject for the fifth plenum.

Rather than discussing the five-year economic plan – which they addressed last year – the focus has shifted to party governance.

Xi’s anti-corruption drive, launched shortly after he took the party reins in 2012, has only intensified in recent years – bringing down scores of high-level officials across regions and policy areas.

Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at the National Institute of Strategic Studies, Tsinghua University, said the statement from Thursday’s Politburo meeting underlined the leadership’s acute awareness of the threat that corruption posed to the party.

It also highlighted a determination to filter out compromised candidates as preparations for next year’s reshuffle began, Xie added.

“The party will continue to learn from the corruption cases and come out with new preventive measures, new solutions in its anti-corruption toolkit, to select better candidates [for its new line-up in the 21st party congress],” he said.

The Politburo statement acknowledged “numerous new situations and problems facing the work of strengthening party discipline”, and attributed them to “profound changes in the circumstances in the outside world, within China and the ruling party”.

It also called on all members to develop a “deep understanding of the great significance [of] persistently advancing the comprehensive and strict governance of the party”.

This must be approached from the “strategic height” of consolidating party rule, drawing on “valuable experience” from the anti-corruption campaign through “higher standards and more concrete measures”, it said.

The coming plenum is expected to also endorse decisions made by the Politburo on changes to the sitting Central Committee.

China’s defence ministry announced in January that Zhang Youxia – a Politburo member and the first-ranked vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC) – was under investigation for corruption along with Liu Zhenli, a Central Committee member and chief of the CMC’s Joint Staff Department.

In April, anti-corruption authorities announced that former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui was under investigation, making him the second Politburo member ensnared this year and the third overall since 2022.

Ma has since been expelled from the party and removed from his public posts, under a decision endorsed by the Politburo on June 30 and expected to be ratified in the coming plenum.

A number of Central Committee members have also been detained by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection – the party’s top anti-corruption and political disciplinary body – since the last plenum, held in October last year.

They include full committee members Sun Shaocheng, the former party chief of Inner Mongolia, former emergency management minister Wang Xiangxi, former Jiangxi and Zhejiang party boss Yi Lianhong, and former Chongqing mayor Hu Henghua.

Xu Liuping, an alternate committee member and former party secretary and vice-chairman of the All-China Federation of Trade Unions, was placed under investigation in May.

Another alternate member, Li Yunze, was abruptly removed from his position as chief of the National Financial Regulatory Administration in April. He later lost his seat in the National People’s Congress, China’s top legislature.

Tsinghua University’s Xie said the statement from the Politburo meeting also indicated that the fifth plenum would elaborate on Xi’s political thoughts on party building.

He said party governance was an important part of the latest branch of Xi’s political thought launched in June’s national party building conference, which stressed the need to govern the party with discipline and unified leadership.

“It is a comprehensive approach to ensure the party’s long-term rule and ability to achieve its goals,” Xie said.

“Besides party governance, the latest thought also emphasised the importance of a unified and centralised leadership and insisted on an organisational system that is cohesive across different levels. All of these will be thoroughly discussed and endorsed at the plenum.”

Deng Yuwen, former deputy editor of the Study Times, the official publication of the cadre-training Central Party School, said the disciplinary infrastructure should screen for both political loyalty and personal integrity in its selection process.

“An official can appear to be extremely loyal in public and be unambiguous in policy implementation, while turning their position into a source of private and family benefits,” he cautioned.

Deng cited the recent downfall of Ma to underline his point. He argued that Ma’s ability to engage in corruption despite the Xi-led crackdown being in full swing showed that while the party’s anti-corruption apparatus was very powerful at punishing wrongdoing, it still needed to tighten routine oversight.

item.title: [SCMP] Can China’s EV boom give it decisive edge in geopolitical tech war?
item.description:
China may increasingly seek to use its dominance in the global electric vehicle industry as geopolitical leverage, giving Beijing greater influence over countries dependent on its technology and supply chains, according to analysts.

“With China, the strategy is different. It’s to overwhelm the industry, capture it, and use it ultimately as leverage,” said Michael Dunne, CEO of Dunne Insights, an auto advisory firm.

“When it comes to crunch time, they say, ‘Oh, by the way, we’re the source of all manufactured cars today. How about that?’” Dunne said during a discussion hosted by the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI).
item.content:encoded:
China may increasingly seek to use its dominance in the global electric vehicle industry as geopolitical leverage, giving Beijing greater influence over countries dependent on its technology and supply chains, according to analysts.

“With China, the strategy is different. It’s to overwhelm the industry, capture it, and use it ultimately as leverage,” said Michael Dunne, CEO of Dunne Insights, an auto advisory firm.

“When it comes to crunch time, they say, ‘Oh, by the way, we’re the source of all manufactured cars today. How about that?’” Dunne said during a discussion hosted by the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI).

“And you’re dependent on us for cars, and we want this and this and this from you on other political issues.”

China’s slowing domestic auto market has pushed its carmakers to expand overseas, with monthly vehicle exports surpassing one million for the first time in June and projected to reach around 12 million by year-end.

The global expansion of cheaper, high-quality Chinese electric and hybrid vehicles has sparked concerns in many countries over Beijing’s alleged “overcapacity”, which governments attribute to state subsidies – a charge China denies.

They are now weighing how to protect their domestic manufacturers, preserve industrial capacity and reduce strategic reliance on China.

US continues to limit Chinese carmakers’ access to its market

While Canada and parts of Europe have taken a more conditional approach by allowing Chinese investment in their auto sectors in the hope of encouraging “reverse technology transfer”, the US has adopted a more restrictive stance, using steep tariffs and regulatory curbs to limit Chinese carmakers’ access to its market.

“It’s a party state converting your car market into its leverage,” said Michael Kovrig, a former Canadian diplomat and senior advisor at the International Crisis Group.

“The EVs are the perfect instrument because they’re the biggest manufactured good in world trade.

“They’re simultaneously an energy asset, a data platform, the anchor of the battery, drone, robotics – the industrial base of the 21st century.”

Speaking at the ASPI event, Kovrig also criticised Canada’s January deal with China, which dropped its 100 per cent tariff on up to 49,000 Chinese EVs a year in exchange for auto investment and tariff-free access for Canadian canola exports.

According to him, Beijing had already begun using EV access as leverage, pointing to Chinese Ambassador to Canada Wang Di’s warning in April that bilateral ties would suffer if Ottawa continued sending military vessels through the Taiwan Strait or allowed lawmakers to visit Taiwan.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Kovrig also alleged that Beijing was attempting to use “Canada as a back door to crack into the United States”, noting that “it’s possible the US may not even let Canadians who have bought a Chinese vehicle in Canada take that vehicle into the United States”.

Dunne echoed that assessment, arguing that the American car market remains the “ultimate target” for Chinese carmakers.

“The Chinese would more or less kill for access,” he added.

“What does it take for us to get in there? They’re working every conceivable angle at the same time that people in [Washington] DC are trying to fend them off.”

The US has kept tariffs above 120 per cent on Chinese vehicles and restricted EVs using China-linked software and hardware.

Last month, the Trump administration blocked Chinese-owned Polestar from selling new vehicles under a connected vehicle rule targeting foreign technology deemed a data security risk.

Congress has also pushed for stricter measures, with bipartisan lawmakers introducing several House and Senate bills aimed at restricting China-linked electric vehicles from the US market.

Beyond domestic measures, Washington is discussing with Canada and Mexico ways to keep Chinese EVs out of the North American market as part of the ongoing review of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) trade agreement.

Beijing denies its industrial overcapacity stems from state subsidies, weak domestic demand

China on Tuesday issued a position paper rejecting claims that its industrial overcapacity stems from state subsidies and weak domestic demand, saying that its manufacturing strength was instead driven by technological innovation, market competition and structural reforms.

“There is no necessary connection between industrial subsidies and overcapacity,” the commerce ministry said in the paper.

The document argued that governments widely use subsidies to support their own development goals, pointing to the US$750 billion Inflation Reduction Act passed by Washington in 2022, to spur domestic EV production.

“It is imperative that all countries make the pie of global development bigger and introduce subsidies and other industrial policies in a rational and compliant manner, rather than use them as a tool to constrain the development of others,” it added.

In early July, the Chinese embassy in Washington also defended Beijing’s EV policies and criticised the US restrictions.

“Advocating protectionism and establishing trade barriers in the name of ‘fair competition’ and ‘national security’ goes against the principles of market economy and WTO [World Trade Organization] rules,” embassy spokesperson Liu Chang told the South China Morning Post.

“Electric vehicle [manufacturing] is a globalised industry. Only division of labour and cooperation can bring mutual benefits, and only fair competition can bring technological progress.”

Dunne, however, contended that the option of a reverse “technology transfer” is a “great idea on paper” but remains impractical, especially for the US market.

“One, the Chinese will be very careful, call it stingy, about handing over any technology,” he said.

“Secondly, I’m not convinced that American companies in joint ventures would know how to secure the technology in the same ways that the Chinese were able to do.”

“We don’t know how to play the game.”

To address the issue, Kovrig argued that “tariffs alone” will not be enough and advocated cooperation among Western countries on drafting common policies on software security, investment screening and rules of origin requirements.

“I think a grand coalition unity is unlikely, but rather functional convergence,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] New yacht travel scheme makes waves but can Hong Kong cash in on marine economy?
item.description:
For the first time, veteran sailor Thomas Wong Kam-chuen and his partners set sail from Hong Kong on their 46-foot yacht on a two-day trip earlier this month to a holiday island in Zhuhai, testing the waters for more leisure travel to mainland China.

After a five-hour voyage from the Causeway Bay typhoon shelter on a sunny weekend, they anchored their Danish-built yacht, DBX2, at Guishan Island, went ashore for a seafood lunch with beer and stayed overnight.

“Food is really economical. We had 11 people, and a seafood meal was only HK$112 [US$14] per person. If you eat seafood in Hong Kong, it is at least HK$600 to HK$700 a person,” said the 79-year-old structural engineer, who has 52 years of sailing experience.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, veteran sailor Thomas Wong Kam-chuen and his partners set sail from Hong Kong on their 46-foot yacht on a two-day trip earlier this month to a holiday island in Zhuhai, testing the waters for more leisure travel to mainland China.

After a five-hour voyage from the Causeway Bay typhoon shelter on a sunny weekend, they anchored their Danish-built yacht, DBX2, at Guishan Island, went ashore for a seafood lunch with beer and stayed overnight.

“Food is really economical. We had 11 people, and a seafood meal was only HK$112 [US$14] per person. If you eat seafood in Hong Kong, it is at least HK$600 to HK$700 a person,” said the 79-year-old structural engineer, who has 52 years of sailing experience.

DBX2 joined nine other vessels in a flotilla organised by the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club in collaboration with the Zhuhai Yacht Association, with the early batch of sailors navigating Greater Bay Area waters under a new individual yacht travel scheme.

The trip was made possible after Beijing approved the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau individual yacht scheme in June, allowing Hong Kong owners to sail their vessels to designated ports as part of a broader “yacht economy” strategy for the Greater Bay Area.

The bay area is a central government initiative to link Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in neighbouring Guangdong province into an integrated economic powerhouse.

Some boat owners and maritime experts note that the yacht scheme currently operates as one-way traffic, generating economic gains for mainland destinations. They have urged Hong Kong authorities to seize the opportunity to upgrade the city’s marine infrastructure to attract southbound yachts.

They have also called on the government to prioritise high-end maritime services – such as trading, financing and design – and to use an ongoing public consultation for Hong Kong’s first five-year development plan to capitalise on the marine economy.

“What we hope for in the future is to place Hong Kong’s yacht industry – including yacht exhibitions, design and trading – in Hong Kong,” said Professor Chen Jihong, director of the Shenzhen International Maritime Institute, who was involved in research and planning for the cross-border individual yacht scheme.

“In the future, Hong Kong can definitely play a greater role in high-end services and financial value addition.”

An ‘economically unbalanced’ voyage?

The scheme is currently limited to northbound Hong Kong yachts, pending mainland approval for yachts there to sail to the city under a southbound arrangement.

The northbound section operates under strict parameters, capping vessel capacity at 12 people and requiring captains to hold Chinese citizenship and have home-return permits and to submit digital clearance hours in advance. Home-return permits allow Hong Kong and Macau people to travel freely between their home city and the mainland.

Potentially, a vast market is waiting to be tapped. Wong Sai-fat, director of marine, citing estimates from multiple media and political party research reports published between April and June, earlier said that once the yacht economy reached maturity, it could generate annual economic benefits of HK$4.4 billion to HK$22.5 billion for Hong Kong.

From 2023 to 2025, an average of 77 yachts visited Hong Kong annually, 35 of which came from the mainland, according to InvestHK, the government’s investment promotion arm.

However, the new scheme is accelerating movement.

Liao Kai, president of the non-profit Zhuhai association, said 38 Hong Kong and Macau yachts had obtained temporary ship nationality certificates issued by mainland authorities as of mid-July.

Twenty of them applied specifically to visit Zhuhai. Without affecting their original ship registration, these certificates allow individual yacht travel within the waters of the nine mainland cities in the bay area.

“In just half a month, we have processed nearly half as many yachts as the roughly 60 that entered [Hainan] under a free travel scheme between Hainan, Hong Kong and Macau over the past six to eight years,” said Liao, whose association is registered under Zhuhai’s civil affairs bureau to advocate for cross-border yacht travel.

The Hainan scheme was implemented in 2019, allowing visiting yachts from Hong Kong and Macau to remain in the southern mainland island province for 30 days.

In Wong’s case, he and his partners paid about HK$5,000 in fees related to the application and preparation of certificates for the Guishan Island trip, excluding spending on meals and entertainment.

Located about three nautical miles (5.5km) southwest of Lantau Island, Guishan is known as a selfie hotspot for sunsets and seafood.

Whether the trip was worthwhile is open to debate.

“Do you think it’s worth it, doing so many procedures just to go for one night and two days? Even going somewhere as close as Guishan, travelling took about five hours each way – that’s 10 hours of sailing within less than 48 hours,” Wong said.

“Factoring in sleep time, the actual leisure time is very short. Those expenses – HK$5,000 – are basically mandatory, so if you only go for two days, it feels a bit economically unbalanced for a two-day trip.”

Still, some yacht owners, such as Simon Deng Wenjian, who visited Nansha in Guangzhou with friends earlier this month, felt the cost was acceptable.

Deng sailed his 53-foot yacht from the Gold Coast in Tuen Mun to Nansha Marina in about 5½ hours, noting that customs clearance at the passenger terminal was efficient and took about 20 minutes.

“Most of the things you do, like the AIS [automatic identification system, a marine tracking tool], are a one-off. If you deduct this cost, the actual cost of each trip is very low,” Deng said, adding that mainland marinas charged an agency and berthing fee of about 6,000 yuan (US$890) per trip.

Deng said prospective yacht owners deterred by high berthing costs might now choose to buy vessels in Hong Kong and register them there, using the travel scheme to sail them back to the mainland.

He said he believed this influx of new buyers purchasing tax-free vessels in Hong Kong would stimulate yacht sales and boost the city’s yachting industry.

To make the northbound scheme more attractive, Lawrence Chow, chairman of the Hong Kong Boating Industry Association, proposed that the city’s Marine Department expand its eSeaGo navigational chart app to cover Greater Bay Area waters so captains could chart their voyages.

Chow also pointed to a private website compiling information on northbound and southbound yacht travel so everyone could access the same information.

Liao said the Zhuhai association was exploring with the Guangdong provincial government the adoption of Hong Kong’s flexible capacity rules and the implementation of the English-language version of the application. Mainland maritime law strictly caps all yachts at 12 people including crew, regardless of the vessel’s size.

Bill Lau, founder of service company Voy Yachting, and Simon Kung, chief executive of Baypoint, both handle applications for yacht owners.

They said that due to complicated paperwork and unaligned systems, end-to-end processing took up to a month.

While Lau charges about HK$6,000 for standard processing, Kung noted that the high-end market commanded vastly different prices.

“For an 80-foot yacht, we are asking for HK$50,000 for the entire application fee,” Kung said. The charge covers paperwork, related fees for the first northbound journey, three days of management expenses with a mainland yacht club and berth rental in Zhuhai.

However, confusion remains among owners over an important issue.

“Many people think applying for the free travel scheme allows them to go for repairs or maintenance, which is not allowed. Actually, your yacht must enter and exit in the original condition,” Kung said.

Instead, owners must use a separate, recently launched bonded scheme in Zhuhai’s Jinwan district to bypass massive import taxes for heavy refits, he said.

Is Hong Kong ready for southbound yachts?

To prepare for the southbound scheme, the Marine Department has introduced several measures.

These include allowing visiting yacht operators to complete Hong Kong qualification exams on the mainland since June 12, submitting all health, immigration and port clearances through a one-stop electronic business system launched on June 29, and applying for five designated public anchorages without pre-booking private marina berths from July 8.

The anchorages are at Stanley Bay, Tai Tam Bay, Repulse Bay, Three Fathoms Cove in Sai Kung and Tai O.

To prepare mainland captains for Hong Kong’s busy waters, the department authorised two mainland centres in Shenzhen and Nansha to conduct local navigation exams and approved seven mainland institutions to offer certified courses.

As of July 24, 160 of 176 applicants had passed the exam or completed training since mid-June.

Once the southbound scheme was approved, mainland visitors could enjoy tax-free fine wines and imported seafood after arriving in Hong Kong by yacht, Kung and Liao said.

Pointing to the designated anchorage areas, Lau stressed the urgent need for better landing facilities and public shuttle boats to take passengers ashore.

“Getting on and off the boat is quite troublesome,” Lau said. “If you anchor in Stanley, how do you get ashore? When it’s so remote, there are no landing facilities.”

The Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club’s commodore, David Norton, who joined the Guishan voyage, said the club was organising another northbound trip in the coming month.

He said he believed the southbound scheme would not only cater to the ultra-rich, but also to sport sailors.

“The cost of mooring is like the cost of parking a car,” Norton said.

He added that a large number of people from fleets of smaller yachts generated far more economic activity onshore than a single superyacht.

However, the lack of an English-language system and Hong Kong’s congested harbours limited the scheme’s full potential, he added.

“Those sorts of facilities are things that the government should be working on – and they are working on it,” he said.

Beyond the yacht economy

Lawmaker Steven Ho Chun-yin said that the sector’s value extended far beyond basic tourism, aligning with calls to develop a supporting service industry chain covering yacht marketing, maintenance, certification and insurance.

“When superyachts come to Hong Kong, the owners are often here to discuss business, which drives our financial sector,” Ho said.

He said unlocking the sector’s potential required addressing institutional barriers to infrastructure investment.

He urged the government to allow operators to retain land for shipyards and improve amenities for sustainable investments, noting that 80 to 90 per cent of local firms held short-term tenancies of about seven years.

“Who would throw billions into a facility to only give it back in seven years?” Ho said.

He also called for more focus on the marine economy in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan.

Through the ongoing public consultation for the five-year plan, the government has signalled a willingness to gather views from all sectors of society to forge consensus on Hong Kong’s development road map.

“We need to establish a higher-level maritime economy committee,” Ho said. “Without a cross-departmental body, an individual department like the Marine Department will only focus on its own specific safety regulations.”

Hong Kong is facing a severe shortage of berthing spots, with 12,500 licensed yachts competing for only 4,300 available berths.

To ease the crunch, Lau, of the yacht service platform, suggested officially zoning existing typhoon shelters to separate leisure yachts from fishing boats and industrial barges.

“If the government regulates it well, it can be like a civilian yacht club,” he said.

Chen, of the institute, said he hoped the yacht industries in Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area could integrate at a higher level, with Hong Kong focusing on exhibitions, design and trading.

“Once this service matures in the Greater Bay Area, the model can fully be promoted to places like Shanghai, Qingdao and other coastal regions,” Chen said.

He noted that the yachting scheme was a vital piece of China’s goal to rise as a marine superpower in the national 15th five-year plan for 2026 to 2030.

Hong Kong could serve as the hub for high-end maritime services for all of China, including design, trade, manufacturing, refinancing and insurance, he added.

“Hong Kong can serve as a bridgehead, as a brilliant pearl,” Chen said. “In this way, we can break the current Western monopoly on these high-end services and value addition.

“Hong Kong’s [role] in China becoming a marine superpower, what is its function? It must be this high-value-added shipping service.”

item.title: [SCMP] US sanctions mainland China, Hong Kong shipping firms over Iranian oil deliveries
item.description:
The United States on Wednesday sanctioned a group of mainland Chinese and Hong Kong shipping companies accused of operating vessels that transported Iranian oil to China, extending Washington’s economic campaign against Tehran alongside its naval blockade.

The US State Department said eight companies were designated for operating vessels that moved Iranian crude oil and petrochemical products to China and the United Arab Emirates as part of Iran’s sanctions-evading “shadow fleet”.

Six of the eight vessels identified by the US Treasury Department were specifically accused of carrying Iranian crude to China, in some cases transporting millions of barrels during 2026.
item.content:encoded:
The United States on Wednesday sanctioned a group of mainland Chinese and Hong Kong shipping companies accused of operating vessels that transported Iranian oil to China, extending Washington’s economic campaign against Tehran alongside its naval blockade.

The US State Department said eight companies were designated for operating vessels that moved Iranian crude oil and petrochemical products to China and the United Arab Emirates as part of Iran’s sanctions-evading “shadow fleet”.

Six of the eight vessels identified by the US Treasury Department were specifically accused of carrying Iranian crude to China, in some cases transporting millions of barrels during 2026.

The designations freeze any assets belonging to the targeted companies within US jurisdiction and generally prohibit US individuals and businesses from dealing with them.

Foreign financial institutions and other companies could also face sanctions exposure if they continue to conduct certain transactions involving the designated firms.

“Today’s designations support the US Navy’s enforcement of a blockade on Iranian ports and coastline,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said.

The action also targeted two Iranian companies accused of forcing commercial vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz to purchase maritime insurance against risks, including seizures, that Washington says are created by Tehran itself.

One of the sanctioned vessel-management companies is based in mainland China, while five others are based wholly or partly in Hong Kong, according to Treasury.

The South China Morning Post has contacted the Chinese embassy in Washington for comment.

“With its economy in free fall and inflation in the triple digits, the regime is desperate for cash,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

“The United States will not allow Iran to hold global commerce hostage or use international shipping to finance the IRGC’s terrorism, aggression and repression.”

Pigott said protecting navigational rights and freedoms in the strait was a “global interest” and that Washington would work with allies to isolate Tehran until it stopped what he called destabilising behaviour.

His statement explicitly linked the economic measures to the US naval blockade, saying the sanctions supported its enforcement along Iran’s ports and coastline.

China a central target in US campaign against Iranian oil exports

China has emerged as a central target of Washington’s campaign against Iran’s oil exports. US officials have repeatedly accused Chinese buyers and shipping networks of providing Tehran with an economic lifeline by purchasing discounted crude despite American sanctions.

Among the companies designated on Wednesday was mainland China-based Qi Hang Ship Management Limited, the owner and operator of the Marshall Islands-flagged Well Sail.

Treasury said the tanker carried hundreds of thousands of barrels of Iranian petroleum products to the United Arab Emirates this year.

It also sanctioned Hong Kong-based Confident Apex Limited, which owns and operates the Mozambique-flagged Lily. The vessel has transported millions of barrels of Iranian oil since 2025, according to the department.

The other targeted vessels had more explicit links to China-bound shipments.

Treasury said the Al Salmi, owned and operated by Hong Kong-based Billion Nexus International, had delivered hundreds of thousands of barrels of Iranian oil to China since last year.

The Breeze V, operated by Hong Kong-based Nevada Spirit Company, allegedly transported millions of barrels to China this year, while the Natsumi, managed by Hong Kong-based Marinova Freight, had carried millions of barrels of Iranian crude to China since 2022.

Another tanker, the Crystal, is owned and operated by Vast Mighty Limited, which Treasury described as based in Hong Kong and the Marshall Islands. It allegedly carried millions of barrels of Iranian oil to China this year.

Two other vessels managed by Marshall Islands-based companies – the Nireta and Yehope – transported hundreds of thousands of barrels of Iranian crude to China during 2026, Treasury said.

Beijing has consistently opposed unilateral US sanctions against its companies and defended its economic relations with Iran as legitimate.

US also targets Iran-based organisations over Hormuz extortion claims

The latest action also targeted the Persian Gulf Marine Insurance Company and the Hormuz Safe Marine Services Authority, an Iranian digital insurance business that accepts bitcoin and other digital assets.

Treasury accused the two companies of helping Iran impose mandatory insurance charges on ships seeking to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy corridors, in an “extortion scheme”.

The policies purportedly protect vessels against risks including seizures, but those dangers are “overwhelmingly created by Iran itself”, the department said.

Treasury said Hormuz Safe, developed by Iran’s Ministry of Economy, offers insurance, traffic control, security and emergency-response services while generating revenue for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The State Department described the insurance arrangements as coercive schemes in which Iranian entities “manufacture risk” and then charge commercial vessels for protection against dangers created by the government.

Revenue generated by the arrangements supports IRGC operations and Iran’s broader regional activities, according to Washington.

Trump administration puts pressure on Iran-China relationship

The sanctions come as Washington steps up both military and economic pressure on Tehran over control of the strait and the continued movement of Iranian energy exports.

The Trump administration has sought to prevent vessels trading with Iran from passing through the waterway while accusing Tehran of attempting to profit from restrictions on commercial shipping.

Washington said it would continue targeting Iran’s shadow-fleet operations and “deceptive financial schemes” while working with allies to isolate Tehran diplomatically and economically.

Treasury said it had sanctioned more than 100 vessels linked to Iran’s shadow fleet since the beginning of the year.

The ships form part of a network that uses foreign flags, shell companies, obscured ownership arrangements and other methods to keep Iranian oil flowing despite Western restrictions.

China is the leading destination for Iranian crude, much of which is sold at a discount and transported through networks intended to disguise the oil’s origin and ownership.

Washington has previously targeted small Chinese refineries, shipping companies, port operators and storage facilities accused of taking part in the trade. Beijing maintains that normal commercial relations between China and Iran should not be subject to US jurisdiction.

item.title: [SCMP] How Trump’s call for Asia-Pacific allies to raise defence spending may backfire on US
item.description:
Donald Trump’s demands that American allies in the Asia-Pacific region share more of the defensive burden have renewed questions about how far they can rely on the United States to help deter the likes of China and North Korea.

Such concerns have led to an increasing focus on developing their own defence industries – but analysts have said that may eventually weaken American dominance in the global arms trade.

Questions over Washington’s commitment
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s demands that American allies in the Asia-Pacific region share more of the defensive burden have renewed questions about how far they can rely on the United States to help deter the likes of China and North Korea.

Such concerns have led to an increasing focus on developing their own defence industries – but analysts have said that may eventually weaken American dominance in the global arms trade.

Questions over Washington’s commitment

In the National Security Strategy released in December, the Trump administration urged allies such as Japan and South Korea to spend more on collective defence to strengthen their ability to deter “aggression”.

It said this was “necessary to deter adversaries and protect the first island chain”, a series of islands and archipelagos that runs from Japan to the Philippines and Borneo.

The chain stands between mainland China and the Pacific and has been identified as a strategic barrier that could be used to block access to the open waters.

Its significance is heightened by the fact that Taiwan sits at its heart.

Beijing regards the island as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to bring it under its control.

Most countries, including the US and its allies, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to seize the island by force and is legally bound to supply Taipei with defensive weapons.

Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth drove home the message about defence spending in June, when he told the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore that the era of the US “subsidising the defence of wealthy nations is over”, and that his country needed “partners, not protectorates”, with alliances built on “shared responsibility, not dependency”.

Doubts about the US commitment to the region have been growing since the National Security Strategy designated the western hemisphere as its top priority.

The war against Iran has raised further questions after Washington relocated Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defence anti-missile system batteries from South Korea to the Middle East to top up US stockpiles that were depleted by the war.

Benjamin Barton, an associate professor of international relations at the University of Nottingham Malaysia, said recent efforts by Asia-Pacific countries to develop their own defence industries seemed to be driven by Washington’s “erratic grand strategy”.

Barton said the US had “castigated” its allies for not spending enough on defence in the hope they would “increase expenditure as a means of fuelling demand in the American military-industrial complex” but this seemed to be “backfiring”.

“Allies have responded by increasing military spending to purchase weapons systems built locally or by sometimes diversifying away from the US due to trust issues,” Barton said.
