“China and North Korea’s military build-ups do count too, but these threats have been fairly constant. Consequently, the stronger variable of the two seems to be coming from the growing unreliability of US foreign policy.”

The US is the world’s largest arms exporter, with 42 per cent of the global market share between 2021 and 2025, and is especially dominant when it comes to advanced weapons such as warplanes.

Major US allies in the region are among the biggest recipients of these sales, with Australia, Japan and South Korea all among the top 10 buyers of US weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

Domestic arms development

South Korea has been at the forefront of the drive to develop its domestic defence industry and was the only US regional ally to feature in the institute’s list of the top 10 global arms exporters over the past five years.

It has announced plans to develop a nuclear-powered submarine and later this year will start delivering 4.5-generation KF-21 fighters to its air force. Seoul is also planning to upgrade the fighter to at least fifth-generation status in the future.

Bence Nemeth, a senior lecturer in defence studies at King’s College London and executive director of the King’s Centre for Defence Economics and Management, said other countries in the region were also developing their domestic defence industries but were lagging behind South Korea in this regard.

“This is not simply a reaction to the current political climate: Seoul has systematically developed its defence industry for roughly five decades,” Nemeth said.

“Today, over 80 per cent of South Korean arms procurement is domestic, including combat aircraft, main battle tanks, armoured vehicles, naval vessels, submarines and missile systems. Depending on the weapons system, the localisation rate can range from roughly 50 to 90 per cent.”

Japan is also stepping up efforts to build up its military and plans to raise defence spending to 2 per cent of GDP by 2027.

It is also attempting to diversify by developing advanced long-range missiles, including Type-12 anti-ship missiles, that would allow them to strike back in the event of an attack.

It is also a member of the Global Combat Air Programme, which aims to develop a sixth-generation warplane by 2035, along with Britain and Italy.

“Japan has a capable defence-industrial base in some areas, especially in naval shipbuilding and selected advanced technologies … but it has historically been more constrained politically and industrially than South Korea,” Nemeth said.

Its post-war constitution renounces the use of force to settle disputes and states its armed forces can only be used for defensive purposes, but Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is seeking to revise it – a move certain to fuel tensions with China.

This shift has also seen it stepping up its arms exports – a development highlighted by the recent deal to supply Australia with Mogami-class frigates.

Australia is also likely to acquire the ability to build its own nuclear-powered submarines within two decades as part of the Aukus pact with Britain and the US, which will allow technology transfers from Washington.

Nemeth said these developments could “strengthen” the allied network by increasing the ability to maintain and develop arms supplies.

“Overall, I would not interpret regional defence indigenisation as a rejection of the US alliance system per se. It is better understood as a hedge against uncertainty and as a response to the fact that the US cannot and does not want to provide everything, everywhere, at the speed and scale required,” Nemeth said.

Tom Corben, a research fellow with the United States Studies Centre at the University of Sydney, said there was a “widespread perception” that the “regional strategic balance is shifting and that the risks of a regional conflict are growing”.

“That’s driven by a combination of China’s relatively opaque military build-up and perceptions that, while America remains indispensable to regional security, its relative military power in Asia is declining,” Corben said.

He said there were “clear incentives” for countries in Asia to develop their own weapons, but there was “no such thing as absolute self-reliance on this score”.

“Many regional countries – including US allies – perceive a growing need to boost their own national defence capabilities not only to better look after their own national security priorities, but also to make themselves more attractive and reliable defence partners for other like-minded states in the region, including the US,” Corben said.

China’s response

Meanwhile, China’s own military modernisation drive continues to gain momentum as it works towards a “centennial” goal in 2027 – the 100th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Liberation Army.

It has never specified what this goal is, but it is widely believed by outsiders to be related to deterring the US and ensuring the People’s Liberation Army has the ability to take Taiwan by force.

China is currently developing sixth-generation fighter jets, known unofficially as the J-36 and J-50, and is now thought to have the world’s largest navy.

Its third and most advanced aircraft carrier, the Fujian, entered service last year, and the Pentagon has said China plans to build six more by 2035.

Xiao Liang, a researcher for the Military Expenditure and Arms Production Programme at the Stockholm Institute, said the overall trend was “clear”: almost all Asia-Pacific countries were trying to strengthen their domestic arms industries, but China was the only one capable of producing complex weapon systems for all sectors.

In contrast, Australia, Japan, and South Korea specialised in certain areas, with Seoul being the “most successful recent case”.

“China’s military modernisation is still the most important driver, while uncertainty about long-term US commitments has reinforced and accelerated efforts to strengthen domestic industries and reduce dependence on foreign suppliers, although to the same extent as European Nato allies,” Liang said.

“But replacing leading US capabilities in areas such as stealth aircraft, engines, ISR [intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance], advanced semiconductors or integrated command-and-control systems remains extremely difficult and expensive. I would expect more co-development and diversification rather than outright replacement of US systems.”

Liselotte Odgaard, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute in Washington, said divergent standards or protectionism could “weaken” cohesion between allied nations.

She added that critical chokepoints, such as chips, propulsion and software, would “remain globally concentrated, limiting full autonomy”.

“Beijing will largely see it as containment continuity, not US withdrawal. Indigenous build-up by allies will be framed as US-aligned balancing and used to justify China’s own military expansion, while also worrying about tighter, more resilient regional coalitions,” she said.

Barton said this trend had “not gone down well in Beijing”, and may “not bode well” for future regional stability if China responded by increasing its own military spending.

“Although leaders in China may be satisfied to see growing evidence of a US strategic retreat – which is clearly what underpins Chinese grand strategy in Asia – they may not be reassured by the increasing ability of some of its neighbours to strike out alone and/or serve themselves as suppliers or security guarantors for others in the region,” Barton said.

“Were China to face multiple simultaneous threats along its eastern and southern periphery, this would force it back to a situation akin to the 1960s, where instability and unpredictability – which are not beneficial for growth – was the order of the day.”

Bence Nemeth, a senior lecturer in defence studies at King’s College London and executive director of the King’s Centre for Defence Economics and Management, said that indigenisation is developing at “very different levels” across the region, with South Korea clearly being the “most advanced case.”

“This is not simply a reaction to the current political climate: Seoul has systematically developed its defence industry for roughly five decades. Today, over 80 per cent of South Korean arms procurement is domestic, including combat aircraft, main battle tanks, armoured vehicles, naval vessels, submarines and missile systems,” said Nemeth.

item.title: [SCMP] Limited dual citizenship gives Indonesian diaspora hope of return, better future
item.description:
Indonesia’s attempt to lure back its native talent scattered around the world through limited dual citizenship has highlighted a long-held demand of the diaspora for such a scheme before they would consider returning home.

The proposed revision to the citizenship law would mark a major shift for a country that has largely allowed only single citizenship since independence in 1945. Currently, children of mixed marriages can hold dual citizenship until they reach 18 years of age, when they are given three years to choose a single country.

Under the new proposal, dual nationality would not be open to all Indonesians abroad, but only to selected individuals whose expertise is considered important to national development, such as scientists, medical specialists, athletes and others recommended by ministries, state agencies or reputable institutions.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia’s attempt to lure back its native talent scattered around the world through limited dual citizenship has highlighted a long-held demand of the diaspora for such a scheme before they would consider returning home.

The proposed revision to the citizenship law would mark a major shift for a country that has largely allowed only single citizenship since independence in 1945. Currently, children of mixed marriages can hold dual citizenship until they reach 18 years of age, when they are given three years to choose a single country.

Under the new proposal, dual nationality would not be open to all Indonesians abroad, but only to selected individuals whose expertise is considered important to national development, such as scientists, medical specialists, athletes and others recommended by ministries, state agencies or reputable institutions.

For Indonesians such as Ayu, who has built a life in France in the last 13 years while holding to her Indonesian passport, even a limited reform would be meaningful for her.

“I feel like this is giving us hope that maybe we could also have our birthright of always being an Indonesian, even though we’re not living there any more,” she told This Week in Asia from Paris.

For some Indonesians living abroad, acquiring foreign citizenship has meant giving up their original nationality – a choice that has long frustrated members of the diaspora who still want to maintain legal, political and emotional ties to their country.

In June, the Ministry of Law revealed that more than 8,000 Indonesians had applied to renounce their citizenship over the past five years, mostly because of marriage to foreigners.

Data from the Ministry of Immigration and Corrections showed that nearly 4,000 Indonesians exchanged their citizenship to become Singaporeans between 2019 and 2022.

Among those who have renounced their Indonesian nationality to acquire citizenship from their host countries are those working in advanced technology and medicine.

Justice Minister Supratman Andi Agtas said last week that Jakarta would ask the House of Representatives to include the limited dual citizenship scheme in the draft bill as part of the revisions to the 2006 Citizenship Law.

“For example, a nuclear expert or [athletes] playing for our national team, in all sports, or [top] chemists. So, it can’t be just anyone,” Supratman said on July 23, as cited by Kompas.

“We said we wanted to accommodate our best talents, right? Many of our diaspora are reluctant to give up their foreign citizenship, especially those with expertise in nuclear, chemical and medical fields,” he added.

The single citizenship principle had also been creating “a problem” for children from mixed marriages between Indonesians and foreigners, Supratman said.

As the proposal remains at an early stage, the government has yet to determine which areas of expertise would be eligible for limited dual nationality.

Supratman emphasised that approval from lawmakers was needed for the measure to be adopted into the draft bill.

The dual citizenship proposal follows a series of efforts by Southeast Asia’s biggest economy to reconnect with wealthy investors, highly skilled workers and the Indonesian diaspora, including its Golden Visa and Global Citizenship schemes.

Glimmer of hope

Ayu, who asked that her last name be withheld, said she supported the measure because it would “open more possibilities for super talented people to be able to give back to Indonesia and not just leave because they have other opportunities in another country”.

While she has “adapted well” to her “second home”, Ayu said she still held her Indonesian passport despite the travel-related difficulties that came with it.

“If I had to give up my Indonesian passport, that means I cannot vote any more, that means that I can no longer put my voice into something that I believe in for the country,” the 39-year-old said.

“In a way, people who are still holding on to Indonesian passports mean that they are still hoping for a better future for Indonesia.”

Legal forfeitures, such as the inability to own land or the difficulty of running a business as a foreigner, also weighed on her decision to maintain her Indonesian nationality, she said.

Ayu said she would feel “really sad” when her daughter had to decide, once she turned 18, whether to choose her Indonesian or French citizenship.

“Indonesia as a country will miss out, as they will lose people just because of their [curbs on] dual nationalities,” she said.

“A lot of mixed-nationality children are probably going to choose the other country just because it is more developed.”

Eddy Setiawan, a researcher at the Jakarta-based Indonesian Citizenship Institute, said the proposed measure could help stem Indonesia’s brain drain, as talented diaspora members “might not have to give up their Indonesian citizenship if they need to pursue a career at a certain level that requires [foreign] citizenship”.

“With people like that, technology and knowledge transfer can occur. Investors with a certain amount of investment can also create jobs in Indonesia,” Setiawan said.

Questions over impact

Hikmahanto Juwana, a professor of international law at the University of Indonesia, however, said there was “no need” to expand limited dual citizenship beyond children of mixed marriages.

“Do we really have a shortage of talented people? Is there any data that backs up this claim?” Hikmahanto said.

“As for nuclear scientists, we have plenty of them.”

He also warned of potential social tensions arising from dual citizenship, including concerns over unemployment and limited land ownership among Indonesian citizens.

But even among those who welcome the proposal, dual citizenship is only one part of a larger question about whether Indonesia can persuade its diaspora to return.

For Ayu, even if she were to obtain dual citizenship, it would not be a decisive factor in her deliberation whether to return to Indonesia or stay in France.

“I think we would like to have a country where there’s just less corruption,” she said.

“I feel like that’s a basic [request], but it’s really hard to [achieve] because that would just ask for the restructuring of the whole country.”

item.title: [SCMP] Is China’s biotech boom at risk? Fear of policy backlash after death in gene-editing trial
item.description:
The death of a six-year-old girl after receiving an experimental gene-editing therapy has been described by scientists as a tragedy that highlights the need to improve trial safeguards.

But some in the biotechnology industry fear Chinese policymakers may curtail the regulatory flexibility that scientists have long enjoyed in initiating clinical trials – a key mechanism behind China’s competitive edge in frontier treatments.

“I hope this tragedy does not have a lasting negative impact on China’s investigator-initiated clinical-research system, but there is a real risk of a regulatory backlash,” said Wang Haoran, chief executive of Neoland Biosciences, based in Shandong province.
item.content:encoded:
The death of a six-year-old girl after receiving an experimental gene-editing therapy has been described by scientists as a tragedy that highlights the need to improve trial safeguards.

But some in the biotechnology industry fear Chinese policymakers may curtail the regulatory flexibility that scientists have long enjoyed in initiating clinical trials – a key mechanism behind China’s competitive edge in frontier treatments.

“I hope this tragedy does not have a lasting negative impact on China’s investigator-initiated clinical-research system, but there is a real risk of a regulatory backlash,” said Wang Haoran, chief executive of Neoland Biosciences, based in Shandong province.

“China has advanced rapidly in several frontier areas, partly because the mechanism has provided greater flexibility for carefully supervised early clinical exploration. That speed has increased the sense of urgency across the biotechnology industries in the United States and Europe.

“This case appears to reveal serious failures in risk assessment, transparency and institutional oversight. Stronger safeguards are clearly necessary, especially for first-in-human gene-editing treatments involving children.”

The girl, identified only as Mei, died days after receiving a bespoke therapy designed to correct a neurodevelopmental genetic mutation in March last year, according to a joint investigation by Retraction Watch and the journal Science published on July 23.

The revelations sent shock waves through global research and biomedical communities, with the report framing the tragedy as “a new stumble in China’s push to rival the United States as a biotech power”.

The trial was led by Qiu Zilong, a neuroscience researcher at Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s brain centre, through an investigator-initiated trial (IIT), according to the report.

Under China’s IIT framework, researchers need clearance only from research hospitals rather than national regulators to test novel therapies on humans – an institutional set-up that has helped drive China’s biotech boom.

Unlike traditional clinical trials requiring rigorous approval from national authorities, IITs offer a nimble route for companies and institutions to determine whether experimental treatments are promising, according to industry outlet Endpoints News in an article published in December.

This mechanism had helped China’s biotech sector catch up with Western rivals, particularly by cementing China’s position as a competitive force in cell and gene therapy, the article said.

However, Wang criticised the culture among some Chinese researchers, particularly younger academics whom he said rushed to generate quick clinical data to secure grants, projects and promotions.

“In this case, many scientific and technical problems had not been solved, yet the principal investigator still pushed forward brashly,” Wang said.

“Cell and gene therapies are often easy to design, but the closer they get to clinical application, the harder they become. Academics often underestimate that difficulty.”

Mei suffered from Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations in the CHD3 gene, which can lead to developmental delays, speech impairment, intellectual disability and autistic traits. Her symptoms, however, were relatively mild.

In July 2023, Mei’s father contacted Qiu, saying the family was willing and able to cover the research and treatment costs. After months of preparation, the trial was conducted in March last year at the Shanghai-based Xinhua Hospital.

Qiu’s team used an adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector – the most common delivery vehicle in gene therapy – to deliver a base editor into Mei’s cerebrospinal fluid, aiming to alter the disease-causing CHD3 gene in her brain.

Had it succeeded, Mei would have been the first person in the world to receive a brain-directed gene-editing therapy. Instead, she died days later of a severe immune reaction reportedly linked to the treatment.

The therapy carried high risks, mainly because of the massive viral dose required, according to several life scientists.

Because only a small fraction of these viruses reach their target cells and activate the base-editing machinery, correcting enough brain cells would demand hundreds of trillions of viral particles.

“Gene-editing therapies using AAV vectors are highly dose-dependent in terms of toxicity; and because Qiu’s therapy was injected directly into the cerebrospinal fluid, the toxicity profile may have been different,” said Cui Xiang, a senior scientist at the multinational biotech firm, Novartis.

The investigation revealed that all four monkeys receiving the therapy during preclinical testing developed moderate to severe liver damage regardless of dosage, yet the human trial was not suspended.

Cui noted that the hospital ethics committee had failed to adequately verify the safety of the technology or properly assess the treatment’s risk-benefit ratio.

The Novartis scientist pointed out that while an infant with a life-threatening metabolic disorder successfully received a personalised CRISPR gene therapy in the US in May last year, Mei’s condition was “far from life-threatening”.

This incident might “cause a long-lasting impact” on the reputation of China’s rapidly rising biotech industry, Cui said.

China’s efficiency and lower development costs have attracted international pharmaceutical giants seeking cheaper cutting-edge assets and clinical research capabilities.

But whether this incident would change how foreign investors and multinational drug makers viewed China’s biopharmaceutical sector remained to be seen and deserved close attention, Cui said.

If, in the aftermath, the Chinese government handles the case seriously and strengthens oversight through legislation – including imposing tougher penalties for violations – it may yet be able to rebuild investors’ confidence, according to Cui.

However, a bioethics expert cautioned that the full impact could only be evaluated once a comprehensive investigation was published.

“Currently, the relevant information comes mainly from the media, and an authoritative independent third-party investigation has not yet been published. If what is said in the Science report is true, this exposes many loopholes in ethics reviews, scientific regulation and institutional oversight,” said Zhai Xiaomei, executive director of the Centre for Bioethics at the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences.

“We should adhere to laws, regulations and objective facts when judging this case, and not be influenced by public opinion.

“We look forward to the national independent investigation publishing the truth as soon as possible so that further judgments can be made based on the facts.”

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia moves to protect local firms as cheap Chinese goods fill market
item.description:
Malaysia is stepping up scrutiny of foreign-run businesses amid concerns from local operators over competition from China. The government wants to retain Chinese investment, technology and affordable consumer goods, while assuring local small and medium enterprises (SMEs) that foreign competitors are not subject to different rules.

Former trade and investment minister Tengku Zafrul Aziz, now chairman of the Malaysian Investment Development Authority, said government social media analysis had identified concerns over Chinese businesses as a significant issue before the Johor state election earlier this month.

“We did a sentiment analysis one week before Johor. One of the top five issues is China coming in. The survey was done for politics, we just flipped through [it] last week and [it was] still a major issue,” Zafrul told This Week in Asia.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia is stepping up scrutiny of foreign-run businesses amid concerns from local operators over competition from China. The government wants to retain Chinese investment, technology and affordable consumer goods, while assuring local small and medium enterprises (SMEs) that foreign competitors are not subject to different rules.

Former trade and investment minister Tengku Zafrul Aziz, now chairman of the Malaysian Investment Development Authority, said government social media analysis had identified concerns over Chinese businesses as a significant issue before the Johor state election earlier this month.

“We did a sentiment analysis one week before Johor. One of the top five issues is China coming in. The survey was done for politics, we just flipped through [it] last week and [it was] still a major issue,” Zafrul told This Week in Asia.

He said the issues remained salient even after the poll, in which the Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition, long dominant in Malaysian politics, won a supermajority in the state legislature at the expense of federal partner Pakatan Harapan, led by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

While consumers in Malaysia benefit from cheaper Chinese products and faster services, local SMEs say they are struggling to match mainland competitors’ scale, supply chains and pricing.

A survey of business owners and senior managers in November last year by the Associated Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry of Malaysia found that 45.1 per cent of the 245 respondents were pessimistic about their industry’s ability to compete with Chinese firms over the next five years.

Some 70.9 per cent described the competition as intense or very intense. Price pressure was the most commonly reported effect, at 86.4 per cent, followed by loss of market share at 61.2 per cent. Another 52.9 per cent said the presence of unlicensed operators had created an uneven playing field.

The concerns carry political weight because micro and SMEs are central to Malaysia’s economy. In 2024, they accounted for 96.1 per cent of business establishments and hired 8.1 million people, or 48.7 per cent of total employment, according to official statistics.

Zafrul said the pressure was being felt in services ranging from interior design and retail fit-outs to car servicing and photography.

In renovation work, for example, he said Chinese companies could measure and simulate a site design quickly, send orders to the mainland for fabrication, and deliver completed fittings at a price and speed local firms struggled to match.

“There’s a problem, right? Because the consumer, they are happy. The local SMEs are upset,” he said, adding that open economies required a “careful” balance.

Instead of restricting the market, he suggested Malaysia should help local firms improve productivity, adopt technology and reduce reliance on foreign labour. “We need to help by getting them up, rather than close down the economy, and invest in our companies to be more productive.”

From studios to furniture

In Melaka, wedding photographer Jordison Tan said although clients still preferred local operators for actual-day event photography, the impact of foreign Chinese competition was most visible in pre-wedding, portrait and costume shoots.

China-based teams had increased competition for heritage-style shoots using Melaka’s Peranakan backdrops, he said. Some advertised packages from US$73 on popular social media platform RedNote, then charged separately for editing, selected photo files and other add-ons.

“It has been bad for pre-wedding and portraiture, because they can offer very low prices, and it’s distorted the market because new clients come in thinking that’s the price,” Jordison said.

The same issues have also emerged in furniture retail.

Yeoh Tze Siang, a Penang-based furniture retailer and installer, said direct sales on Chinese platforms such as Shopee, Lazada and Pinduoduo had changed a market once dominated by local stores.

“Before the pandemic, competition was mostly between local stores,” he said. “Even [with] price competition, we had a bottom line that we would not cross.”

As online sales grew, customers began photographing furniture in his showroom and searching for cheaper similar-looking products online, Yeoh said.

His business has been badly hit since 2023, pushing firms like his further towards installation work – where workers often encounter shoddily made items such as cabinets with thin or warped back panels that need reinforcement. “They are cutting corners just to move products. Malaysians are happily buying it because it’s cheap.”

Yeoh said he could not verify what testing or regulatory checks individual products had undergone. “The government should look into [online platforms] and limit those coming in. There are many Chinese companies ‘collaborating’ with locals to enter the market. But nothing is done to care for direct purchases through legal channels.”

‘Not an easy balance’

The government’s challenge is to respond to local SMEs without removing the consumer benefits of an open economy, Zafrul said.

A purely market-based answer, such as asking businesses to improve productivity and efficiency, was unlikely to satisfy politically. “If we say that, voters will say then next election we’ll make sure you’re voted out,” he said.

Broad restrictions could also provoke a consumer backlash and raise prices. “If you stop it, the consumer is angry, the inflation goes up. It’s not an easy balance,” Zafrul said.

Putrajaya has framed the issue around compliance and fair competition rather than a problem with Chinese businesses specifically.

In June, Anwar ordered a nationwide, multi-agency crackdown on illegal business activity involving foreign nationals, including alleged abuse of tourist and student visas and the unlawful acquisition or misuse of business licences. Deputy Finance Minister Liew Chin Tong said then the effort was to ensure a level playing field and full compliance with Malaysian laws and regulations.

Last month, Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir said the government was considering possible legal changes to tackle illegal foreign business activity – such as immigration-pass abuse, proxy arrangements with local vendors and leasing of business licences. Planned responses include stronger vendor compliance checks, agency data sharing, risk-based monitoring and greater industry capacity to identify and report such activities.

Enforcement was also high on the list for respondents to last year’s chamber survey, with 75.7 per cent calling for stronger action against abuse of Malaysia’s visa-free facility and work-permit systems, and 55.8 per cent supporting enhanced guidelines on local participation and inclusion in supply chains.

‘Need to adapt’

Some politicians have called for more forceful measures too. Lawmaker Tan Kar Hing urged the government to suspend e-commerce platform Pinduoduo’s Malaysian operations until an effective cross-border anti-dumping mechanism was created.

In a social-media post on Monday, the Gopeng MP said the factory-to-consumer model allowed overseas manufacturers to sell directly to Malaysian consumers at prices local manufacturers, wholesalers and distributors could not match.

He proposed local data-storage requirements for cross-border platforms, as well as mandatory partnerships with Malaysian manufacturers, suppliers and logistics providers, alongside technology transfer and SME training.

“The suggestion … is not blind protectionism, but an adjustment period to ensure local SMEs can compete in a fair, transparent and balanced environment, rather than be killed directly by price wars,” Tan said in his post.

Malaysia could no longer depend on lower wages as its main competitive edge, said economics analyst Geoffrey Williams.

“The competition from cheaper Chinese products is mostly a legitimate cost advantage, rather than unfair practices,” the visiting fellow at Universiti Malaya said. “What is often described as dumping because of the large volumes involved is now mostly a production advantage.”

China’s economies of scale were “simply a reality of the competitive environment”, he said.

Williams warned that protectionist intervention would harm consumers and prove unsustainable in the long run. “Businesses need to adapt, not rely on protection.”

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Take sides’? Malaysia insists on conditional neutrality amid US-China tech rivalry
item.description:
Malaysia is finding it increasingly difficult to stay neutral in the US-China rivalry as the superpowers lock horns over trade, investment and the security of advanced technology, according to a top government adviser.

“They don’t make us take sides when it comes to foreign policy,” Tengku Zafrul Aziz, senior political adviser to Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, told This Week in Asia. “They ask me to take sides when it comes to security of technology.”

Malaysia’s solution was conditional neutrality, he said, backed by stronger regulations, closer scrutiny of sensitive technologies and assurances that neither side’s hardware or know-how would end up in the other’s hands.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia is finding it increasingly difficult to stay neutral in the US-China rivalry as the superpowers lock horns over trade, investment and the security of advanced technology, according to a top government adviser.

“They don’t make us take sides when it comes to foreign policy,” Tengku Zafrul Aziz, senior political adviser to Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, told This Week in Asia. “They ask me to take sides when it comes to security of technology.”

Malaysia’s solution was conditional neutrality, he said, backed by stronger regulations, closer scrutiny of sensitive technologies and assurances that neither side’s hardware or know-how would end up in the other’s hands.

The challenge is particularly acute for Malaysia’s growing data-centre sector, with policymakers needing to convince Washington that advanced US artificial intelligence chips will not be diverted to China, while assuring Beijing that tighter controls do not amount to choosing sides.

They ask me to take sides when it comes to security of technology

Tengku Zafrul Aziz, political adviser

“Today the first question I always get asked is whether Malaysia is aligned with China or the US,” said Zafrul, a former finance minister who also served as Malaysia’s trade chief from 2022 to December last year, “Companies then make decisions based on that [answer]. It used to be driven by efficiency, cost, but now it’s driven by alignment.”

Last year, Washington alleged that Chinese engineers had circumvented US export controls by renting Malaysian data-centre capacity equipped with high-end Nvidia chips to train AI models.

Malaysia responded by imposing tighter restrictions on the export, transshipment and transit of high-performance AI chips of US origin.

Zafrul argued that such controls made Malaysia a more attractive, trusted location for the deployment of advanced hardware, turning compliance into a competitive advantage.

Abdul Halim Md Lassim, group COO of HeiTech Padu, a Malaysian data-centre and cloud service operator, said security, resilience and environment, social and governance compliance were factors investors increasingly prized.

“Malaysia remains well-positioned for growth because of its location” and government agencies’ efforts “to strengthen the digital economy”, Abdul Halim said.

‘Catch-all’ controls

American technology companies continue to design many of the most sought-after AI chips, allowing the US government to set the regulatory standards and export controls governing their sale.

In July last year, Malaysia issued a directive under its Strategic Trade Act 2010 to establish “catch-all” controls on unlisted goods, requiring trade permits for US-origin AI chips if businesses suspect shipments could be diverted for restricted activities.

Under the directive, anyone exporting, transhipping or moving specified advanced AI chips through Malaysia must give 30 days’ notice if they know, believe or have reason to suspect the chips could be linked to such activity. The Strategic Trade Secretariat then decides whether a permit is needed.

The provision, originally written to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and their delivery systems, also regulates “intangible transfers of controlled technology”, according to legal experts.

It could in theory “cover controlled technology, software or know-how transferred through digital or data-centre environments, even where no physical hardware crosses a border”, customs and trade lawyers Jeff Sum and Chloe Ng at Wong & Partners said in a joint response to questions.

The rules allowed Malaysian regulators to demand access to documents and digital records when a breach was suspected, they added, but a lack of legal precedent meant that “how they would be applied in practice … remains largely untested”.

Privacy vs compliance

Farlina Said, director of cyber and technology policy at the Institute of Strategic and International Studies Malaysia, said controlling chip usage would still leave data-centre operators with little visibility into what clients actually did with rented computing capacity.

“This makes it difficult to provide the end-user assurance sought by technology-owning countries,” she said. “Moreover, forcing operators to inspect computing activity too closely might also run into privacy concerns.”

Data-centre operators could be expected to “conduct appropriate customer due diligence, but they cannot realistically know every downstream AI workload running on their platforms”, Abdul Halim said.

He added that operators had a responsibility to respect customer confidentiality and data sovereignty while providing secure and compliant infrastructure.

Farlina suggested Malaysia could build credibility as a host for sensitive technology by setting clear, technology-neutral standards covering cybersecurity, data protection and information-systems management.

“We have to think about our own capability to detect and enforce, our own capability to detect, think about our capabilities to build the ecosystem that we want,” she said, noting that Malaysia was still trying to make the move from technology adopter to technology developer, while relying on systems and components from the US, China, Japan, South Korea and elsewhere.

Politics complicates matters further. What one government considers a national security threat may not be viewed the same way elsewhere, complicating enforcement when export controls change.

Malaysia needed a framework that was “welcoming but also structured”, Farlina said, because businesses sought stability to operate in an open trading economy.

Abdul Halim said a trusted-host model should be based on “governance, security and openness rather than geopolitical alignment”, adding that HeiTech aimed to remain technology-agnostic while complying with applicable laws.

The anxieties run both ways: as Malaysia has pushed to process rare earths domestically rather than simply export the raw ore, Zafrul says Chinese investors have raised their own version of the same concern – that their processing technology could leak to competitors.

“They want to ensure that the technology they bring in is protected,” he said, adding that Malaysia’s approach was to stay open to investment while strengthening safeguards for sensitive technology.

Political ambitions

As for Zafrul, since his Senate term ended last year, he has made clear he intends to seek elected office.

“I’ve stated clearly, publicly as well and of course to the prime minister … that I intend to contest,” he said when asked about his political aspirations. “I hope I will be given the opportunity.”

Zafrul said he would leave it to Anwar and the People’s Justice Party (PKR) to decide whether he runs for a parliamentary or state seat. He has previously been linked to the parliamentary seat former economy minister Rafizi Ramli vacated when he quit the party earlier this year.

“I’m OK … Parliament, state or both,” he said, adding that he had joined the multiracial PKR because he supported parties campaigning on policies and issues, rather than “weaponising race and religion”.

Before entering government, Zafrul was a career banker and group CEO of CIMB, one of Malaysia’s largest banking groups, from 2015 to 2020. He became finance minister under Malaysia’s eighth prime minister, Muhyiddin Yassin, in March 2020 and retained the portfolio under Muhyiddin’s successor Ismail Sabri Yaakob.

Zafrul previously contested the Kuala Selangor parliamentary seat in 2022 as a candidate for the United Malays National Organisation, which he joined in 1997. He left Umno in May last year to join PKR.

item.title: [SCMP] The Philippines, sovereignty and the Pax Silica Industrial Hub – how US’ Helberg sees it
item.description:
The struggle between the US and China over who will lead in artificial intelligence is one of the defining competitions of our time. In the third part of our exclusive interview with a key player defining Washington’s policy on AI, Jacob Helberg, US undersecretary of state for economic affairs, gives a commitment to the Philippines on the Pax Silica Initiative.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr used his State of the Nation address in Manila on Monday to staunchly defend a proposed US-backed artificial intelligence hub, promising it would create “quality jobs” and inject new life into the economy.

The venture is the flagship project in a US-led coalition seeking to build China-free AI supply chains spanning critical minerals, semiconductors and logistics.
item.content:encoded:
The struggle between the US and China over who will lead in artificial intelligence is one of the defining competitions of our time. In the third part of our exclusive interview with a key player defining Washington’s policy on AI, Jacob Helberg, US undersecretary of state for economic affairs, gives a commitment to the Philippines on the Pax Silica Initiative.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr used his State of the Nation address in Manila on Monday to staunchly defend a proposed US-backed artificial intelligence hub, promising it would create “quality jobs” and inject new life into the economy.

The venture is the flagship project in a US-led coalition seeking to build China-free AI supply chains spanning critical minerals, semiconductors and logistics.

“A product of the 23-member strong and US-led Pax Silica Initiative, the Pax Silica Industrial Hub will create an ecosystem that will have AI at its core,” Marcos said.

“It will bring quality jobs to our people, accelerate our industrial competitiveness, and revitalise our economy.”

The promise is to establish an advanced manufacturing and logistics centre in the global AI and technology value chain.

But critics warn that the project could erode Philippine sovereignty, displace farming communities, and cause environmental harm.

In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post earlier this month, one of the US government architects of the Pax Silica Initiative rejected suggestions that US interests within the zone would have special treatment.

“We will ensure that the zones will uphold the sovereignty of the host country,” said Jacob Helberg, US undersecretary of state for economic affairs.

Helberg said the US administration was “still in the process of negotiating the shape of these long-term agreements” but the concerns of the Philippines and the investors would be met.

The new economic zone would provide “international investors with the kind of policy and regulatory certainty that they need in order to allocate large pools of capital to do a significant industrial buildout”.

The hub, he added, would also help “American companies secure strategic inputs that they need for their supply chains”.

We will ensure that the zones will uphold the sovereignty of the host country

Jacob Helberg, US undersecretary of state for economic affairs

Manila, a close US ally, joined the Pax Silica Initiative in April as repeated confrontations with Beijing in the disputed South China Sea worsened already-frayed relations between the two Asian nations.

The initiative is the framework for the proposed 1,619-hectare (4,000-acre) industrial hub in New Clark City, 100km (60 miles) north of Manila, the anchor project of the Luzon Economic Corridor – a trilateral connectivity project led by the United States, Japan and the Philippines.

The hub plans reflect deepening economic cooperation between Manila and Washington as they seek to reduce their dependence on Beijing for critical supply chains, including in rare earths, an area that Beijing dominates and is increasingly willing to leverage.

In May, Philippine officials said American officials had requested that the zone be placed under US jurisdiction, but they “did not agree to that”.

Helberg’s assurances were welcomed by Philippine ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez, who said they affirmed that the “proposed economic security zone will uphold Philippine sovereignty as its host country”.

“This is fully consistent with the Philippine government’s position that all development initiatives within the country operate under the Philippine Constitution, Philippine laws, and Philippine jurisdiction.”

Retired American diplomat Edgard Kagan said he took Helberg “at his word” on sovereignty, adding that Washington fully understood the importance of “full respect” for Philippine jurisdiction.

“There is neither interest in nor precedent for the United States seeking sovereignty in an economic zone,” said Kagan, the US ambassador to Malaysia from December 2023 to February this year.

The economic zone also featured last week during US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to the Philippines for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations foreign ministers’ forum.

“From the South China Sea to Pax Silica and the Luzon Economic Corridor, the US-Philippine Alliance makes both our countries stronger, safer and more prosperous,” Rubio said after his meeting with Marcos in Manila.

As part of its commitment, Washington would deliver US$100 million in new foreign assistance for the Luzon corridor to upgrade infrastructure and advance logistics and energy projects, the State Department said.

“Secretary Rubio and President Marcos also discussed opportunities related to the Philippines’ membership in Pax Silica and hosting the initiative’s first Economic Security Zone in Clark,” the department said.

Romualdez said both sides were “committed to developing a framework under Pax Silica that advances mutually beneficial economic objectives”.

“The focus of both governments is to establish an investment environment that is competitive, transparent and predictable, enabling high-value industries to flourish and bilateral trade relations to thrive better than ever before,” he added.

Wendy Cutler, a senior vice-president at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said the plan suggested that the Donald Trump administration was “serious about experimenting with different and innovative approaches to build secure supply chains particularly when it comes to AI”.

“Unlike free trade agreements, this zone covers only a limited geographical area, does not include tariff-free reciprocal access, and seems to be limited in scope in terms of lifting restrictions and regulations,” she added.

Zack Cooper, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, said the details about the project were “still coming together” and he expected there would be “robust support from US policymakers to ensure that the Philippines benefits from this arrangement”.

“I think the critical thing here is that the US government has been consistent from [Joe] Biden to Trump in trying to invest in the Philippines to help demonstrate the value of the alliance in both Manila and Washington,” he said.

Despite assurances of a win-win partnership, the proposal has drawn criticism from opposition parties, environmental groups and farmer organisations.

“The dynastic government is just ripping us off. They brought in Pax Silica. They are seizing more than 4,000 hectares from farmers in Central Luzon,” labour rights leader Leody De Guzman was quoted as saying by Philippine news outlet Inquirer.net on Monday.

Activist groups say the project will displace farming communities, reduce agricultural land, and strain local water resources.

Supporters of the project, including the Philippine ambassador to the US, who is also Marcos’ second cousin, argue that it has the “potential to create hundreds of thousands of jobs over time while reinforcing the country’s long-term industrial competitiveness”.

“The AI-native industrial acceleration hub represents an important opportunity to strengthen the Philippines’ position in the global value chain for semiconductors, critical minerals processing, advanced manufacturing and artificial intelligence-enabled industries,” Romualdez said.

Neither side asks the harder question: not whether Pax Silica is desirable, but what is traded for it

Jewellord Nem Singh, Stimson Centre

The Philippines, the world’s second-largest nickel producer and biggest exporter of raw nickel ore, sends the bulk of its output to China and Chinese-owned processing facilities in neighbouring Indonesia.

The government hopes that the project will help the country move beyond exporting raw ore to China at low prices by developing domestic processing capacity, creating more value at home and supplying the US market.

However, in a Substack post on Monday, Jewellord Nem Singh, a non-resident fellow at the Stimson Centre, said one big issue was still to be addressed.

“Neither side asks the harder question: not whether Pax Silica is desirable, but what is traded for it,” Singh wrote.

“Used well, it could anchor the productive base the state has yet to build for its industrial goals. Used badly, as critics point out, it could simply become an export platform, for allied rather than Chinese buyers.”

item.title: [SCMP] Can China and Indonesia’s strong financial ties withstand ‘resource nationalism’?
item.description:
Back in 2009, when China’s economy was expanding at about twice today’s pace, a little-known private firm made a quiet bet on uncharted territory: Indonesia.

The company was on a quest: to secure nickel, a vital industrial metal used in stainless steel production and, increasingly, to power advanced batteries.

That bet proved lucrative. By leveraging Indonesia’s vast nickel reserves – the world’s largest – and securing greater control over upstream supplies, Tsingshan Group has grown into a leading global stainless steel producer. It joined the Forbes Global 500 in 2021, and in 2025 generated 432 billion yuan (US$63.8 billion) in revenue, with operations spanning from Zimbabwe to the United States.
item.content:encoded:
Back in 2009, when China’s economy was expanding at about twice today’s pace, a little-known private firm made a quiet bet on uncharted territory: Indonesia.

The company was on a quest: to secure nickel, a vital industrial metal used in stainless steel production and, increasingly, to power advanced batteries.

That bet proved lucrative. By leveraging Indonesia’s vast nickel reserves – the world’s largest – and securing greater control over upstream supplies, Tsingshan Group has grown into a leading global stainless steel producer. It joined the Forbes Global 500 in 2021, and in 2025 generated 432 billion yuan (US$63.8 billion) in revenue, with operations spanning from Zimbabwe to the United States.

The company, founded in Wenzhou in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, is one of a growing number of Chinese enterprises helping to forge deeper trade and industrial ties between the world’s second-largest economy and Southeast Asia’s largest.

What began as a push to secure raw minerals has evolved into a broader commercial relationship spanning resources, downstream metal processing, manufacturing and, most recently, financial services – though one increasingly shaped by Jakarta’s shifting domestic priorities.

“Indonesia provides the resources, while China contributes capital, technology and manufacturing expertise, creating an increasingly integrated economic ecosystem,” said Zhao Xijun, a finance professor at Renmin University of China in Beijing.

Chasing the battery boom

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s administration has prioritised capturing greater added value from the nation’s mineral deposits since taking office in late 2024, said Hu Jie, executive director of the Southeast Asia Centre at the Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance.

Among the most important is nickel: a critical input in electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing and lithium-ion batteries, leading Jakarta to court foreign capital in downstream processing, said Hu, who keeps close ties with Indonesian officials and provides advisory services to Chinese firms looking to invest in the country.

Faced with weak domestic demand and industrial oversupply at home, Chinese producers are driven to deepen their presence in Indonesia

Hu Jie, Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance.

This ambition has quickly translated into aggressive domestic targets. Indonesia has set a goal of deploying 2 million EVs and 12 million electric two-wheelers by 2030. According to data from its Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources (MEMR), the nation currently has about 11 million active cars on its roads.

To meet this demand, Chinese car manufacturers are expanding local production facilities. In April, local media outlet Jakarta Globe reported that BYD’s factory in West Java – designed to deliver up to 150,000 EVs annually – was scheduled to begin operations and produce its first vehicles this year, with a total investment of 11.2 trillion Indonesian rupiah (US$616 million).

China’s industrial footprint in Indonesia has also shifted further downstream along the nickel supply chain, with technology-focused players taking centre stage. Earlier this month, Shenzhen-listed Azure Corporation unveiled plans for a US$290 million lithium battery manufacturing facility there. The project is expected to have an annual production capacity of 5 gigawatt-hours for a range of lithium batteries.

However, industry analysts stressed that attracting foreign investment formed part of a much larger Indonesian blueprint. The International Institute for Sustainable Development, a Canada-based think tank, wrote in a 2025 research report that “the ambition is not only to create a market for EVs – the country has the largest nickel reserves in the world and aims to become a leading producer of EV batteries.”

According to the Jakarta Globe, EV sales in the country surged 141 per cent year on year in 2025 to more than 100,000 units, hitting a record in December.

“Chinese manufacturers and Indonesia’s market are naturally aligned. Faced with weak domestic demand and industrial oversupply at home, Chinese producers are driven to deepen their presence in Indonesia,” said Hu from the Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance.

And as Chinese businesses become more deeply embedded in Indonesia’s industrial ecosystem, a parallel financial architecture is also taking shape.

Alternative payment channels

In June this year, the People’s Bank of China designated Bank of China (Hong Kong)’s Jakarta branch as Indonesia’s official yuan clearing bank, while Bank Mandiri became a direct participant in the Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) – Beijing’s payment infrastructure often seen as an alternative to the Western-dominated Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, commonly known as Swift.

That same month, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the PBOC and Bank Indonesia, the Southeast Asian country’s central bank, also signed a trilateral memorandum to ease the use of the rupiah and offshore yuan in transactions between Indonesia and Hong Kong. This followed the PBOC and Bank Indonesia expanding a 2021 bilateral local-currency settlement framework last year to cover all balance-of-payments transactions.

This institutional push builds on the rapid growth seen in 2025, when bilateral local-currency settlement between the two countries more than doubled to US$13.19 billion from US$4.9 billion in 2024, according to Indonesia’s central bank, as cited by Chinese state news agency Xinhua.

“A mutually reinforcing ecosystem is gradually taking shape,” said Matteo Giovannini, a senior finance manager at the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China.

“Resource cooperation supports industrial investment, which in turn creates greater demand for cross-border financial services, local currency settlement and trade financing.”

Deeper trade and investment ties, he added, would make the yuan “naturally more attractive” by lowering foreign-exchange costs and reducing reliance on third currencies.

Indonesia has also begun tapping China’s capital markets through its inaugural 7 billion yuan issuance of panda bonds – yuan-denominated debt securities sold in China’s domestic bond markets.

Giovannini, also a non-resident associate fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation, said these recent developments underscored Indonesia’s growing role in Beijing’s push to internationalise its currency.

“Indonesia represents an important testing ground for the gradual expansion of the yuan’s use in [the Association of Southeast Asian Nations], particularly if local-currency settlement mechanisms continue to mature,” Giovannini said, though he acknowledged the US dollar would remain dominant for the foreseeable future.

This growing financial alignment, however, is unfolding against a shifting domestic backdrop in Indonesia, where operations on the ground are running up against political currents.

Tightening the screws?

What many Chinese scholars describe as a wave of “resource nationalism” has swept across Indonesia this year. The trajectory of domestic companies, especially Tsingshan Group, captures both sides of the story: a company that built its global dominance on the country’s nickel riches, only to face a more challenging policy landscape years later.

In its “Macroeconomic Policy Report on Indonesia” published in June, the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences said “policy overhauls targeting nickel mining, in particular, have dealt severe blows to foreign investors, with Chinese enterprises already bearing the brunt of the fallout.”

As part of this shift, Indonesian President Prabowo has adjusted domestic policies on nickel production. Reflecting a tightening regulatory grip, Indonesia’s MEMR has capped the national production quota for 2026 at 260 million to 270 million tonnes, implying a 30 per cent year-on-year decline.

Weda Bay Nickel in Indonesia – the world’s largest nickel mine – is a joint venture formed by Tsingshan Group, French miner Eramet and local firm Antam, with Tsingshan holding a majority share. In June, Eramet told Mining Weekly, a South African trade magazine, that production there had been suspended since late May and that the company had reduced its workforce and entered a maintenance phase.

“The mining output quota has been exhausted,” said Jerome Baudelet, chief executive of Eramet Indonesia.

Such operational halts reflected a calculated strategy, analysts said. “Jakarta hopes to wield its regulatory toolkit as an effective policy lever to underpin nickel prices. Global benchmark nickel did rally to a peak before pulling back, leaving it with gains of roughly 20 per cent from the late 2025 level,” said Xu Yu, analyst at Orient Futures.

“The country also raised relevant tax levies. The rationale behind this regulatory tweak is plain to see – elevated nickel prices would lift fiscal receipts and fuel broader economic expansion.”

Chinese enterprises must evolve to manage policy risks and adapt to the shifting strategic interests of the host country – this is a lesson every company going global must learn

Zhao Xijun, Renmin University of China

According to the Indonesian government, the nation’s budget deficit is expected to widen to 2.85 per cent of gross domestic product this year, surpassing both its prior forecast of 2.68 per cent and last year’s reading of 2.81 per cent.

At the same time, blowback from the Iran war is spilling over into the domestic economy while pressure from the United States is mounting. Faced with challenges at home and overseas, the Indonesian rupiah has sustained a steep depreciation.

Against this backdrop, the market’s earlier trailblazers could be weighing a pullback. In June, Reuters reported that Tsingshan Group was considering a major development in Madagascar, while Hong Kong-listed Lygend Resources – a Chinese operator offering services across the full nickel value chain – was mulling a project in Tanzania.

“President Subianto’s [Prabowo’s] policies – marked by resource nationalism and protectionism favouring domestic enterprises – have left some Chinese investors more cautious about committing capital today”, said Hu of the Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance.

At the same time, “Chinese capital remains pivotal to its economic development, a reality well acknowledged by their government officials,” Hu said.

The future of the partnership

Despite Jakarta’s push for self-reliance, the numbers reveal a stark truth. According to the Chinese embassy in Jakarta, China has remained Indonesia’s largest trading partner for 13 consecutive years and had been among its top three sources of foreign direct investment over the past decade.

Bridging that dependence with domestic ambition, analysts noted that recent policy tightening marked an attempt to leverage Indonesia’s natural resources to bolster the domestic economy, rather than simply laying the groundwork for others to reap the benefits.

“Chinese enterprises expanding into Indonesia are undergoing a profound shift: their strategy is evolving from merely ‘going global’ to deeply embedding themselves within local industrial ecosystems,” said the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences in its June report.

“In the near term, Indonesia will no longer offer a low-cost and low-threshold investment destination.”

Aaron Ang, non-executive director at Hong Kong-based cybersecurity firm Edvance, also flagged investment hurdles in Indonesia, including “a tangled regulatory landscape and skilled talent shortages”.

“Our strategy centres on collaborating with local commercial partners instead of competing against them. This approach will allow us to establish a lasting foothold there,” Ang said.

As Chinese firms recalibrate their local strategies amid mounting challenges, policymakers in Beijing and Jakarta are also stepping in to keep bilateral cooperation on track.

Responding to concerns about whether Chinese firms were becoming less welcome in Indonesia, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said on Tuesday that Jakarta had “on multiple occasions expressed readiness to deepen cooperation with China on industrial and supply chains, and welcome Chinese enterprises to invest in the country”.

“We believe that Indonesia will continue to protect the lawful rights and interests of Chinese companies and foster a sound environment for investment and operation there,” Lin added.

During the World AI Conference in Shanghai earlier this month, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met Airlangga Hartarto, the Indonesian coordinating minister for economic affairs. The Southeast Asian nation became one of the founding members of the World AI Cooperation Organisation, a new China-led initiative promoting global artificial intelligence governance.

Wang said he hoped Indonesia would provide a fair and equitable business environment, while Airlangga stated that Indonesia had continued to welcome Chinese enterprises to invest.

“Over the long run, the key determinant of Chinese firms’ sustainable success in the country is to become a co-developer rather than remaining mere product exporters,” said the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences in its report on Indonesia.

But navigating Jakarta’s evolving domestic priorities is likely to remain a delicate balancing act. Zhao from Renmin University said China and Indonesia’s complementary strengths had fostered an increasingly integrated economic partnership but cautioned the relationship was not without friction.

“Chinese enterprises must evolve to manage policy risks and adapt to the shifting strategic interests of the host country – this is a lesson every company going global must learn,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] North Korea sending 30,000 troops to Russia is a ‘win-win’: analysts
item.description:
North Korea is rumoured to be sending tens of thousands more troops to Russia in support of its war in Ukraine, marking a deepening of the two countries’ defence ties and a major escalation of Pyongyang’s involvement in the conflict, if confirmed.

Late on Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky revealed that preparations had been under way in Russia’s Voronezh region to receive another 30,000 North Korean troops since last month.

He also claimed Pyongyang was planning to send additional missile launchers to support Moscow’s military campaign.
item.content:encoded:
North Korea is rumoured to be sending tens of thousands more troops to Russia in support of its war in Ukraine, marking a deepening of the two countries’ defence ties and a major escalation of Pyongyang’s involvement in the conflict, if confirmed.

Late on Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky revealed that preparations had been under way in Russia’s Voronezh region to receive another 30,000 North Korean troops since last month.

He also claimed Pyongyang was planning to send additional missile launchers to support Moscow’s military campaign.

“This is quite a plausible claim,” said Oh Gyeong-seob, a North Korea-focused political scientist and senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification. “It would be a win-win deal for both countries.”

It would be a win-win deal for both countries

Oh Gyeong-seob, political scientist

A steady stream of cheap frontline troops from North Korea offered Russia “a cost-effective way to recruit soldiers”, Oh said, “while Pyongyang receives money and military technology in return”.

An estimated 14,000 North Korean soldiers and thousands of additional military engineers were first sent to Russia’s Kursk region in late 2024 in support of Moscow’s war effort. Pyongyang confirmed the deployment in April last year.

Current estimates suggest the number of North Korean frontline forces remains at similar levels today.

Oh said Russia’s pool of willing recruits had shrunk as the war – launched in February 2022 – ground past four years and five months, making North Korean manpower an increasingly attractive stopgap solution.

Estimates of the death toll vary, but Western intelligence assessments claimed in May that nearly 500,000 Russian soldiers had been killed or injured.

In January, the Centre for Strategic and International Studies think tank put the Russian military death toll at around 325,000, out of some 1.2 million casualties since the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelensky said on Saturday that preparations for the latest North Korean deployment had been detected in the Voronezh region from June. The border area lies close to the war’s front lines and has been a frequent target of Ukrainian drones and missile strikes.

“This is a threat not only to Ukraine,” the Ukrainian president warned in his nightly address, “but to everyone in Asia within range of North Korean missiles”.

“Russia is helping North Korea learn how to wage war, improve its weapons and gain real combat experience in using them,” he added.

Trading troops for tech

North Korea maintains one of the largest standing armies in the world, with an estimated 1.2 million soldiers on active duty.

Oh said the deployment of an additional 30,000 troops to Russia “would be an attractive proposal” for Pyongyang as it offered them valuable battlefield experience, adding that North Korea had long struggled to maintain its massive military while also pouring scarce resources into its nuclear weapons and missile programmes.

Zelensky’s remarks at the weekend followed a four-day visit to Moscow by North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui, who met both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

“The two sides could have discussed pending alliance issues, including additional support for Russia’s war effort,” Oh said, noting speculation that it might have also laid the groundwork for North Korean leader Kim Jong-un to visit Moscow.

Putin invited Kim to Moscow during the Russian president’s own visit to Pyongyang in June 2024, when the two signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty that forms the basis of their military cooperation.

Another deployment would likely be justified under that treaty’s mutual defence clause, according to Lim Eul-chul, a professor of North Korean studies at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies.

“North Korea could exploit global geopolitical instability to further entrench its status as a de facto nuclear weapons state while accelerating military modernisation through transfers of advanced Russian military technology,” he said, citing the benefits of exposure to drone warfare, modern battlefield intelligence and satellite systems for a military that had spent decades in relative technological isolation.

For Russia, meanwhile, North Korean boots on the ground offer a way to reinforce depleted ranks without risking the domestic political backlash that another large-scale mobilisation could invite.

Lim added that North Korea had dramatically ramped up production in recent months of its solid-fuelled, road-mobile short-range ballistic missile systems – known as KN-23 and KN-24, or Hwasong-11A and Hwasong-11B – and “now appears to have sufficient capacity not only to equip its own military but also to continue manufacturing and supplying weapons for export to Russia”.

Raising the risks

The rumoured deployment of more North Korean troops is not without its risks, however.

Heavy losses could become a domestic issue for Pyongyang and raise the odds of defections or captures – despite reports that troops have been ordered to avoid capture at all costs.

Lim also highlighted the risks of North Korean special forces suffering a lasting blow, unwanted information seeping back into the isolated state as a result of Ukrainian and Western psychological operations, and the psychological effects of war.

“Soldiers returning from high-intensity warfare dominated by drones and advanced firepower may suffer combat trauma and struggle to readjust, potentially creating instability within the military,” Lim said.

Heavy North Korean casualties or the lack of a decisive Russian victory could also weaken Kim’s “leadership and the legitimacy of his decision to deploy troops”, he added.

Not all analysts are convinced that a second wave of frontline North Korean troops is imminent.

Yang Uk, a defence analyst and research fellow at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, said Pyongyang might consider its obligations under the defence treaty already met, having helped Russia reclaim much of the Kursk region.

He suggested that North Korean troops might instead be used to operate long-range artillery and missile systems from Russian soil, or to handle rear-area security, in exchange for Moscow providing advance military technology.

Lim said the deployment would “serve as a warning” to the US, South Korea and Japan and was also “intended to signal that Russia could intervene immediately in the event of a contingency on the Korean peninsula”.

A North Korean military seasoned “with extensive modern combat experience and backed by advanced Russian military technology” would pose a markedly greater threat to regional security, he added.

South Korea, which has condemned the invasion of Ukraine and joined international sanctions against Russia, has since been labelled an “unfriendly country” by the Kremlin.

Its support for Kyiv has been limited to humanitarian assistance and non-lethal military equipment, however, as it seeks to avoid direct confrontation with Russia while standing with Western allies and partners.

South Korean officials have previously voiced their concerns about Russia repaying North Korea’s military support with transfers of advanced missile, drone and submarine propulsion technologies to enhance Pyongyang’s military capabilities.

item.title: [SCMP] The West should stop blaming China for its economic woes
item.description:
If a cure for cancer were discovered, wouldn’t it be a cause for celebration? Not if China discovered it. At least that’s the view of the congressionally appointed US-China Economic and Security Review Commission.

“Imagine they [the Chinese] cure cancer. A shock would go through the system as we’ve never seen – our approach would have failed,” Commissioner Leland Miller told a public forum earlier this year.

“We want someone to cure cancer, but we don’t want China to control the pipeline for that cure. If China has enormous success in AI, quantum, and biotech, it shows we are failing on the national security side. I’m not against cooperation, and obviously, everyone wants cancer cured. But if there’s going to be a winner in that race, US industry – which funds enormous R&D – should be it.”
item.content:encoded:
If a cure for cancer were discovered, wouldn’t it be a cause for celebration? Not if China discovered it. At least that’s the view of the congressionally appointed US-China Economic and Security Review Commission.

“Imagine they [the Chinese] cure cancer. A shock would go through the system as we’ve never seen – our approach would have failed,” Commissioner Leland Miller told a public forum earlier this year.

“We want someone to cure cancer, but we don’t want China to control the pipeline for that cure. If China has enormous success in AI, quantum, and biotech, it shows we are failing on the national security side. I’m not against cooperation, and obviously, everyone wants cancer cured. But if there’s going to be a winner in that race, US industry – which funds enormous R&D – should be it.”

So a Chinese cancer discovery would be a threat to US national security. Any Chinese success, no matter the obvious public benefits it would bring, automatically means an American failure.

What Miller really means is that the US should discover the cure for cancer, control “the pipeline for that cure” and if necessary, weaponise it against other countries, notably China.

At least Miller was being honest. Sadly, though, this is typical Washington thinking: what is good for China is bad for the US. Vice-President J.D. Vance, for example, has repeatedly blamed the rise of the Chinese middle class for the decimation of the American middle class. Global Impulse, a current affairs YouTube channel, provides a good summary of Vance’s absurd claim.

In the commission report released to the US Congress late last year, this whole China threat is framed as “China shock 2.0”. “While China professes to be a responsible steward of the global economy, in practice it has continued to flout international trade rules even as it is the biggest beneficiary of those rules. Its heavily state-distorted economic model has resulted in systemic dumping and massive excess supply,” it said. “Left unchecked, this wave of predatory overcapacity threatens to hollow out not only developing economies but also key segments of US and allied manufacturing – eroding the industrial base essential to national security.”

You know something is up when the same spurious claims and arguments are suddenly repeated ad nauseam by think tanks, pundits, politicians and supposedly independent academics.

“China Is Sabotaging the World That Enables Its Rise: Beijing’s Risky Bet Against the West”, which appears this month in Foreign Affairs, repeats virtually all the points made in the commission report; more on this below. The European Union is now threatening a trade war citing the same arguments almost point by point.

Chinese state subsidies – subsidies are practically what the EU is built on – trade surplus, overcapacity and unfair competition are no longer just economic malpractices but direct threats to national security and industrial survival. That’s rich, considering the current American political regime poses a far more direct economic and security threat to the EU and Nato than China.

Writing in his newsletter, Global Currents, Jostein Hauge, an associate professor in development studies at the University of Cambridge, offers an excellent summary and critique of “the China 2.0 narrative”.

“The largest industrial subsidy programme in modern history is the US Chips and Science Act – roughly US$280 billion, signed in 2022 by a country that championed free trade only as long as it was convenient,” he wrote. “The EU has its own defence-oriented industrial strategy that seeks to mobilise up to €800 billion [HK$7.14 trillion] in public and private funds to strengthen Europe’s defence infrastructure and innovation.”

In absolute terms, China’s export volumes result in the world’s largest trade surplus. But that’s only because of the size of its economy and population. In per capita terms, China’s exports rank only around 104th globally. “[It’s] well below Germany (26th), the UK (42nd), and the United States (63rd),” Hauge wrote.

Other economists have pointed out that China’s export-driven economy is the slip side of America’s deindustrialisation and financialisation of its economy. This is the Faustian bargain the two countries have made with each other. Neither can extricate themselves from it despite the destructive fallouts.

China shock 1.0 was about cheap Chinese goods flooding Western markets. China shock 2.0 is really the West’s unhappiness that China has moved up the hi-tech value chain and flooded their markets with advanced but affordable goods from EVs to robotics and drones.

“When China moved up that chain, the West decided the rules of trade were no longer fair,” Hauge wrote. This is a description of a hierarchy, not a rules-based order, and the complaint is that China refused to stay in its assigned tier.”

Korean economist Chang Ha-joon has called such Western critics “bad Samaritans”.

The Foreign Affairs article repeats one such argument made (in)famous by Michael Pettis, a Beijing-based economist. It is that “suppressed consumption and excess domestic savings have forced China to export both goods and capital, requiring other economies – historically, above all, the United States – to absorb Chinese surpluses through trade deficits and capital inflows,” it said. “European analysts are now extending this argument to the EU.”

So, Chinese consumption suppression leads to Western trade deficits. If ever there is a simplistic economic claim that borders on caricature, this is it. As many economists have pointed out, deficits and surpluses are accounting items; they are the results of complex trade dynamics, not the causes.
