Anyone who has been to a shopping centre or humongous supermarket in a Chinese city may find it hard to believe the Chinese consumer is suppressed. I live in Canada and I am more financially repressed (high taxes) and consumption-suppressed (highly inflated shop prices) than my relatives in China.

It’s impossible to determine whether a nation’s consumer-citizens are suppressed. Should they amass unrepayable debts to fuel consumption, as many do in the US? In fact, post-Mao, the Chinese population has experienced the largest and fastest sustained expansion of the consumer economy and living standards in modern history.

What Western critics are really unhappy about – because that has been the ambition of the West ever since Britain’s Lord Macartney’s failed sales pitch to the Qing Emperor Qianlong – is that they couldn’t make Chinese their consumers. The US is so deindustrialised and EU so uncompetitive that they will not be able to meet the demands of Chinese consumers if the mainland market is flung open to them.

item.title: [SCMP] How America’s 250-year China dream became its greatest strategic challenge
item.description:
One morning in February 1784, a converted privateer called the Empress of China sailed out of New York harbour. It was bound for a country almost no one aboard had ever seen – China, then ruled by the Qing dynasty.

Six months later, it dropped anchor at Canton, the only port where the Qing government allowed Western maritime trade.

At the time, the Declaration of Independence was less than a decade old, and the Treaty of Paris recognising American independence had been signed less than a year before.
item.content:encoded:
One morning in February 1784, a converted privateer called the Empress of China sailed out of New York harbour. It was bound for a country almost no one aboard had ever seen – China, then ruled by the Qing dynasty.

Six months later, it dropped anchor at Canton, the only port where the Qing government allowed Western maritime trade.

At the time, the Declaration of Independence was less than a decade old, and the Treaty of Paris recognising American independence had been signed less than a year before.

The newborn republic had no navy and little standing in the world. What it did have was a dream of China.

Two and a half centuries later, the country that once drew American merchants across the Pacific has become Washington’s principal competitor. The United States and China, now the world’s two largest economies, are locked in a struggle over trade, technology, security and the shape of the global order.

For historians, that first voyage marked the beginning of a relationship in which America repeatedly reinvented what China represented – from coveted market to admired civilisation, from missionary project to strategic rival. Each reinvention said as much about America as it did about China.

Even during his visit to Beijing in May, US President Donald Trump invoked the Empress of China during the state banquet hosted by President Xi Jinping, recalling the first American merchant ship to reach Chinese shores.

The market

It is easy to forget how important the idea of China was to the founding of America, according to Xu Guoqi, the David H.Y. Chang Professor of Chinese History at the University of Hong Kong (HKU).

The tea that was dumped into Boston harbour in 1773, the act of defiance that helped ignite the revolution, was Chinese tea.

“The dream of independence for future Americans came, to a certain extent, from their dream of the China market,” said Xu.

Tea, which Americans called “green gold”, was effectively a hard currency, he said.

“Everybody seemed obsessed with Chinese tea after the British brought it to the West.”

That fascination predated the US itself, Xu added. “Europeans had dreamed of finding a route to China since the days of Marco Polo, a quest that famously sent Christopher Columbus across the Atlantic in 1492,” Xu said.

“That is the irony of the shared history between China and America – it was interconnected from the very beginning.”

When the Empress of China sailed to Canton in 1784, it embodied a belief that access to the Chinese market could help to secure America’s future.

That belief endured for more than two centuries.

In the 19th century, it took the form of the China trade and, later, the Open Door Policy – Washington’s call for equal commercial access to China rather than allowing foreign powers to divide it into exclusive spheres of influence. It was an era when a weakened Qing empire, battered by the opium wars and unequal treaties, was being forced open by imperial powers.

A century later, the same aspiration reappeared in the language of reform and engagement.

By the time China joined the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2001, many in Washington and on Wall Street believed opening up the Chinese economy would not only create one of the world’s largest export markets but also reinforce the assumptions of the American-led global economic system.

These hopes were captured in then-US president Bill Clinton’s 2000 remarks supporting China’s WTO accession.

“Economically, this agreement is the equivalent of a one-way street. It requires China to open its markets – with a fifth of the world’s population, potentially the biggest markets in the world – to both our products and services in unprecedented new ways,” he said.

But rather than converging towards the American economic model, China developed a state-led system that Washington increasingly viewed as a strategic challenge instead of an opportunity.

The first Trump administration launched a trade war in 2018. The second expanded it in 2025, signalling a new consensus that China itself had become the challenge.

A mutual misunderstanding

If Americans first imagined China as a market, they also imagined it as one of the world’s great civilisations. But the China they admired was often one they barely understood.

“Americans now easily forget that the United States was a very small country back then, when everything was just being founded,” said Wang Yuanchong, an associate professor of history at the University of Delaware.

“At the start China was strong and America was small, and only slowly did that situation reverse,” Wang said.

When the Empress of China arrived, Wang said, its crew carried a “sea letter”, a kind of all-purpose passport, addressed to no one in particular and merely listing every title its bearers could think of.

“That actually proves they knew nothing,” he said.

“They were completely in the dark about China’s administrative system, its society, its history and culture. They simply came.”

Qing officials, for their part, knew little about the new republic. They saw foreign visitors through the old imperial lens of tribute and trade.

Two centuries later, the ignorance is not mutual, Wang said.

Ordinary Chinese, he said, could name several American presidents, while many Americans “can’t name a single Chinese leader”.

As Americans imagined China, historians suggest that they were also constructing an image of themselves.

Unlike the European empires carving up Qing China, the young republic preferred to see itself as a more progressive kind of power.

One reason was America’s comparatively restrained presence in China during the 19th century.

Unlike other Western powers like Britain and France, the US seized no colonies on Chinese soil and championed the Open Door Policy, which called for equal commercial access rather than exclusive spheres of influence.

In 1868, the Qing court invited the departing US minister to China, Anson Burlingame, to represent China on a mission to the West. Burlingame acted as a mediator between China and Western countries and won the trust of Chinese officials.

The Burlingame Treaty that followed recognised that the two peoples could travel between the countries as equals and study in each other’s country.

Later, the US returned part of the Boxer Rebellion indemnity to fund Chinese schools and scholarships for study in America, benefiting the predecessor of Tsinghua University.

But historians warn that this picture of a kinder America leaves out a lot.

Xu at HKU argues that America’s difference reflected a genuine sense of exceptionalism. Having recently broken from the British monarchy, the US saw itself as fundamentally different from Europe’s imperial powers.

“The US looked down on the old European countries,” Xu said. “They thought they were corrupt.”

Wang of the University of Delaware said that throughout the 19th century, “America’s main focus in China was commerce.”

It had no garrison in China as Britain did, and until it took the Philippines from Spain in 1898, it had little real armed force in the western Pacific, according to Wang.

“It was just a country that came to share the spoils,” Wang said. “The ones out front were mostly Britain, France, Russia and Germany.”

Gordon H. Chang, Olive H. Palmer Professor in Humanities at Stanford University, similarly cautioned against romanticising America’s role.

“It’s a myth that America did the Boxer indemnity for China’s purposes,” he said, adding that former president Theodore Roosevelt’s calculation “was to advance American influence in China”.

The idea of an innocent America also sits uneasily alongside the experience of Chinese migrants within the US itself.

Thousands of Chinese labourers helped to build the transcontinental railroad, completed in 1869. Thousands more worked in mining, agriculture and small businesses, Chang said.

But their contribution was soon buried by the politics of exclusion.

“The fact that it was forgotten or neglected or covered up is part of that history of discrimination,” Chang said.

The mission to change China

If commerce was America’s first Chinese dream, transformation became its most enduring ambition.

“The sense that the United States should shape, mould or change China is quite deep,” Chang said – first turning China into a Christian country through missionaries, then a capitalist one, and now a non-communist one.

The ambition, he said, was always trailed by frustration, because “China continues to be what it is, regardless of what the United States wants.”

Wang dated the start later.

For most of the 19th century, he said, Washington stayed mostly silent on China’s political system. The belief that America should design and drive change in China did not truly take hold, Wang argued, until “after the second world war, in the Cold War years”.

Richard Nixon’s 1972 visit to China is often remembered as a realist turn, a strategic opening designed to balance the Soviet Union. But the normalisation of diplomatic relations in 1979, Deng Xiaoping’s visit to the US and China’s reform and opening-up soon encouraged a view in Washington: that engagement itself could transform China.

After the Cold War, supporters of engagement argued that trade, investment and China’s integration into global institutions would not only expand commerce but gradually encourage political liberalisation.

China’s entry into the WTO became the clearest expression of that belief.

In Beijing, however, many top leaders drew the opposite conclusion.

The strategy that Americans described as engagement was often interpreted as an effort to reshape China’s political system. That suspicion was reinforced by the Cold War concept of “peaceful evolution”, the idea that communist governments could eventually be transformed through the gradual spread of Western political values rather than military force.

It is a doubt rooted deep in the minds of generations of Chinese leaders, who have repeatedly warned that the same could happen in China – even though both the Biden and Trump administrations have assured Beijing they do not seek regime change.

Chang remained cautious about these assurances.

“If Donald Trump could snap his fingers, of course he would like to have a change in China,” he said.

“We’re going back to the past,” he said. “But the past is the 1950s, not the 1990s. The period from 1990 to around 2015 was the unusual period, and I don’t think we’re going back to it.”

The reversal of power

If America’s ambition was to shape China, history had another surprise in store: the balance of power itself would not remain fixed.

When the two countries first encountered one another in the late 18th century, China was the older, richer and more established civilisation. The US was a fragile new republic looking for its place in the world.

That balance began to shift around the turn of the 20th century.

As China reeled from the Boxer crisis and the occupation of Beijing, the US – its civil war long settled – was enjoying the prosperity of the Gilded Age and emerging as a Pacific power.

“The US is a late-developing country, founded just as the industrial revolution was beginning, so it caught the express train from the start,” Wang said.

“China’s misfortune is that its whole 19th century was a descent, while America rose the whole way – two completely opposite trajectories.”

Today, many Chinese see history as turning once again.

In January 2021, just days after the riot at the US Capitol, Xi advanced the argument that “the East is rising and the West is declining”, signalling China’s growing confidence in its development model and international standing.

The theory has since been discussed throughout official and popular Chinese discourse.

That reversal also changed how Washington viewed the world, Wang argued.

Before the two world wars, and especially before the second, Wang said, the US never had a fixed global rival. Treating first the Soviet Union and then China as its primary adversary, he said, was a strategic logic that emerged only after the US became a global power.

Fixing another country as a “main enemy” to be managed over the long term had not been a constant in more than two centuries of Sino-American contact, he said.

Hope, fear and the road ahead

If the US repeatedly reinvented China, China also reinvented the US.

Before the end of the first world war, Chinese intellectuals held up then-US president Woodrow Wilson as a symbol of idealism, hoping his principle of national self-determination would help China recover its rights.

The Paris Peace Conference’s decision to give Japan control of Germany’s former privileges in the Chinese province of Shandong shattered that hope.

After 1919, Xu said, “the Chinese became radical, became desperate, and turned to a third civilisation: Russia”.

Looking back across 250 years of contact, Chang at Stanford sees a recurring pattern.

Rather than moving steadily from friendship to rivalry, he argues, the relationship has repeatedly swung between excessive optimism and excessive fear.

Both, he suggests, have obscured a more complicated reality.

Wang believes that reality depends on maintaining contact, even as political tensions deepen.

“Without exchange, there is nothing,” he said. “Wasn’t ping-pong diplomacy exactly this?”

None of the historians who spoke to the South China Morning Post expected the warmth of an earlier age to return easily.

Chang put it bluntly: “The idea that China and the United States should become great friends has never been the case, and I don’t think it ever will be.”

But for Rana Mitter, S.T. Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School, the point was that the relationship had never stood still, and never stopped mattering.

“China and the US have been rivals, enemies, partners and collaborators during the past two centuries, in particular the last century,” Mitter said.

“It’s worth remembering that history changes over time but the two countries remain important to each other.”

item.title: [SCMP] How Xinjiang offers Hong Kong a bridge to Central Asia — and what the risks are
item.description:
Hong Kong businesses can leverage Xinjiang’s connectivity with Central Asia to expand into new markets while the city’s financial, trade and professional services can help businesses in the region enter Southeast Asia, according to political analysts.

But an economist and a textile industry veteran have warned of potential risks for Hong Kong businesses building ties with Xinjiang in northwestern China.

Western countries have imposed sanctions on officials and entities tied to the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region over alleged suppression of ethnic minority members – accusations Beijing has repeatedly denied.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong businesses can leverage Xinjiang’s connectivity with Central Asia to expand into new markets while the city’s financial, trade and professional services can help businesses in the region enter Southeast Asia, according to political analysts.

But an economist and a textile industry veteran have warned of potential risks for Hong Kong businesses building ties with Xinjiang in northwestern China.

Western countries have imposed sanctions on officials and entities tied to the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region over alleged suppression of ethnic minority members – accusations Beijing has repeatedly denied.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu led his largest delegation to date to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in May and June, aiming to explore new markets amid geopolitical uncertainties and help mainland Chinese companies go global.

Li Lifan, a research fellow at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, said Xinjiang could play a role in fostering collaboration between Hong Kong and Central Asia.

Li noted that Xinjiang had two major railway hubs in Alashankou and Khorgos at its border with Kazakhstan, a country through which most freight trains running between China and Europe passed.

“Xinjiang is essential to trade between Hong Kong and Central Asia,” he said, adding that the region had a strong appetite for advanced and innovative electronic products.

“For example, products can be designed in Hong Kong, manufactured in Xinjiang and exported to Central Asia.”

Li added that Hong Kong commercial associations could consider setting up offices in key Xinjiang border cities, such as Khorgos, to help foster connections for their counterparts in Central Asia.

Ethnic Kazakhs in prefectures close to Kazakhstan could help Hong Kong firms communicate with stakeholders, he suggested.

Additionally, Hong Kong could assist Central Asian and Xinjiang businesses in expanding into new markets as they currently relied on the port of Lianyungang in eastern Jiangsu province to export to Japan and South Korea, he said.

“Hong Kong serves as a good gateway for Xinjiang and Central Asia to venture into the Southeast Asian market,” Li said.

The analyst added that companies in Xinjiang and Central Asia could source capital from Hong Kong and use the city’s mediation and legal services in case of any trade disputes.

Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said Hong Kong could serve as a springboard for Xinjiang businesses seeking new and friendly markets outside Western countries.

Lau noted that Xinjiang had one of the fastest-growing economies in China and served as a hub connecting the rest of the country with Central Asia and Europe under the Belt and Road Initiative, while Hong Kong was tasked with helping mainland businesses go global.

“Most importantly, both places should leverage their strategic positions to cooperate and facilitate development,” he said.

Hong Kong could take advantage of Xinjiang’s location and its cross-border infrastructure as it looked to build ties with Central Asia, Lau added.

Xinjiang has for years been a source of strain between Beijing and Washington.

Western countries have imposed sanctions on China over its alleged use of forced labour and detentions in the region, a claim that Beijing has strongly denied.

The Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act that came into force in 2022 blocks the import of all goods sourced wholly or partly from Xinjiang unless the companies involved can prove their supply chains are free of coercive practices.

Esquel Group, a Hong Kong-based textile and apparel company, and two of its mainland-based subsidiaries were blacklisted over their cotton sources.

A Hong Kong textile industry veteran, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the chances were slim for other Hong Kong companies to expand into the region due to costs and sanction-related concerns.

The insider said Esquel’s presence on the mainland was unique as it had expanded in Xinjiang since the 1990s and built its supply chain.

The representative said that the appetite for Xinjiang cotton was also low, except among mainland brands, as global apparel companies could avoid trouble by using cotton from Pakistan and India at competitive prices.

Gary Ng, senior economist at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank, said cotton and food products from Xinjiang had been heavily politicised, and companies would try to minimise their risks of being targeted.

Instead of sourcing materials from the region, the city could help re-export Xinjiang products to overseas markets where there was a demand and promote the area’s tourism, he said.

Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways last year launched direct passenger flights to Urumqi, the region’s capital.

The South China Morning Post recently visited Xinjiang on a media trip, where the local cotton industry sought to clear its name.

Zhao Xin, who owns 113 hectares (279 acres) of cotton fields in the city of Shihezi in Xinjiang, said in response to accusations of forced labour that many procedures had already been automated and mechanised.

He pointed to the general application of drip irrigation technology, which involves installing small hosepipes underneath a thin plastic sheet covering the soil to irrigate crops while preventing evaporation and retaining heat.

Zhao added that farmers relied on satellites to increase precision when sowing seeds and operating harvesting machines.

“It has significantly saved manpower and increased productivity,” he said.

“Forced labour does not exist. All modernised efforts have removed the need for manpower. How can we exploit them? It has been mechanised.”

A manager at a factory of Shihezi Baifeng Cotton Industry Company, which processes cotton into yarn, also said automation had cut employee headcount from 900 to 250, with workers focusing on monitoring and maintaining the machines.

The factory is located in the 180-hectare Shihezi Textile Industrial Park, which is home to 17 businesses less than two years after its opening.

With an occupancy rate of more than 60 per cent, the park also brings in waterless dyeing technology from Esquel.

Liu Zhen, general manager of Shihezi Jingyi Technology, a company formed by Esquel and a Xinjiang business, said the technology helped tackle a bottleneck in the industry, as textile dyeing caused pollution and water was scarce in the region.

“We hope to introduce green and sustainable technologies to promote positive development in the industry,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Investment with Chinese characteristics: how Beijing’s money is reshaping tech ventures
item.description:
On the surface, China’s cutting-edge tech sector – from the algorithmic breakthroughs of DeepSeek and Zhipu AI to the hardware of Unitree Robotics and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) – mirrors Silicon Valley’s venture capital-backed ecosystem.

But a closer look at their financing histories reveals a common investor: the Chinese state.

Beijing’s strong presence underscores a more profound structural shift in how China’s frontier technology is being funded. As Western venture capital and domestic private wealth retreat, the government has been steadily expanding its role in the market, constructing a state-capitalist apparatus which blurs the line between public policy and private equity.
item.content:encoded:
On the surface, China’s cutting-edge tech sector – from the algorithmic breakthroughs of DeepSeek and Zhipu AI to the hardware of Unitree Robotics and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) – mirrors Silicon Valley’s venture capital-backed ecosystem.

But a closer look at their financing histories reveals a common investor: the Chinese state.

Beijing’s strong presence underscores a more profound structural shift in how China’s frontier technology is being funded. As Western venture capital and domestic private wealth retreat, the government has been steadily expanding its role in the market, constructing a state-capitalist apparatus which blurs the line between public policy and private equity.

Rather than operating via a single entity, this public capital flows through a layered matrix of national funds, local investment vehicles, state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and privately managed funds. It is a system that converts top-down policy priorities into private-market bets, with an alternative perspective on what can be considered a return on investment.

Last year, state-affiliated investors supplied more than 90 per cent of the committed capital tracked in China’s private-equity market, a surge from just under 79 per cent in 2021, according to domestic data provider Zerone.

This mandate comes directly from the top. At a high-level national science and technology gathering in Beijing on July 8, President Xi Jinping urged financial capital firms to “invest early, invest small, invest for the long term and invest in hard technology”.

How this capital is deployed could determine whether China will succeed in its ambitions to become a self-reliant tech superpower – or suffocate its economy under the weight of state-engineered overcapacity.

How the money moves

“2018 was roughly the turning point for us,” said Shen Qinhua, founding partner of Puhua Capital, a Hangzhou-based investment firm with about 40 billion yuan (US$5.91 billion) under management. Puhua aimed to raise between 7 billion and 8 billion yuan in 2026, with state-affiliated investors expected to account for about 90 per cent of the total, he said.

According to Shen, it was around eight years ago that traditional private-business owners in eastern Zhejiang province started to pull back their investments in Puhua, as they realised that venture funds’ long holding periods had failed to match their liquidity expectations.

China’s enormous industrial advantage has not yet translated into a profit advantage

– Zhou Kaibing, Hangzhou Venture Capital Association

Around the same time, dollar funds began retreating amid escalating US-China tensions. More recently, restrictions on investment in sensitive technologies from both sides have deepened the financial divide, while Beijing’s aggressive push into strategic technologies has drawn a diverse array of state investors.

This state support arrives in vastly different forms and at distinct stages of a company’s life cycle.

For CXMT, which is headed for a blockbuster public market debut in Shanghai next week, a combination of national, provincial and municipal investors supplied the massive capital, credit support and project construction resources required to build a capital-intensive memory chipmaker from scratch. Industrial and private investors came later.

It is one of the clearest examples of the “Hefei model”, under which the provincial capital of central China’s Anhui uses state investment vehicles to back strategic industries, absorb early risk and anchor companies locally before bringing in market capital.

By contrast, state funds entered Unitree Robotics much later in the game. That financing came after the robot maker had already proven its technological and commercial viability, timing that aligned with Beijing’s elevation of robotics to a strategic priority.

Unicorn artificial intelligence firm DeepSeek, initially funded entirely by private wealth, only recently drew backing from the national AI fund after emerging as a powerful symbol of China’s challenge to US tech supremacy.

Hong Kong-listed Zhipu, whose market cap at the market close on Friday was HK$585.95 billion (US$74.72 billion), attracted a cluster of local government funds when it neared its initial public offering in January, as cities vied for a stake to secure a share in the booming AI sector – or remain economically relevant.

One main delivery mechanism for state capital is the fund-of-funds model.

Puhua Capital, for instance, has twice been selected to manage sub-funds backed by the National SME Development Fund, which is financed by central and local fiscal capital alongside smaller state and institutional investors.

In this set-up, the national fund typically provides a 30 per cent anchor commitment. Puhua would raise another 30 per cent to 40 per cent from provincial, municipal or district-level state vehicles, before securing the remaining balance and deciding where to base the fund.

Puhua would retain its day-to-day investment autonomy, but operate under strict oversight. An appointed observer, separate from the investment committee, could join deal discussions from an early stage and veto proposed investments.

Furthermore, at least 70 per cent of the capital must be deployed into “522” companies – businesses with no more than 200 million yuan in annual sales, 200 million yuan in assets and 500 employees. Performance metrics and related-party transactions would be regularly audited.

“The requirements are higher,” Shen said, “but so is the support for policy direction and industrial coordination.”

In this way, a fund-of-funds brings in broader outside capital while steering it to policy priorities. Meanwhile, the National Venture Capital Guidance Fund, launched late last year, operates further upstream, channelling central fiscal money through regional funds into hundreds of professionally managed sub-funds focused strictly on early-stage technologies.

Some point towards specific industries. For example, the “Big Fund” – China’s flagship semiconductor investor – concentrates capital into this fiercely competitive arena, taking equity stakes directly and backing specialist funds across the chip supply chain.

Others can be deployed through local platforms that take stakes or finance construction, as in Hefei, as well as via investments and acquisitions by state-owned companies.

Who bears the risk?

Capital is pouring into strategic industries through funds with longer lifespans as exit routes expand. Platforms like Shanghai’s Nasdaq-like Star Market and the Hong Kong stock exchange now allow these companies to go public sooner, enabling broader retail investors to share in the potential gains.

“A loop is gradually taking shape, directing more capital towards hard tech companies,” said Mi Lei, founder of CAS Star, a venture-capital firm spun out of an institute under the state-run Chinese Academy of Sciences. The firm’s early bets on China’s photonics sector have begun to see tangible returns amid the AI boom.

However, state investors and private funds do not always share the same scorecard. While a market fund is judged mostly on financial returns, local governments must also account for the number of factories built, jobs created and taxes generated – competing goals that can weaken financial discipline and fuel intercity rivalries.

This local tournament has made China’s industrial policy unusually entrepreneurial – and competitive. Beijing signals the strategic direction, while cities fiercely contest fund structures, industrial estates, credit support and real-world applications.

In the nascent stages of an industry, this rivalry can foster healthy development, or what Shen described as “a hundred flowers blooming”. But it can also lead to severe overcrowding, driven by local governments’ fear of missing out on the next big macroeconomic wave.

The solar panel and electric vehicle (EV) sectors offer stark cautionary tales for today’s policy darlings, such as AI, semiconductors and embodied intelligence.

Expanding production capacity can benefit a single city seeking to boost its local economy, but when dozens of cities replicate the strategy simultaneously, the result is crippling overcapacity and collapsing profit margins on a nationwide basis.

“China’s enormous industrial advantage has not yet translated into a profit advantage,” said Zhou Kaibing, chairman of the Hangzhou Venture Capital Association. He noted that some companies with little initial appetite for scaling up began to aggressively add capacity after winning government support.

The structural risks of this approach were highlighted by state broadcaster CCTV in April through the downfall of Neta, a once-prominent EV brand owned by Hozon Auto.

Local governments in Tongxiang in Zhejiang province, Yichun in central Jiangxi province, and Nanning in Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region all took equity stakes in Hozon, providing factories, land, subsidies and financing to secure production bases within their regions – even as the carmaker remained deeply unprofitable.

As its products lost ground in a brutally competitive domestic market, the company fell into court-supervised restructuring in 2025. The failure has put billions of yuan in state-backed equity, subsidies and fixed industrial assets at risk.

This raises an uncomfortable question for policy architects: are these losses an acceptable cost of doing business in a nascent industry, or do they represent a fundamental failure of discipline in public investment?

Zhou argued that to mitigate these risks, governments should avoid trying to act as talent scouts themselves. Instead, they should delegate capital management to professional fund managers, who are better equipped to pick market winners and diversify risk.

The state investment system excels at moving money, but it is still learning how – and where – to take risks, he said.

Course correction

Beijing, however, is very much aware of these structural vulnerabilities.

At the same science and technology gathering in Beijing, Xi issued a pointed warning, saying that regions must adapt policy to local conditions rather than blindly chase hot sectors or engage in wasteful, copycat development and “involution-style” competition.

The nature of venture capital is to take risks and tolerate failure. You only need one winner to deliver an outsize return

– Mi Lei, CAS Star

Policymakers are now attempting a delicate balancing act: mobilising unprecedented capital for technology while imposing rigorous discipline on how it is deployed.

In recent years, this policy response has been rolled out in stages. The State Council’s 2024 policy document, which introduced 17 guidelines on promoting high-quality venture capital, served as the sector’s broadest overhaul since 2016.

It encouraged “patient capital” with a more long-term outlook, shifting the evaluation metrics from a deal-by-deal basis to that of a fund’s full life cycle, while protecting managers from liability for honest failures and broadening exit strategies beyond initial public offerings.

By 2025, new rules shifted the focus directly onto government fund management. This guidance curbed overlapping funds and duplicate local investments, demanded more professional management and called for a greater tolerance for legitimate, due-diligence-backed investment losses.

This year, the State Council’s guidance for investment approval extended the course correction to the factories, industrial estates and public liabilities that often accompany state-backed investments. It also tightened its oversight of fixed-asset projects, enabling it to halt disorderly capacity expansion while introducing lifetime responsibility for officials whose unlawful investment decisions cause serious economic consequences.

“The nature of venture capital is to take risks and tolerate failure,” said CAS Star’s Mi. “You only need one winner to deliver an outsize return.”

The ultimate test for the equity investment model with Chinese characteristics is whether its bureaucracy can not only learn to accept the inevitable losers that are inherent to venture capital, but also retain the discipline required to cut their losses after failed bets.

item.title: [SCMP] Nobel laureate Simon Johnson on the AI race and China’s ‘over-automation’ problem
item.description:
Simon Johnson is a professor of entrepreneurship at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). A former chief economist of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), he won a joint Nobel Prize for economics in 2024 for his research into how institutions shape national prosperity. On June 8, the British government announced Johnson as chair of its new AI Economics Institute.

In this interview, conducted on the sidelines of the UBS Asian Investment Conference in Hong Kong, Johnson discussed the rise of artificial intelligence, the future of US-China competition, and how the technology poses unique challenges to both economies.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
item.content:encoded:
Simon Johnson is a professor of entrepreneurship at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). A former chief economist of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), he won a joint Nobel Prize for economics in 2024 for his research into how institutions shape national prosperity. On June 8, the British government announced Johnson as chair of its new AI Economics Institute.

In this interview, conducted on the sidelines of the UBS Asian Investment Conference in Hong Kong, Johnson discussed the rise of artificial intelligence, the future of US-China competition, and how the technology poses unique challenges to both economies.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

As your research focuses on AI, how do you expect AI to change the job market globally? Will the impact be positive or negative for human workers?

It is obviously very early in the process, so we do not know for sure yet. But what seems to be likely, call that the default, is that AI will replace a lot of people who currently have relatively routine tasks in all businesses.

This is going to affect a lot of people in the middle of organisations, including white-collar workers at the beginning of their careers, or in information processing or compliance. These sorts of tasks are definitely in the line of fire.

For example, as long as people have money to invest, then you are going to need some people in any banking organisation to manage those relationships. But when it comes to making decisions about where to deploy the money and other processing functions – preparing statements, customer service and making adjustments to people’s accounts – a lot of that can already be handled by AI.

Every company needs some high performers. You do need some people to manage relationships. But you may not need all the other people that you currently have in banking or other sectors. In a sense, it means that the number of people that you need is just fewer than before.

AI has two sides – of the same coin – and they are inseparable. One is automation, which means replacing people with algorithms. That means no more jobs for some people in existing functions. The other side of the coin is that AI will help create new tasks and new activities, and young people (and others) can go into these new activities that do not currently exist.

The question is: at what pace do we automate jobs compared to the pace at which we create new tasks for humans? It is early days to answer this question. However, what the preliminary evidence suggests is that the automation effect is bigger than new task creation.

The United States and China are competing fiercely in a range of hi-tech industries. Which side looks best positioned to win this race, and why?

The US is having a difficult moment because we are retreating from our investments in science, and we are cutting the number of graduate students and the amount of science that is created. That is really very important for future tasks in the job market.

Right now – during the second administration of US President Donald Trump – the flow of new science creation is down about 10 to 20 per cent in the US, which is heading in the wrong direction, by any measure. If the US wants to compete with China, we should be investing a lot more in science, not less.

This is obviously a dynamic conversation. There are many people on Capitol Hill who would agree with me that we should spend more on science. And Congress, in principle, does control the budget. But the administration is not on board with that, and their policies are unfortunately undermining the US.

The current focus on automation is probably a bit too extreme in China

What are your biggest concerns regarding AI development in China and the US?

The issue for China could be over-automation. Given the wage level in China and the number of people who want to have a job, including young people, it is not clear that you should have so much automation in manufacturing and the service economy.

The kind of automation that is being developed in the US and China makes sense for high-wage economies. Now, some parts of China are relatively high-wage, but a lot of China is not. So, if you bring high-wage technology to a medium or lower-wage place, what happens to the workers? This is an issue in some parts of the US, so China’s not alone on this.

The current focus on automation is probably a bit too extreme in China. If you had an expansion of China’s service economy and shifted away from a capital-intensive investment strategy, the market would take care of itself. Hong Kong is obviously very different from mainland China, with a much stronger service sector, and that is perhaps a lesson for the rest of China.

Regarding the US – I am British by origin and moved to the US 40 years ago to get my PhD. The population of the US has increased by 100 million since then – now, it’s almost 350 million people. The US has this ability to bring talented people from around the world – people who want to work hard – and plug them into a society that is fairly dynamic.

Foreign skilled labour is complementary to, not a substitute for, domestic labour. I am very happy to see more foreign-born people come to graduate schools – MIT and other places. That is the secret sauce of America. If we can continue to allow immigration at all levels, including graduate students and scientific inventors, then the US will do well. That is the key political choice.

Are US export controls effective tools for delaying China’s AI development? What else can the US do to compete with China?

Not really, no. I understand why export controls are deployed, and you can argue that in a particular moment it might have some value. But honestly, it just encourages China to develop technology that uses different kinds of chips and build their own chip industry. I do not think this will slow them down very much. I am not sure if it is helping China, but it is not substantially changing the terms of that competition.

The best way for the US to compete with China is to invest more in our own science and technology, which we are good at and we have excellent mechanisms for doing it. But we are cutting back for political reasons. That is a missed opportunity, and everything else is, I would say, a distraction.

We will see which of President Trump’s ideas and preferences last beyond him. Some of the China rhetoric that he has – sometimes he obviously changes back and forth – is excessive. But on Capitol Hill, where you have a much wider range of views, there are some positive responses to the competition from China. There is also probably too much anti-China rhetoric.

Unfortunately, the Americans and others have a tendency to blame their own home-grown problems on other people, like immigrants or China. It is not very healthy. Most of what we are grappling with in the US is about us. Most of it is about underinvestment in science and technology and not generating enough new jobs through those investments. The trade threat from China is significant, but it is not the main problem.

AI is bringing sweeping changes. What can people do to adapt to those changes?

The debate is evolving very quickly. People are beginning to understand the downside of this technology. The release or the pre-release of Claude Mythos in the US has made it clear that this technology – if it falls into the wrong hands – could do a lot of damage. For example, it could be used to break commercial-level cybersecurity, which could be a huge problem in many economies.

As for evolution, we are not yet changing the biology of humans. In that sense, humans have to learn to work with algorithms and computers in new ways. And some of those new ways will be hard to imagine.

I have written a science-fiction novel about this very problem, because I find economics is good for thinking about the situation today, yesterday, and a little bit tomorrow. But if you want to think out 25 years, then economics is not that useful. You have to imagine everything changing between technology, society, culture and economics.

Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, a lot of people have started to imagine different futures. Of course, science-fiction writers have been thinking about this for a long time, as have people who make sci-fi movies. The broader population is now out of the box. But the question is still struggling to get oriented.

There have been many predictions in recent years that China will overtake the US as the world’s largest economy. Do you think China is still on track to become the world’s No 1 economy, and how long will this process take?

I think we are talking about gross domestic product measured in terms of market exchange rates rather than purchasing power, because China is already very large in those terms. China has a good chance. It has 1.4 billion people, compared with 350 million people in the US. If China can come up to half of the American wage level, or GDP per capita, then it will surpass the US.

It is not baked in. It is not necessarily the outcome yet, because a lot depends on productivity and what happens in terms of productivity gain. The Americans will keep at it. The US could do better. We could accelerate, which we are not doing. And China is obviously pushing on.

The next 10 to 15 years will be quite decisive, because China has a demographic adjustment coming. The Chinese population has peaked and is coming down. A lot of young people in China need jobs. Whether they can get into a productive position in a hyperactive economy will be a very important variable for what happens subsequently.

We have seen other places that competed very effectively with the American model for a period, such as the Soviet Union in the 1950s and 60s, Japan in the 1970s and 1980s, and Europe more recently. What is interesting is that all those places had very different characteristics, and they are not the same as China.

They all went through a phase when they were running neck and neck with the Americans on frontier technologies, such as space technology, vehicles or aircraft. But none of them could stay the course.

It is actually not easy to run at the front of the pack. If you ride a bicycle, the person who rides at the front has to use more energy than the others behind them. Similarly, it is relatively easy, although not trivial, to be the country that slipstreams; that follows; that adopts the technology. And it is quite hard to be at the front of the technology pack and stay at the front, because that requires you to continue to renew your economy.

If you let some people and companies become big and successful, and stay there without being challenged, then they go to sleep and they do not remain innovative. That is what happened in these other economies. Only the US has been able to retain this level of dynamism.

The United Kingdom, where I was born, is a classic example. This was, by far, the most productive place in the world in the early 19th century. It lost that lead and is now substantially behind and needs to catch up.

What are the weaknesses of the Chinese economy? How will these weaknesses slow China’s progress in surpassing the US?

There is no secret that Chinese consumers are quite worried and do not spend enough money because they save a lot. They lost a lot of money on property. And the policy preferences are to encourage capital investment as opposed to encouraging consumer spending and supporting consumer financial security in a way that would be conducive to more robust consumption.

All these features have been with China for quite some time. When I was at the IMF in the early 2000s, we were talking about almost the same issue. But they are real issues and definite constraints.

Another key issue is over-automation. Where are the good jobs? Who is getting the good jobs? Do young people become discouraged? Do they drop out of the labour force or not pursue ambitious careers?

Industrial policy is an interesting topic. China has had some remarkable successes, including on infrastructure, energy and most spectacularly electric vehicles. This is an area where the US should be competing head to head with China, but we have retreated. So, China has a remarkable global opportunity.

There has been a set of policies in China that have encouraged overcapacity in lots of sectors. Obviously, President Trump threatened tariffs and Chinese President Xi Jinping countered with critical minerals and magnets. So that is a little bit of a stand-off.

It is not easy to sell even the best Chinese products at the scale that is desired around the world, because people want China to buy from them too. The trade has to flow both ways, but who is going to buy in China if the consumer is hampered and feels handicapped?

You have criticised Trump’s tariff policies. How are tariffs affecting the US economy?

The Trump tariffs, as they are called, have a number of fundamental problems. One is that they are illegal. We have laws about what rules can be imposed, including by the presidency. I signed an amicus brief – opinion provided by experts to the American courts – on the original Trump tariffs from 2025. The arguments in our expert brief said these tariffs are illegal and must stop.

Now, the Trump administration replaced those tariffs with another set of tariffs earlier this year, which in my view are also illegal and not consistent with the legislation. I signed an amicus brief to the Court of International Trade on that, and this is still going through the court system. It will also be appealed and will presumably go to the Supreme Court.

In addition to not being legal, these tariffs are also not a good idea because what you are essentially doing is putting a tax on your own consumers. And those consumers are often relatively low-income people in the US who shop at Walmart, for example, which sources a lot from mainland China and other places.

You are also putting a tax on your own companies that buy imported inputs. So, you are undermining their ability to manufacture in the US. The goal of the policy is to help manufacturers, but this kind of tax is completely counterproductive. You can offset it with various kinds of special privileges and exemptions, but that becomes extremely complicated.

It also opens the door to corruption. This is not specific to America; this is something that happens all around the world. When you get complicated tariff systems, you tend to have some political favours, some facilitation payments, some bureaucratic discretion. All of which is a complete mess, and not the right way to organise foreign trade.

Corruption is a standard feature of complicated trade systems. I am not saying we have seen direct evidence or court cases on this yet, but that is what we should expect. Even if it is not overtly corrupt, then it just makes investment much harder and less predictable. It discourages you from entering into long-lasting foreign trade relationships.

It is really the kind of policy that undermines job creation. The Trump administration says that they want job creation, but their policies are counterproductive in this case.

[We will have] more volatility than between 2010 and 2020, which was a relatively calm decade

Given the Trump administration’s tariff policies and the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran, are we heading towards a recession?

There is always some risk of recession, and I do think the situation in the Strait of Hormuz is very dangerous. It is quite difficult for the US to resolve this situation by itself. I am writing about ways in which China could help with that.

But I do not think China is yet willing to play the kind of expansive role we are recommending, which would suggest that we will get a lot of instability and continued disruption through the Strait of Hormuz.

At the same time, Russia is playing quite a destructive role – not just in Ukraine, but also with regard to supplying Iran with drones. Remember, a lot of these drones were actually developed in Iran, sold to Russia, and now Russia has improved the design.

The Russians are the big winners from the Strait of Hormuz closure and the Iran war, because now they can sell more oil at a higher price. Before the invasion, they were selling at about US$60 a barrel. Now, they can sell at the full [global oil benchmark] Brent price between US$100 and US$110 per barrel. That is a big windfall for the Kremlin.

This kind of physical game is very bad for the global economy. It adds pressure on the central banks because of inflationary effects; it disrupts access to energy for a lot of economies, particularly the ones that do not have deep pockets or strategic reserves; it introduces uncertainty around investment.

There is also big tension within Nato about whether the US will continue to support it. I do think the US will try to acquire Greenland, and it may do that in ways that are not violent. This would send a not entirely peaceful and conducive signal to Russia and mainland China. These are big risks swirling around the global economy.

If a recession does come, how can the global economy bounce back?

There is a resilience to the global economy that is admirable. And the AI boom, as long as it lasts, will be helpful there.

At the same time, we should remember what happened during some historical episodes of big technological transformations. For example, railways did transform and boost the productivity of many economies, including the US. But in 1873, there was a big financial crash around railways, and a years-long depression over the following decade in the US.

So, even though the railways were profoundly transformative and very positive from the point of view of economic development, you can still have big bumps in the road around the deployment and valuation of new technology.

The world is a big place, and the world is quite resilient. There are definite tensions. But I do not see any reasons why the world economy would go down and stay down. The future is more about volatility, I would say, not recession. More volatility than between 2010 and 2020, which was a relatively calm decade.

item.title: [SCMP] Fields Medal win: Wang Hong, Deng Yu are first Chinese nationals to score top maths honour
item.description:
For the first time, China has produced Fields Medal winners educated on its own soil – and two at once.

Chinese mathematicians Wang Hong and Deng Yu took the honour, alongside John Pardon and Jacob Tsimerman.

The Fields Medal is the top honour for young mathematicians under 40 years of age. The medals, along with a modest cash prize, were given out on Thursday at the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) in Philadelphia.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, China has produced Fields Medal winners educated on its own soil – and two at once.

Chinese mathematicians Wang Hong and Deng Yu took the honour, alongside John Pardon and Jacob Tsimerman.

The Fields Medal is the top honour for young mathematicians under 40 years of age. The medals, along with a modest cash prize, were given out on Thursday at the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) in Philadelphia.

The prestigious medal, often called the “Nobel Prize of mathematics”, has been awarded since 1936, but this is the first time a Chinese national has won it.

It is also the first time that two mathematicians who completed their undergraduate training in mainland China have shared the prize in the same year.

With this, China becomes the fifth country – after the United States, France, Britain and Russia – to produce two Fields laureates in a single ceremony, and the first Asian nation to do so.

Only two other ethnic Chinese mathematicians have won the Fields Medal: Shing-Tung Yau in 1982 and Terence Tao in 2006, but neither held Chinese citizenship at the time. China’s mathematics community had been waiting for this moment for decades.

“I am very happy,” Yau, who returned to China full-time in 2023 to help nurture young mathematical talent, told Chinese media.

He said he had long hoped that at least one Chinese mathematician would win the prize, but was especially delighted that two outstanding young mathematicians received it this year.

Wang and Deng were both admitted to Peking University in 2007. Now they stand together on the world’s highest stage for mathematicians.

Deng was honoured for work in partial differential equations, and connecting fundamental laws of physics to equations describing the behaviour of gases and fluids. Yau said the research addressed a question first raised by German mathematician David Hilbert more than a century ago and pursued by generations of leading mathematicians.

Wang won for major advances in harmonic analysis and geometric measure theory, including her work on the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture. Yau described her efforts with a collaborator as a “landmark contribution”, saying the problem had evaded solution for decades.

The twin victories showed that China could produce world-class mathematical talent, Yau said. He added that the next milestone would be to nurture Fields Medallists who receive their full training in China and make their most important discoveries there.

He said he had “repeatedly invited” Wang and Deng to return to teach in China in the hope of helping train the next generation.

Wang Hong: solving the 3D Kakeya conjecture

During a press conference after the announcement, Wang said the award meant a great deal to her and her collaborators.

She recalled first hearing about the Fields Medal as a high school student, reading in a mathematics magazine about Terence Tao’s 2006 win. “I was quite excited [then],” she said. “So I’m also excited today.”

Born in 1991 in Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, Wang Hong enrolled at Peking University at just 16 – first in the School of Earth and Space Sciences, then transferring a year later to the highly competitive mathematics programme.

She earned her bachelor’s degree in 2011. After that, she went to France to study at Ecole Polytechnique and Paris-Sud University, obtaining both an engineering degree and a master’s degree in mathematics.

She then moved to the US to earn her PhD at Massachusetts Institute of Technology under Larry Guth, winner of the 2016 New Horizons in Mathematics Prize for his solutions to long-standing problems in different branches of mathematics. She completed her doctorate in 2019.

After postdoctoral work at the Institute for Advanced Study in New Jersey, she held a faculty position at the University of California, Los Angeles.

She is now a professor at New York University’s Courant Institute as well as a permanent professor at the Institut des Hautes Etudes Scientifiques (IHES) in France.

She is recognised for her breakthrough contributions to harmonic analysis and geometric measure theory.

In 2025, she and collaborator Joshua Zahl published a 127‑page paper proving the three‑dimensional Kakeya conjecture – a problem that had baffled mathematicians for over a century.

Their work provides a fresh analytical framework for signal processing applications such as radar and remote sensing.

She has also received the Salem Prize and the Clay Research Award for this achievement. She is the third woman ever to win the Fields Medal.

Wang said she believed China was already producing world-class mathematical research.

She pointed to collaborators who had recently returned to China, including Joshua Zahl, who joined Nankai University’s Chern Institute of Mathematics last year. “I believe they will just continue making an impact,” she said.

Deng Yu: cracking Hilbert’s sixth problem

During the press conference, Deng called the award “a really great honour”.

Deng recalled that while reading a novel he received an email from the president of the International Mathematical Union in January requesting a Zoom meeting. Having heard that Fields Medal recipients were typically notified around that time, he suspected what it meant.

“I thought that was it,” he said. “So then I just kept reading the novel.”

Born in 1989 in Shenzhen, Deng showed early mathematical talent. In 2006, he won a gold medal at the Chinese Mathematical Olympiad with a perfect score. That same year, he took the gold at the International Mathematical Olympiad.

He was admitted to Peking University without entrance exams in 2007, but transferred to MIT in 2009, earning his bachelor’s degree in mathematics in 2011.

He completed his PhD at Princeton University in 2015 under Alexandru Ionescu, whose work relates to the long-term dynamics of solutions of partial differential equations.

After a postdoctoral appointment at NYU’s Courant Institute and a faculty position at the University of Southern California, he became a professor at the University of Chicago in 2024.

Deng is recognised for his pioneering work in partial differential equations, fluid dynamics and probabilistic analysis.

Last year, together with Zaher Hani and Xiao Ma, Deng solved a narrow version of Hilbert’s sixth problem – one of 23 challenges posed by German mathematician David Hilbert in 1900.

Ionescu, Deng’s Princeton adviser, said the work would “almost certainly win a Fields Medal”.

In 2021, Deng received the Sloan Research Fellowship, awarded to outstanding early-career researchers.

China narrows the gap in mathematics

The Fields Medal winners highlight the broader trend of China’s growing prominence in mathematics.

“Looking at just this year’s ICM invited speakers, there are 12 Peking University undergraduate alumni,” said Chinese mathematician Lin Huaxin in an interview with National Business Daily earlier this month.

“That shows PKU’s mathematical level has climbed more than one notch over the past three or four decades.”

“While the United States still holds a strong lead globally, China is narrowing the gap, and one important sign is that China is attracting mathematicians from around the world,” Lin added.

Lin himself left his tenured position at the University of Oregon at the end of 2024 to return to China full‑time, joining the Shanghai Institute for Mathematics and Interdisciplinary Sciences.

Zahl, Wang’s collaborator, accepted an invitation from Chinese mathematician Guo Shaoming to join Nankai University full-time last year.

Before Thursday’s official announcement, many speculated that both Wang and Deng would win the Fields Medal.

Rumours surfaced on July 14 after their names were apparently leaked due to a coding error on the ICM website, though the organisation has not commented on the matter.

On the eve of the ceremony, at an International Mathematical Union gathering in New York, Glasgow beat Hong Kong and Tokyo to become the host of ICM 2030.

item.title: [SCMP] The best guest shifts in Hong Kong and Macau amid Asia’s 50 Best Bars 2026
item.description:
All of Hong Kong and Macau are gearing up for a week of mixology festivities as Asia’s 50 Best Bars looks to descend on our sister SAR for its second year, announcing this year’s list next Tuesday.

In the days before and after, both Macau and Hong Kong will be flush with the region’s top mixologists, either here to receive awards or soak in the cities – or to take over many of our city’s world-class bars. From mega shifts like at Argo or Wing Lei Bar to unique one-off shifts featuring bars from Mongolia, Nepal, Phnom Penh and, of course, Singapore, Bangkok and Seoul, here are the guest shifts this week you don’t want to miss.

Friday, July 24
item.content:encoded:
All of Hong Kong and Macau are gearing up for a week of mixology festivities as Asia’s 50 Best Bars looks to descend on our sister SAR for its second year, announcing this year’s list next Tuesday.

In the days before and after, both Macau and Hong Kong will be flush with the region’s top mixologists, either here to receive awards or soak in the cities – or to take over many of our city’s world-class bars. From mega shifts like at Argo or Wing Lei Bar to unique one-off shifts featuring bars from Mongolia, Nepal, Phnom Penh and, of course, Singapore, Bangkok and Seoul, here are the guest shifts this week you don’t want to miss.

Friday, July 24

Green Room x Three x Co

Ranked the No 15 best bar in Asia last year, Kuala Lumpur’s Three X Co is heading all the way up to the 49th floor of Upper House to take over Green Room for one night only. Represented this time by bar manager Rachel Hor and senior bartender Chris Ang, Three X Co focuses on contemporary cocktails such as those from its IndiVDuality menu. The Quiet Quinn riffs on the martini with a Tanqueray 10 base, a chrysanthemum infusion and Yzaguirre Dry Reserva Spanish vermouth, topped with orange bitters and grapefruit zest.

Where: Green Room, 49/F, Upper House Hong Kong, Admiralty

When: 6.30pm-9.30pm

The Local Pour – Dara x Flair Up

Dara, celebrated for its modern Filipino dishes and vibrant neighbourhood atmosphere, is teaming up with “flairtender” Washam Limbu for a special collaboration titled The Local Pour.

Limbu is the co-founder of Flair Up and frequently participates in the Young Chef, Young Waiter, Young Mixologist (YYY) competitions. He took home the 2026 YYY Story Teller Global title and was named the Young Mixologist of the Year in 2025, when he was also crowned champion in the 2025 Ichiko Cocktail Competition Hong Kong event.

Guests can expect high-energy performance, artisanal craft cocktails and a commitment to locally produced ingredients.

Where: Dara, Shop 3, Soho 189, 189 Queen’s Road West, Sai Ying Pun

When: 7pm until sold out

Saturday, July 25

The Road Less Travelled – Wing Lei Bar x Nomad Lab x Barc x Kiki Lounge

Even though Wynn Palace and Wing Lei Bar start their festivities earlier in the week, one of our favourites on the itinerary has to be this one – gathering bars from Mongolia, Nepal and the Isle of Man.

All three bars are represented by their co-founders. Nomad Lab’s Awaraa Awarzed is coming in from Ulaanbaatar as the self-proclaimed “first cocktail lab in Mongolia”, while Barc’s Abhishek Tuladhar is arriving from Nepal. The latter won the 2025 Michter’s Art of Hospitality award from Asia’s 50 Best Bars last year. Rounding out the takeover is Drew Fleming from Kiki Lounge in Isle of Man, the winner of the Spirits Business Awards Bar of the Year in 2024.

Where: Wing Lei Bar, West Esplanade, G/F, Wynn Palace, Avenida da Nave Desportiva, Coloane-Taipa, Macau

When: 5pm-8pm

25:00 x Thaipioka

Bartenders Hope Narawut and Supawit Thinpitayanurat, also known as Miguel, are arriving from Bangkok to take over 25:00 Twenty Fifth Hour, representing Thaipioka, which focuses on equal parts cocktails and music. Back home, Thaipioka offers fruit-centric cocktails like the Kyoho Balsamic Negroni, adding vinegar, shiso bitters and kyoho grapes to the traditional profile, or the Orange Thai Milk Tea, which soups up the citrus drink with rum, coffee, caramel and fresh orange.

Where: 13/F, Luk Yu Building, 24-26 Stanley Street, Central

When: 9pm-1am

Sunday, July 26 (early)

C108 celebrates its second anniversary with Sora Bar

C108’s second anniversary on Old Bailey Street is coming hot on the heels of its updated menu earlier in the month. Taking centre stage for Sunday’s anniversary party is a guest shift by Jonas Vittur, director of bars at Rosewood Phnom Penh’s rooftop bar, Sora, and its head bartender Phirun Lek.

Last year, the sky bar was ranked No 65 on Asia’s 50 Best Bars list and won the Ketel One Sustainable Bar Award. C108 is also working with Good Stuff to have four DJs play music all night long.

Where: 15 Old Bailey Street, Central

When: 7pm-10pm

The Old Man x AABBCC

Start your Sunday night at the top of the alphabet as AABBCC arrives from New Delhi to take over The Old Man on Aberdeen Street. The “retro-futuristic archive” bar sends co-founders Jairaj Singh Solanki and Aditi Singh, who are bringing cocktails such as a twist on the Godfather with dandelion, a Bellini using cacao butter, a caprese salad rendered in alcohol form, and a drink called the Mushroomisu.

Solanki’s former concept, Lair, also based in New Delhi, was ranked the 8th best bar in Asia last year.

Where: The Old Man, LG/F, 37 Aberdeen Street, Soho, Central

When: 6pm until sold out

Sunday, July 26 (late)

Dio x Bar Woody

There’s so much happening on Sunday and Monday that it’ll be easy to catch an early shift and a late shift on either night. Bar Woody has made a name for itself in Chengdu by anchoring its concept on the complexity of wood and herbs, with its signature cocktails such as the Cedar, the Benzoin and Sandalwood. Now there is a chance to try those earthy sips at Dio on Sunday, when Bar Woody’s Keith Lo and Austin Guo serve their wood-forward creations supported by Mizunara, featuring The Hachi Shochu and Wakshio 424 Gin.

Where: Dio, 8 Aberdeen Street, Central

When: 8pm till sold out

The Diplomat x Offtrack

Singapore’s Offtrack, last year’s No 23 best bar in Asia and known for its high-energy music and equally excellent focus on cocktails and food, arrives in Hong Kong to take over The Diplomat for one night only. At home, Offtrack’s co-founder Aslam Zainal and his team serve straightforward, inventive drinks like the Cora Middleton, combining raspberry, white almond, rum, lime, hibiscus and egg white. It makes perfect sense for Zainal to stage a guest stint at one of Hong Kong’s best bars for martinis, Irish coffees and burgers.

Where: The Diplomat, LG/F, H Code, 45 Pottinger Street, Central

When: 8pm till sold out

Monday, July 27 (early)

Quinary x Native x Milli x Chanel Adams

Hong Kong’s first home of molecular mixology, Quinary, is starting the party early on Monday with a triple-header featuring Singapore’s Native and Milli, alongside a special guest. Native is represented by co-founder Vijay Mudaliar and mixologist Amillie Chan, who are showcasing their unique approach to obscure and foraged ingredients, while Danny is bringing a menu of playful cocktails from Milli, a rooftop bar atop Singapore’s National Gallery. Rounding out the line-up is Chanel Adams, who most recently worked at the Mandarin Oriental Bangkok, and at Please Don’t Tell in Hong Kong before that.

Where: Quinary, 56-58 Hollywood Road, Central

When: 7pm-10pm

Tell Camellia x Gong-Gan

Gong-Gan, famed for its zero-waste philosophy, arrives from Seoul to take over tea-inspired cocktail joint Tell Camellia. Ranked No 74 on Asia’s 50 Best Bars this year, Gong-Gan is represented by co-founders Evan Noh and Willy Park. Their signature cocktails include the Si-Jang, featuring the premium Korean spirit Igangju alongside bourbon, lemon juice, roasted rice and banana beer.

Where: Tell Camellia, 45 Pottinger Street, Central

When: 8pm onwards

Monday, July 27 (late)

Kinsman x Bar Truce x Bar Notes

Wong Kar-wai-inspired Kinsman brings together Indonesia and South Korea in a double header featuring Bar Truce from Jakarta and Seoul’s Bar Notes. The former is grounded in Japanese mixology tradition with a twist, serving cocktails like the Ogura Dream as a clarified twist on the Alexander. Meanwhile, Bar Notes puts its focus on storytelling – its owner Ricky is also a freelance writer – serving concoctions like the Ssanghwa, inspired by the portmanteau “halmae-nial” – a combination of “halmae”, meaning granny, and “millennial”, referring to millennials enjoying foods normally associated with the elderly – containing rum, cream, egg and the eponymous bitter tea.

Where: Kinsman, 65 Peel Street, Central

When: Bar Truce: 8pm-10pm; Bar Notes: 10pm-12am

Socio x Modernhaus

One of Jakarta’s best – Modernhaus – arrives to take over Socio, Hong Kong’s main venue focused on upcycling community ingredients. Modernhaus was named the No 12 best bar in Asia last year and focuses on conceptual, minimalist cocktails. At home, they serve drinks like the Turmeric, which involves a turmeric gin, coconut chai milk, cream, salted tamarind and lemonade soda, and the Apple, which spotlights smoked manalagi apple brandy, koji, umami bitters and apple miso.

Where: Socio, 17 Staunton Street, Central

When: 8.30pm onwards

Tuesday, July 28

Campari x Wynn Palace Asia’s 50 Best Bars after-party

Tuesday is the day we’ve all been waiting for. After our region’s most excellent bars get their flowers, Wynn Palace is joining hands with Campari to host an all-out after-party in Macau. Responsible for the vibes are some of the region’s best. Look out for veterans of the list to host this get-together: Singapore’s Cat Bite Club (No 86, 2026); The Cocktail Club (No 12, 2024) and Carrots (No 34, 2025), both from Jakarta; Opium from Bangkok (No 43, 2025); and Bengaluru’s Soka (No 28, 2025).

Where: Palace Reserve Club, Wynn Palace, Avenida Da Nave Desportiva, Cotai, Macau

When: Post-ceremony till late

Wednesday, July 29

Argo Mega Friends Takeover

Argo plays host to an exceptional night of mixology as Argo Mega Friends returns with three new regional names. This collaboration brings together teams from three of Asia’s top-ranked bars. Bangkok’s Bar Us is represented by co-founders Aum Veerach and Taln Sudarat; Dry Wave Cocktail Studio sends founder Supawit “Palm” Muttarattana and bartender Ammie Suparada; and Taipei duo William Wu and Cloris Huang of The Public House round out the line-up.

Expect a vibrant atmosphere where these master mixologists serve up inventive, culinary-forward cocktails, such as Bar Us’ famous Jackfruit & Sticky Rice.

Where: Argo, Four Seasons Hotel Hong Kong, 8 Finance Street, Central

When: 6pm-9.30pm

Terrible Baby x Moebius Milano

Moebius Milano, ranked No 7 on the World’s 50 Best Bars last year, is housed inside a Milanese textile warehouse where Michelin-starred gastronomy, live jazz and avant-garde mixology collide.

For one night only, Moebius’ owner Lorenzo Querci and bartender Andrea Giraldo are taking over Eaton HK’s Terrible Baby. On the menu are cocktails like the Cocco & Salvia Negroni, which contains Bulldog gin and Del Professore Vermouth Rosso, as well as the aperitif Raspberry Lavorato Secco, which contains Campari and Rabarbaro Zucca.

Where: Terrible Baby, 4/F, Eaton Hong Kong, 380 Nathan Road, Kowloon

When: 7pm till sold out

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Disbelief, shock’: Singapore PM on Faishal’s inappropriate messages with woman
item.description:
A married Singapore minister’s sudden resignation amid revelations he had exchanged inappropriate messages with a woman has rocked the city state’s establishment circles, with a groundswell of sentiment calling for him to be retained.

Amid online petitions and calls to keep former minister-in-charge of Muslim affairs Faishal Ibrahim following his resignation on Monday, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong shed further light on the controversy, suggesting the matter was more serious than previously believed.

Faishal resigned from the cabinet, parliament and the People’s Action Party (PAP) after accepting he had fallen short of standards expected of him in his online interactions with a woman, which resulted in harassment accusations by both parties.
item.content:encoded:
A married Singapore minister’s sudden resignation amid revelations he had exchanged inappropriate messages with a woman has rocked the city state’s establishment circles, with a groundswell of sentiment calling for him to be retained.

Amid online petitions and calls to keep former minister-in-charge of Muslim affairs Faishal Ibrahim following his resignation on Monday, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong shed further light on the controversy, suggesting the matter was more serious than previously believed.

Faishal resigned from the cabinet, parliament and the People’s Action Party (PAP) after accepting he had fallen short of standards expected of him in his online interactions with a woman, which resulted in harassment accusations by both parties.

Wong learned of the interactions after the woman emailed him with details of their exchanges.

Speaking to local media on Wednesday, Wong said he initially thought the contents in the “detailed” email were fabricated.

“My initial reaction was disbelief and shock.”

Police were called in to investigate the accusations but no criminal action was taken.

Faishal, 58, who was also senior minister of state for home affairs, said in his resignation letter that while there was no physical relationship between him and the woman, and he did not intend for the interactions to develop into one, there was a “lapse of judgment” in how he handled the matter.

Wong noted that he had attempted to see if there was a way for Faishal to continue in office despite the circumstances, but the complaint against Faishal had made it a public matter.

Several key colleagues on his team independently reviewed the evidence and reached the same conclusion, Wong added.

The prime minister stressed that if any other MP from the ruling PAP had been in a similar situation, the same standard would have applied.

He said he recognised the temptation to make an exception for Faishal, but “doing so will only cause more damage and harm to Singapore”.

“We have to do the right thing, and we have to continue to uphold the trust that Singaporeans have in our political system and in our public institutions,” Wong said.

“He accepts that he made a very serious mistake in engaging her, even when the nature of the interactions crossed the line, and he also accepts that his responses, his interactions with her, objectively speaking, were questionable and inappropriate,” Wong added.

On Tuesday evening, Wong, the new acting minister in charge of Muslim affairs Zaqy Mohamed and Home Affairs Minister K. Shanmugam met members of the Malay-Muslim community.

It was understood that the issue of retaining Faishal was raised during the meeting.

Earlier on Wednesday, Shanmugam revealed on social media that there was a series of online interactions between Faishal and the woman, and Faishal expressed concern that the woman might react negatively if he abruptly cut her off.

Faishal himself … acknowledged that he should not have allowed his exchanges with the lady to carry on

Home Affairs Minister K. Shanmugam

“Nevertheless, his responses were, objectively, inappropriate and questionable. They come across as engaging with her. Indeed, that was how the lady interpreted his responses, and said she was encouraged to continue,” Shanmugam said.

According to Shanmugam, the standards governing personal conduct in these situations are straightforward: where a matter remains private and the inappropriate conduct stops after counselling, it can remain private.
