However, when the matter enters the public domain through a complaint or otherwise, it must be examined and if impropriety occurred, action must follow.

Therefore, once the woman emailed the prime minister, the matter was no longer a private, consensual one between two people and became “semi-public”. Since she lodged a complaint against a public office holder, the Prime Minister’s Office had to “consider the appropriateness of Faishal’s interactions”.

“Faishal himself reflected on the matter and acknowledged that he should not have allowed his exchanges with the lady to carry on, and he should have established clear boundaries from the start,” Shanmugam said.

Independent political observer Felix Tan said Wong and Shanmugam’s comments reinforced the point that the interactions were egregious enough to warrant Faishal’s resignation.

He noted that the comments and petition in support of Faishal appeared to be gaining traction among Singaporeans, suggesting that segments of the public questioned whether the response was proportionate to the circumstances.

“Having to deal with such an issue early in his tenure is far from ideal, so the government is signalling that the decision was not made lightly or on a whim, but followed careful consideration,” Felix Tan said.

“By addressing the matter decisively, PM Wong is also seeking to prevent the issue from escalating into a prolonged distraction for the government.”

Political observer and law professor Eugene Tan said he believed the minister’s comments on Wednesday had to do with the public clamour over whether Faishal’s lapse of judgment warranted his resignation.

“I think the preference was not to go into more detail, but there was probably pressure to demonstrate that Faishal’s resignation was warranted,” Eugene Tan said.

Regarding the principle Shanmugam laid out concerning when personal conduct required examination, Eugene Tan said that standard was not evident or well articulated until now.

“Where there is a complainant, the consideration that the matter could go public – and thus the government could lose control of the narrative – means it would not be surprising that a proper inquiry be conducted and a fair hearing accorded to the MP or political officeholder as well as the complainant,” Eugene Tan said.

He noted that what was clear now was that not every inappropriate relationship warranted a resignation: “The consequences may be clear to the PAP MPs, but it appears not to be so for the public trying to understand how different personal indiscretions are dealt with by the party.”

An online petition urging Wong to reject Faishal’s resignation has since garnered 1,340 signatures.

The petition’s creator, Ridjal Noor, wrote that Singapore needed “experienced, steady public leaders who understand the realities people face and can keep serving without disruption”.

“We therefore appeal to the Prime Minister of Singapore to reject the resignation and confirm that Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim should remain in his position,” Ridjal said.

“This decision would reflect respect for public service, confidence in proven leadership, and a commitment to keeping capable ministers where they can continue to do the most good.”

Some political observers also spoke against Faishal’s resignation.

On Tuesday, Walid Jumblatt Abdullah, an associate professor of public policy at Nanyang Technological University, said on social media that while the public did not know much about the interactions, what was known was that they were not criminal and were unrelated to his public work.

“I therefore do not think he should have resigned. And I wonder whether we are setting impossible standards to meet for (aspiring) politicians, and whether younger people would be deterred from stepping forward to join politics because of that,” Walid said.

Former nominated member of parliament Calvin Cheng said on Facebook on Monday: “A good man should not have his whole career and life destroyed for something like this.”

Cheng said Faishal should be allowed to apologise and be transparent, while community leaders could decide whether he should keep his Muslim affairs position. A by-election could also be called in his ward to see if he should retain his MP position.

“We don’t live in 17th century Puritan England. The people will understand,” Cheng said.

item.title: [SCMP] Beijing and Manila should avoid South China Sea ‘miscalculation’: top diplomats
item.description:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met his Philippine counterpart in Manila on Wednesday, with both sides highlighting the need for “reducing the risk of miscalculation” and maintaining stability in the South China Sea.

The meeting on the sidelines of the Asean foreign ministers’ gathering marked the first formal talks between the top diplomats since Maria Theresa Lazaro assumed office in July last year.

It also came days after fresh tensions in the disputed waters, with Chinese coastguard and Philippine Navy vessels clashing on Monday near the Second Thomas Shoal, the first serious maritime encounter in months between the rival claimants.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met his Philippine counterpart in Manila on Wednesday, with both sides highlighting the need for “reducing the risk of miscalculation” and maintaining stability in the South China Sea.

The meeting on the sidelines of the Asean foreign ministers’ gathering marked the first formal talks between the top diplomats since Maria Theresa Lazaro assumed office in July last year.

It also came days after fresh tensions in the disputed waters, with Chinese coastguard and Philippine Navy vessels clashing on Monday near the Second Thomas Shoal, the first serious maritime encounter in months between the rival claimants.

The Philippine foreign ministry described Wednesday’s meeting between Wang and Lazaro as “candid, comprehensive and constructive”.

“The two sides underscored the importance of maintaining peace, security, and stability in the region, reducing the risk of miscalculation, and sustaining dialogue on matters of mutual concern,” it said in a read-out.

The talks covered a wide range of topics, including maritime disputes, security, law enforcement, trade and investment cooperation as well as tourism and regional issues, according to the ministry.

It said Lazaro reiterated Manila’s protest against “violent actions” by China Coast Guard personnel near the Second Thomas Shoal, known as Renai Jiao in China and Ayungin Shoal in the Philippines.

She also reaffirmed the Philippines’ position on the maritime dispute and raised concerns over Chinese actions that “have infringed on the maritime rights and entitlements, including incidents affecting the safety of Filipino personnel and fishermen”.

Beijing has accused the Philippines of instigating Monday’s incident by sending small rubber boats to approach its coastguard vessel, while Manila says one of its navy personnel was struck on the head with a wooden baton.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr summoned the Chinese ambassador on Tuesday, condemning the incident as a matter of national security.

Hours earlier, the Philippine envoy in Beijing had been summoned by the Chinese foreign ministry, which accused Manila of provocation.

The Wang-Lazaro meeting also came days after a diplomatic row over a Chinese state media video mocking the 10th anniversary of a South China Sea arbitral ruling favouring Manila.

The video, published by China Daily on July 10, showed a monkey dressed in traditional Philippine attire being manipulated by figures representing the United States and Japan before being blasted by water cannon, something China has been alleged to have deployed against Philippine vessels in contested waters.

Manila strongly condemned the depiction as racist propaganda and lodged a formal diplomatic protest.

Beijing distanced itself from the video, saying it did not represent an official position, while asserting its territorial claims.

Lazaro raised the issue with Wang, according to her ministry.

“Disagreements over legal and political issues do not justify resorting to disturbing imagery,” she was quoted as saying.

She also described the video as “deeply offensive, distressing, and unacceptable”.

“The Philippines emphasised the need to exercise restraint, avoid actions that increase tensions, and resolve disputes peacefully in accordance with international law, particularly the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and the 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award,” the read-out said.

Lazaro also reiterated Manila’s one-China policy, it added.

Additionally, both sides underscored the importance of “maintaining open channels of communication, enhancing mutual understanding, and strengthening confidence-building measures”.

According to the read-out, both foreign ministers highlighted progress on the South China Sea Code of Conduct and reaffirmed their commitment to wrapping up related negotiations this year.

The Philippines is this year’s rotating chair of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Manila is hosting regional ministers this week for discussions on regional flashpoints ranging from the South China Sea to Myanmar and the economic impact of the Middle East conflict.

In separate meetings on Monday with Asean Secretary General Kao Kim Hourn of Cambodia and Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan, Wang emphasised that maritime disputes should not derail ties and called for joint efforts to exclude perceived external meddling.

During his talks with Kao, Wang described the South China Sea as a shared home for regional countries while hailing Beijing as “the most important anchor of stability in the region”.

“Certain forces within the Philippine military and maritime law enforcement ranks have deliberately provoked incidents in the South China Sea to serve the interests of external forces, undermining the process of improving China-Philippines relations as well as peace and stability in the South China Sea,” Wang told Kao.

On July 12, the Philippines marked the anniversary of the 2016 arbitral ruling with a joint statement alongside the US, Japan and 11 other nations. Beijing denounced the declaration as “a distortion of facts and an act of vilification against China”.

The Wang-Lazaro meeting would be significant, Asean spokesman Dominic Xavier Imperial of the Philippine foreign ministry had said on Monday, noting it would cover not only bilateral relations but also regional issues.

“We believe that this engagement is very important because not only will it address … the bilateral relations between the Philippines and China, but it will also have something to do with … the impact of what’s happening globally to the region, to Asean,” he said, according to the Manila Bulletin.

Imperial added that negotiations on the South China Sea code of conduct, ongoing for nearly 17 years, would “always be part of the discussions” during both bilateral and Asean meetings.

In 2023, Asean and China agreed to speed up talks with the goal of concluding the agreement within three years, but progress has been slow as both sides still dispute the legal basis of Beijing’s claims in the strategic waterway.

Despite expanding trade and Chinese investment in the Philippines, the South China Sea dispute remains central to their relations, which have fluctuated between tension and engagement since Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr took office four years ago.

Encounters between Chinese coastguard vessels and Philippine ships have become more frequent, particularly around Scarborough Shoal and Second Thomas Shoal, over which Beijing asserts “indisputable sovereignty” alongside much of the South China Sea.

While China sees Asean as a critical arena to push back against what it considers “external interference” led by the US and Japan, the Philippines has hardened its stance in recent months, accusing the Chinese of aggressive manoeuvres.

Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr, sanctioned by Beijing last month over “erroneous remarks”, has asserted that the Philippines is justified in avoiding defence engagements with China.

Manila has strengthened military ties with the US, Japan and their allies over the years, while maintaining bilateral channels with Beijing to manage disputes and avoid escalation.

Both sides have also kept communication channels open, despite frequent clashes and maritime incidents.

During a working-level dialogue in Manila on June 30, Liu Jinsong, director general of the Chinese foreign ministry’s Asian affairs department, urged the Philippines to “honour its commitments and match words with deeds”, while expressing “serious concerns” over what Beijing saw as negative moves.

Philippine officials at the meeting, led by Marshall Louis Alferez of the foreign ministry, reaffirmed a commitment to dialogue and the one-China principle, while expressing a readiness to manage disputes constructively and avoid unintended incidents.

Philippine read-outs described the talks as building on earlier bilateral sessions this year in Cebu, Beijing and Quanzhou, where officials discussed South China Sea issues, provisional arrangements to reduce incidents during resupply missions and potential practical cooperation.

item.title: [SCMP] Wang Yi and Marco Rubio at Asean discuss Xi’s planned US visit, South China Sea clash
item.description:
The Chinese president’s planned trip to the US and the Beijing-Manila South China Sea dispute led the agenda when the top Chinese and American diplomats met in the Philippines on Wednesday.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met in the Philippine capital, Manila, for 90 minutes of talks on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations foreign ministers’ meeting, which ends on Thursday.

According to a readout published by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, Wang described the meeting as “pragmatic, positive and constructive”, and urged both sides to pursue “strategic stability” and “peaceful coexistence”.
item.content:encoded:
The Chinese president’s planned trip to the US and the Beijing-Manila South China Sea dispute led the agenda when the top Chinese and American diplomats met in the Philippines on Wednesday.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met in the Philippine capital, Manila, for 90 minutes of talks on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations foreign ministers’ meeting, which ends on Thursday.

According to a readout published by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, Wang described the meeting as “pragmatic, positive and constructive”, and urged both sides to pursue “strategic stability” and “peaceful coexistence”.

Without explicitly mentioning the issue, Wang said he had conveyed China’s position on the “recent series of negative words and actions by the US” and called on Washington to respect China’s core interests.

“Our responsibility now is to follow the path set by the two heads of state, eliminate interference and overcome obstacles, and ensure that the consensus reached by the leaders is translated into consensus and action across the entire government and all sectors,” Wang was quoted as saying.

Rubio also said there were still differences between the two countries but that their job was to manage them.

He added that there were areas of potential cooperation, and they discussed President Xi Jinping’s planned trip to the US, according to Reuters.

“The work we need to do now [for] September is to identify what those areas are, so that we can lay the groundwork for a very positive visit … we talked a lot about that,” Rubio said.

He described Monday’s clash between Beijing and Manila over Second Thomas Shoal as very negative and benefiting no one.

When asked about the progress of arms sales to Taiwan – a sensitive subject at the China-US summit in May – Rubio said they were still under internal review because Washington had to take its own stockpile and availability into consideration.

“There is a huge effort on our part to restart a definite defence industrial base and restart its ability to produce,” he said.

Washington is reviewing a US$14 billion weapons package to the island and has not yet formally submitted the proposed sale to Congress, with the delay attributed to production capacity and ammunition reserves.

After his trip to Beijing in May, US President Donald Trump said that holding off on the package could be a “negotiating chip”.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary.

Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

On the subject of America’s conflict with Iran, Rubio described China as in some ways cooperative with the US.

“One thing in particular is that they have been pretty clear that they don’t support any tolling or restrictions on global shipping through international waterways,” he said of China.

Before Rubio’s trip to Manila, the US State Department said the visit was meant to advance “a clear US priority: a free and open Indo-Pacific that delivers safety, security and prosperity for the region and for the American people”.

The diplomatic engagement comes as a rekindled US-Iran war puts Southeast Asian economies under intense economic and energy strain, and follows Washington’s allegations of Chinese electoral interference in the 2020 presidential election.

In a prime-time speech last week, Trump accused China of meddling in US elections, alleging it obtained 220 million American voter records beginning in the 2020 election cycle for “the largest compromise of election data in history”.

Beijing firmly rejected the accusation on Friday.

On Wednesday, Rubio said the allegations of election interference were not discussed in his meeting with Wang.

He also said the state of China-Japan ties was “troubling”, and that deep cooperation between Washington and Tokyo would continue.

Wang and Rubio last spoke in early July in what both sides described as a “positive and constructive” phone call. It was the first reported cabinet-level communication since Trump’s state visit in May.

The dialogue is a critical follow-up to the summit in which both countries pledged to establish a “new vision of building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability”, with Beijing committed to buying more planes, agricultural produce and energy products.

The rival powers are in a fragile trade truce reached by Xi and Trump in October last year and are trying to manage risks and stabilise ties to avert a total decoupling.

But their underlying tensions and rivalry – such as on critical supply chains and advanced technology – remain unchanged.

China has increasingly said it calls for managed competition rather than confrontation, while avoiding major concessions on issues over trade or Taiwan.

Meanwhile, on Friday, the US did not renew a national emergency declaration over Hong Kong and lifted sanctions on nine government officials from Hong Kong and mainland China.

The move was welcomed in Beijing, which described Washington’s decision as “an important step in fulfilling the consensus reached in bilateral talks”.

On Tuesday, Trump signalled that Washington would confront Beijing over the alleged interference but played down the prospect of retaliation.

“We’re going to talk to them about it,” Trump said, adding that the alleged interference “took place a long time ago” and that China might be “a little bit different today than it was then”.

“They do things to us and we do things to them,” he said. “I’ll be honest, we do things to them too. It’s not a one-way street, but we’ll be talking to them.”

Both sides have indicated that Xi’s planned visit remains on track.

On Sunday, before heading to Manila, Rubio said Xi’s trip was still expected to happen in September.

And on Monday, China’s foreign ministry said that both sides had kept in contact on the arrangements for the heads of states’ interactions later this year.

“We anticipate that the trip is happening in September. They’ve continued to send over their teams to prepare for it, and I’ve heard nothing otherwise,” Rubio said.

item.title: [SCMP] Discover India’s ‘last village’: a hub of Balti culture on the Pakistan border
item.description:
An inky darkness blankets the road as I step out of the car. I blink to get my bearings, the silhouettes of trees slowly forming beneath a startling canopy of stars.

“Sorry to make you walk in the dark, but this is a shortcut,” says Rashidullah Khan, our companion and guide for the evening. He leads the way up through the trees, our phone torches illuminating pebbled, muddy slopes.

After 10 minutes, we reach a narrow lane flanked by stone walls punctuated with wooden doors. A sculpture of a large bird perches above one doorway, an unassuming entrance to what a sign identifies as the Yabgo Palace Turtuk. Inside the central courtyard of the wooden building, intricately carved upper balconies appear in the candlelight, plush bolster cushions and low tables clustered below: the setting for dinner with Turtuk’s king.
item.content:encoded:
An inky darkness blankets the road as I step out of the car. I blink to get my bearings, the silhouettes of trees slowly forming beneath a startling canopy of stars.

“Sorry to make you walk in the dark, but this is a shortcut,” says Rashidullah Khan, our companion and guide for the evening. He leads the way up through the trees, our phone torches illuminating pebbled, muddy slopes.

After 10 minutes, we reach a narrow lane flanked by stone walls punctuated with wooden doors. A sculpture of a large bird perches above one doorway, an unassuming entrance to what a sign identifies as the Yabgo Palace Turtuk. Inside the central courtyard of the wooden building, intricately carved upper balconies appear in the candlelight, plush bolster cushions and low tables clustered below: the setting for dinner with Turtuk’s king.

I am in the “last village” of northern India, a few kilometres from the Pakistan border. Living in a corner of the Ladakh desert – India’s northernmost region, known for its stark and arresting landscape – the villagers of Turtuk, Thang, Tyakshi and Chalunka consider themselves part of Baltistan, but flipped nationality overnight, after the 1971 Indo-Pakistani war. Families were split as the now Indian villages were separated from the larger Balti population on the other side of the border.

Until 2010, this sensitive area was closed to outsiders. Now, through tourism, residents are gently asserting their Balti identity, eager to share their heritage with the wider world.

Turtuk is deliciously lush, rich with apple and apricot orchards and green buckwheat fields, cut through by the icy blue Shyok River. At around 3,000 metres (9,843 feet), it sits at a relatively low elevation within Ladakh, but during the first few days anywhere in the area, the altitude makes activity strenuous.

My journey begins in Leh (around 3,500 metres/11,483 feet), Ladakh’s capital, where the air is palpably thin and, initially, a heavy head and breathlessness are common after even gentle walking. To prevent altitude sickness, visitors must acclimatise here for a couple of days before travelling onwards. Non-residents require a permit to travel beyond Leh – Inner Line Permits for Indians and Protected Area Permits for foreigners – which can be applied for in advance, or obtained through Leh travel agents, the process taking between 24 and 48 hours.

I spend my first day resting, hydrating and gazing at the purple mountains from the window of my room at The Pal Hotel. A brief stroll to Leh market reveals that the crowds weaving around and through the souvenir shops and cafes serving cakes and steaming momos – Tibetan dumplings filled with meat or vegetables – are larger than usual, in anticipation of the visiting Dalai Lama’s public address the following day.

Leh is more than a pit stop in which to, literally, catch your breath. It’s an introduction to the region’s history and culture, the Buddhist leanings visible in fluttering prayer flags and a landscape dotted with monasteries. The world’s highest peace pagoda, the white-domed Shanti Stupa, spans two circular levels filled with reliefs depicting the life of the Buddha and offers panoramic views of Leh and the surrounding mountains.

Twenty kilometres (12 miles) away, the stupas, paintings and statues of the 15th century Thiksey Monastery, one of the largest in the area, amount to a treasure trove of Buddhist art. Some visitors circle and prostrate themselves before a 15-metre-high (49-feet-high) Maitreya Buddha, a bodhisattva believed to be a future Buddha; others sit in quiet contemplation.

Juxtaposed against these peaceful symbols are stark reminders of conflict. Ladakh remains heavily militarised, having been the site of clashes between India and Pakistan or China. Leh’s Hall of Fame museum and memorial has displays on the 1999 Kargil war; Ladakhi culture; soldiers’ personal memorabilia; and the challenges of high-altitude warfare, as well as life in general.

From Leh, the drive to Turtuk winds through constantly changing landscapes – rugged peaks marbled with purple, gold and rust stripes; sandy deserts; the lush, boulder-strewn river plains sliced through by the Shyok; and the dizzying Khardung La pass, at around 5,400 metres (17,717 feet), before finally descending into the Shyok Valley.

“The Himalayan region of Baltistan, famously known as Gilgit-Baltistan, was on the Silk Route,” says Turtuk’s king, Yabgo Mohammad Khan Kacho, at dinner. “Some of the world’s highest peaks – Karakoram one and two [K1 and K2] – and prominent glaciers like Baltoro and Siachen are here [on the Pakistani side of the border].” Pakistani Baltistan is often known as “Little Tibet” due to its alpine scenery.

His title is unofficial but Kacho is a direct descendant of the Yabgo dynasty, Baltistan’s rulers for 2,000 years.

Wearing an elegant cream shuqa – a traditional men’s woollen overcoat – embroidered with flowers, and an ivory and gold turban, his soft yet clear voice floats gently through the courtyard, as he recounts Baltistan’s tumultuous history with invaders, including Genghis Khan (in the 13th century) and Alexander the Great (in the 4th century; although historians doubt either made it this far). We talk over a traditional Balti meal: buckwheat crepes with tangy yogurt and spinach dip; baleh, a buckwheat noodle, thyme and vegetable soup; and meat dumplings with a punchy chilli oil.

“We still eat many of our traditional dishes,” says Kacho, although his son says he prefers a less carbohydrate-heavy, more protein-rich diet, to better suit his gym regimen.

The 14th century wooden palace doubles as Kacho’s residence and a museum. Weapons, maps and artefacts showcase Balti history while Buddhist and Islamic art reflect the region’s mixed heritage.

Like most of his “subjects”, Kacho was separated from family in 1971.

“My sisters and cousins are in Pakistan. My riyasat [princely state] is there,” he says.

This division becomes tangible in nearby Thang, where Indian visitors (Thang is off-limits to non-Indians) can view the Line of Control between their country and Pakistan. Guide Rukiya Bano directs my gaze through binoculars, pointing out which mountains and bunkers are Indian and which are Pakistani. Her finger points to fields across the river: “That is Pakistan.” It is just 2km (1.2 miles) away yet feels much more distant for the residents of these four villages, as getting a visa to visit relatives is challenging.

Thang is home to botanist Mohammed Ali Bari, known as Goba Ali, whose colourful house overflows into a flourishing garden. Ali was five years old when he was separated from his parents.

“During the 1971 war, many feared the consequences if our village was captured. So, the women and most children went to hide a little further away. My grandfather, brother and I stayed,” says Ali, offering me grapes and dried apricots. When the war was over, the border was redrawn in haste, and those in hiding on that fateful December night were stranded on the wrong side of the new divide.

Ali speaks gratefully of the Indian Army for having raised him and his brother, a childhood with no formal education and a tent in a soldiers’ camp for a home. “They would dress me in red and take me to a spot where my parents could see me through binoculars from across the border and know that I was all right.”

In 2014, he was granted permission to visit his family in Pakistan, reuniting with them for 10 months. Photos from that trip hang in a small museum in his home and include one of Ali resting his head on his mother’s shoulder, household items and work tools in the background representing Balti culture. This separation from their larger community has made it difficult for many of the villagers to piece together their heritage. It took Rashidullah Khan seven years and several conversations with family in Pakistan to replicate the design of a traditional palace in his 12-room boutique hotel, Virsa Baltistan, in Turtuk.

“Virsa is the dream of a boy who grew up in this war-torn area, with very little money. This was intended to be more than a hotel, but a representation of Balti culture and identity,” says Khan.

The structure, with intricately carved windows and balconies, was created by 200 local woodcarvers, blacksmiths and stonemasons using riverbed mud, timber and hand-carved wood. Guest experiences include visits to traditional weavers, potters and metalworkers, and a five-course Balti tasting menu prepared by local women.

Under apricot trees, Zainab didi (“older sister”, a term used to address elder women in India) makes buckwheat crepes on a griddle while Khan plates each course: kisirnarang-thur, crepes cut into thin strips and a dollop of tangy yogurt dip placed on a leaf; praku, a thumb-pinched pasta cloaked in walnut sauce; and phading, a dessert of boiled apricots, apricot kernels and basil leaves shaped into a sticky caramelised square.

“These ladies think that my plating and portions are stingy,” laughs Khan. “I explain a tasting menu to them, but they believe food should be served generously and eaten with the hands to enjoy it.”

Finding hospitality professionals in this remote area is challenging and Khan has trained former mechanics and clerks, valuing their willingness to learn and cultural knowledge over industry experience.

“Involving the community is an integral part of Virsa,” he says.

Evenings bring music and dance to the hotel’s orchard – drummers and woodwind players accompany performers re-enacting Balti legends with swirling swords and athletic leaps.

Music plays an integral role in another Balti tradition: polo.

This free-spirited, rougher version of the game is accompanied by live instruments, the horses trained to musical cues.

Unfortunately, no game is scheduled for when I’m visiting, but while passing a pitch – sandy, uneven ground, with fading lines demarcating the goals – it’s easy to imagine how boisterous it gets when two teams of six players jostle on such a narrow strip, the first to score 10 goals being the winners. The prize is meat, sometimes a goat or sheep. Although a trophy is a recent addition, celebratory “goat parties” are still popular.

The four villages have eight teams, competing in tournaments for a few weeks starting at Navroze (the Persian New Year, in late March, which also signals the arrival of spring) and later, in July or August.

“We also hope to take the game beyond Turtuk, and represent Baltistan in national tournaments,” says Nassir Hussain, a player on Khan’s Virsa team.

Ordinarily, visitors en route to the border have stopped in Turtuk only to eat lunch at its riverside cafes. But with more guest houses, homestays and camping facilities now available, villagers are encouraging tourists to stay for longer, to fully experience what the area has to offer.

A steep but short hike to the Turtuk Monastery is rewarded with sweeping views over mountains, river, fields and a cascading cemetery.

Within the village, a 140-year-old home has been converted into the Balti Heritage Museum, with a display of utensils and traditional clothes: well-worn, rugged, functional-looking items made from animal skin and fur, for warmth; loose trousers of coarse cloth; fur-lined coats and tunics in cream, beige and rust hues. Among the fancier robes are shuqa in cream accented with bright embroidered flowers.

The house was built using traditional construction techniques – interlocked wooden and stone structures that serve as pillars, reinforced timber lacings and a half-timbering method – to protect against earthquakes and provide insulation in the extreme cold of winter. The pillars and doorframes are intricately carved with Buddhist and Bon (an ancient spiritual tradition that predates Buddhism and Islam in the region) motifs: left-facing swastikas, or yungdrung; florals; and knots of eternal loops, weaving back into each other.

Nearby is a centuries-old nangchung, meaning “cold house”, one of eight in the area. These bunkers were built in such a way that cool mountain air could circulate through gaps between the stones. Before electricity and fridges arrived in Turtuk, these served as communal stores for perishable food.

Elsewhere, the Bunker of Memories recalls the region’s history as a war zone. Used by the Ashoor family (the nearby Balti Heritage Museum is their ancestral home) during the Kargil war, the sturdy underground stone shelter displays military detritus, several pieces repurposed as utilitarian objects: jerrycans as water carriers and thaps – traditional stoves; ammunition boxes as safes; and rocket shells as butter churners.

It’s a sobering space, and a reminder of the resilience shown by Baltis in challenging conditions.

Later, while sipping on apricot juice with nutty kernels bobbing on top at The Balti Kitchen restaurant, Abdul Rashid Khan, Rashidullah’s father, recalls the dust and rubble during the 1999 war. “It was scary, and several people retreated from the village. I chose to stay home. When it was over, the calm and silence were disorienting,” says the jovial, soft-spoken man, who now runs a speciality store selling jams, nuts, dried apricots, oils and other local products.

“Before 1971, there was a smaller population, and few schools. Now there are more schools and girls are educated.”

A balancing of gender roles is also evident in the visibility of women in tourist businesses, noticeably at a cafe managed by the Women’s Empowerment and Welfare Association and at The Balti Kitchen, which is run by Khan’s sister and set on an open wooden platform amid organic flower and vegetable gardens. The menu lists specialities such as tsapon, home-baked bread toasted in white butter, onion and spices; squu, a potato, barley, pea and Himalayan herb stew; and kambo kushu, apple-flavoured cookies topped with mulberries and chocolate syrup.

Outside tourism, there is an ambition among the villagers to showcase their identity beyond Turtuk, whether through representing Baltistan in national polo tournaments or taking part in Khan’s plans to launch a Balti design label with local artisans. This aspiration represents preservation and renewal for a community whose identity has been defined by borders, and is now eager to move beyond those restrictions.

item.title: [SCMP] The mystery of one man’s fortress in Longgang
item.description:
On the northeastern fringes of Shenzhen, standing among the low-rise tile houses of Longgang district, is a monolith that refuses to explain itself.

Erected during the late 1970s and 80s, the seven-storey building towers over the market town, a monument to something known only to its long-gone creator. Vegetation grows wild on the roof. Iron fencing and rusty cages crown its top. At night, it stands unlit; by day, its bare concrete facade looms over the narrow surrounding streets with the air of a wartime watchtower, attracting young explorers who ride Shenzhen’s Metro Line 3 to Shuanglong station, crossing the city just to see “Longgang’s Weird Building” for themselves.

A glance at the near-windowless exterior provides only hints of the man behind the Weird Building: Wen Yaoguang, a Longgang native who appears to have made his fortune in Hong Kong.
item.content:encoded:
On the northeastern fringes of Shenzhen, standing among the low-rise tile houses of Longgang district, is a monolith that refuses to explain itself.

Erected during the late 1970s and 80s, the seven-storey building towers over the market town, a monument to something known only to its long-gone creator. Vegetation grows wild on the roof. Iron fencing and rusty cages crown its top. At night, it stands unlit; by day, its bare concrete facade looms over the narrow surrounding streets with the air of a wartime watchtower, attracting young explorers who ride Shenzhen’s Metro Line 3 to Shuanglong station, crossing the city just to see “Longgang’s Weird Building” for themselves.

A glance at the near-windowless exterior provides only hints of the man behind the Weird Building: Wen Yaoguang, a Longgang native who appears to have made his fortune in Hong Kong.

What is known of Wen’s life has been pieced together through oral accounts from neighbours, local lore passed between households and recounted to inquisitive visitors. As filmmaker Zhang Shengjia discovered while conducting research for his 2025 documentary, The Haunted Folk Fortress, Wen was, seemingly, an ordinary man driven by an extraordinary vision.

It is thought that Wen was born in Longgang and, sometime before World War II, crossed into Hong Kong, where he found work as a seafarer and later took over some farmland. He lived in Hong Kong through the Japanese occupation (1941-1945). During the city’s economic boom in the 60s, he is said to have received a sizeable land-requisition payout. After 1978, when mainland China began to open up under Deng Xiaoping, Wen returned to Longgang with his fortune and began to build.

Although it has never formally been opened to the public, the curious have found their way inside the Weird Building over the years. Their online accounts and footage – available through a virtual-reality tour – offer further understanding of its interior.

Longgang’s Weird Building is remarkably compact, with a footprint of roughly 36 square metres. Pass through the front entrance grilles and you are met with steep stairways leading both down to a dark, now-flooded basement and up to a small living area and kitchen.

Wen devised alternating-tread stairs as a space-saving solution; left and right feet land on separate, staggered steps, halving the width of each staircase. Throughout the property, staircases are adapted to their particular location; some veer off at unlikely angles, while others do not resemble conventional staircases at all.

Despite the building appearing to have few windows, much of the interior is well-lit and the upper floors offer panoramic views. What looks from the outside like solid concrete is, on one facade, in fact sheets of stainless steel punched with holes measuring roughly 5mm across.

Cast-in-place concrete furnishings are embedded into the structure of the third floor and most of the fourth floor is given over to bathtubs and water tanks, the purpose of which is unknown.

There may be as many as 20 bathtubs and eight toilets in the building, estimates Feng Guochan, executive chief architect at the Shenzhen General Institute of Architectural Design and Research, who had been allowed access by the local government to survey the building. Precise counts are difficult given the non-linear floor plans, says Feng.

The rooftop terrace, with its pavilion, is believed to have once served as a garden.

Rather than bricks or prefabricated blocks, Wen chose to pour everything – walls, floors, curved concrete benches arranged around tables – in situ.

“Choosing this approach is quite a challenge,” says Feng. Cast-in-place concrete requires a lot of formwork and carries the risk of blowouts, where wet material bursts through moulds. “And it’s very slow.”

That may explain why the building took more than a decade to complete but the permanence of concrete is perhaps the point, as the furniture is the building, fused with the structure. “When primitive people lived inside caves, they organised their lives according to the contours of the cave,” says Feng. “Instead of this being imposed by nature, [here] it occurs through one’s own thinking.”

In many ways, Longgang’s Weird Building echoes the qualities of Chinese vernacular defensive architecture, examples of which include the Kaiping diaolou of Guangdong province (fortress-like residences bearing elements of Western architectural traditions built by Chinese who returned from overseas in the 20s and 30s) and the Hakka paolou (fortified watchtowers erected on the peripheries of walled villages in Shenzhen).

Structures built by returnees “often reflect what the owner experienced abroad”, Zhang tells me. “As [this] owner was once a seafarer, the interior of the Weird Building not only reflects this experience at sea – with cabin-like spatial layouts – but continues the functional traditions of diaolou. It has massive water tanks, plots for raising chickens and growing vegetables – all built for self-sufficiency in a crisis.”

While the rest of China was opening up, Wen seemed to want to seal himself off, “like he was preparing for the end of the world”, says Feng.

In Zhang’s documentary, one local resident recalls Wen sitting under a banyan tree on a street corner, contemplating how his building could be modified: “I believe he is much like those of us who enjoy creative work – he is an artist and architect, and he possessed enough passion to persevere with the construction.”

Wen was probably also inspired by feng shui, says Zhang: “It’s rumoured that a feng shui master advised him to keep building to ward off bad luck, and there was definitely some consideration to feng shui principles indoors, too.”

Whatever the inspiration, the idiosyncratic construction has spatial complexity. Floors of differing heights flow into one another and bring to mind Austrian architect Adolf Loos’ Raumplan concept, which conceives of a building as an intertwined three-dimensional puzzle.

Feng describes the structure as resembling a Chinese puzzle lock – each space interlacing with the next, with no continuous floors. It is unlikely that Wen encountered Loos’ work, but the parallels are striking.

“I suspect he never used a floor plan to build this house, because it’s impossible to draw one,” says Feng.

As with Raumplan designs, Wen’s bland facade conceals lavish interiors. The upper floors are adorned with ceramic-tile paintings of Guilin scenery, portraits of women, scenes from traditional Chinese opera and aluminium panelling bearing images copied from the Louvre museum in Paris, France. Wen decorated an entire room with tiles inscribed with moral teachings rendered in calligraphy that were bought in Qingyuan, Guangdong. “In the traditional framework of the diaolou, Wen built a rather hedonistic interior, and you can see that from the design and the structure of the space, centred entirely around his life,” says Gu Ling, a curator who hosted a screening and panel discussion of Zhang’s documentary in February. “There were a lot of these so-called artwork or decorative pieces, and they were all rather valuable.”

Wen had his own way of doing things, adds Feng. “This person is simply someone who’s broken away from the ordinary, who’s always courageously pursuing his own self.”

Feng believes that the Weird Building was possible only because of the times in which it was constructed: after reform and opening up had begun but before a series of regulations introduced between 1982 and the 1990s placed restrictions on urban land ownership and construction.

“It’s a self-built home from a unique era, and the fact that it’s a self-built home within an urban setting makes it such a rare specimen,” he says. “There will never be another Weird Building. You need the right conditions for it to emerge, and currently, those conditions don’t exist.”

The fascination with Longgang’s Weird Building is part of a broader impulse among young Chinese, particularly in the Greater Bay Area, to seek out and document local history before it is swallowed by development and forgotten.

As people who have known eccentrics such as Wen, Zhang Suying, who built a castle out of scavenged material in Longnan city, Gansu province, and Yang San-er, who took 18 years to build a unique timber-framed house in Pingtung, Taiwan, grow elderly, oral histories are becoming increasingly hard to find. The Haunted Folk Fortress is Zhang’s attempt to decrypt Wen’s story before it is lost to time, but his quest has been challenging and his attempts to track down archival footage have proved largely futile: Hong Kong’s ATV filmed the Weird Building but the broadcaster went bankrupt and it’s not clear how its archive can be accessed; TVB also covered it but declined to share the material. Nothing of Wen’s life in the city surfaced in Hong Kong’s public records, either.

It is thought that Wen died around 2000 and, at some point after his death, his family sold the building to a developer that subdivided it into rental units. Online, Zhang found dozens of mentions by people who claim to have lived in the Weird Building or met the owner – but none responded to his requests for an interview.

One key interviewee among the local residents who would talk to Zhang was the father of his cinematographer, who used to haul sand and cement to what was then just a construction site and spoke at length about the man behind the architectural anomaly: “People all said the same thing – that he was strange. Before reform and opening up, there weren’t even buildings taller than three floors. So when he built that big house, everyone thought, ‘Wow, this guy must be really rich to build something like that.’”

Other interviewees speak of construction methods and materials, including green ceramic tiles that were imported from Hong Kong. Their recollections form the backbone of the film, the final version of which remains a work in progress.

It is pure luck that Wen’s structural legacy still stands. In 2013, when local authorities gazetted a nearby Hakka walled village as intangible cultural heritage, the Weird Building happened to fall within its radius of protection.

“Without it, the Weird Building would be gone,” says Gu.

However, “a certain level of conservation is required, since the building has a unique character; the government hopes to develop the entire area, including the Weird Building, and carry out restoration work”. Unfortunately, those plans have been put on hold due to a lack of funds amid a downturn in the mainland property market.

For Feng, who has studied the building for more than a decade, what endures is something more personal than architectural history: “I see a freedom in this old man that I kind of envy. He pursued his own spiritual world, and sensitively expressed his desires.

“People should be able to express themselves through their space.”

item.title: [SCMP] Only in Hangzhou: Hang Lung’s new Westlake 66 complex blends hi-tech and history
item.description:
Hangzhou is a city of contradictions. It is home to West Lake, a Unesco World Heritage site that has inspired poets and painters for more than 1,000 years, since at least the Tang dynasty (AD618-907). It is also the birthplace of Alibaba (owner of the South China Morning Post) and a growing centre of artificial intelligence and robotics, thanks to Zhejiang University’s engineering pipeline and a local government that offers subsidies, low-cost rentals and a hands-off approach, creating an ecosystem that has made the city a natural home for companies such as DeepSeek and Unitree Robotics.

One of the seven ancient capitals of China – once praised by Marco Polo as the “city of heaven” – is now one of the country’s most dynamic tech hubs. Building something that honours Hangzhou’s multilayered identity is no small feat, but that is exactly the opportunity the creative minds behind Westlake 66, Hang Lung Properties’ newest mixed-use development, in the Wulin Central Business District, saw in the project.

“Hangzhou is one of the most incredible cities I’ve ever experienced,” says Jeffrey Kenoff, FAIA, design principal at Kohn Pedersen Fox (KPF) architectural firm. “It’s a city with centuries of history, yet being reinvented by Alibaba and its peers as a kind of ‘Silicon Valley of Asia’. Westlake 66 gave us a chance to rethink office, hospitality and retail for a new generation.”
item.content:encoded:
Hangzhou is a city of contradictions. It is home to West Lake, a Unesco World Heritage site that has inspired poets and painters for more than 1,000 years, since at least the Tang dynasty (AD618-907). It is also the birthplace of Alibaba (owner of the South China Morning Post) and a growing centre of artificial intelligence and robotics, thanks to Zhejiang University’s engineering pipeline and a local government that offers subsidies, low-cost rentals and a hands-off approach, creating an ecosystem that has made the city a natural home for companies such as DeepSeek and Unitree Robotics.

One of the seven ancient capitals of China – once praised by Marco Polo as the “city of heaven” – is now one of the country’s most dynamic tech hubs. Building something that honours Hangzhou’s multilayered identity is no small feat, but that is exactly the opportunity the creative minds behind Westlake 66, Hang Lung Properties’ newest mixed-use development, in the Wulin Central Business District, saw in the project.

“Hangzhou is one of the most incredible cities I’ve ever experienced,” says Jeffrey Kenoff, FAIA, design principal at Kohn Pedersen Fox (KPF) architectural firm. “It’s a city with centuries of history, yet being reinvented by Alibaba and its peers as a kind of ‘Silicon Valley of Asia’. Westlake 66 gave us a chance to rethink office, hospitality and retail for a new generation.”

All of this enthusiasm reflects a deeper shift that has reshaped Hangzhou, propelled by the “Six Little Dragons” – Game Science, DeepSeek, Unitree Robotics, Deep Robotics, BrainCo and Manycore Tech – setting up operations in the city. With a population of 12.62 million, according to a 2024 census, including a growing number of AI and tech workers, Hangzhou has a pressing need for spaces where people can connect, collaborate and unwind beyond the office. It calls for a different approach from the one that has shaped many American cities, and one that New York-based KPF was keen to explore.

“A lot of modern [American] cities developed in the 1980s and 90s were leaning towards more efficiency,” says Kenoff, describing them as “single‑use districts: all residential, all office, all shopping. People were driving on highways back and forth from destination A to destination B”.

In his view, that obsession with efficiency hollowed out a sense of community, something China is trying to rebuild by looking to “reinvent the way that people actually occupy public space”.

For KPF, that meant rejecting the generic glass-and-steel monument that “ticked all the boxes” – they wanted a building “that couldn’t exist anywhere else”. So, they turned to Hangzhou itself for guidance.

Hangzhou’s geography was the obvious place to start. Westlake 66 occupies a unique position midway between the Grand Canal and West Lake, creating a natural pathway between the two landmarks. “What dawned on us was to lean into that seclusion. Rather than thinking about ‘architecture as building’, it was really more about ‘architecture as landscape’,” Kenoff explains, adding that his team drew inspiration from Huang Gongwang’s famed 14th century shanshui painting, Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains, translating its layered, terraced landscapes into the project’s stepped towers and sky park. Its design allows light to filter down to street level, while the site’s location informed a vision of the complex as a green valley rather than an isolated block.

Reverence for the city’s natural landscape carried over into the project’s sustainability ambitions. “It had to be conceived with nature at its centre,” says Kenoff, adding that the building received LEED Platinum, China Green Building Label 3-Star and WELL Platinum certifications. “But the goal was not just to build a ‘green’ building. We wanted to create a space that encourages sustainable behaviour as well.”

Surrounded by metro stations, the complex promotes mass transit and reduces car dependency. It uses low-carbon concrete bricks – a first for commercial developments in mainland China and Hong Kong – and solar panels installed on rooftops. Its five towers, each with its own distinct design and height, bend and open in different ways to maximise light and breeze, reducing energy consumption throughout.

All of the architectural pieces are linked through “The Oasis”, a 10,000-plus square metre “urban sanctuary” that connects the shopping mall, office towers and upcoming hotel within a panoramic corridor. “It’s an invitation to meander,” Kenoff says. “I love architecture that pulls people in.”

Another element binding Westlake 66 together is a 550-metre-long facade of modular metal panels, lined with warm-toned, glazed terracotta to wrap the project’s various components – a nod to local traditional material and craft while lending the complex a textured, “human-scale” presence that glass towers often lack. Kenoff explains that the “terracotta materiality respects culture; the cell modularisation humanises scale. It breaks down such big buildings and makes them more pleasurable to walk along. Its fluidity echoes the West Lake experience”.

It also extends the project’s longevity. Kenoff cites “the time between conception and completion” as the biggest challenge with such buildings. “By the time they are built, there are a million changes. What you think is a store becomes a restaurant, and that means the facade is constantly being asked: should it be transparent glass, solid or mechanical for venting?” He posits that “the cell solves this common problem”.

Respect for Hangzhou’s heritage didn’t stop at the facade; the city’s time as the capital of the Southern Song dynasty (1127-1279), when commerce, art and scholarship thrived, was a rich source of inspiration, and the same local terracotta tradition caught the attention of James Pierce, senior director at the Oval Partnership, the retail interior design consultant for Westlake 66. “It inspired both the materiality and colours we used. For the interior, the team chose a muted palette, with soft, rich textures that reference period ceramics, but also West Lake.”

As visitors move through the space, from north to south, he adds, colours shift subtly from warm to cold, while materials and forms transition between metals, stone and marble. In the south atrium, blue tones conceptually evoke the lake itself.

Just like KPF, Pierce’s team made heritage central to their design narrative, but their approach extends to the visitor experience itself, as the goal was to create a place where history was felt, not just observed.

“Historically, the area [Baijingfang] was known as the ‘place of 100 wells’, where people gathered, drew water and socialised,” Pierce explains. “So, that idea became the foundation of our design. We created well-like forms that cut through the floor plates, bringing light through the space and giving it a powerful sense of immersion.”

The Oval Partnership carried that same thinking through to the lower level, where a gallery with glass flooring allows visitors to literally walk over the past, a fitting solution for a project that incorporates Song and Yuan dynasty relics in a 2,700 square metre in-mall exhibition hall. Explains Pierce, “It’s thought of as a functional space where the mall can host events; there have been catwalk shows, educational programmes and community gatherings. It’s really intended as a hub within a hub.”

For all its tributes to Hangzhou’s former existence, the Oval Partnership also embraced modern technology.

“In our relics area, a huge video screen will play the site’s history like a movie sequence,” Pierce says.

Hang Lung is also thinking beyond the site itself; the company has taken a lease on the neighbouring building to give Westlake 66 a front door on Wulin Square, with interconnected bridging levels. In the future, the existing 105,900 square metre retail area is expected to grow by another 40 per cent.

In a city that balances ancient heritage with futuristic ambition, Westlake 66 is designed for today and whatever comes next. If Hangzhou’s past is any indication, the best chapters are still being written.

item.title: [SCMP] A Vietnamese refugee returns to the Hong Kong island where echoes of a lost childhood remain
item.description:
“This is where my bed was.”

Katie Aung stands at the centre of Tai A Chau, an uninhabited island south of Lantau, with former marine police officer Les Bird, pointing to a spot on the ground.

“This is where I lived.” She turns slightly, and gestures again. “My bed faced this way. Head this end, feet down here. I lived right here for many years of my childhood.”
item.content:encoded:
“This is where my bed was.”

Katie Aung stands at the centre of Tai A Chau, an uninhabited island south of Lantau, with former marine police officer Les Bird, pointing to a spot on the ground.

“This is where I lived.” She turns slightly, and gestures again. “My bed faced this way. Head this end, feet down here. I lived right here for many years of my childhood.”

In the 1990s, it was to this 1.2 sq km speck of land in the South China Sea that Aung, a former Vietnamese refugee, was confined.

Tai A Chau today is almost entirely reclaimed by nature – a deserted outcrop. But its past as a detention centre remains etched into the landscape, lingering beneath the undergrowth: the concrete spine of a former camp cutting through the island, the foundations of village houses that once stood there – quiet, stubborn reminders of what once was. It is this past that Aung and Bird, who oversaw the search-and-rescue operations for tens of thousands of Vietnamese refugees in Hong Kong across three decades, have come to recall.

After disembarking at the old jetty of Tai A Chau, Aung walks inland with Bird. Along the way, they spot an ornate, rocky fish pond, built by other refugees who had once inhabited the island. Aung recognises it immediately; she and the other children would gather around its edge, watching the colourful fish that darted through the water.

Upon entering the main clearing of the island, Aung slows and looks around. Framed by hills on both sides, the space opens up before her, its present at odds with what it once held. Here is where she makes sense of her old sleeping quarters.

“We both stood there in silence for some time,” Bird says, recalling the visit he made with Aung in February. “Katie was lost in her memories in a moment that must have been pretty poignant for her.”

In the late 70s through to the 90s, waves of refugees fled Vietnam’s post-war turmoil, risking their lives on rickety boats in the South China Sea. Many were rescued – or intercepted – by authorities. Under British colonial administration, Hong Kong established temporary detention centres on isolated islands and former military sites. One of them was Tai A Chau, where children and adults alike spent months, or even years, under tightly controlled conditions. For them, these camps became formative, often traumatic, spaces.

“In my mind, I still see the island as it was during that first week in 1989 [when the camp was opened],” says Bird. “We received about 3,000 desperate people. We had to provide shelter, food and fresh water – and there was nothing on the island. It was mayhem.”

What unfolded in those early days was improvised survival. “I remember fathers, dressed in rags, scavenging for materials – broken boats, tree branches, anything – to build shelter, and mothers, many with babies, trying to find ways to feed them. There were no sanitation facilities. No power. At night, the island was in complete darkness,” Bird says.

He recalls the threat of disease being inescapable. “We knew, in the heat of the day, it wouldn’t be long before something would spread.” Even now, the sensory memory lingers. “As Katie and I walked across the island, I could still see those scenes,” he says. “I could still smell the smoke from the fires people used for cooking – and that strong ointment of White Flower Oil everyone relied on, hoping to keep illness away.”

After a few years of operating as a ramshackle “tent city”, the government built an all-purpose holding centre on Tai A Chau, in 1991. Life on the island continued to be regimented and constrained.

Detainees were housed in shared halls, movement was restricted and repetition often replaced any sense of freedom. But within these walls, small acts of resilience – learning new languages, forming friendships and even building fish ponds – offered the faintest glimmers of normality.

Aung was just nine years old in 1989, when she left her parents and hometown of Da Nang to join her two aunts aboard a small dinghy. Boat No 761 carried 77 people on a perilous journey to Hong Kong that would last seven days and seven nights.

“We had to leave at night, then head to the mountains for a night or two,” she recalls. “We left during the Lantern Festival, so there was a lot of distraction; that way, the police didn’t catch us.”

Much of the journey remains blurred. “I don’t remember a lot of details,” Aung says. “The strange thing about memory is that the brain blocks most of the trauma.” What endures are fragments: the confined space of the boat and the physical reality of survival.

“All I remember is being in a tiny cabin, curled up – kind of like hugging your knees.”

Aung recalls men in green uniforms transferring them, one by one, from the sinking boat to a larger vessel, its deck crowded with others bound for Hong Kong’s Green Island, then used as a processing centre for new arrivals, as well as detainees awaiting release or relocation.

“I remember arriving late at night at the dock, and they sprayed me,” she says. “They asked me to turn 360 degrees so they could spray me with pesticide – to kill any germs or bacteria I might have carried. They basically treated me like an insect.”

As a child, Aung remembers life on Tai A Chau as something akin to imprisonment. “Guards opened the door, and then it shut, and they locked it,” she says, describing the camp being made up of large, hut-like structures. “You weren’t allowed to go outside. Everybody stayed in their bunk beds. I’ve never been to prison, but what I imagine it to be – this was it.”

For Aung, the years that followed were marked by constant movement. “I was at Whitehead [Ma On Shan] – that was the worst – and then they moved me to Tai A Chau.”

It was there, around 1992 or 1993 until 1996, that she spent the longest stretch, before being transferred through several more detention camps. Guards, she recalls, came from a range of backgrounds, and included Afghan and Indian personnel. Daily life was defined by a quiet, unrelenting monotony.

“As a child, I didn’t know what hopelessness was, but I knew what boredom was,” she says. “Every day was the same.”

But during those years, Aung picked up Cantonese through shows such as Enjoy Yourself Tonight – the camp was allowed one hour of television each evening – and began learning English at a school in the camp.

Her name appeared on deportation lists more than once. “Each time, somehow, I was left off.” Eventually, after her aunt – who had secured her own release – advocated on her behalf with the help of a lawyer, Aung was granted her freedom.

“At first, I thought they were calling me again for deportation. But this time, they told me I was free to go.”

She spent a final few months at a detention centre near Kai Tak, which she calls a “freedom camp”, while awaiting relocation to her next destination.

Later, during a period of looser restrictions, Aung was allowed to work outside the camp as a seamstress, in a factory producing hospital gowns bound for the United States, though she had to return each night.

In 1997, Aung left for the US, closing the chapter that had defined her early life and, in many ways, rewrote its trajectory. She arrived in Louisiana with little English, navigating high school through sheer determination before earning a place at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, where she studied chemistry before building a career as an analyst at a chemical company. But her story did not settle into a single path.

In time, she met her husband, started a family and quietly began building something of her own. Now, she is the force behind ventures such as Yummi Sushi in Dallas, Texas, where she is based – a successful entrepreneur whose journey speaks not just of survival, but of reinvention.

Last year, Aung came across Bird’s book, Along the Southern Boundary: A Marine Police Officer’s Frontline Account of the Vietnamese Boatpeople and their Arrival in Hong Kong (2022), an encounter that saw long-dormant memories resurface, drawing her back to Hong Kong. It began with a childhood friend from the Tai A Chau Detention Centre, who had tracked down Bird after researching the island and later organised a reunion for former residents.

“She found Les and asked if he could take us back,” Aung recalls. After initial contact in January, Bird reconnected with her ahead of her trip to Hong Kong in early February.

On the boat to Tai A Chau, Bird showed Aung a PowerPoint presentation featuring photographs from 1989, when the island had been turned into a refugee camp.

“She was fascinated by every image, studying them closely – searching for faces, for fragments of memory, for anything or anyone she might recognise,” he says. “When she did recognise something, she would tell me the story behind it. I found that fascinating. It became a kind of history lesson for me as well, shaped by Katie’s own experiences.”

Each photograph prompted further questions, the answers to which pieced together a clearer picture of the past.

“By the time we arrived at Tai A Chau,” Bird says, “I had a fairly good idea of where Katie would have lived on the island during her time there.”

Since the release of his book, Bird has been contacted by numerous former refugees eager to share their stories. One of them, Connie Sam, reached out after seeing a photograph of Vietnamese refugees on the deck of the people-smuggling freighter Huey Fong. Others have written to say, “That’s me in your book”, or, in one case, “That’s my mother looking directly at the camera – and that small child standing next to her is me.”

“Once something like that happens, I pack a bag and go wherever they are,” Bird says. “I’ve travelled to some pretty remote places, and the meetings are always emotional. I can’t plan or imagine what I’ll say. It’s surreal, having someone who appears to be a complete stranger hug you and refuse to let go of your hand, and then listen to their stories.”

In 2022, Bird gave a talk at the Vietnamese Heritage Museum in Orange County, California, where the impact of these connections was clear: “Everyone in the audience was a former refugee, many rescued from the South China Sea, who had spent time in the Hong Kong camps. My talk lasted 45 minutes; the Q&A continued for three hours. People stood up to tell their stories. For many, it was the first time they had found the courage to speak publicly about what they had endured. It impressed on me how difficult it is for people to talk about trauma – even when they have survived almost certain death and gone on to thrive.”

Like Aung, many former refugees went on to achieve remarkable things. David Tran, featured in Bird’s book, created hot-sauce producer Huy Fong Foods and the popular Sriracha brand. Oscar-winning actor Ke Huy Quan has spoken publicly about his own refugee journey.

The Tai A Chau’s detention centre closed in 1996 and its buildings were demolished. Although it now stands empty and eerie, the island stirred memories for Aung.

“I haven’t fully processed the trip yet,” she admits. “I’m a busy mum, businesswoman and wife, so I haven’t had the time.”

Still, the journey brought clarity. “I don’t see myself as a victim. I appreciate the time I spent in the camp. It trained me, in a way, for the road map I’m on today.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong restaurants score extra HK$500 million thanks to World Cup
item.description:
The World Cup brought in an extra HK$500 million (US$63.8 million) for Hong Kong’s catering sector this year, an industry leader has said, after restaurants and shopping centres hosted overnight viewings of the final with dim sum, snacks and milk tea.

Businesses were also urged on Monday to devise creative strategies and set competitive prices to maintain the momentum from the city’s World Cup fever.

The final between Spain and Argentina drew crowds of football fans, including children and the elderly, who flocked to shopping centres at 3am – packing every floor of Tuen Mun Town Plaza, Olympian City, MCP in Tseung Kwan O and Kai Tak Mall.
item.content:encoded:
The World Cup brought in an extra HK$500 million (US$63.8 million) for Hong Kong’s catering sector this year, an industry leader has said, after restaurants and shopping centres hosted overnight viewings of the final with dim sum, snacks and milk tea.

Businesses were also urged on Monday to devise creative strategies and set competitive prices to maintain the momentum from the city’s World Cup fever.

The final between Spain and Argentina drew crowds of football fans, including children and the elderly, who flocked to shopping centres at 3am – packing every floor of Tuen Mun Town Plaza, Olympian City, MCP in Tseung Kwan O and Kai Tak Mall.

Simon Wong Ka-wo, president of the Hong Kong Federation of Restaurants and Related Trades, estimated that the catering industry had pocketed an additional HK$500 million between June 30 and Monday, representing an uptick of about 6 per cent from its initial estimate in July.

In Tuen Mun Town Plaza, cheers erupted as Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal appeared on a 540-inch screen, building to a crescendo when Spain clinched victory 1-0 after extra time.

Stalls and restaurants sought to capitalise on the crowds, setting up booths nearby to offer bubble tea or delivering dim sum directly to the viewing area.

Supermarket chain ParknShop stayed open overnight, selling drinks and fruit, while some spectators ordered food deliveries to the venue.

Many vendors offered promotions such as “buy three, get one free” to attract customers. Taxis also lined up at the mall’s entrance, ready to pick up passengers after the match.

Nini Man, manager of Nap Tea’s Tuen Mun branch, said the World Cup pop-up stand had only started turning a profit in the last two matches after the spot opened for a trial run on July 3.

She said she was inspired by the strong turnout at the mall for the Brazil-Japan match earlier in the tournament. As more vendors joined, the screenings evolved into a plaza-wide event.

“It was worth continuing [during the World Cup],” she said.

Man added that the exposure had helped introduce the shop to nearby residents who had never visited before.

“We have become like old neighbourhood friends,” she said, referring to the rare opportunity to interact with customers face-to-face.

Terence Chan Tak-ming, general manager of the portfolio leasing department at Henderson Land, said MCP recorded double-digit growth in both foot traffic and sales turnover throughout the World Cup.

He noted that tenants offering sports, lifestyle retail goods, or food and drinks had performed particularly well, creating business opportunities outside traditional peak hours.

In addition to vendors offering snacks and drinks ranging from coffee to craft beer, MCP also arranged free shuttle buses to Central and Mong Kok to help fans travel directly to work on Monday morning after watching the final.

Catering sector leader Wong said that while the significant time difference between Hong Kong and North America had dampened the usual business boost over the match period, many fans still visited restaurants and shopping centres to watch the final.

Venues raking in extra business included traditional Chinese dim sum restaurants.

“Restaurants need new directions in operations to attract new clientele. For important matches in the future, now that large screens have been installed, restaurants can roll out different activities and discounts to attract customers,” Wong said.

Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui, who watched the final at Kai Tak Mall, said that even with mega-events, businesses need to think creatively about strategies to attract customers.

She highlighted the emerging trend of traditional dim sum restaurants live-streaming World Cup matches as a successful example.

“I used to think watching a match in a dim sum restaurant might seem out of place, but it is actually feasible,” Law said. “That is why everyone has to rack their brains and examine their own strengths to discover more business opportunities.”

She added that a proactive approach from these businesses would help boost the economy.

Economist Simon Lee Siu-po said he believed business among restaurants and retailers would return to baseline levels after the World Cup, given lukewarm nighttime spending sentiment.

He urged the catering industry to be transparent and creative to attract patrons, citing the example of Lin Heung Lau’s Sheung Wan branch.

The restaurant rolled out an HK$3,888 eight-person VIP package and a HK$368 set for singles for the final match, with tea and service charges included.

Lee said the operator addressed the two pain points of Chinese restaurants by setting out their prices clearly and catering to the needs of solo diners.

“Hong Kong has too many options. With a competitive price and quality food, patrons will be interested,” he said, adding that restaurants could offer smaller meal portions to attract those dining alone.

Among those drawn to the city’s shopping malls for the final match’s “vibrant” atmosphere was Tuen Mun resident Shannon Dias, 42, who came to support Spain.

“A lot of people are here for both teams. It feels like a stadium – it’s better to be here,” he said.

Although he had eaten before the match, Dias said services by vendors at the shopping centre were “pretty good”.

“They’re doing their best to set up shop, especially for an event like this,” he said. “It definitely helps boost the economy.”

Another fan, Kit Ching, attended with his family after seeing promotions on social media.

Despite the crowds, he said he enjoyed the atmosphere and spent about HK$50 on drinks and snacks from ParknShop before kick-off.

“It was good to have something to eat while watching,” he said.

But some Argentina supporters left disappointed after the final whistle.

McQueen Zeng, who watched the match with friends, said it was a “pity” Argentina could not defend their title.

“I applaud Spain, and I also applaud our Argentinian players because they kept making efforts and trying to score,” he said. “I’m grateful to them for that.”

Zeng added that he would continue to support the team and hoped to watch a future World Cup in person, noting that Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay would co-host the opening three centenary matches for the 2030 Fifa tournament.

Additional reporting by Jess Ma

item.title: [SCMP] Asia’s AI boom has a dirty secret: the coal that powers it
item.description:
Asia sits atop vast amounts of coal, nearly three-fifths of the world’s known reserves by some estimates.

Cheaper and more reliable than imported oil and gas, and far less vulnerable to disruptions caused by foreign wars, coal is also dirty, polluting – and the region’s No 1 “stopgap source” to power the AI infrastructure roll-out.

“AI demand is materialising faster than clean energy generation can be commissioned,” said Alexander Kheder, a market research analyst at BMI who tracks global AI infrastructure spending and data centre expansion.
item.content:encoded:
Asia sits atop vast amounts of coal, nearly three-fifths of the world’s known reserves by some estimates.

Cheaper and more reliable than imported oil and gas, and far less vulnerable to disruptions caused by foreign wars, coal is also dirty, polluting – and the region’s No 1 “stopgap source” to power the AI infrastructure roll-out.

“AI demand is materialising faster than clean energy generation can be commissioned,” said Alexander Kheder, a market research analyst at BMI who tracks global AI infrastructure spending and data centre expansion.

Solar and wind, for all their recent progress, still could not deliver the relentless, round-the-clock baseload that the data centres powering artificial intelligence demanded, he said.

In Malaysia’s pioneering smart city of Cyberjaya, dozens of data centres are already in operation, with more planned for the future.

“The impact is going to be very, very visible,” said Adit Rahim, 49, a local resident and communications executive who worries about the strain all this development is placing on utilities.

“What no one is really addressing is whether resources like water and electricity are keeping pace,” he said.

Data centres never sleep. Their servers hum around the clock, training and running the artificial-intelligence models that are transforming the global economy – and their appetite for electricity is voracious.

That hunger has been a boon for companies such as Johnson Controls, whose Asia-Pacific vice-president for project delivery and data centre solutions, Ali Badreddine, has been fielding a flood of urgent requests from his base in Singapore.

“Customers are telling us they need everything faster,” he told This Week in Asia.

His company’s backup power systems – essential to prevent catastrophic data loss at AI data centres, where an unexpected power outage can destroy months of model-training progress – used to ship within months, but now come with waiting times of two years or more.

“Even if you are willing to pay, there simply isn’t enough manufacturing capacity available,” Badreddine said.

Southeast Asia’s AI workload demand will, in all likelihood, continue outpacing renewable energy supply for some years yet, according to Kheder, which is why coal has become the No 1 “stopgap source to bridge this gap”.

War woes

Asia imports the bulk of its oil and gas, much of it through a chokepoint strait that has been largely sealed off amid the US-Israel war on Iran.

Oil prices have whipsawed this year from lows of around US$60 a barrel in January to nearly US$120 at the height of the conflict in April. A ceasefire agreed in June helped stabilise the market for a few weeks until US President Donald Trump declared the truce “over” on July 8 following a fresh round of tit-for-tat attacks, sending prices rising again.
