Second, Southeast Asian countries often pursued industrial strategies that reduced pressure on local firms to upgrade. Indonesia emphasised resource nationalism and commodity downstreaming. Thailand protected large domestic conglomerates that dominated the services sector. Both approaches allowed high returns behind protective walls rather than forced firms to compete globally.

At the same time, multinational corporations that outsourced part of their production to these countries kept their high-value functions such as research, design and complex engineering in their home countries, leaving Southeast Asian operations in lower-value assembly roles. This model produces impressive foreign direct investment statistics in the short term, but little wage growth or technological diffusion.

Third, governments have been slow to manage the other side of China’s economic pressures: its export surge since the Covid-19 pandemic. Weak domestic demand in China combined with Western tariffs has pushed excess capacity into regional markets. Ceramics factories in northern Thailand have closed in large numbers. Indonesian textile workers have lost jobs. Malaysian retailers and logistics operators complain of being undercut by e-commerce platforms and opaque “zero-dollar transport” arrangements that exploit regulatory loopholes.

What must change

If Southeast Asia is to turn the current difficult environment into an opportunity, a few concrete shifts are required.

First, governments must restore or build credible, independent economic institutions. This means protecting central bank independence, rebuilding professional economic teams and ending the practice of using state power to extract resources from the private sector. Without policy predictability and institutional trust, even generous investment incentives will fail to produce sustained capital formation.

Second, industrial policy needs to shift from protection and resource nationalism towards forcing competitiveness. This involves reducing the barriers that allow inefficient firms to survive, aligning vocational training with the skills demanded by modern manufacturing and services and actively supporting the formalisation of large swathes of the workforce. Informal employment above 50 per cent, as seen in Thailand, is incompatible with productivity growth.

Third, infrastructure and logistics must be treated as urgent national priorities rather than secondary concerns. Thailand’s relatively weak ranking in global logistics performance already undermines its attractiveness for high-value supply chains. Improving ports, roads, digital connectivity and trade facilitation would raise returns on existing investment and make relocation more attractive.

Fourth, countries need a more realistic approach to managing import competition from China. This does not mean blanket protectionism that hurts consumers and invites retaliation. But it does mean stronger enforcement against illegal imports, better use of trade remedies where dumping can be proven and support for domestic firms to upgrade quality and move into higher-value segments. At the same time, governments should press for greater reciprocity, including duty-free access for labour-intensive exports from lower-income members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations into the Chinese market.

Finally, political incentives must change. Leaders should be rewarded for delivering productivity growth and formal employment rather than for short-term spending or populist measures. This requires a national consensus that escaping the middle-income trap requires sustained effort across administrations.

The window created by supply-chain diversification remains open but is narrowing. Countries that subordinate their economic strategies to short-term political gains will find themselves squeezed from both sides – losing the relocation benefits they had hoped for while watching their industries lose competitiveness. Those willing to make the critical reforms still have a realistic chance to turn pressure into progress. The choice is increasingly stark.

Anna Fong is a Master of Business Administration candidate at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. Donald Low is Senior Lecturer and Professor of Practice in Public Policy at the same university.

item.title: [SCMP] Apple’s biggest-ever leak happened in India. Will firms rethink their China relocations?
item.description:
When Apple set its sights on India as its next promising market, CEO Tim Cook planned to take a leaf out of the company’s China playbook – a retail and manufacturing strategy that had paid hefty dividends to the US tech giant.

“We are, in essence, taking what we learned in China years ago and how we scale to China and bringing that to bear,” Cook told investors in February 2023. The company had just seen record quarterly sales in the Indian market, and was just weeks ahead of the opening of Apple’s first stores in the country. “India is a hugely exciting market for us.”

At the time, Cook’s optimism in India also carried a degree of pragmatism. To navigate the rising trade tensions between the world’s two largest economies and avoid US tariffs on China-made goods – both the duties already in place and those likely to be imposed in the future – Apple had bet on India to become its next manufacturing hub.
item.content:encoded:
When Apple set its sights on India as its next promising market, CEO Tim Cook planned to take a leaf out of the company’s China playbook – a retail and manufacturing strategy that had paid hefty dividends to the US tech giant.

“We are, in essence, taking what we learned in China years ago and how we scale to China and bringing that to bear,” Cook told investors in February 2023. The company had just seen record quarterly sales in the Indian market, and was just weeks ahead of the opening of Apple’s first stores in the country. “India is a hugely exciting market for us.”

At the time, Cook’s optimism in India also carried a degree of pragmatism. To navigate the rising trade tensions between the world’s two largest economies and avoid US tariffs on China-made goods – both the duties already in place and those likely to be imposed in the future – Apple had bet on India to become its next manufacturing hub.

India began to deliver. In 2022, the country produced around 6 per cent of all iPhones, but by 2026, that figure was expected to surpass 25 per cent, according to data from Counterpoint Research.

However, this year Cook’s vision faced a sobering reality check. In June, a massive cyberattack by hacking group World Leaks hit Tata Electronics, Apple’s Bengaluru-based partner for iPhone parts and assembly, leaking more than 200,000 files on the dark web. Analysts called the leak the biggest in the company’s history.

“India has proven it can scale production; now it must prove it can scale trust,” said Christopher Tang, a professor specialising in global supply chain management at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).

While India managed to ramp up labour-intensive assembly, attract major suppliers such as Foxconn and Tata, and leveraged government incentives, the incident revealed that the ecosystem still needed to catch up in three vital areas: information governance, supplier discipline, and cyber-operational integration, Tang noted.

“India can become a major global manufacturing hub,” Tang said. “But overtaking China as the world’s premier factory is a much higher bar.”

The breach may slow Apple’s willingness to transfer its most sensitive product data

Christopher Tang, UCLA

Made in India?

The files from the Tata leak included Apple’s component and supplier lists, as well as photos of the firm’s unreleased iPhone 18 Pro, exposing sensitive details of the chips on its main circuit board as well as hundreds of parts, according to Reuters.

Apple, Tata and the Indian authorities were reportedly investigating the incident. Neither company immediately responded to requests for comment.

“This leak is significant because Apple’s secret sauce that creates its competitive advantage depends not only on Apple’s own systems but also on every node in its manufacturing network,” Tang said.

“The breach may slow Apple’s willingness to transfer its most sensitive product data or highest-complexity product ramps too quickly to newer hubs,” he added.

This year’s leak was only the most recent test of India’s fast-expanding manufacturing capabilities. In 2024, Tata suffered a fire that led to a production halt at its facilities in Tamil Nadu, a state in the country’s south.

Despite the fallout, analysts said they did not expect the breach to diminish the importance of India in Apple’s ongoing efforts to diversify its global manufacturing.

“The current situation will be very much of a remediation-and-move-on situation, rather than an existential threat to Tata’s partnership with Apple,” said Tarun Pathak, research director at Counterpoint Research.

“Ultimately, we believe this doesn’t halt India’s momentum, but it will surely lead to an industry-wide re-evaluation” of the information technology infrastructure of electronic manufacturers, Pathak said.

Still, the breach cast a shadow over Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s “Make in India” initiative to transform India into a global manufacturing and innovation hub, challenging China’s dominance as the “world’s factory”.

The expansion of Apple’s manufacturing network in India helped drive the country’s broader industrial upgrade. In recent years, the US tech giant’s major suppliers, including Foxconn and Tata, have scaled up operations heavily across the country from Tamil Nadu to neighbouring state Karnataka.

Foxconn, also known as Hon Hai Precision Industry, injected another US$1.5 billion into its India unit last year.

However, Apple’s aggressive expansion plans in India also faced pressure from its home country. US President Donald Trump said publicly last May that he had asked Cook to stop building plants in India and step up production in America.

Beyond Apple, India has also attracted South Korea’s Samsung and Chinese handset makers including Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo to build production bases there.

India has surged to become the world’s second-largest mobile phone maker by volume, with 99.2 per cent of its locally sold handsets produced inside the country, according to official data.

Just last week, New Delhi unveiled a new US$6.5 billion initiative, the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme, to incentivise smartphone brands that produce their devices locally and source domestic components. The initiative targets US$460 billion in domestic mobile phone production over the next five years, with a significant increase in exports.

Hedging or diversifying?

India has been gaining an increasingly significant role in Apple’s supply chain. Last year, Cook revealed that most of the iPhones sold in the US were produced in India. In the meantime, almost all iPad, Mac, Apple Watch and AirPods products sold in the US market were made in Vietnam.

China, on the other hand, would continue to manufacture the vast majority of products sold in the rest of the world, according to Cook.

Apple’s geographic diversification efforts, known as the “China plus one” strategy, sought to shift away from total reliance on the Chinese manufacturing powerhouse amid geopolitical tensions and a supply bottleneck.

The diversification efforts accelerated during the Covid-19 pandemic, when virus control protocols in China dragged some of Apple’s product shipments to a halt at one point.

“For Apple, ‘China plus one’ is primarily a hedge against geopolitical risk, rather than a decision driven purely by commercial efficiency,” said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy.

“This incident will not reverse its strategy, but it reminds Apple that diversification is not a simple copy-and-paste of the China playbook,” Sun said.

When talking about China’s manufacturing advantages, observers have usually focused on China’s low cost, efficiency and sheer scale, while underestimating its suppliers’ ‘soft power’ in commercial confidentiality, rapid response and systemic risk control, he added.

“Supply chain security is, in itself, a core manufacturing capability,” Sun said.

While Apple has previously faced product leaks in the form of unauthorised photos and smuggled parts from factory floors – including facilities in China – the scale of the recent cyber breach was unprecedented, according to analysts.

Every added node is an added point of vulnerability

Sun Chenghao, Tsinghua University

Sun noted that a leak of this magnitude was highly unlikely to hit long-established Chinese Apple suppliers, although the possibility could not be wholly dismissed.

“The key is not just firewalls; it’s the organisational discipline, tiered authorisation, physical isolation, supplier compliance auditing and a culture of secrecy forged over decades of collaboration,” Sun said.

A global supply chain alert

Analysts noted that the strategy, adopted to mitigate geopolitical risks, inadvertently exposed the supply chain to other risks.

“The more fragmented a supply chain becomes, the more a company must share blueprints, test data, supplier lists, quality standards and internal workflows across more touch points,” Sun said.

“Every added node is an added point of vulnerability.”

A source within Apple’s supply chain noted that cyberattacks are a universal threat, which is increasingly prevalent after the explosion of artificial intelligence technology.

“It’s not just Tata; all suppliers have been under attack in some way,” said the person, who asked to remain anonymous due to the sensitivity of the matter. “What happened to Tata sounded an alert across the supply chain globally.”

While India faces immediate scrutiny, experts stressed that cybersecurity required an ongoing arms race extending beyond any single company or region.

“No country or supplier ecosystem is immune,” UCLA’s Tang said.

item.title: [SCMP] In Indonesia’s island paradise, slavery remains a daily reality
item.description:
Two hours from the tourist beaches of Bali, slavery is alive and well on the Indonesian island of Sumba, where people are still born into bondage.

They work from dawn to dusk without pay, are passed on in marriage, and are sometimes beaten and raped by their masters. Yet most are resigned to their fate because their status “cannot be wiped away”, as one young slave – or ata – Kanisius Kanyali Hambarita said.

Slavery has been illegal in what is now Indonesia for more than 160 years, but it survives in Sumba’s rigid caste system, particularly in the island’s east.
item.content:encoded:
Two hours from the tourist beaches of Bali, slavery is alive and well on the Indonesian island of Sumba, where people are still born into bondage.

They work from dawn to dusk without pay, are passed on in marriage, and are sometimes beaten and raped by their masters. Yet most are resigned to their fate because their status “cannot be wiped away”, as one young slave – or ata – Kanisius Kanyali Hambarita said.

Slavery has been illegal in what is now Indonesia for more than 160 years, but it survives in Sumba’s rigid caste system, particularly in the island’s east.

Kanisius and his master, Umbu Ana Rara, 31, who is three years younger than him, live in the village of Tenggedu, whose turquoise waterfalls draw intrepid tourists looking for a “hidden tropical paradise”.

It is a place out of time, reached by a rocky road between arid hills and the sea where you have to dodge stray cows, goats and wild horses. There is no mobile phone signal and food is cooked over a wood fire.

Umbu Ana said he treats his slave “like a member of the family” as the two sat chewing betel nuts – a mild stimulant that stains the gums red – in the late morning heat, with chickens and geese wandering at their feet.

Both master and slave sleep on mats on the floor of one of the village’s towering traditional thatched houses – built to resemble buffalo horns – that are often grouped around the tombs of the masters’ ancestors.

Umbu Ana allows his ata to earn a little money as a motorcycle taxi driver and to grow his own food on a small plot of land.

“I don’t object to it, that’s how it is,” said Kanisius of his status as a slave. “It’s not a weight on our shoulders. It’s only the symbol of a tradition inherited from our ancestors.”

Others tell a different story away from their masters.

“I was beaten from childhood if I didn’t work enough,” said an ata in his forties from the nearby village of Napu.

“They would hit me, throw water on me,” he said, forcing him to work in the fields after school, feeding the pigs or cooking for his master. “I tell my children: ‘I don’t want you to go through what I went through.’”

Eight of out 10 of Sumba’s population of 685,000 people are Christian, but its older marapu belief system, that blends animism and ancestor worship, has deep roots.

It divides society into three castes: “the nobles, called maramba – often large landowners – ordinary people called kabihu and the slaves/servants, the atas,” said rights activist Martha Hebi, author of several studies on the subject.

The religion is “the essence of social stratification”, marapu priest Umbu Remi Deta said. Legend “says that the marambas acquired atas when they arrived in Sumba”.

The island’s isolation – 2,000km (1,200 miles) east of the capital Jakarta – has helped preserve these ancestral social structures.

Despite having the world’s largest Muslim population, Indonesia is dazzlingly diverse. While slavery is banned under its 1945 constitution, written when the country broke free from Dutch colonial rule, some traditional customs are tolerated.

Estimates vary as to how many slaves are on Sumba. A social worker, who asked not to be named, said there were “around 1,700” in East Sumba among a population of 350,000. But others put their number at several thousand.

Rooted in tradition

Forced labour exists elsewhere in Indonesia, with temporary bondage practised by “the Dayak indigenous community in Kalimantan for debts,” said historian Bondan Kanumoyoso of the University of Indonesia in Depok.

But the slavery in Sumba was unique, he said, going from generation to generation, with masters and slaves living in similar conditions under the same roof. If it was not for the atas’ work-worn faces, it is often hard for outsiders to work out who is who.

The maramba masters have long underpinned the domination of their slaves with physical and sexual violence. “The master can ‘use’ his maidservant,” said pastor Marlin Lomi, the head of the influential Protestant synod of East Sumba, “and that is considered normal”.

“If I like a female slave but she refuses me, I will beat her husband,” said one maramba, who confirmed the practice on condition of anonymity.

“If you are a girl, you belong to the master,” said Andy Yentriyani, a former head of the National Commission on Violence Against Women. “So sexual intercourse is not considered rape. It is only using your authority [over] your belonging.”

The violence often goes unpunished “because the victims don’t dare testify”, said Hebi, who founded the NGO Solidarity for the Women and Children of Sumba.

An 18-year-old slave who said she had been raped since she was 13 by her master and his son, reported them to the police in Waingapu, the capital of East Sumba, in 2024 after having a child.

But two years on the investigation still had not been concluded, said Dian Sasmita, of the Indonesian Child Protection Commission, urging the authorities “to shed light on these cases”.

The young victim, initially taken in by an NGO, now lives under protection in her village.

Pastor Marlin, 57, said the Protestant synod also helps in cases of violence against women and children “if the victims speak up”.

But the caste system is very deeply rooted, said Gidion Mbilijora, who was the bupati or head of the East Sumba district for 13 years. He owns two atas himself.

“We need a long process of changing the mindset” of the nobles, he said during the enormous funeral of one of them close to the capital, to which 4,000 guests, including atas, were invited.

The funeral was marked by the ritual sacrifice of two horses as part of the marapu rite, which most inhabitants of Sumba still follow, whether Christian or Muslim.

Until the early 1990s, the police kept a close eye on such funerals for fear of human sacrifices, according to the American anthropologist Janet Hoskins. In the not so distant past, marapu ritual required a slave to be buried with his master.

Small steps

Rights groups like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have urged Jakarta to enforce its constitutional ban on slavery as well as anti-discrimination conventions it has signed. Amnesty Indonesia’s Haeril Halim said the government “is aware of the situation in Sumba” but “has so far taken no measures to eliminate slavery”.

Indonesia should “declare the freedom of all ata people from their maramba masters,” said Andreas Harsono, of Human Rights Watch Indonesia.

The country’s human rights minister Yusril Ihza Mahendra said that while the constitution banned slavery, “Indonesia is a highly plural society, and social development differs among ethnic groups”.

“The government does not wish to impose change suddenly – rather it follows the social development of each community step by step,” he said. “We are convinced that education will change everything.”

Former district head Gidion echoed this. With the local elite almost entirely drawn from the nobles – most of whom own slaves – he said change will only “come step by step”.

“I think it will definitely change … advances in knowledge will enable people of the lower class to realise … that this social bond is no longer appropriate,” he added.

Some nobles have tried to improve the atas’ lot.

“One way of reforming this rigid system is to start with our own families,” said Norlina Rambu Jola Kalunga, 54, a noblewoman who inherited five atas when she married the son of a royal family.

The 54-year-old pastor, a former rector of the Christian University of Sumba, wants atas to be emancipated. But she cannot free her own because it would go against custom, even though her grandfather “granted freedom to all the atas” when he was leader of the Protestant community in neighbouring Central Sumba.

Another maramaba noblewoman Tamu Rambu Margaretha – widely known as Mama Margaretha – has long sought to loosen the bonds of slavery in her village of Prailiu, even travelling to Jakarta to advocate emancipation.

She sent all her atas to school along with her children because “if someone is illiterate, there are many things they won’t understand”.

Her son Umbu Remi, the marapu priest, runs a gallery where 20 local women, several of them atas, sell their spectacular ikat handmade textiles – which take months to weave and dye – to passing tourists.

Mama Margaretha and her atas and their children live together in several traditional houses, which look like tall witches’ hats, ranged around her family’s tombs. She provides for them and they tend her land and livestock.

She said she would “not oppose” her atas leaving her, saying it would be “fine” if they “ran away on their own”. But lacking any real means, none have.

Even those atas who try to break away often find themselves shackled to their old masters.

Having been used and abused throughout his youth, the man from the village of Napu raised his family outside the household of the maramba who beat him in a house his old master no longer used.

He even managed to send two of his four children to university with the help of government grants by selling livestock he reared by himself.

But the land where he grows corn, cassava and vegetables is still his master’s, so “when they need us, we go. If not, we do not”.

“It’s so easy for them to order us around. But I did not directly fight back. I made my own path. I could see what freedom looked like,” he said. “Now there are rules … laws that protect us. Maybe the maramba understands that, so they do not bother us too much any more.”

He is still a slave but he dreams that his children will be “free from the maramba … If we have knowledge, then we are free.”

item.title: [SCMP] The human faces of China’s belt and road strategy, through Liu Heung-shing’s lens
item.description:
It is barely light when Liu Heung-shing starts the day in his art-filled Happy Valley apartment. But then, the photojournalist has always believed in getting to the story before everyone else.

Liu, 74, wakes at 5am to spend three hours reading the news, coffee in hand. Despite being “long retired”, the Pulitzer Prize-winning photographer takes note of where he might want to visit next.

“There are so many ways to tell a story. Sometimes, the most difficult decision is when not to press the shutter, rather than when to press the shutter,” he says, while cooking and sipping a glass of Chablis. He has invited me to his home for dinner and to discuss his most recent book, Old Road New Connections: China Builds a Different World, for which his shutter charted a global odyssey following the tentacles of China’s Belt and Road Initiative. If the initiative sounds abstract in policy papers – six economic corridors, hundreds of billions in cumulative investment, more than 150 participating countries and 230 cooperation agreements – Liu’s book is an attempt to humanise that scale.
item.content:encoded:
It is barely light when Liu Heung-shing starts the day in his art-filled Happy Valley apartment. But then, the photojournalist has always believed in getting to the story before everyone else.

Liu, 74, wakes at 5am to spend three hours reading the news, coffee in hand. Despite being “long retired”, the Pulitzer Prize-winning photographer takes note of where he might want to visit next.

“There are so many ways to tell a story. Sometimes, the most difficult decision is when not to press the shutter, rather than when to press the shutter,” he says, while cooking and sipping a glass of Chablis. He has invited me to his home for dinner and to discuss his most recent book, Old Road New Connections: China Builds a Different World, for which his shutter charted a global odyssey following the tentacles of China’s Belt and Road Initiative. If the initiative sounds abstract in policy papers – six economic corridors, hundreds of billions in cumulative investment, more than 150 participating countries and 230 cooperation agreements – Liu’s book is an attempt to humanise that scale.

“I knew it was also a human story of Chinese going around the world, doing things, changing things and putting a uniquely Chinese stamp on different parts of the world.”

In many ways, the project is typical Liu: ambitious, self‑assigned and pursued with a mixture of stubbornness and curiosity.

“I think I’m somebody whose brain works 24 hours a day,” he laughs.

He likes to say that his books all begin with a simple editorial question: “If this is going to be one of the defining stories of the 21st century, and nobody has framed it properly yet, what can I do?”

Born in Hong Kong in 1951, Liu spent his early childhood in Fuzhou, Fujian province, with his mother, witnessing famine during the Great Leap Forward. His family eventually returned to Hong Kong.

In 1969, Liu left for New York, in the United States, where he studied politics at Hunter College. He remembers the year clearly because it was then that he saw Jimi Hendrix and Janis Joplin perform up close at the Woodstock festival.

More specific education came when his mentor, Albanian‑born photographer Gjon Mili, took him to the 28th floor of the Time & Life Building, which was where the photographers at Life magazine and other Time Inc titles were based.

“On that floor,” Liu says, “the world unfolded through photography.”

It was for Time Inc that Liu first returned to mainland China, in 1976, to photograph a nation coming to terms with the death of Mao Zedong.

As a foreign correspondent in China until the early 90s, he documented the pivotal decades that followed. Later, as the executive vice-president of News Corp China, Liu shuttled between tycoon Rupert Murdoch and party cadres.

Fundamentally, the photographer divides his understanding of modern China into three eras: China 1.0, the Maoist times he glimpsed as a child; China 2.0, launched by Deng Xiaoping’s 1978 reforms; and China 3.0, the country that is developing at breakneck speed, with the belt and road a defining initiative.

“This book is my exploration of that new world,” he writes in Old Road New Connections. “I used my camera to capture a resurgent nation spreading its wings.”

Doing so involved more than 270,000km of travel, “roughly the distance of seven times around the globe”, on multiple self-funded journeys over a three-year period. He covered five continents, 21 countries and 54 regions, spending a great deal of time in factories, mines, ports, deserts and train drivers’ cabins, as well as on the road, and that was after months of negotiation for access to the businesses, state-owned and otherwise, operating along the routes.

The resulting book turns one of this century’s most ambitious infrastructure projects into something unexpectedly intimate and personal: a portrait of a world quietly reordering at China’s direction.

“It’s capturing the contradictions sometimes, the smallest details that lend poetic meaning to life,” says Liu. “That is much more enduring than what’s in the latest news cycle.”

Following new lines of steel in Indonesia, he rode the Jakarta-Bandung high‑speed Whoosh, photographing Chinese and Indonesian operators shoulder to shoulder in the cab as Southeast Asia’s first bullet train, launched in 2023, zipped at 350km/h past villages and roads still heaving with traffic jams.

“You can show [a picture of] a high‑speed train once,” he says. “You show it twice, it’s already a repeat. After that, what interests me is who’s riding it, who’s driving it, who’s being moved and who finds their village cut in half.”

His journey through western China began on the old Silk Road: Xian’s terracotta warriors; camel caravans re‑enacted in Dunhuang. In complete contrast, he then visited the country’s first 100-megawatt molten‑salt solar thermal power station, which uses 12,000 mirrors and looks like a sci‑fi sun.

Some of Liu’s favourite photos from this project emerged along the sand ridges of the Gobi: young dancers from the Beijing Modern Dance Company performing in the desert, their body language, movement and skin tones coalescing with the sand dunes.

In Thailand, he watched workers construct concrete pillars that will one day connect Kunming, in China’s Yunnan province, to Bangkok and then Malaysia and Singapore, a rail artery replacing old Maritime Silk Road routes.

In Kazakhstan’s Aktau port, Liu slept uncomfortably “in a small converted shipping container”, he recalls, while sharing a worksite with engineers of the Citic Environmental Group, who were trying – not without problems – to hand over a water-treatment plant to a local team.

He met a couple in the old city of Kashgar, in the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region; Hadiya Msham Abdulla from Tanzania studied at Fujian Medical University and now runs a cafe with her Uygur partner, Dilshat Tursun. As their staff made a latte for Liu, the couple proudly introduced him to their baby daughter.

“What is the most important factor in storytelling? I believe it’s trust,” he says. “I’m a humanist to the core, because I’m interested in everything. I’m interested in why this woman wants to look beautiful. I’m interested in athletes, how this man can run so fast.”

He’s also interested in the Kenyan manager at the Mombasa-Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway control centre who dispatches instructions in fluent Mandarin. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, Liu and his camera descended down a suffocating 1,150-metre-deep underground lift into the Kamoa-Kakula copper mine, which has Chinese investors. He snapped portraits of local miners, South African technicians and Angolan labourers working side by side with Chinese engineers.

Elsewhere in Africa, he encountered a Chinese lion conservationist, Xing Ba, in the Masai Mara wildlife reserve and a young Chinese engineer who has no plans to “go back” – Africa, for her, had become home.

His photographs from Iran date from just before the current conflict in the Middle East. While in the country, his interpreter asked him when more much-needed trains would be coming from China for Tehran’s metro. China helped build several of the city’s lines.

Liu captured a ladies’ Zumba class in Xinjiang; Brazilian cowboys; and a courier making AliExpress deliveries on horseback in a satellite town outside Moscow, Russia. He even peeked inside a Shanghai factory producing satellites deployed in the US-China space race.

A post-dinner snoop around his apartment finds a small framed picture of Liu’s, above his desk. It’s of Richard Nixon holding a bucket of Tsingtao beers and play-acting as a waiter on a Hangzhou-to-Shanghai train. The former US president was acting goofy on returning to China in 1982, to commemorate the 10th anniversary of the signing of the Shanghai Communiqué, which paved the way to normalising bilateral relations between China and the US.

On another wall is a picture that helped earn Liu his shared Pulitzer – as well as a punch from a KGB guard inside the Kremlin: a 1991 shot for Associated Press of Mikhail Gorbachev announcing his resignation and the dissolution of the Soviet Union. It shows the departing president sitting at a table, his shoulders slightly slumped, a blur of paper – an empire dissolving between one breath and the next.

“I was the only foreign photojournalist inside the great hall at the time,” recalls Liu. “I was really running around like crazy that day.”

His contributions to culture grew in 2015, when he founded the Shanghai Centre of Photography, which quickly became a mainstay of the West Bund art district before closing in December 2023. Running a non-profit, fundraising and training 10-plus staff proved rewarding but ultimately too taxing. He now divides his time between Hong Kong, Europe and mainland China.

With Old Road New Connections, Liu shows he is still more interested in being on the road than at the podium. Although conceived as a China 3.0 travelogue of sorts, a book on how China’s infrastructure push translates into lived experience is perhaps a logical addendum to a lifelong project of bearing witness to world-defining tipping points.

His photographs and anecdotes do not resolve into a neat verdict on the belt and road, or China’s far-spanning cross-border development. Instead, they register the speed of progress and the human ways by which capital and culture, Chinese or otherwise, flow. It’s not the panoramas of bridges, trains or ports that are most poignant, but the images of people absorbed in daily life as the world around them is being rewired.

“If the 21st century is to be China’s, as the last was America’s, I wanted to see the making of that century where it was happening, no matter how far away,” he writes.

“I’ve photographed so many people, in so many stories, in so many different countries, but I’m still interested,” he says, finishing the Chablis, “because my next picture could just be my best.”

Old Road New Connections: China Builds a Different World will be officially launched at Liu Heung-shing’s talk with Bernard Chan, chairman of the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority board, on Thursday July 16, at the 36th Hong Kong Book Fair, which runs until July 21, at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines’ Marcos uses national address to promise relief, but funding questions loom
item.description:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr used his 2026 State of the Nation Address (Sona) on Monday to promise relief from taxes, electricity charges and high rice prices, while pledging to pursue corruption cases linked to a flood-control scandal that has battered his administration.

But while analysts said the one-and-a-half-hour speech addressed issues Filipinos had expected Marcos to confront, they questioned how the government could afford the handouts and why he announced no austerity or revenue-raising measures to address continuing financial and economic pressures and a deepening debt burden.

Marcos began his speech by returning to the corruption issue that dominated last year’s address: an inquiry into alleged irregularities in flood-control projects, including claims of ghost, substandard and overpriced works, that investigators said had channelled public funds through kickbacks to politicians, public works officials and contractors.
item.content:encoded:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr used his 2026 State of the Nation Address (Sona) on Monday to promise relief from taxes, electricity charges and high rice prices, while pledging to pursue corruption cases linked to a flood-control scandal that has battered his administration.

But while analysts said the one-and-a-half-hour speech addressed issues Filipinos had expected Marcos to confront, they questioned how the government could afford the handouts and why he announced no austerity or revenue-raising measures to address continuing financial and economic pressures and a deepening debt burden.

Marcos began his speech by returning to the corruption issue that dominated last year’s address: an inquiry into alleged irregularities in flood-control projects, including claims of ghost, substandard and overpriced works, that investigators said had channelled public funds through kickbacks to politicians, public works officials and contractors.

The scandal has become one of the biggest tests of Marcos’ anti-corruption drive, not least because it has implicated former House speaker Martin Romualdez, the president’s first cousin and long-time political ally, who stepped down last year amid mounting pressure over the controversy.

In his speech, Marcos said cases had already been filed against – and some arrests made of – contractors, senior Department of Public Works and Highways officials and lawmakers.

He said that, according to the Ombudsman, the country’s anti-corruption body, authorities were close to filing “multiple cases against the former speaker”.

Without naming Romualdez, Marcos said: “This pains me, but we have to do what is right. I am not the president of my family. I am not the president of my friends. I am the president of the Philippines, and my duty is to the Filipino people.”

Romualdez has denied wrongdoing and said he is prepared to face any charges.

Marcos said the flood-control probe had resulted in the recovery, freezing or preservation of almost 25 billion pesos (US$405 million) in money and assets.

To help Filipinos cope with multiple crises, Marcos said he would ask Congress to pass laws that would remove the charge of “system loss” – the cost passed on to consumers for electricity lost in the power grid or through pilferage – from all electricity bills, raise the tax exemption threshold for individual taxpayers from 250,000 pesos to 350,000 pesos and remove the minimum corporate income tax on microenterprises.

He also announced an amnesty period for those with unpaid income tax, estate tax and donor tax, as well as value-added tax.

Marcos said he would expand the coverage of his rice subsidy programme, which sells rice at 20 pesos per kilogram instead of at current market rates of more than twice that amount, to up to 8 million families from the present 2.5 million families.

Former agriculture undersecretary and policy expert Fermin Adriano told This Week in Asia that the president’s speech was “filled with spending but no mention of how his government will raise required revenues”.

“In developed countries, any programme or project mentioned will require a calculation of how much it will cost, where the money will be generated or shifted from one priority to another,” Adriano said.

Financial risk analyst Jonathan Ravelas also told This Week in Asia: “After listening to the whole speech, the only thing I can think of is – where will the money [to do all that] be coming from?”

Ravelas, managing director of eManagement for Business and Marketing Services and retired chief market strategist of the Philippines’ largest bank BDO, noted that Marcos’ speech mentioned a lot of revenue cutbacks and more foreign direct investment.

But he said the country was currently in “a state of permanent crisis” because of economic difficulties brought on by the Russia-Ukraine war and the Middle East conflict.

“In a country where you have an emergency and you talk of continued spending, isn’t there something wrong with that?” he said.

He also cautioned that the revenue-easing measures Marcos announced would still need congressional approval.

Last week, Marcos’ public affairs undersecretary Claire Castro had said the speech would be “earth-shaking”.

However, Dr Jean Franco, a political-science professor at the University of the Philippines, was underwhelmed.

“It was not earth-shaking at all, but he said what people expected of him, given the crisis and the spectre of the flood control scandal,” she told This Week in Asia.

She also pointed out that it was not enough to file cases against those involved in the flood-control scandal without also proposing measures to reform the system. “Otherwise, the cycle of corruption continues.”

Franco said Marcos “did not stress long-term solutions to prevent another flood control scandal”, citing the need for a flood-control master plan to coordinate priority projects, funding and agency responsibilities rather than rely on piecemeal works.

“The implication is that he wants to be perceived as a president responsive to the demands of the people. I think he is humbled by his low approval and trust ratings, which somehow is a repudiation of his landslide win in 2022.”

Hours before the Sona, private pollster OCTA Research released its second-quarter survey showing both Marcos and Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio – his 2022 running mate and former ally turned political enemy – had fallen below 50 per cent on at least one key performance or trust measure.

Marcos’ performance rating fell by eight percentage points, from 55 per cent in March to 47 per cent, while his trust rating slipped from 54 per cent to 49 per cent, according to the survey conducted from July 4 to 11.

Duterte-Carpio’s performance rating slid from 50 per cent to 45 per cent, while her trust rating dropped from 55 per cent to 47 per cent, with the polling period coinciding with the opening of her Senate impeachment trial over allegations including misuse of public funds and threats against Marcos and first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos.

Duterte-Carpio has denied wrongdoing and accused Marcos’ allies of political persecution.

The vice-president, who was abroad, was a no-show, along with Marcos’ estranged elder sister, Senator Imee Marcos, and former Senate president Alan Peter Cayetano, who now leads the Senate minority.

Imee, whose relationship with her younger brother has deteriorated as she aligned herself more closely with the Duterte camp, wore black and a patchwork dress made of fabric scraps at the Senate session hours before the Sona, saying it reflected the “fragmented (gutay-gutay), sliced up (hiwa-hiwa), broken up (biyak-biyak)” state of the Philippines under his presidency.

Marcos turned to the South China Sea only near the end of the speech, framing the dispute not just as a sovereignty issue but also as a question of national dignity.

Although he did not name China, his remarks appeared to reference a diplomatic row over an AI-generated editorial video posted on state-run news outlet China Daily’s Facebook account, which Philippine officials condemned as racist and dehumanising over its depiction of Filipinos as monkeys. China’s foreign ministry said the video did not represent Beijing’s official position.

“A common threat lies before us, directed against our dignity and self-respect. Of late, our very humanity has been called into question,” Marcos said.

“Let me remind our friends and our detractors. Filipinos are a noble, kind, gracious and great race. We are not greedy. We are not racist. We are not liars. We are respectful and we are dignified. We are Filipinos and we do not yield.”

Marcos said his government “will do all that is necessary to continue upholding [the 2016 arbitral] award, utilising every peaceful and legal means available”, referring to the international tribunal ruling that rejected Beijing’s sweeping claims in the South China Sea and upheld Manila’s sovereign rights in its exclusive economic zone.

item.title: [SCMP] From marches to memes: why India’s youth turned against Modi
item.description:
As India picks up the pieces in the aftermath of a youth protest that deposed an education minister, questions linger over the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) failure to connect with younger generations.

Analysts say the scale of youth participation in the protest suggests a loss of faith in Prime Minister Narendra Modi, with the real test coming at the ballot box in key state elections next year.

Thousands of young people joined the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) march to parliament on Monday demanding examination reforms and the resignation of education chief Dharmendra Pradhan.
item.content:encoded:
As India picks up the pieces in the aftermath of a youth protest that deposed an education minister, questions linger over the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) failure to connect with younger generations.

Analysts say the scale of youth participation in the protest suggests a loss of faith in Prime Minister Narendra Modi, with the real test coming at the ballot box in key state elections next year.

Thousands of young people joined the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) march to parliament on Monday demanding examination reforms and the resignation of education chief Dharmendra Pradhan.

The impetus behind the protest was medical school entrance paper leaks, which forced a resit and affected 2 million students, driving at least 12 to suicide.

It was one of the largest displays of public dissent against Modi’s government over his 12 years in office, fuelled by existing discontent over job prospects and corruption.

Kartik Verma, 20, a student at Aligarh Muslim University, said he and his family had been staunch Modi supporters but “the arrogance of the BJP with no accountability shook my belief”.

“Despite my family’s restrictions, I still went ahead to join the protest. This was now or never for me,” Verma said, adding he would “never vote for the party again”.

Hoping to change his family’s views, Verma said he could not let them remain andhbhakts (blind devotees) of the BJP.

Asim Ali, a political analyst at the Centre for Policy Research, said it was the first time young people from the upper class and higher castes and even BJP-supporting families joined the protest.

“We haven’t seen anything like this before. Youth have become a key political demographic in India,” he said.

It has been almost 50 years since India saw such a massive student protest. In 1974, tens of thousands took part in the Jayaprakash Narayan movement, a student-led political demonstration in Bihar state decrying corruption and economic hardship.

But whether the shift in youth sentiment will translate into punishment of the BJP at the ballot box remains to be seen, according to Ali.

“Elections are fought with different strategies. Young voters may still vote based on religion, caste or regional identity,” he said, pointing to BJP’s victory in the 2024 Haryana assembly election despite a farmers’ protest three years earlier.

Dented aura

Monday’s protest began peacefully with young people holding placards, waving Indian flags and singing patriotic songs. But chaos ensued when security forces fired tear-gas shells and resorted to baton charges after protesters attempted to breach barricades around the parliament building.

Many protesters were injured in the clashes. While several received first aid at the scene, others were taken to hospital for further treatment.

After Pradhan quit on Saturday, protesters celebrated their victory, with the CJP urging supporters to disperse.

Health Minister J.P. Nadda and other officials then held a joint press conference with CJP members, with Nadda saying the government had accepted all demands of the protesters – which included exam reforms, dropping police cases against protesters and compensating families of students who died by suicide after the exam leaks.

Authorities also restored mobile internet services and resumed train services around the protest site. The concessions were a surprise as Modi is known for his hardline stance.

The CJP emerged in May after Chief Justice Surya Kant called unemployed youth and activists “cockroaches” and “parasites”. Reclaiming the slur in an act of defiance, young Indians launched the satirical CJP, a play on the ruling BJP, which gained over 22 million Instagram followers within a week.

The protest had dented the aura of Modi and the fear of the government, and could have consequences far beyond the youth demographic, said Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.

“Persistent paper leaks have killed their hope, and an unresponsive government has pushed them to the breaking point. Rising youth unemployment has added fuel to this fire,” Donthi said.

Unencumbered by the past, the youth wanted to hold the government accountable for its failures, he said.

“They are unimpressed by issues such as religious nationalism that older generations are beholden to. The deeply skewed and unfair education system in India holds the key to a better future for millions of children and their families.”

Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council, said the movement revealed the “anger” among critical masses who felt the government had ignored their grievances, particularly over youth unemployment.

The movement should serve as a warning for the Modi administration, he said.

“There have been periodic protests here and there but they have not come to the fore. With this movement, it really has come to the surface in a big way, clearly a wake-up call for the government and its large support base.”

Meme fest

To express dissent, Gen Z protesters have used Instagram Reels with hip-hop tracks, memes, irreverent humour and even jokes on Modi, attracting millions of views and drawing more young people to the movement.

The videos not only injected humour into the movement but also helped counter mainstream media portrayals that sought to frame the protests as antinational and Pakistan-backed.

During the protests, mainstream TV reporters were heckled with chants of “Godi Media” (lapdog media), prevented from filming and physically assaulted.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by India Tales | News | Memes | Culture (@thetalesindia)

Swati, 28, from Gwalior, who requested to be identified by her first name, said that her father, a BJP supporter with a Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh background, was unaware of the Monday events because he mainly relied on the mainstream media.

“I have been arguing with my father since 2017 [about the BJP] but to no avail,” said Swati.

She joined the protest over what she described as the government’s refusal to take responsibility.

“People dying due to improper infrastructure, attacks on minorities, deaths due to manual scavenging, gig workers’ accidents, unemployment, there is a lack of accountability for several problems in the nation,” Swati said.

The medical exam paper leak and subsequent police action were the last straw for Gen Z, said Anurag Minus Verma, an Indian cultural critic.

“It was then the whole idea of tear gas was fought with laughing gas – a meme warfare that young protesters used pretty well,” said the author of The Great Indian Brain Rot.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by 𝘼𝙉𝙆𝙄𝙏 (@alex.ankitt)

Verma said memes became a central part of the protest, which neither the police nor the BJP understood.

“There was a clear disconnect between Gen Z and the ruling party. [The BJP] failed to understand what Gen Z wanted and how they communicate.”

On Thursday midnight, Modi, departing from the usual practice of delivering a televised address, chose a selfie video seemingly aimed at young protesters to assure them that the government stood with them.

However, Verma argued that the BJP’s social media apparatus was behind the times, focusing on X and Facebook, rather than Instagram. BJP initiatives such as Bhajan Clubbing, a youth-driven cultural trend, and creator awards have also failed to gain traction.

“When Modi came to power in 2014, he used selfies to engage with youth. But that generation is already 12 years old, and the new generation has moved on to Instagram, where the BJP has no base,” the author said.

item.title: [SCMP] Cambodia’s war on scammers needs a blueprint built to last
item.description:
Online scams have become one of the world’s most pressing non-traditional security threats in recent years, with Southeast Asia emerging as the site of rampant transnational criminal activity.

In response, Cambodia has stepped up efforts to fight back, moving in recent months from ad hoc enforcement towards more centralised, coordinated action.

While the political will is clear, implementation is now the issue. The question is not whether Phnom Penh is fighting the war against online scams, but whether it can win it.
item.content:encoded:
Online scams have become one of the world’s most pressing non-traditional security threats in recent years, with Southeast Asia emerging as the site of rampant transnational criminal activity.

In response, Cambodia has stepped up efforts to fight back, moving in recent months from ad hoc enforcement towards more centralised, coordinated action.

While the political will is clear, implementation is now the issue. The question is not whether Phnom Penh is fighting the war against online scams, but whether it can win it.

The government has enacted the Law on Combating Online Scams, which came into force in April, to provide a dedicated legal basis for criminalising technology-enabled fraud, organised scam operations, money laundering, illegal recruitment, forced labour and related offences. In November, it established the Commission for Combating Online Scams (CCOS) as a national coordinating body to detect, disrupt and dismantle scam networks.

Between November and May, Cambodian authorities reportedly raided more than 400 locations, revoked 25 casino licences and deported around 20,000 foreign nationals linked to scam operations.

These are important steps. They show that Phnom Penh now treats online scams not only as a law-enforcement issue but as a challenge to national security, the economy, governance and its reputation.

Prime Minister Hun Manet has framed the crackdown as part of efforts to restore Cambodia’s international standing. This matters. For a country seeking investment, tourism, digital transformation and regional credibility, an association with scam compounds is costly.

Despite these efforts, however, structural challenges remain. Cambodia is unlikely to eliminate online scams entirely in the short term. It might need one more year. A more realistic objective for now is sustained disruption: breaking the chain of operations and ending impunity for the culprits.

The online scam economy endures because it adapts. Recent reporting suggests that Cambodia’s crackdown has placed real pressure on scam operators, but it has also pushed some to change tactics and locations. Their durability lies in their networks, which sit at the intersection of transnational organised crime, human trafficking, illegal gambling, money laundering, corruption, weak regulation, porous borders and digital vulnerability.

Three structural constraints stand out:

First, the scam economy is transnational. Victims may be located in Singapore or China; workers can be recruited from one country, trafficked through another and forced to operate in Cambodia. Money moves through banks, crypto wallets, informal brokers and offshore companies. Servers, platforms and messaging channels may be hosted beyond Cambodian jurisdiction.

This cross-border security threat demands cooperation, not a blame game. Cambodia and its neighbours need to share real-time intelligence, conduct joint investigations, offer mutual legal assistance and pursue extradition arrangements and coordinated victim repatriation.

Partners including China, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Vietnam and the United States have already engaged on this front. These efforts should be further institutionalised.

Second, enforcement must move up the chain. Arresting frontline scammers or even ringleaders is insufficient if the landlords, recruiters, forgers, telecoms providers, payment intermediaries, financiers and others above them are not apprehended.

A serious crackdown requires a whole-of-system approach: tracing assets, enhancing oversight of company registries, regulating casinos and real estate, and strengthening financial and telecoms compliance – paired with consistent law enforcement, transparent reporting and space for public scrutiny. Some of these measures have been inclusively implemented but they need to be more coherent and systemic.

Third, credibility depends on transparency. International partners will not assess the sincerity of Cambodia’s crackdown based solely on official statements; they will look for verifiable outcomes.

CCOS has shared regular reports with key stakeholders and the general public, but it needs to offer more independent verification where possible. Cambodia has cooperated with embassies and victim-support groups and the government has claimed that prosecutions proceed regardless of a suspect’s social standing or connections. The message should be clear here: nobody is above the law.

A victim-centred outlook is equally essential. Screening procedures should distinguish between commanders of vast scam networks and the coerced foot soldiers beneath them. The latter need safe shelters, translation services, consular access, legal assistance, medical support and pathways for repatriation.

A more durable strategy should combine five tracks.

Command coordination: CCOS must be empowered to serve as a permanent national secretariat with real authority to coordinate law enforcement, immigration, justice, telecoms, banking, local administration and foreign affairs. A long-term war against scams requires such an approach.

Legal enforcement: the new law must be tested through serious prosecutions, especially of organisers and financiers. Convictions will matter more than arrests.

Financial disruption: Cambodia should target money flows, including cryptocurrencies, freeze suspicious assets, monitor high-risk real estate and casino-linked transactions, and strengthen cooperation between banks, payment providers and financial intelligence units.

Border and digital governance: border checkpoints, visa records, work permits, telecoms registration, internet service provision and company licensing should be integrated into a risk-based monitoring system.

International cooperation: Cambodia needs to further enhance cooperation and coordination with regional and global partners to crack down on online scams. Hosting the international conference on combating online scams in September demonstrates Cambodia’s efforts to promote international cooperation while creating a platform for sharing information and best practices.

Can Cambodia eradicate online scams? Not completely, and certainly not quickly. The criminal ecosystem is too mobile, too profitable and too transnational. Even countries with stronger institutions struggle to stamp out cyber-enabled fraud. As the Khmer Times has argued, Cambodia’s campaign against online scams is a major test of state capacity, law enforcement and the culture of accountability.

But Cambodia can do something more practical and politically meaningful. It can make itself inhospitable to scam networks, close off the space for impunity, raise the operational costs and protect victims. It must demonstrate that enforcement reaches every layer of the criminal enterprises and, in doing so, convert a reputational crisis into a governance reform agenda, transforming its image from a country ridden by online scams to a source of best practices for others.

The government’s call for an unrelenting crackdown on online scams must now be matched by concrete outcomes. The political will is clear, but implementation capacity remains the decisive test.

Dr Chheang Vannarith is Visiting Senior Fellow at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. This article was first published by the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesia’s Bali financial hub ‘a matter of survival’: economic tsar
item.description:
Bali has “aura” and political titan Luhut Pandjaitan wants to channel it to transform Indonesia’s famed resort island into an international financial centre.

But President Prabowo Subianto’s special adviser and economic tsar is not relying on subtle nods to Gen Z slang to sell paradise. Instead, he conjures up a striking image to make his case.

A friend recently sent him a photograph of kamikaze drones lighting up the skies over Abu Dhabi, accompanied by a plea: help us get out.
item.content:encoded:
Bali has “aura” and political titan Luhut Pandjaitan wants to channel it to transform Indonesia’s famed resort island into an international financial centre.

But President Prabowo Subianto’s special adviser and economic tsar is not relying on subtle nods to Gen Z slang to sell paradise. Instead, he conjures up a striking image to make his case.

A friend recently sent him a photograph of kamikaze drones lighting up the skies over Abu Dhabi, accompanied by a plea: help us get out.

Indonesia, safely removed from the Iran war’s turmoil, was the obvious choice, he said.

“They said ‘We’d like to move our assets, we’d love very much to stay away from here and live in Bali, because it’s so peaceful in Bali’,” he recalled. “The Middle East conflict is not going to end next month or next year, I don’t believe that.”

Speaking to This Week in Asia on the sidelines of the Nusa Dua Forum in Bali on July 17, the 78-year-old chairman of Indonesia’s National Economic Council was a study in moustachioed calm – a far cry from the crisis of confidence that has roiled Southeast Asia’s largest economy this year.

For us … it’s a matter of survival

Luhut Pandjaitan, National Economic Council chairman

Investors, spooked by scepticism over Prabowo’s populist policies and rattled further by a global energy crisis that sent fuel prices soaring, have pulled billions out of Indonesia in recent months.

Acknowledging the market rout and concerns over money laundering, Luhut pledged greater transparency and to stamp out corruption.

“Without this, it’s very hard to gain trust and credibility,” he said, going on to describe the financial hub in existential terms. “For us … it’s a matter of survival.”

On Tuesday, Indonesia’s parliament passed legislation paving the way for the new financial centre just 20 days after talks on it had first begun.

Its precise location and the full range of associated incentives are still under wraps, but Luhut says the legislative speed should come as no surprise – he first floated the idea two years ago.

The centre could be up and running as soon as next month, he said, hinting that Prabowo might time an official announcement to coincide with the country’s independence day on August 17.

Instead of Indonesia’s civil code, the centre will operate under international commercial law, according to Luhut, who drew a parallel with Hong Kong.

“It’s like one country, two systems,” he said. “Which is not the ideal … But the purpose is to improve the credibility and trust of Indonesia.”

Sceptical of the notion that only Singapore, Hong Kong or the United Arab Emirates could host such hubs, Luhut said he had consulted a range of investors – from American hedge fund manager Ray Dalio to the Porsche family – and found them in agreement.

“They said they love the aura of Bali,” he quipped.

Separately, at the forum – co-organised by the South China Morning Post and Indonesian sovereign wealth fund Danantara – Indonesia’s former coordinating minister of maritime and investment repeated his pitch to a room filled with officials, investors and family office principals.

“We’re going to be very transparent. We’re going to be more efficient, there’s going to be less corruption,” he declared. “I’m pretty confident about that.”

Unshaken optimism

Luhut’s optimism does not end at the new international financial centre. He is convinced Indonesia’s digitalisation push and its young, skilled workforce can deliver Prabowo’s target of lifting economic growth from 5 to 8 per cent by 2029.

“I think 8 per cent – with digital infrastructure support, artificial intelligence and also with the family offices – I don’t think it’s a big deal,” he said, brushing off economists’ scepticism.

Technological progress over the past few years had been nothing short of “beautiful”, Luhut said, outlining how data collected from eight government ministries and major institutions now fed into an AI-supported system to drive efficiency gains.

“Indonesia will be different within two years,” he vowed, referring to a local “brain and talent factory” he founded where students are selected based on IQ scores and put through a curated curriculum.

Addressing the prevailing gloom surrounding coverage of Indonesia’s economy and policies, Luhut blamed a failure of messaging and argued that there was an information disconnect between the government and the public.

Earlier this year, global index provider MSCI warned it could downgrade Indonesia from emerging to frontier market status amid concerns over transparency and stock market manipulation. A May deadline it set to see signs of progress has since been pushed back to November.

A brighter spot came earlier this month, when S&P reaffirmed Jakarta’s sovereign credit rating, forecasting that recent financial strains would ease thanks to higher commodity prices and spending cuts.

The government projects its budget shortfall to widen to 2.85 per cent of gross domestic product this year, just shy of the 3 per cent statutory ceiling. Prabowo’s flagship free meals programme – a cornerstone of his populist economic agenda – has drawn much of the flak for exacting a heavy toll on state finances since its launch in January 2025.

On Tuesday, the programme’s budget was slashed again – now reduced by more than 100 trillion rupiah (US$5.6 billion) from its original allocation – and the agency chief charged with overseeing it resigned a day later, citing health reasons.

Luhut defended the scheme as essential to inclusive growth and insisted the administration had committed to making it more “targeted” by focusing on remote areas.

“You have to adjust, because every province faces a different situation,” he said.

Indonesia’s troubleshooter

Luhut’s current role is just the latest chapter in a political and business career spanning four decades.

A former four-star army general, he first entered politics as Indonesia started its transition to democracy in the late 1990s, before stepping away several years later to build a business empire in energy, minerals and coal.

He returned in 2014 after helping finance Joko Widodo’s successful presidential campaign that year, becoming his chief of staff – a newly created position – and trusted troubleshooter, later spearheading both Indonesia’s downstreaming strategy and its pandemic response.

Also Widodo’s point man on China, Luhut called Jakarta-Beijing relations “very good”, revealing plans for an impending meeting between Prabowo and around 20 Chinese firms invested in Indonesia.

In May, Chinese businesses had raised concerns about Jakarta’s rising levies and stricter enforcement, with several Indonesian ministers pushing back, insisting the country must prioritise sovereignty over its natural resources.

To avoid misunderstandings, Luhut said Prabowo’s relationship with Chinese leader Xi Jinping had to become “much closer”.

“I said to the president, the biggest investor in this country is still China, whether you like it or not,” he said, noting that Beijing was “very willing” to share its technology and research capabilities.

Prabowo’s stricter demands of tycoons – including a plan to funnel proceeds from palm oil exports and other key resources through sovereign wealth fund Danantara to curb under-invoicing – has further unnerved investors, but Luhut shrugs off the unease.

“This country, with a 300 million population, it’s not easy to govern,” he said. “But we explain to them that the best time to invest in Indonesia is today.”

During the 2024 presidential election, when Luhut backed Prabowo’s campaign, he declined any ministerial post, opting instead to remain an adviser, according to state news agency Antara.

Asked about Widodo’s surprise return to the political stage this year – touring the country to support his son Kaesang Pangarep’s Solidarity Party – Luhut was philosophical,

“Jokowi is still active because, of course, he has to survive,” he said, referring to the former president by his popular nickname. “Otherwise, if you retire fully, it’s easy to get very old.”

Luhut described urging both presidents to maintain a harmonious relationship for the country’s sake, which Widodo did in 2019 when he made former electoral rival Prabowo his defence minister.

“He was my deputy, and now he’s my boss,” Luhut said of the current president. “If it’s just the two of us, we talk in a very relaxed way. But I still respect him, because this is an institution. And we have to respect that.”

For a man widely seen as one of Indonesia’s most influential unelected figures, Luhut professes being content with his position just beneath the summit of power.

“I’m happy with what I am. That’s my destiny,” he said. “Everything under this sky, whatever it is, I try to contribute as much as I can because I love this country.”

Fittingly, he closed his pitch to investors at the Nusa Dua summit not with numbers, but a feeling. “You’ll never get bored in Bali,” Luhut said. “Whenever I land in Bali I can feel friendliness, harmony and hope.”

item.title: [SCMP] What is Beijing thinking? Why Washington is struggling to understand its rival
item.description:
After Donald Trump’s high-stakes summit with Xi Jinping in May, the idea of US-China “strategic stability” appeared in readouts from both sides.

While the White House framed this vision as a “constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of fairness and reciprocity”, Beijing said only that it was a “constructive bilateral relationship of strategic stability”.

China watchers zoomed in on the phrase – especially the Chinese version – debating what it could reveal or conceal about Beijing’s long-term ambitions.
item.content:encoded:
After Donald Trump’s high-stakes summit with Xi Jinping in May, the idea of US-China “strategic stability” appeared in readouts from both sides.

While the White House framed this vision as a “constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of fairness and reciprocity”, Beijing said only that it was a “constructive bilateral relationship of strategic stability”.

China watchers zoomed in on the phrase – especially the Chinese version – debating what it could reveal or conceal about Beijing’s long-term ambitions.

The episode highlights the importance of language in US-China diplomacy. And according to analysts, while Beijing has become better equipped linguistically to parse American strategy, the US is struggling to do the same.

They put that down to funding cuts to language programmes in America as well as dwindling student exchanges and less interest in learning Chinese.

The result is a disjointed network of government programmes, think tanks and independent researchers seeking to translate and interpret China’s latest moves.

Analysts say that fragmentation could make it harder for Washington to understand its most critical bilateral relationship.

“A decline in government support and interest among American students leaves a major gap in Chinese language capabilities,” according to Kyle Chan, a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Centre at the Brookings Institution.

“This could lead to a wider gap in understanding China.”

Since Trump’s return to the White House, numerous federal language programmes have been disrupted.

Overseas fellowships such as the State Department’s Critical Language Scholarship have seen funding interrupted, while programmes including the National Resource Centre and Foreign Language and Area Studies – which provided millions of dollars in grants, tuition and stipends for university students nationwide – have been halted.

However, defence-centric initiatives under the Pentagon’s Defence Language and National Security Education Office have been largely preserved.

Similarly, language training through the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Office of the Director of National Intelligence and Central Intelligence Agency remains funded, though some programmes face operational bottlenecks due to tightened security clearance.

Shengyu Wang, a researcher at the Asia Society Policy Institute, noted that defence-related language programmes were important but he said a wider approach was needed.

“Language knowledge should not be built only around defence needs,” Wang said. “If civilian language programmes weaken, Washington may lose the broader cultural, historical, political and social knowledge needed to interpret China as a system.”

A bipartisan group of US lawmakers attempted to establish a civilian language centre in 2024 through the Open Translation Centre Act.

The legislation aimed to set up a separate, federally funded research centre tasked with locating, translating and analysing open-source materials. The bill noted that “a lack of foreign language speakers greatly hinders US policymakers, academics, students and others’ ability to understand China and other nations”. But the legislation stalled in Congress.

Rosie Levine, executive director of the US-China Education Trust, said fewer than 2,000 Americans were currently studying in China – a dramatic drop from around 11,000 in 2019.

Conversely, more than 265,000 Chinese students were enrolled in US universities during the 2024-25 academic year.

She said factors including China’s pandemic-era visa restrictions, geopolitical tensions and higher travel costs had contributed to the decline and warned that recent funding cuts could worsen the situation.

“If that trend continues … the US will face a critical shortage of grounded China expertise within a decade,” Levine said.

Apart from fewer student exchanges, Beijing has also imposed tighter controls on Western researchers and journalists in China as the focus on national security and geopolitics intensifies.

With their access to China limited, Washington think tanks and policy analysts have turned to translating and analysing open-source official texts to try to work out Beijing’s thinking.

In recent years, leading research organisations have launched translation-specific initiatives with support from both the federal government and private foundations.

One significant example is the Council on Foreign Relations. Its China Strategy Initiative features a dedicated database called the China Open Source Observatory – a project launched in 2024 that aims to translate key Chinese official papers and policy documents, with a collection that spans from 1990 to 2023.

The initiative asserts that the “future of Western-China relations now rests on open-source analysis” and notes that the project bridges the translation gap by “locating, translating and annotating documents of historic or strategic value that are currently only available in Chinese”.

It also makes use of artificial intelligence, involving engineers from Anthropic and Google to optimise large language models for translation. Through this partnership, it claims to have achieved “near-perfect accuracy” when translating military and diplomatic texts.

Georgetown University’s Centre for Security and Emerging Technology meanwhile maintains a “discovery tool” for Chinese-language news and commentary on technology issues, with more than 5,000 articles featuring analysis on AI, quantum technology and aerospace.

Individual Substack accounts such as Pekingnology, The East is Read and Sinification are also actively involved in translating and analysing Chinese-language material.

Sourabh Gupta, a resident senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies, argued that while some of these efforts were welcome, “current initiatives are scattershot and lack a certain coherence”.

“Unless presented coherently, systematically and consistently, these translation initiatives will, more or less, lack purchase and resonance within the consuming community,” he said.

However, Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute said “some degree of fragmentation is natural”. He said the real challenge was “when translations circulate without enough explanation of method or context”.

A debate over context arose in October when the Rand Corporation – a Washington think tank mainly funded by the Pentagon – released and then quickly withdrew a 115-page report accusing prominent Washington-based experts with Chinese skills of “hawkish” distortions of Beijing’s terminology.

The study, titled “Stabilising the US-China Rivalry”, warned that several analysts – including Rush Doshi, director of the China Strategy Initiative and a former National Security Council official in the Joe Biden administration – had translated Chinese terms with “more hawkish English alternatives than the original Chinese language sources may imply”.

The report highlighted a specific example from a 2021 book by Doshi, which translated the Chinese phrase xianshouqi as “offensive moves”.

It argued that Doshi had overstated the phrase’s significance to claim Beijing’s strategy was more assertive than it was, noting it is actually a board game metaphor that literally means “first hand” and contextually translates to “taking the initiative”.

In response, Doshi said the paper had engaged in “creative conceptual reinterpretation”.

“In most cases they muster only 200 words of critique against several thousands words of my own empirical support, which is a bit superficial,” he wrote on social media.

The report was swiftly taken down and replaced with a note saying: “This document has been withdrawn for further review.”

Gupta from the Institute for China-America Studies said that if the goals of translation were narrow and “almost ulterior” it would reinforce a more skewed and “securitised beltway view of China”.

“The end purpose of translation is not to reinforce a view of China as the ‘other’; rather, it should be to obtain a more objective assessment of China,” he said.

But Wang noted that China’s official language “often creates room for several plausible interpretations”.
