“A phrase can be linguistically accurate but politically incomplete … China’s political system is difficult to read by design,” he said.

“Its official language is formal, repetitive, coded and often intentionally ambiguous. That ambiguity gives the leadership flexibility and helps it speak to different audiences at once.”

Chan of the Brookings Institution – who has also compiled a public database of Chinese government documents – emphasised that the undertaking would always be an “imperfect project”.

“There will always be some degree of selection bias in terms of which voices get translated and read by American audiences. At the same time, it’s much better to translate a limited selection of important texts rather than to leave a vacuum of understanding,” he added.

For Levine from the US-China Education Trust, translation efforts were “better than nothing”, but she said there was no substitute for on-the-ground experience.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Singapore PM Wong moved swiftly on Faishal Ibrahim’s resignation
item.description:
Singapore’s acting minister-in-charge of Muslim affairs Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim resigned about a month after the prime minister learned of his improper interactions with a woman, a move observers say shows Lawrence Wong’s swift handling of the first scandal under his watch to contain any political fallout.

They told This Week in Asia that while there was no affair in Faishal’s case, it made sense for the party to deal with the consequences quickly in case of leaks as the woman was a member of the public, not a party member whom the ruling People’s Action Party (PAP) could counsel or discipline.

Furthermore, Faishal’s position as acting minister-in-charge of Muslim affairs meant Wong had to be sensitive to the community’s reaction – and potential embarrassment – if the matter was not swiftly extinguished and a replacement sought for the post.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore’s acting minister-in-charge of Muslim affairs Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim resigned about a month after the prime minister learned of his improper interactions with a woman, a move observers say shows Lawrence Wong’s swift handling of the first scandal under his watch to contain any political fallout.

They told This Week in Asia that while there was no affair in Faishal’s case, it made sense for the party to deal with the consequences quickly in case of leaks as the woman was a member of the public, not a party member whom the ruling People’s Action Party (PAP) could counsel or discipline.

Furthermore, Faishal’s position as acting minister-in-charge of Muslim affairs meant Wong had to be sensitive to the community’s reaction – and potential embarrassment – if the matter was not swiftly extinguished and a replacement sought for the post.

On Monday, Faishal resigned from the cabinet and parliament after inappropriate interactions he had with a woman that resulted in harassment accusations by both parties became known to the prime minister.

No criminal action was found but Faishal, 58, who was also senior minister of state for home affairs, reflected and accepted that his conduct fell short of the standards “expected of a political office holder and MP”, Wong said in a statement on Monday.

Wong revealed that most of their interactions took place through online messages and they also met on the sidelines of public events. Both parties later made allegations of harassment against each other, and the matter was referred to police.

Faishal, who is married with two children, wrote in his resignation letter from government and his party: “While there was no physical relationship between us, and I did not intend for the interactions to develop into one, there was a lapse of judgment on my part in the way I handled the interactions, and in failing to establish clearer boundaries at an earlier stage.”

Faishal’s case inevitably drew comparisons with another explosive revelation in July 2023, when former speaker of parliament Tan Chuan-Jin and MP Cheng Li Hui, both from the PAP, resigned from their positions after being in an extramarital affair.

Political observers noted the much shorter timeline in Wong’s handling of Faishal’s resignation compared with the affair between Tan and Cheng, which then prime minister Lee Hsien Loong found out about after the 2020 general election, at least two years before they stepped down in 2023.

Lee said in a press conference in July 2023 that as recently as February that year, he had counselled the lawmakers involved to end it. Tan offered his resignation then, but Lee said he told him to ensure his constituents were taken care of first and that the affair had to end.

Lee added then that he had “very recently” come across information strongly suggesting the pair’s relationship had continued.

Teo Kay Key, senior research fellow at the Institute of Policy Studies, noted that the full details of Faishal’s interactions were unknown, making comparisons difficult. However, the difference in timelines was “quite clear”, perhaps reflecting lessons learned from the public reaction to Tan’s affair, she said.

“Of course, given that the woman had sent details to the PMO [Prime Minister’s Office] and also that both parties had actually made harassment allegations, there is a possibility that the news would have gotten out from other channels and that it would have been more expedient to deal with the whole matter swiftly,” Teo said.

While the details of the relationship were scant and what actually happened was unclear, Teo added that this incident, taken together with the previous resignations, revealed the PAP’s expectations for how its MPs and political office holders should behave in their personal relationships and how this would affect their political careers.

Independent political analyst Felix Tan raised concern that the lack of details could lead to greater public speculation online.

He said Wong was not being stricter than his predecessor but wanted to stem the damage early instead of letting it “evolve into something greater that he has to deal with in the future”.

“One possible question that may arise is whether Faishal’s decision to step down was intended to bring the matter to a close, particularly if there was concern that it could become public or be pursued further. While there is no evidence to support such a conclusion, it is the kind of question that may emerge in the absence of greater clarity,” Felix Tan said.

He also noted that Leader of the House Indranee Rajah had earlier this year stressed integrity and honesty regarding Workers’ Party chief Pritam Singh’s conviction for lying to a parliamentary committee, and this was a reflection of how the PAP believed parliamentarians should conduct themselves.

Former nominated MP (NMP) Calvin Cheng wrote on social media that Faishal should not resign since he did not have an affair. “One has to balance losing a good minister/MP with small failings that all human beings have,” Cheng said.

Walid Jumblatt Abdullah, an associate professor of public policy at Nanyang Technological University, said on social media that given what was known about the interactions, he did not believe Faishal had to resign and that impossible standards were being set that would deter young people from politics.

“The criteria I would use is: is Singapore better off today than yesterday? I think the answer is no. He was a good minister for the country,” Walid said.

Yet Zulkifli Baharudin, a former NMP, told This Week in Asia that the office of Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs had to be held to a higher standard.

“The institution of the Muslim minister is a very peculiar one,” he said. “It’s one that’s based on preserving the dignity and the position of Malay Muslims in Singapore and Lawrence Wong must treat the institution of Muslim minister very sensitively so even a minor indiscretion will not be tolerated.”

While some might not consider Faishal’s actions a big or serious deal, Zulkifli noted that the prime minister was taking an uncompromising and high standard expected of the minister-in-charge of Muslim affairs, which would strengthen the institution in the long run.

“It is a tragedy and the community is embarrassed and upset. But one, this is human failure and two, at the end of the day, this will strengthen the institution. This is not just another ministry, it reflects the standing and position of Malay Muslims in Singapore,” Zulkifli said.

Faishal, who has a PhD in management science, entered politics in 2006 in the then Marine Parade group representation constituency following an uncontested walkover.

He was appointed minister of state for national development and home affairs in 2020 and replaced Masagos Zulkifli as acting minister-in-charge of Muslim affairs following the 2025 election, when he was also co-opted into the central executive committee of the ruling PAP.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s survival strategies written in flavours
item.description:
The first time I ate proper Sichuan food in Chengdu, my mouth went numb. Not spicy-numb. Anaesthetised numb, like a dentist had been at my tongue with lignocaine. The waiter saw my face and laughed. “Málà,” he said. Numbing spicy: the specific sensation of Sichuan peppercorn meeting chilli oil, a flavour combination so particular to this basin-locked province that there’s no English word for it.

I look Chinese and I should appreciate this, except I am not quite. What I didn’t understand then, eating my way through a bowl of mapo tofu while my face leaked involuntary tears, was that I wasn’t experiencing cuisine. I was experiencing climate adaptation disguised as dinner.

Sichuan is a basin. Humid, isolated, subtropical. Before refrigeration, before modern preservation, the question wasn’t “what tastes good?” The question was “how do we stop food rotting in 90 per cent humidity while we’re eating it?” The answer: you overwhelm. You use so much chilli and peppercorn that bacteria doesn’t stand a chance. You pickle everything that can be pickled. You dry what can be dried. You ferment what’s left. The intensity isn’t indulgence, it’s necessity turned into culture over 2,000 years.
item.content:encoded:
The first time I ate proper Sichuan food in Chengdu, my mouth went numb. Not spicy-numb. Anaesthetised numb, like a dentist had been at my tongue with lignocaine. The waiter saw my face and laughed. “Málà,” he said. Numbing spicy: the specific sensation of Sichuan peppercorn meeting chilli oil, a flavour combination so particular to this basin-locked province that there’s no English word for it.

I look Chinese and I should appreciate this, except I am not quite. What I didn’t understand then, eating my way through a bowl of mapo tofu while my face leaked involuntary tears, was that I wasn’t experiencing cuisine. I was experiencing climate adaptation disguised as dinner.

Sichuan is a basin. Humid, isolated, subtropical. Before refrigeration, before modern preservation, the question wasn’t “what tastes good?” The question was “how do we stop food rotting in 90 per cent humidity while we’re eating it?” The answer: you overwhelm. You use so much chilli and peppercorn that bacteria doesn’t stand a chance. You pickle everything that can be pickled. You dry what can be dried. You ferment what’s left. The intensity isn’t indulgence, it’s necessity turned into culture over 2,000 years.

This is what Chinese food actually is, once you strip away the romanticisation and the “gastroporn” and the idea that cuisine is primarily about pleasure. It’s a historical record of what people needed to survive, written in flavour.

The basin: Sichuan’s humidity problem

Sichuan sits in a depression surrounded by mountains, with the Tibetan Plateau to the west, the Qinling range to the north. Moisture gets trapped. The air stays thick. In summer, it’s a greenhouse. In winter, it’s a damp cold that seeps into your bones and won’t leave. This creates a preservation crisis that coastal and northern China don’t face. Food spoils faster, mould is constant, storage is a battle against biology. So, Sichuan cooking became aggressive: doubanjiang (fermented broad-bean paste) by the handful, and hotpot, where everything gets boiled in chilli oil hot enough to sterilise on contact.

The food overwhelms your senses because it had to overwhelm microbes first.

I’ve eaten mapo tofu in London, in Singapore, in Chinese restaurants across three continents. It’s never the same as eating it in Chengdu, where the humidity is 85 per cent and your clothes never quite dry and the málà makes sense as something other than a flavour preference. Twice-cooked pork, dan dan noodles, fish-fragrant aubergine – every signature Sichuan dish follows the same logic: bold flavours that mask spoilage, high heat that kills bacteria, preservation techniques that buy time.

This is survival cuisine that became so successful it convinced the world it was always about pleasure.

The coast: Cantonese confidence

If Sichuan cuisine is about fighting humidity, Cantonese food is about not needing to fight anything.

Guangzhou sits at the Pearl River Delta, where river meets ocean, where trade brought wealth and wealth brought abundance, and abundance produced restraint. When you can get fresh fish daily, when vegetables grow year-round, you don’t need to preserve anything because tomorrow will bring more.

Cantonese cooking is quiet. Steaming, not frying. Light soy, not heavy bean paste. Ginger and spring onion, not chilli oil. The food doesn’t shout because it doesn’t need to. I’ve watched how Cantonese cooks prepare fish; steamed whole, soy sauce drizzled, nothing else. The point is showing off the fish, proving it’s so fresh that anything more would be vandalism. This is prosperity cuisine, abundance cuisine, cuisine that says, “we’re so secure, we can afford to do nothing”.

Dim sum, the elaborately folded dumplings, the delicate shrimp har gow, the translucent rice rolls, is restraint dressed as complexity. It is maximum technique applied to minimal ingredients, showing skill through precision rather than force. The Cantonese saying goes, “eat in Guangzhou”, not because the flavours are loudest, but because they’re truest. Coastal confidence written in steamed fish and morning yum cha.

The plateau: Shaanxi’s arid survival

Shaanxi province is characterised by yellow earth, cold winters, not enough water, wheat instead of rice because rice needs irrigation, the plateau can’t provide. This is northern China and the food reflects it: heavy, durable, built to fuel physical labour in cold, dry air where every calorie counts.

It gives us biang biang noodles, hand-pulled, wide as belts, served with chilli oil and vinegar because that’s what you’ve got and that’s what stores; roujiamo, flatbread stuffed with slow-cooked meat, eaten by hand, portable fuel; yangrou paomo, mutton soup with torn bread, eaten for breakfast when you need 2,000 calories before you start work.

I ate biang biang noodles in a tiny restaurant in Xian’s Muslim Quarter, watching the cook slap dough against a metal table until it stretched into noodles 60cm (two feet) long. The sound echoed off the walls – biang biang biang – which is supposedly how the dish got its name. The character for biang (𰻝) has 58 strokes and isn’t in standard dictionaries because it was invented by illiterate noodle sellers who needed a word for the sound. The noodles were thick, chewy, coated in chilli oil and vinegar, topped with vegetables and a bit of pork. Not delicate or subtle. Just: here’s wheat, here’s heat, here’s what keeps you upright when the plateau cold tries to put you down.

Shaanxi food is northern Chinese pragmatism rendered edible. It values sustenance over pleasure, durability over delicacy, survival over refinement.

The delta: Jiangnan’s sweet abundance

South of Shaanxi, east of Sichuan, you get Jiangnan, which sits “south of the Yangtze”, centred on Suzhou and Hangzhou – waterways, fertile land, relative peace for centuries. The scholar-official class developed here. The imperial examination system produced more successful candidates from Jiangnan than anywhere else. This is where Chinese literati culture comprising painting, poetry, gardens and aesthetic refinement grew the deepest roots.

The food reflects that. Jiangnan cuisine is subtly sweet, using sugar to balance rather than dominate. Think of xiaolongbao – soup dumplings in which the broth is delicately flavoured, not aggressively seasoned, and West Lake vinegar fish from Hangzhou – sweet-sour, restrained. This is cuisine developed by people who had time to think about aesthetics, who had enough security to value harmony and balance over intensity. When you’re not fighting for survival, you can afford elegance.

I ate xiaolongbao in a Shanghai restaurant where each dumpling was folded with 18 pleats, not because 18 is functionally necessary, but because 18 is the traditional number and tradition matters when you’re performing refinement rather than just feeding people.

Jiangnan food is what happens when prosperity lasts long enough to become culture.

The freeze: Dongbei’s preservation imperative

Finally, there’s the northeast: Manchuria, where winter lasts six months and temperatures hit minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit), and the question isn’t “how do we keep food fresh?” but “how do we keep food at all?” The answer: you pickle. You ferment. You preserve everything possible in autumn because nothing grows between November and April.

Pickled cabbage, fermented in massive jars, stored for winter, the base of dozens of Dongbei dishes. Stews that cook all day because when it’s minus 30 degrees Celsius outside, the stove stays on anyway. Dumplings filled with pork and cabbage, boiled in vast quantities, frozen outside, retrieved as needed.

This is the cuisine of cold-climate survival. The food is heavy, repetitive, calorically dense. You’re not eating for pleasure, you’re eating to generate body heat, to maintain function, to survive until spring.

I visited Harbin in January, when everything was frozen solid. Beautiful and profoundly cold. The locals were eating hotpot at outdoor tables, wearing three layers, drinking baijiu to stay warm. The food was pure fuel. When I asked a Harbin native what defined Dongbei cuisine, she said: “We eat what doesn’t freeze.”

What the food reveals

Together, these five cuisines cover the fundamental climates and geographies that shaped how a billion people eat.

Each cuisine is a survival strategy that worked so well it became culture. Once it’s culture, wrapped in tradition and nostalgia and regional pride, it stops looking like adaptation and starts looking like identity.

Chinese food isn’t mysterious. It’s just geography rendered edible, climate written in flavour, history you can taste if you know what you’re tasting for. Every dish becomes a climate map, every regional speciality a survival footnote, every meal a reminder that culture is just successful adaptation given enough time to forget it was adaptation in the first place.

This is an exclusive essay by Lu-Ann Ong, whose forthcoming book, Experience China: What Maps Don’t Tell, explores contemporary China through landscape, cuisine, history and memory.

item.title: [SCMP] Black Lake CEO’s strategy to sell AI solutions to factories: turn to food couriers
item.description:
When Zhou Yuxiang, founder and CEO of Shanghai-headquartered Black Lake Technologies, wanted to sell his artificial intelligence (AI) automation solutions to millions of family-run factories across China, he came up with an unconventional strategy: hiring food delivery workers to make sales.

His entire sales team, hired from various industrial cities, survived a gruelling five-day boot camp on articulating how AI can solve specific manufacturing pain points.

“They are very street-smart,” the 36-year-old said in an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post. “Good college graduates are often thin-skinned. They linger in front of a factory and can’t get in.
item.content:encoded:
When Zhou Yuxiang, founder and CEO of Shanghai-headquartered Black Lake Technologies, wanted to sell his artificial intelligence (AI) automation solutions to millions of family-run factories across China, he came up with an unconventional strategy: hiring food delivery workers to make sales.

His entire sales team, hired from various industrial cities, survived a gruelling five-day boot camp on articulating how AI can solve specific manufacturing pain points.

“They are very street-smart,” the 36-year-old said in an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post. “Good college graduates are often thin-skinned. They linger in front of a factory and can’t get in.

“But for food delivery guys, they just give a cigarette to the security guard and get in … They can also bypass guard dogs, or find a back door to get into a factory to meet the owner because they deliver food.”

With a sales force of more than 420 delivery workers, Black Lake, established in 2016, has grown to serve 35,000 factory clients, 95 per cent of which are small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

The International Data Corporation also ranks it as mainland China’s top provider of cloud-based production management software.

Hong Kong ‘very attractive’ for next step

This success earned Zhou an invitation to meet Premier Li Qiang in October last year to brief him on how to use agentic AI to digitise the backbone of the mainland’s economy against the backdrop of technological self-reliance as a key goal for the next five-year plan.

To Zhou, the key factor that will determine the country’s competitiveness in manufacturing is how to make nearly 5 million manufacturing SMEs and factories agile, flexible and able to swiftly respond to market demands.

By launching tailored products for them in 2021, what began as a socially responsible initiative has evolved into a highly profitable business with more than 100 per cent annual growth providing cloud-based software-as-a-service.

At the Nusa Dua Forum in Bali organised by the SCMP, Zhou said Black Lake would soon expand into Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines later this year.

The emerging tech company currently has a reported valuation exceeding 7 billion yuan (US$1 billion). While Zhou remained tight-lipped on whether the business had plans to list in Hong Kong, he acknowledged the allure of the financial hub.

“We’re born in China, but we’re going global. I think capital market-wise, Hong Kong has attracted the smartest and most diverse group of international savvy investors who can appreciate our value, who can see our potential, and their long-term positioning rather than short-term arbitrage,” he said in his first interview with a Hong Kong media outlet.

“If we move to the next stage, I think Hong Kong is a very attractive place.”

He also revealed that Black Lake was collaborating with two universities in Hong Kong on AI and supply chain research, describing scholars in the city as “world-class” and possessing a “global vision and understanding of China”.

From ‘cheap and good’ to on-demand produce

Zhou said that Black Lake was expanding across China, going from its traditional coastal industrial strongholds, including the Yangtze and Pearl River Deltas, into inland provinces such as Sichuan, Hebei and Hubei.

“The booming e-commerce market gave Chinese consumers a much stronger voice on what they want,” the Dartmouth College alumnus said.

A common theme he spotted among small businesses was that they all needed supply chains that could react instantly to address niche, fast-changing demands.

But he noted that such businesses lacked the know-how, while sizeable enterprises had heavily relied on Western players for industrial automation.

“In China, there is a paradigm shift from just making things ‘cheap and good’ to producing based on real-time demand,” he said. “It’s beyond the human brain … That’s why AI technologies and digital tools come into play.”

Among its popular products for SMEs were mini-programs that allow workers to simply scan bar codes in a factory via WeChat to trigger tasks, and wearables to digitise shop floors.

He observed that two more trends accelerated the rapid adoption of AI in mainland manufacturing: the trade war-related restructuring of global supply chains and a rapidly ageing workforce of veteran factory managers.

“We are building AI brains to replace these retiring workers to continue the miracle of the Chinese manufacturing sector,” he said.

Agility in action: two success stories

Those partnered with Black Lake to rewire manufacturing with AI ranged from giant chains to family-run businesses.

One of its largest clients was beverage chain Mixue Bingcheng. In 2018, founder Zhang Hongchao set his sights on overseas expansion but wanted to deviate from the standardised menu model of competitors such as Starbucks.

He required the company to roll out five to six new flavours every month without facing stock-outs on popular items.

By digitising their supply chain – from farm to processing to logistics – with the help of Black Lake, Mixue achieved the agility needed to scale globally. The beverage brand now has nearly 60,000 stores worldwide.

Zhou said another smaller yet telling example was a plastic packaging factory in Suzhou.

Founded in the 1990s, the parents’ generation relied on massive, predictable bulk orders such as lipstick tubes from traditional giants, including L’Oreal and Unilever. But margins were squeezed as cheaper labour emerged in Southeast Asia.

Zhou said that when the factory founder’s daughter took over, she realised that they could not predict the market a year ahead or produce the same thing all year round. She instead pivoted to serve smaller e-commerce cosmetics brands.

Black Lake’s CEO said these brands demanded tiny initial batches, for example, 10,000 units instead of 300,000, but required the factory to ramp up production within five days if a product went viral on TikTok.

By equipping workers with wearable devices guided by real-time data, the factory eliminated reliance on human guesswork for material transfers. They squeezed line-changeover idle times from six hours down to just one hour.

“Previously, the dad only gave the daughter 5 per cent capacity for those agile orders … When we visited them two years ago, 60 per cent of the orders were agile orders,” he said. “If you only produce standardised products, you very quickly lose the market.”

The future: AI’s ‘Google moment’

As mainland companies expand overseas, Zhou argued that agility was even more valuable than improving efficiency, while agentic AI – capable of real-time, data-driven decisions – could also bridge cultural divides.

Despite these advancements, the entrepreneur said he believed the AI industry was only just getting started.

“If we compare AI with the internet, we are still at the ‘Yahoo moment.’ We have chatbots. But how do we put the AI capability into workforce enhancements or replacements? I think there’s still a lot to do,” he said.

He said Black Lake currently had three agentic AI products deployed and seven more in incubation – ranging from converting design files into automated workflows to AI-driven quality assurance and procurement dispatching.

“In certain scenarios, our AI has already achieved 97 per cent reasoning accuracy, successfully replacing roles traditionally done by humans. But there are still 80 per cent of roles left to address,” he said.

“In the next two to three years, the spotlight will move from foundation models to the application layer. That is when everything changes … That will be the ‘Google moment’ for AI.”

item.title: [SCMP] Were the German courts too soft on Chinese members of drug rape network?
item.description:
Minutes after a Berlin court sentenced a Chinese man to five years in prison for aiding and abetting aggravated rape and sexual coercion, two women who had sat through the trial hugged each other and cried.

But the case left one of those women, named Kristina, balancing mixed emotions as she struggled to reconcile her desire to see the perpetrators punished and questions about what justice really meant in a case of this nature.

The 32-year-old accused, who was studying medicine, was jailed for five years earlier this month.
item.content:encoded:
Minutes after a Berlin court sentenced a Chinese man to five years in prison for aiding and abetting aggravated rape and sexual coercion, two women who had sat through the trial hugged each other and cried.

But the case left one of those women, named Kristina, balancing mixed emotions as she struggled to reconcile her desire to see the perpetrators punished and questions about what justice really meant in a case of this nature.

The 32-year-old accused, who was studying medicine, was jailed for five years earlier this month.

The man – who under German law could only be identified by his given name as Zhiting S. – was one of four Chinese nationals convicted and sentenced to up to 14 years in prison after investigators uncovered an online network where perpetrators exchanged tips on drugging and sexually assaulting women.

Kristina, who is studying in the German capital, was one of the many Chinese women who spent months sitting through the hearings. Some of them have criticised these sentences as too lenient.

Punishing some perpetrators does not make this kind of thinking disappear. It is like a smell in the air

Kristina, Chinese student in Berlin

She, like other observers, had a complicated reaction to the case – one shaped by anger towards the perpetrators, desire for justice and the challenge of understanding a legal system with a different approach to punishment compared with China.

The guilty men

The four convicted men were members of a Telegram group known as the “German driving school for experts”.

The eight-member group – all but one of whom was Chinese – used code words to discuss drugging and sexually assaulting women in a network that stretched from Germany to Los Angeles.

They referred to women as “cars”; finding a new victim as “looking for a car”; sedatives as “oil” or “fuel” and particularly attractive women as “luxury cars”. Sedated women were described as “dead pigs”.

They also filmed their crimes and shared recordings in encrypted online group chats to boast about their actions.

The identified victims were mostly Chinese women who were partners, colleagues, friends or acquaintances of the perpetrators. Most of them had been unaware of the assaults until they were contacted by police.

The exact number of victims remains unclear, and investigators have identified several similar online groups, one of which had around 4,500 members.

Their trials coincided with the exposure of similar sexual assault networks across Europe and North America, the most high-profile of which was the Gisele Pelicot mass rape trial in France.

The Telegram group’s activities were exposed after Dapeng Z., a 44-year-old Frankfurt-based IT engineer, was arrested in November 2024. Forensic analysis of his digital devices led investigators to other suspects.

Sizhe Weng, a former University of Southern California doctoral student, was charged last year with drugging and raping three women in the United States. Another suspect in Germany reportedly died by suicide and two others have not been publicly identified.

Dapeng Z. was sentenced to 14 years in prison for aggravated rape and attempted murder. Zhongyi J., a 28-year-old Chinese student in Munich, received more than 11 years for similar charges.

Meanwhile, Tong Z., a mechanical engineering student in Berlin, received five years and nine months for aggravated rape, grievous bodily harm and privacy violations.

German courts have described the crimes as involving a high degree of planning and appalling contempt for women.

In sentencing Zhiting S., a Berlin judge said sexual offences themselves were not new, but added: “What is new is that such crimes are not only committed, but are subsequently uploaded to the internet and applauded.”

The Munich judge who sentenced Zhongyi J. made a similar point, warning that “we have entered uncharted legal territory”.

The judge added it was “not a Chinese or French phenomenon, but also a German one. A global one”.

‘Culture shock’

For many Chinese observers, the sentences raised a different question: why were the sentences not longer?

Unlike countries such as the US that allow for consecutive sentences for separate crimes, Germany has a “total sentence” system that considers both the seriousness of the crimes and the defendant’s prospects for reintegration into society, according to Cheng Jie, an associate professor of law at the University of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.

In the Zhiting S. case, the court took into account “extensive identifying and prejudicial” media coverage in China, saying the “personal consequences” had been “particularly severe”. He is now appealing against his sentence.

“A lengthy prison sentence, combined with media exposure, professional damage and social exclusion, may leave a defendant with little chance of reintegrating into society after release,” Cheng wrote in an article published in Southern Weekly.

“German courts may therefore, within the limits of the defendant’s culpability, consider a less severe sentence to avoid permanently cutting someone off from society.”

The Federal Court of Justice, Germany’s highest court for civil and criminal matters, has ruled that media reports that prejudged and helped to identify a defendant would be seen as a mitigating factor in sentencing, Lisa Jani, a spokeswoman for the Berlin courts, said in an interview.

Not to do so meant that the verdict might not survive an appeal.

“In Germany, the courts are responsible for finding someone guilty and [delivering] a verdict in a fair trial – not the media,” she said.

A Chinese criminal lawyer who specialises in sexual violence cases said the German court’s sentencing and reasoning initially came as a “culture shock” to her because of the “quite different” legal climate in China.

“The presumption of innocence is a principle of modern justice that is broadly recognised around the world,” the lawyer said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

“While in Germany, it has been fully embedded in the legal system, in China it is discussed and emphasised much less, and it does not translate into consistent judicial practice.”

In some cases, the Chinese authorities were inclined to identify criminal suspects before a verdict was reached, and people might be more accustomed to extensive public discussion beforehand, she added.

For Kristina, the case highlighted these different approaches to justice.

She had initially hoped the defendants would receive the harshest punishment possible. But as she followed the proceedings, her expectations gradually shifted.

She recalled how devastated she felt when the defence lawyer for Zhiting S. submitted an eight-page press dossier containing Chinese and German media coverage and social media discussions about the case, fearing it would benefit the defendant.

By the end of the trial, she no longer saw the five-year sentence – the maximum sought by prosecutors – as disappointing but perhaps the best outcome the legal system could deliver.

Questions of justice

Kristina said she would not simply say whether “justice” had been done or not, because “justice means different things to different people and within different cultural contexts”.

But she argued that based on her understanding of the men and China’s legal and social environment, these relatively light sentences would not necessarily change them.

While she understood Germany’s emphasis on rehabilitation, she warned: “The weight or significance of this system may be in question when it is applied to someone who grew up in China.”

In the cases of Dapeng Z. and Zhongyi J., the sentences included a legal measure known as sicherungsverwahrung, which allows for their continued detention after the end of their jail term if they are deemed to pose a continued threat.

“What shocked me was that victim support was still very difficult to achieve,” said the Chinese lawyer.

“In some ways, this criminal trial can feel like the authorities have carried out their duty to prosecute a crime and complete a task, but providing meaningful support for the victim, who bears the deepest harm, is much harder. This is a global issue.”

Although existing laws may allow offenders to be prosecuted after they return to China, she said the country lacked specific legal provisions to address both sexual assaults where the victim had been drugged and in cases where technology was used to facilitate the crime.

Kristina said she remained pessimistic about whether punishment alone could address this problem.

She has launched an online petition together with other Chinese women in Germany, calling for legal and policy changes in the country, seeking tougher penalties for drug-assisted sexual assaults, recognition of misogynistic motives and stronger risk assessments.

The petition has so far gathered close to 3,500 signatures.

“I still feel a sense of despair,” Kristina said.

“Punishing some perpetrators does not make this kind of thinking disappear. It is like a smell in the air – something that spreads through society and eventually takes hold of certain people, leading them to commit these acts.”

.

item.title: [SCMP] Fields Medallists highlight new wave of Chinese scientists leading global research
item.description:
Two Peking University alumni made history by winning the Fields Medal this week, a victory spotlighting a broader wave of young high-achieving Chinese scientists rising to global prominence.

The International Congress of Mathematicians announced on Thursday that Wang Hong and Deng Yu, both of whom entered the top Chinese university in 2007, were awarded the highest honour for mathematicians under 40.

It is the first time Chinese nationals have received the prestigious award often called the “Nobel Prize of mathematics”.
item.content:encoded:
Two Peking University alumni made history by winning the Fields Medal this week, a victory spotlighting a broader wave of young high-achieving Chinese scientists rising to global prominence.

The International Congress of Mathematicians announced on Thursday that Wang Hong and Deng Yu, both of whom entered the top Chinese university in 2007, were awarded the highest honour for mathematicians under 40.

It is the first time Chinese nationals have received the prestigious award often called the “Nobel Prize of mathematics”.

Mathematician Cai Tianxin, a distinguished professor at Zhejiang University, said China’s research standards had caught up with the West and, with a more flexible academic environment, its young scientists were poised to achieve global recognition.

“Wang Hong and Deng Yu are both courageous in tackling and overcoming challenges.”

Cai cited leading Chinese scientists in the first half of the 20th century, including influential mathematicians Shiing-Shen Chern, Hsu Pao-lu and Wu Wenjun, as well as Nobel-winning physicists Chen-ning Yang and Tsung-Dao Lee.

“[Wang and Deng] are fortunate to have had the opportunity [like the Chinese scientists above] to study at top-tier universities in Europe and the United States in their youth and conduct research under mentors at the global forefront of the field,” he said in an interview.

“The difference today is that maths research at China’s leading universities is approaching world-class standards, with compensation and facilities that rival those of top Western institutions.

“If the academic environment were to become more flexible, I believe that this younger generation of mathematicians will soon achieve results that command global admiration.”

Tian Gang, a Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) academician and the director of Peking University’s maths centre, said in an interview with science outlet The Intellectual that Wang and Deng’s achievements pointed to the rising prominence of China’s maths education system.

“The goal is not the prize itself, but developing young mathematicians ready for the toughest challenges. Their breakthroughs reflect the growing strength of China’s maths education system, not just personal success,” he said.

I believe that China has become a hotbed for basic research

Shing-Tung Yau, Tsinghua University

According to Tian, this year “the number of Chinese mathematicians nominated for the Fields Medal was the highest in history – at least four or five”, although the official nomination list is not made public.

“The emergence of talent is not a sudden spike but the result of a long‑nurtured training ecosystem,” he said.

From the “golden generation” cohort of talented mathematicians who entered Peking University around 2000 – including Xu Chenyang, Liu Ruochuan, Yun Zhiwei and Yuan Xinyi – to the class starting in 2007, including Wang and Deng, and onwards to the younger cohort of Liu Yifeng, Feng Jiandong, Cao Yunlong and Su Jun, he said there was a talent pipeline stretching more than two decades.

Across maths, physics, life sciences and disruptive technologies, a generation of young Chinese scientists in their thirties has produced world-class breakthroughs in recent years.

Making waves in AI

Among young Chinese talents beginning to take centre stage in the AI large-model field are Moonshot AI founder Yang Zhilin, who was born in 1992 and graduated from Tsinghua University with a bachelor’s degree.

After earning his PhD from Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, he turned down a job offer from Apple and returned to China to start his own business.

The open-source Kimi K3 model he developed achieved performance on par with top-tier international standards upon its release, sparking panic among major artificial intelligence (AI) models in Silicon Valley, a jolt reminiscent of the AI shock caused by the Chinese start-up DeepSeek.

Born in 1985, DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng went to Zhejiang University in Hangzhou for his bachelor’s and master’s degrees. The DeepSeek model released at the end of 2024 was a Sputnik moment for many outside China.

Ten days ago, after a financing round, Liang’s net worth soared to US$36 billion.

In China, the heavy, sustained investment in cultivating the home-grown talent pipeline is seen as starting to pay off.

Shing-Tung Yau is the first Chinese-born Fields Medallist – although he was not a Chinese citizen when he received the award in 1982.

Yau, dean of Tsinghua’s Qiuzhen College since retiring from Harvard in 2022, said he hoped Chinese mathematicians educated in China would achieve breakthroughs at home.

“In recent years, President Xi Jinping has repeatedly emphasised the importance of basic research. Over the past decade or so, Chinese maths has made remarkable progress, with some disciplines joining the world’s top ranks, and an increasing number of scholars are making strides towards world-class work,” he said in an interview.

“Currently, China’s support for basic sciences, including maths, is unprecedented and surpasses that of any other country in the world. I believe that China has become a hotbed for basic research.

“I hope that the young generation of mathematicians who have grown up in China can achieve the most crucial breakthroughs on home soil, and carve out our own path for Chinese maths.

“This is the most important step to becoming a mathematical powerhouse, and it is also an inevitable path for China to become a leading nation in science and technology.”

Rising generation of Chinese scientists

Many of the rising stars in China’s science and technology field have studied both domestically and abroad, before returning home to study further, work, innovate and collaborate.

Wang and Deng – who went on to MIT and Princeton for advanced training – and many other scientists share a Chinese foundation combined with advanced studies at foreign institutions.

Liu Yifeng, born in 1985, is now a professor at Zhejiang University’s Institute for Advanced Study in Mathematics.

Like Fields Medallists Wang and Deng, Liu graduated from Peking University’s school of mathematical sciences in 2007 before earning a PhD at Columbia University in the US.

He then taught at MIT, Northwestern and Yale universities in the US. He resigned from his tenured professorship at Yale in 2021 to return to China where his research covers algebraic number theory, automorphic forms and algebraic geometry.

In 2025, his team received the Alexanderson Award – an honour from the American Institute of Mathematics previously given to only four Chinese scholars since its inception in 2018.

He also received a Sloan Research Fellowship for early-career researchers and the SASTRA Ramanujan Prize, which is named for an early 20th century Indian mathematician.

He is now a candidate for academician status at CAS and the Chinese Academy of Engineering, the country’s highest lifelong academic title.

Feng Jiandong, born in 1992, is a Qiushi Distinguished Professor at Zhejiang University.

Feng also started at Zhejiang and at 26, after completing his PhD at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne in 2018, returned to China and established a physical biology laboratory at Zhejiang.

He has developed innovative cross-disciplinary experimental methods combining single-molecule electrical, optical, chemical and quantum measurement techniques, with his research featured on the cover of Nature. In 2024, he received the sixth Xplorer Prize, a prominent Chinese science award.

Scientist Cao Yunlong, born in 1991, is a researcher at Peking University’s Biomedical Pioneering Innovation Centre. During the Covid-19 pandemic, he led systematic studies on B-cell immune responses and the structure and function of specific antibodies against the virus.

Cao did his undergraduate work in physics at Zhejiang University’s Chu Kochen Honours College and studied at Harvard for a PhD in chemistry.

He has written or co-authored more than nine papers in leading journals such as Cell, Nature and Science as first or corresponding author, and was named to Nature’s list of the top 10 people in science in 2022. He too was awarded the Xplorer Prize in 2024.

Biologist Su Jun, born in 1994, is a researcher at the National Institute of Biological Sciences in Beijing.

Su Jun earned his bachelor’s degree at the Chinese University of Hong Kong before pursuing graduate studies abroad and completing postdoctoral studies at the Max Planck Institute in Germany.

He revealed molecular mechanisms behind why human eggs mis-segregate chromosomes, and proposed the first prevention strategy to improve how human eggs organise and safely separate their DNA.

At the age of 28, he appeared on MIT Technology Review’s list of under-35 innovators in China, and at 29 he received the Damo Academy Qingcheng Award, which recognises scientific innovation from scholars under 35.

Additional reporting by Shi Huang

item.title: [SCMP] Syria’s US$216 billion rebuild offers a Hormuz alternative
item.description:
For years, Syria was a wound the world watched fester: a country carved up by war, sanctioned into isolation and reduced to a byword for state collapse.

Its economy needs US$216 billion to rebuild, according to World Bank estimates. This month, for the first time since the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, it began to look like it might actually get there.

On July 8, the government of Ahmed al-Sharaa – a former jihadi commander turned president – established a supreme constitutional court. Four days later, it convened the new national parliament.
item.content:encoded:
For years, Syria was a wound the world watched fester: a country carved up by war, sanctioned into isolation and reduced to a byword for state collapse.

Its economy needs US$216 billion to rebuild, according to World Bank estimates. This month, for the first time since the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, it began to look like it might actually get there.

On July 8, the government of Ahmed al-Sharaa – a former jihadi commander turned president – established a supreme constitutional court. Four days later, it convened the new national parliament.

Together, these acts set in motion the process needed to build a post-Assad state, spurring Washington to announce on July 8 that it would lift its long-standing designation of Syria as a state sponsor of terrorism, following a third face-to-face meeting between Sharaa and US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of a Nato summit in Ankara.

That decision and the impending removal of associated US sanctions clear the way for Syria to rejoin the global financial system, without which the job of national reconstruction cannot begin in earnest.

After 14 years of civil war, the country’s infrastructure lies in ruins. Its institutions are embryonic and its politics still combustible. What it has, instead, is its location at the ancient crossroads of trade between Asia and Europe.

Two forces have revived interest in these long-dormant trade routes: the Strait of Hormuz crisis and a planned logistical corridor connecting the two continents via the Gulf states and Israel that stalled amid the political wreckage of the wars on Gaza and Iran.

Into that vacuum has stepped Syria, offering its eastern neighbour Iraq, the second-biggest oil exporter in Opec, a sorely needed outlet for its fuel.

On July 14, Damascus and Baghdad – with encouragement from Washington – struck a deal to rebuild a moribund pipeline connecting Iraq’s oilfield in Kirkuk to the Syrian port of Baniyas on its Mediterranean coast. US energy giant Chevron is set to lead the project, with mammoth multinational investment bank J.P. Morgan arranging the requisite financing.

Meanwhile, Iraq has signed a separate memorandum of understanding with Jordan to explore reviving a pipeline from Basra to the port of Aqaba, near the Red Sea. Combined, these projects could reroute practically all of Iraq’s oil exports and, in the words of US special envoy Tom Barrack, “make the Strait of Hormuz an afterthought”.

A third project – a rail corridor connecting Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast to Turkey via Jordan and Syria – is also in the works, following the signing of an agreement in June by Ankara and Riyadh.

“Syria has got a lot of problems, but its location isn’t one,” said Aron Lund, a senior analyst at the Swedish Defence Research Agency, calling the country “perfectly placed” to serve as a link between Europe, Turkey and the Gulf.

“But to capitalise on that geographic position, Syria needs a stable and welcoming political and legal climate, which is not the case today,” Lund said.

Get it right and the pay-off “could be hugely significant for Syria’s future”, he added. Get it wrong and “it’s far from certain” these long-term projects will ever be finished.

Caroline Rose, senior director of the New York-based Soufan Centre think tank, agreed. The flurry of pipeline and railway deals “definitely show that leaders and business stakeholders are seeing Syria as a serious alternative” to Hormuz, she said.

But it remains to be seen whether the current political momentum and push to diversify trade routes can be sustained.

“These projects will take many years to conduct,” Rose said. “It won’t be an immediate result, that’s definitely clear.”

A similar asterisk hangs over sanctions relief. Their lifting by the US removed some legal hurdles to trade and investment, said Omer Ozkizilcik, a senior Syria fellow at the Atlantic Council think tank, but “just like in any other post-conflict nation, many economic and administrative obstacles remain”.

‘Scared’ money, raw risk

Though analysts agree that the removal of Western sanctions is likely to accelerate reconstruction, it still “won’t be easy or rapid”, according to Bill Park, a senior lecturer in defence studies at King’s College London.

The scale of the destruction and dislocation means many of the roughly 4.5 million Syrians still living abroad – three-quarters of the 6 million who fled the war – are unlikely “to return in a hurry”, as Park put it.

“There will need to be confidence that Syria has stabilised, and maybe greater stability in the region,” he said.

It will also take time to convince Western financial institutions that Syria is a safe place to invest.

Despite J.P. Morgan’s decision to open a branch in Iraq to support the Baniyas pipeline, Rose said New York bankers she had spoken to were still “scared” of engaging with Syria’s new government.

Lenders have good reason to be circumspect. Trump continues to muse about the prospect of Syrian forces intervening in Lebanon to disarm Hezbollah, despite Sharaa’s denials that any such plan exists.

Israel, meanwhile, continues to occupy parts of southwestern Syria, seized amid the Assad regime’s collapse, having unilaterally declared the area a demilitarised zone – one policed by Druze separatists whom Israeli forces arm and protect, and who run what amounts to a mini-narco state there in cahoots with former Assad loyalists.

Trump’s Hezbollah idea took on new life on July 15, when he told Fox News that Sharaa could target the Iran-allied group “much more precisely” than Israel could – enabling Israel to redeploy its forces and focus on “the bigger issue, which is Iran”.

Israel rejected the notion a day later, but Damascus got the message. It has since announced three major seizures of Iran-supplied weapons, including drones and missiles, that were bound for Hezbollah in a bid to placate the Trump administration.

Tehran’s Revolutionary Guards responded by firing several missiles into the Syrian desert: a reminder of the country’s vulnerability to attacks by Iran’s proxies.

Damascus has tried to defuse the situation. Earlier this month, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani travelled to Beirut, offering reassurances of non-interference to both the government and parliamentary speaker Nabih Berri, a Shia community leader and political ally of Hezbollah.

The landmark visit yielded a border security pact aligning the two governments against the shared threats posed by Israeli occupation and Hezbollah, along with plans to revive business and trade ties and rebuild a railway line connecting Syria to the Lebanese port of Tripoli.

Lebanon. The Iraq pipeline deal. Even overtures to Assad’s former ally Russia, which is negotiating a deal to repurpose its former naval base at Tartus into an agricultural commodity trading hub – all point to Syria rebuilding relationships on every front and hedging against overreliance on any one patron.

As for Washington? Damascus knows it must “keep a very positive face” with the Trump administration, according to Rose – fully aware that this most improbable of relationships could “turn on a dime”.

item.title: [SCMP] Putting the ‘K’ back in K-pop: how Rescene charmed South Korea
item.description:
In an industry built on going global, K-pop’s freshest phenomenon has succeeded by doing the exact opposite: staying home.

Rescene, a five-member girl group from little-known agency The Muze Entertainment, debuted in 2024 but largely flew under the radar until recently.

Now, they are the talk of the town – chart-toppers, brand ambassadors and a name that is suddenly inescapable across South Korea.
item.content:encoded:
In an industry built on going global, K-pop’s freshest phenomenon has succeeded by doing the exact opposite: staying home.

Rescene, a five-member girl group from little-known agency The Muze Entertainment, debuted in 2024 but largely flew under the radar until recently.

Now, they are the talk of the town – chart-toppers, brand ambassadors and a name that is suddenly inescapable across South Korea.

No stadium tours preceded their rapid ascent from relative obscurity. No Hybe-scale marketing budget was behind their rise. Instead, viral YouTube clips and old-fashioned word of mouth did all the hard work.

Their breakthrough, dubbed a “small agency miracle”, was a rare feat in an industry dominated by the big four entertainment agencies – Hybe, SM, JYP and YG.

But Rescene’s rise is more than just a plucky underdog tale.

Their melodic, unhurried songs have more of 2000s K-pop about them than today’s hybrid, genre-blending sounds, setting the group apart with music made for Korean fans first.

In an increasingly globalised industry obsessed with world domination, Rescene has become that rarest of things: a genuine domestic phenomenon.

Humble beginnings

Two years ago, it was a very different story. Back in 2024, major broadcasters and music festivals had little interest in a group from an unproven agency, so the quintet spent their early years playing whatever venues they could find, from junior school field days to local community centres.

Their fortunes changed after Woni, the group’s leader, was chosen to host a self-titled YouTube channel created by a producer with a track record of viral video hits. Rather than polished idol content, the series highlighted each member’s distinct background and personality.

Japanese member Minami’s gleefully exaggerated homage to 1990s Japanese gyaru subculture spawned the now-ubiquitous catchphrase “Geoje, Yahho!”, while later episodes leaned into the Gyeongsang satoori (dialect) of members Woni and Zena, deepening the connection with fans.

A Rescene track soon topped the South Korean music charts, with a follow-up also reaching the top 10, and all five members have now cracked the top 13 of the Korea Corporate Reputation Research Institute’s brand reputation girl-group index, with Woni taking the top spot ahead of idols from Hybe and YG.

They were not the first K-pop group to find major success on a minor label, however.

EXID’s “Up & Down” caught fire in 2014 off a single fan-filmed clip that went viral. A year later, GFriend won the country over when footage emerged showing the group’s members repeatedly slipping on a rain-slicked stage but refusing to stop performing.

And BB Girls, who first made a name for themselves as Brave Girls in 2011, experienced a revival a decade later after videos of soldiers singing along to their songs on military bases spread online.

The BTS playbook

“This is ultimately the power of digital platforms,” said Kim Jeong-sub, a professor of K-culture and entertainment at Sungshin Women’s University in Seoul and author of The Universe of BTS.

“In the past, songs usually became popular first because of a specific moment,” he said, citing appearances in television dramas or a viral sing-along.

“With Rescene, the process worked in reverse. People first became interested in the members themselves and that interest naturally extended to their music.”

He compared the strategy to that of Hybe’s foundational group, BTS. Before they became K-pop royalty, the boy band “couldn’t rely on expensive television promotions, so they documented their daily lives through blogs and YouTube”, Kim said.

By building intimacy with video diaries and personal messages, the group laid the emotional groundwork for what became their global fan base: the BTS Army.

“Rescene has taken that one step further,” Kim said. “Their success has been built on carefully produced content that highlights each member’s personality and individuality.”

The group’s rise has not gone unnoticed by policymakers. South Korea’s culture ministry plans to almost double funding next year for a programme supporting independent agencies abroad.

This year, Rescene’s agency was among 10 that were awarded up to 300 million won (US$203,700) in annual government support, from a 3 billion won pot, for album production, music videos and overseas marketing.

More ‘K’ in K-pop

For pop culture critic Kim Hern-shik, however, the real story is not Rescene’s rise, but what that rise reveals about how much K-pop has changed.

“The reason the group attracted so much attention is precisely because K-pop has spent the past few years looking overseas,” he said.

Since the pandemic, entertainment agencies have poured resources into international tours and global fandom building, often before groups had even established themselves at home.

As that became more common, Korean fans increasingly felt like an afterthought, Kim Hern-shik said, with groups like Stray Kids and XG finding global fame while remaining, in his words, “relatively unfamiliar to the Korean general public”.

Rescene, by contrast, built their popularity by being distinctly Korean. Rather than presenting a polished, placeless image that many idols cultivate for export, they openly celebrate their hometowns, regional dialects and local culture.

“The members proudly talk about where they come from,” Kim Hern-shik said. “In the past, idols from major agencies sometimes even tried to hide their regional backgrounds.”

The ripple effects have been felt in domestic tourism too. South Gyeongsang, Woni’s home province, logged a record 5 million visitors in the first half of this year, with the eponymous Geoje city of “Geoje, Yahho!” fame becoming one of the region’s most-visited spots thanks to Rescene’s videos.

Kim Hern-shik said this reflected a certain reassertion of Korean specificity across the country’s culture industry, pointing to the runaway global success of the animated hit KPop Demon Hunters – which foregrounds Korean culture, despite being American made – and BTS’ decision to stage their long-awaited reunion concert at Seoul’s Gwanghwamun Square with a comeback centred around the Korean folk song “Arirang”.

“Interest in Korea today extends beyond Seoul and the surrounding metropolitan area,” he said. “People are increasingly curious about smaller cities and different regions of the country.”

Rescene reminds people that K-pop also has roots

Kim Hern-shik, Korean pop culture critic

He compared this longing for a “sense of place” to that experienced by practitioners of the Korean martial art taekwondo. Millions practise it worldwide, yet people still travel to Kukkiwon in Seoul because they want “to experience the birthplace”.

“Rescene reminds people that K-pop also has roots,” he added. “Although we use the term ‘K-pop’, what people are ultimately consuming is content produced by individual entertainment companies. The problem is that when fans come to Korea, there often isn’t a physical place that embodies that experience.”

Rescene’s success is proof that authenticity and global appeal were never mutually exclusive, according to Kim Hern-shik.

“By proudly showcasing Korea, and local Korea in particular, Rescene has shown that authenticity itself can attract global attention,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Can Southeast Asia survive more Iran war fuel shocks?
item.description:
Southeast Asia’s governments have spent months trying to blunt the effects of war-driven energy shocks from the Middle East, but renewed fighting between the United States and Iran has exposed how limited those defences are, analysts have warned.

The latest flare-up has revived fears of a second round of fuel disruption across the region, where many economies remain heavily dependent on imported oil and shipping routes linked to the Gulf.

Southeast Asian leaders expressed “grave concern” over the revival of tensions between the US and Iran, urging a “complete and immediate cessation of hostilities across all fronts in the Middle East” at the 59th Asean Foreign Ministers Meeting in Manila on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
Southeast Asia’s governments have spent months trying to blunt the effects of war-driven energy shocks from the Middle East, but renewed fighting between the United States and Iran has exposed how limited those defences are, analysts have warned.

The latest flare-up has revived fears of a second round of fuel disruption across the region, where many economies remain heavily dependent on imported oil and shipping routes linked to the Gulf.

Southeast Asian leaders expressed “grave concern” over the revival of tensions between the US and Iran, urging a “complete and immediate cessation of hostilities across all fronts in the Middle East” at the 59th Asean Foreign Ministers Meeting in Manila on Tuesday.

The diplomats from the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations also called “for the restoration of the safe, unimpeded, and continuous transit passage of vessels and aircraft in the Strait of Hormuz”.

The foreign ministers said the hostilities would negatively affect “regional trade, energy and food security, including energy markets and supply chains, agricultural production, and the stability of agricultural input supply chains, particularly fertilisers”.

The shaky truce between the US and Iran, formalised in June, ended this month after both sides traded accusations of ceasefire violations.

Southeast Asia bore the brunt of the energy crisis that followed the outbreak of hostilities in late February and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, where about 60 per cent of Asia’s crude oil imports come from.

Countries such as the Philippines were particularly hard-hit, with the nation importing more than 95 per cent of its fuel.

Analysts said the ceasefire breakdown revealed underlying weaknesses in the region’s ability to shield itself from external fuel shocks.

Southeast Asian economies remained heavily dependent on imported oil and shipping routes connected to the Gulf, said Joanne Lin, a senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and a visiting scholar at the MIT Centre for International Studies.

Higher energy costs also fed into fertiliser, food, transport and manufacturing, she said, meaning governments would have to keep diversifying suppliers, building reserves, providing targeted support and accelerating renewables, biofuels and regional energy connectivity.

While there “has been some learning over the past months”, Lin said the region could not fully insulate itself from a prolonged conflict if the Strait of Hormuz remained disrupted.

Collins Chong Yew Keat, a foreign affairs, security and strategy analyst at Universiti Malaya, told This Week in Asia that Asean “has not yet learned the deeper structural lesson of the crisis” as it still lacked an operational regional energy security system, with no collective mechanisms such as a strategic petroleum reserve or centralised procurement platform.

“Asean can therefore speak collectively as it has in Manila in calling for an immediate cessation of hostilities and the restoration of safe and free passage through the Strait of Hormuz, but when actual supplies are threatened, member states largely fall back on national and bilateral solutions,” he said.

Uneven response

As countries are likely to rely on national measures to deal with external pressures, responses across the region will be uneven, with some economies more vulnerable than others.

Hunter Marston, director of the Southeast Asia programme at the Lowy Institute in Sydney, said the measures implemented so far were short-term, with a “mix of optimism from countries like Indonesia” but greater volatility for others such as the Philippines given current fuel prices.

“Different member states face different vulnerabilities because of their varying levels of dependence on crude oil and natural gas imports,” said Jaideep Singh, an analyst at the Institute of Strategic and International Studies in Malaysia.

Singh noted that some Asean member states had already taken individual measures to ease dependency on Gulf-sourced fuel.

Malaysia and Indonesia, both palm oil exporters, have expanded the use of palm-based biodiesel to reduce reliance on conventional diesel, while other countries have promoted alternative energy sources, particularly for electric vehicles.

Singapore was accelerating electric vehicle adoption through strong policy support and nationwide charging infrastructure, while Laos was expanding EV uptake through electrification targets and cross-border clean energy cooperation, said Dinita Setyawati, a senior analyst for Asia at energy think tank Ember.

Lin pointed out that some countries might be better equipped to handle disruptions: Brunei and Malaysia enjoyed a greater natural cushion as hydrocarbon producers and exporters, while Singapore had higher adaptive capacity through its trading and refining networks and commercial relationships.

Indonesia sat somewhere in between, she added, as it was also a net petroleum importer in addition to having coal, gas and a major biofuel industry, which could entail large subsidy costs.

“Thailand and the Philippines remain among the more exposed larger economies because of their dependence on imported oil and the importance of fuel to transport and electricity,” Lin said, while Cambodia, Laos, East Timor and Myanmar consumed less energy in absolute terms but had weaker fiscal space and lower household incomes, making price increases harder to absorb.

Singh said Thailand’s substantial stockpiles might cushion the blow and provide some relief.

Vietnam remained vulnerable as it imported 88 per cent of its oil despite having domestic refining capabilities, and “will need to diversify suppliers and long-term supply contracts rather than relying mainly on emergency spot purchases”, Chong said.

Diversifying ties

If the first response to the crisis is domestic cushioning, the longer-term response is likely to be a wider search for suppliers and partners that analysts say may not necessarily amount to a “wholesale geopolitical realignment”.

“We might see more diversification rather than any wholesale geopolitical realignment,” Lin said, adding that Asean could deepen energy ties with Russia, Gulf producers, the US, India, Japan and Australia, depending on who could provide reliable oil, liquefied natural gas, financing and emergency support.

For Marston, “the nature of hedging has already changed” as middle powers in Asean are looking more to one another, as well as partners such as Japan and Australia, to diversify their supply chains.

While the US remained a significant player because of its large oil and gas exports, Marston said China was likely still the most important partner because of the enormity of its strategic reserves.

Southeast Asia might also continue to warm up to Russia as it built up its reserves and improved its resilience in energy security, “but sanctions, insurance and payment risks will limit how far that relationship can expand”, Lin said.

Despite these attempts, however, Asean would not necessarily become more united, Chong said, noting there would be “greater diversification without genuine regional pooling”.

Unless the crisis produced a binding oil-sharing protocol, common strategic reserves and agreed emergency-allocation rules, Chong said, “Asean’s collective energy security will remain more symbolic and declaratory than operational and functional”.

item.title: [SCMP] How China is using film diplomacy to project a better image across Africa
item.description:
Beijing’s soft power drive to win African hearts through cinema was on display recently in Bujumbura, where Chinese dragon and lion dances merged with sacred Burundian drums to open Chinese Film Week.

The Chinese embassy in Bujumbura, the economic capital of Burundi, said the July 15 event offered “a beautiful example of cultural exchanges between the two countries” and that both sides were determined to “make cinema a vehicle for Sino-Burundian friendship”.

Zhu Kewei, China’s ambassador to the East African country, called cinema “a force capable of bridging language barriers, borders and cultures”, adding that “film carries a nation’s historical memories, cultural traditions, values and the emotions of its people”.
item.content:encoded:
Beijing’s soft power drive to win African hearts through cinema was on display recently in Bujumbura, where Chinese dragon and lion dances merged with sacred Burundian drums to open Chinese Film Week.

The Chinese embassy in Bujumbura, the economic capital of Burundi, said the July 15 event offered “a beautiful example of cultural exchanges between the two countries” and that both sides were determined to “make cinema a vehicle for Sino-Burundian friendship”.

Zhu Kewei, China’s ambassador to the East African country, called cinema “a force capable of bridging language barriers, borders and cultures”, adding that “film carries a nation’s historical memories, cultural traditions, values and the emotions of its people”.

“Many African friends have told me that they came to know and understand China through Chinese kung fu movies and martial arts stars,” she said at the event, referring to the famous Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan movies of the 1970s and 1980s.

In addition to the film screenings, China and Burundi plan to expand cooperation through creator exchanges, artist mobility, university partnerships, co-productions and skills transfer.

As part of the China-Africa Year of Human and Cultural Exchanges, the festival in Burundi lined up seven Chinese films, including The Wandering Earth II, Changan and The Snow Leopard.

Screenings took place in major cities like Bujumbura, Ngozi and political capital Gitega.

China’s film diplomacy is a pan-African endeavour, with Beijing in recent months boosting the number of screenings across several countries, including Egypt, Ethiopia, Kenya, Morocco, Nigeria, South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe.

Observers say the expanded screenings and cultural exchanges are part of a wider effort by Beijing to change how Africans view China and build lasting ties with local media and institutions.

Alessandro Jedlowski, an associate professor in political sociology and African Studies at Bordeaux Institute of Political Science (Sciences Po Bordeaux), said China’s travelling film weeks aligned with a broader strategy to reshape African perceptions of the Asian economic giant.

Beijing had invested heavily in media circulation to improve the international image of its footprint in Africa, Jedlowski said.

“These events allow China to present everyday, non‑military narratives that contrast with geopolitical framings and help normalise Chinese modernity as familiar and accessible.”

Beyond public perception, the screenings strengthen institutional connections, he added, suggesting that power arises from a complex, unpredictable dynamic rather than a rigid, top-down strategy.

“China seeks to embed itself in African media ecologies not as a monolithic actor but as one capable of adapting to local contexts.”

In Nairobi, a film about hybrid rice pioneer Yuan Longping headlined a cultural showcase last month, using the scientist’s life story to draw attention to China’s agricultural cooperation with African countries.

The film was paired with Hi, Mom, a blockbuster comedy-drama, and the historical drama Mao Zedong and Qi Baishi, which traces the relationship between the Chinese leader and the master painter.

Zhang Zhizhong, a senior diplomat at the Chinese embassy in Kenya, described films as “a powerful expression of a thriving civilisation and an important window into a country’s culture”.

“Chinese cinema has seen a growing number of brilliant and thought-provoking masterpieces [in recent years],” Zhang added.

Last year, the Chinese animated film Ne Zha 2 took the world by storm, grossing US$2.2 billion to rank fifth in all-time global box office takings while becoming the highest-grossing animated film in cinema history.

“I hope that, through these films, our friends in Kenya can experience the true face of China, the pulse of its development and the charm of its culture,” Zhang said.

The films screened in Kenyan capital Nairobi came from Hunan province, the birthplace of Mao Zedong and the cradle of hybrid rice.

Zhang said Hunan had been approved by the Chinese government as a pilot zone for in-depth China-Africa economic and trade cooperation.

The central Chinese province hosts the China-Africa Economic and Trade Expo every two years and is at the forefront of cooperation with Africa.

“But what you may not know is that Hunan is also a cultural powerhouse in China,” Zhang said. “I have no doubt that Hunan will continue to lead the way in cultural and people-to-people exchanges with Africa.”

Meanwhile, in Morocco to the northwest, the African tour of the revolutionary drama My Maan Ling began on June 29 at the Confucius Institute of Hassan II University in Casablanca, marking its first public screening on the continent.

Inspired by the true story of Hainan province’s all-female Red Army detachment in the 1930s, the film honours the revolutionary ideals and heroism of its fighters.

Additional screenings were later scheduled at Mohammed V University in Rabat and various state-owned enterprise sites in Morocco.

Jedlowski noted that Chinese filmmakers did more than just show their movies in Africa, saying they were also actively collaborating with African partners to co-produce films.

In his research, Jedlowski has come across several initiatives in which Chinese media companies collaborate directly with local entities.

For instance, StarTimes, a large pay-TV operator and digital television infrastructure provider, has become a major player in the distribution and production of African content.

The company produces local drama series such as Alagbara in Nigeria and is developing entertainment formats exported across multiple African countries.

Various Chinese state‑funded frameworks, such as the China–Africa Film and Television Cooperation Project and the Silk Road Film and Television Bridge Project, also support dubbing African films into African languages and encourage joint production, Jedlowski said.

A notable example is the planned Sino-Nigerian feature 30 Days in China, produced by Corporate World Entertainment, FilmOne Entertainment and HuaHua Media.

Although the project was interrupted by the coronavirus pandemic and has yet to be released, it is a clear instance of active co‑production that could serve as a model for feature projects, according to Jedlowski.

That said, audience response has been mixed.

Jedlowski observed that while dubbed dramas found enthusiastic viewers, they also drew criticism, such as from Nigerian filmmakers protesting foreign series dubbed into Yoruba or Hausa.

“Some viewers appreciate relatable everyday narratives. Others prefer Nollywood or local productions,” he said, referring to Nigeria’s film industry.

“Acceptance depends on how well they align with local expectations, linguistic identities and existing media preferences.”

item.title: [SCMP] Fewer opportunities, less passion, no clue? How the US’ China expertise is fading
item.description:
As the United States marks the 250th anniversary of its founding, it confronts a new world order dominated by its relationship with China. In this wide-ranging series, we examine the pressure points and possibilities in those ties, from hard tech to soft power. Here, Meredith Chen looks at how tensions and shrinking academic exchange may be eroding America’s deep, experience-based understanding of China.

Long before China could be studied through satellite images, social media, big data or computer modelling, American scholars learned about the country the slow way.

Many travelled to the country. Some went far beyond its major cities, reaching remote county towns and villages by train, bus and boat to conduct fieldwork.
item.content:encoded:
As the United States marks the 250th anniversary of its founding, it confronts a new world order dominated by its relationship with China.
