In this wide-ranging series, we examine the pressure points and possibilities in those ties, from hard tech to soft power. Here, Meredith Chen looks at how tensions and shrinking academic exchange may be eroding America’s deep, experience-based understanding of China.

Long before China could be studied through satellite images, social media, big data or computer modelling, American scholars learned about the country the slow way.

Many travelled to the country. Some went far beyond its major cities, reaching remote county towns and villages by train, bus and boat to conduct fieldwork.

They spent months, even years, knocking on doors, lingering over tea, combing through archives, and interviewing cadres and ordinary members of the public to build a deep understanding of a country undergoing extraordinary transformation.

This was the reform era. As China reopened and the two countries’ relationship normalised after prolonged Cold War estrangement, American scholars gained access to a society that had been closed to them for decades.

Many of those who entered China in those years would go on to become the backbone of American expertise on the country, shaping scholarship, training future generations and influencing how Washington dealt with Beijing.

As the United States marks its 250th anniversary, however, that intellectual tradition is under strain.

Observers caution that America’s ability to understand China is undergoing a generational rupture, as specialists with deep in-country experience are leaving the stage while the conditions that once nurtured such expertise are disappearing as ties become increasingly tense.

“America’s ability to understand and manage its most consequential strategic relationship is eroding,” according to a report released in March by the US-China Education Trust, a non-profit organisation.

It pointed to the dwindling number of Americans studying in China and warned that the US could face a “critical shortage of grounded China expertise within a decade”.

A fascinated generation

American expertise on China did not begin with reform and opening-up. Earlier generations, including heavyweights such as John King Fairbank, laid the foundations for modern China scholarship and influenced generations of scholars who later came to prominence.

But it was the cohort – political scientists, historians and anthropologists – that entered China in the 1980s and 1990s that gained unprecedented opportunities for sustained, on-the-ground study.

Many of them came of age during the Cold War and experienced the political and intellectual currents of the 1960s and 1970s, experts said.

Two movements were particularly influential in shaping their world view: the anti-Vietnam war movement and the Cultural Revolution.

For many of them, China was a subject of “both fascination and mystery”, and they developed a strong interest in the communist revolution and, “to varying degrees, felt sympathy for China’s socialist experiment”, said Guo Wu, a historian and former professor at Allegheny College in Pennsylvania.

According to Ding Xueliang, professor emeritus at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, when those American scholars began to conduct fieldwork in China after 1979, they confronted the realities of the Cultural Revolution and experienced a bitter process of “waking from a great dream” as they reassessed their beliefs.

This painful disillusionment was channelled into a sustained focus on ordinary Chinese society, including poorer and less-developed communities, he said in an article published online in May.

Cuts and restrictions

Ding is not optimistic about the future of China expertise in the US as the older generation of scholars gradually retires.

“Will there still be deeply knowledgeable China scholars after [this] generation leaves the stage? I certainly hope so, but the outlook is not encouraging,” he said.

Of the many factors behind this darkening outlook, analysts said, the most important was the rapid erosion of opportunities for Americans to conduct on-the-ground research in China as pressure increased from both sides.

The flow of American students into Chinese universities has sharply declined since the onset of the Covid pandemic in 2020 and the continued deterioration of US-China relations.

Today, fewer than 2,000 Americans are studying in China, down from roughly 15,000 a decade ago and still far below pre-pandemic levels, according to the US-China Education Trust.

In the US, growing political scrutiny and cuts to federal funding for China studies have limited research and exchange programmes, while China has tightened controls over visiting scholars and made visas harder to get.

While American scholars were once warmly welcomed and even treated as honoured guests, foreign researchers today are more likely to encounter suspicion about their intentions.

As Chinese society became more globally connected and confident, the West no longer possessed “the same aura of mystery or prestige that it once did”, which made the interpersonal and institutional dynamics that once facilitated scholarly engagement more complex, Wu noted.

For Dennis Wilder, a senior fellow for the Initiative for US-China Dialogue on Global Issues at Georgetown University, the loss of experiential knowledge that comes from living in China contributed to “a serious gap” in US understanding of US-China relations.

“It is not language skills that I worry about,” said Wilder, who formerly held senior roles related to China and East Asia at the US National Security Council and CIA. “But the ‘feel’ for new China and the societal ecosystem can only be learned with long-term immersion in China.”

Passing the torch

Beyond shrinking access, Wu said that US students studying China today increasingly viewed it through the lens of strategic competition and national security, a tendency he attributed in part to the tenor of mainstream discourse on China.

For scholars of previous generations, engagement with the country was often driven by “a personal and intellectual passion”, he explained.

The “deep sense of curiosity about China” had been ruptured, Wu said, along with “the aspiration to travel to China, immerse themselves in its society, and understand it on its own terms”.

Many younger scholars today approach China through well-established disciplinary frameworks, producing important scholarship but also contributing to a “more professionalised and specialised approach” to the field, he added.

“[A] more detached and ostensibly ‘rational’ assessment of China has also become increasingly influential among younger scholars and policy analysts,” he said.

Diao Daming, a professor at Renmin University of China’s School of International Studies, drew a similar contrast.

“The older generation … faced a China that needed to be continually understood,” he said. “While the younger generation confronts a China that is continually developing – a China they increasingly perceive as a so-called rival to the US.”

While the work of the older generation sought to explain China to the US and the wider world and generally favoured stable bilateral relations, he said many younger scholars approached China warily with an underlying orientation towards containing China’s rise and preserving America’s dominant position.

The earlier generation approached China through disciplines such as history, literature, sociology and anthropology, while many younger scholars approached China mainly through the lens of economics, political science and international relations, and often relied more heavily on data than long-term immersion, he added.

The current generation of American China experts “seems to have lost interest in Chinese culture and history”, and may not even possess good Chinese-language skills like their predecessors, Diao said.

Many had not spent enough time living in different parts of China and therefore lacked much of a “personal feel” for the country, he added.

For Ding, the issue was not only the passing of the torch to a new generation but also the marginalisation of older, established China scholars in Washington, which had left policy debates increasingly dominated by superficial assessments, he said in another article published in May.

Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser and trustee chair in Chinese business and economics at the Washington-based think tank Centre for Strategic and International Studies, however, said he had seen no evidence that younger Americans were broadly more critical of China than previous generations or less interested in studying it.

Rather, the changing environment surrounding China itself played a larger role in reshaping the field, argued Kennedy, who has travelled regularly to China for decades.

“China’s domestic politics are tighter. Its engagement with the world has more restrictions. This is less about Americans changing over the course of generations than changes in China that Americans and others are perceiving.”

Blocked pipeline

Neysun Mahboubi, who directs the Penn Project on the Future of US-China Relations at the University of Pennsylvania and regularly brings American students to China for study trips, said his biggest concern was not the current moment, but the pipeline crisis that could leave the country short of qualified specialists in the coming decades.

He also pushed back against framing the issue simply as a generational divide, arguing that a key challenge was increasingly one of material incentives. The erosion of career opportunities had made China studies a less attractive path for young Americans than it once was, he said.

These trends predated the pandemic, he noted, and even emerged before the first Trump administration.

Foreign firms retreating from China or increasingly hiring local talent were not a new phenomenon, Mahboubi explained, while “budget cuts in the federal government displacing many young China analysts is of a more recent vintage”.

“China is the most consequential bilateral relationship for the US right now, but some jobs that used to exist, whether in business or in government, don’t exist any more.”

He added that the picture remained dynamic and that there was “at least some cause for optimism” that US students’ interest in China might rebound.

“Maybe precisely because there’s such a clear sense now that China is the primary geopolitical relationship for the US to be concerned about, so certainly at some schools, especially elite American institutions, there seems to be an uptick in interest in China studies.”

The changing balance of expertise, some scholars said, was also visible from the Chinese side.

Wu added that Chinese studies on America had been greatly enhanced in the past few years, resulting in expanding research interest and output. He also pointed to the “demystification” of the US in contemporary China.

As more Chinese scholars, students and travellers gained first-hand experience of American society, the US had become less an object of “admiration, imagination, or ideological projection”, and more one of Chinese observation, analysis and evaluation, he said.

Chinese studies of the US had contributed to a more nuanced understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of the American political system, he added.

But Chinese scholars studying the US also faced growing challenges in conducting on-the-ground fieldwork, experts said.

Kennedy said he was worried that “we’re actually moving towards scholarly decoupling”.

“If the relationship between the two countries at the political level does not achieve some greater measure of genuine stability, then we will increasingly become strangers with each other,” he warned.

item.title: [SCMP] Rail and road: the benefits of China’s full-system transport makeovers
item.description:
I visited China after the pandemic. The thing that struck me was how different it sounded, and then, once I started paying attention, how different it moved. Every Didi I called in Shanghai was a different make. A BYD, then a Zeekr, then an Avatr I had never heard of. I started waiting for the app to reveal its hand, a small thrill each time, and got a quiet burst of joy whenever it was a Hongqi.

The variety of electric vehicle (EV) brands is in every first-tier Chinese city, but Shanghai is where it gets faintly ridiculous. The city is home to SAIC, one of China’s oldest state-owned carmakers, and to Tesla’s Shanghai Gigafactory. For years, its notoriously brutal licence-plate lottery has waved EV buyers straight through. The result is the highest EV adoption rate of any Chinese city, and a fleet to match: a different marque every ride.

Once, a sleek blue saloon slid past me, and I mistook it for a Porsche – the silhouette, the sloping roofline, the whole stance. A closer look and it was a Xiaomi SU7; Chinese social media got there before I did and nicknamed it “Mi Porsche”. When you think of a phone company building cars that look suspiciously like a six-figure German sports saloon, the mix-up says plenty about how far the design has come.
item.content:encoded:
I visited China after the pandemic. The thing that struck me was how different it sounded, and then, once I started paying attention, how different it moved. Every Didi I called in Shanghai was a different make. A BYD, then a Zeekr, then an Avatr I had never heard of. I started waiting for the app to reveal its hand, a small thrill each time, and got a quiet burst of joy whenever it was a Hongqi.

The variety of electric vehicle (EV) brands is in every first-tier Chinese city, but Shanghai is where it gets faintly ridiculous. The city is home to SAIC, one of China’s oldest state-owned carmakers, and to Tesla’s Shanghai Gigafactory. For years, its notoriously brutal licence-plate lottery has waved EV buyers straight through. The result is the highest EV adoption rate of any Chinese city, and a fleet to match: a different marque every ride.

Once, a sleek blue saloon slid past me, and I mistook it for a Porsche – the silhouette, the sloping roofline, the whole stance. A closer look and it was a Xiaomi SU7; Chinese social media got there before I did and nicknamed it “Mi Porsche”. When you think of a phone company building cars that look suspiciously like a six-figure German sports saloon, the mix-up says plenty about how far the design has come.

In Chengdu, Sichuan province, I walked into a swanky Huawei shop intending to browse phones and laptops. I found what I was expecting – and then full-sized electric cars on display, like an expensive impulse purchase by the till. This is uniquely Chinese: the brand that sold you your phone also sells you the thing you drive it around in.

How the cars got everywhere

In 2020, EVs made up about 6 per cent of new car sales in China. By 2026, that figure had climbed past 60 per cent.

This did not happen by accident. It was by design, through purchase subsidies, mandated sales quotas in big cities, free green licence plates in places where an ordinary plate is auctioned off for a small fortune and a charging network built ahead of demand rather than behind it.

China now has more than 12 million public charging points, more than the rest of the world combined, built mostly within the last decade. That solved the chicken-and-egg problem that has slowed EV adoption everywhere else: nobody buys an electric car if there’s nowhere to charge it, and nobody builds chargers for cars that don’t exist yet. China built both at once and let everyone else argue about which should have come first.

The other surprise was how far down the price ladder this goes. The Wuling Mini EV costs not much more than a decent scooter. Counties have run subsidy schemes for rural buyers and the result is farming towns where EVs are now charged outside vegetable markets. As someone who lives in Singapore, a country that has cornered the market on the world’s most expensive cars, a comparable car and kilowatt-hour cost a sum I cannot mention, for it gives me a genuine heartache just thinking about it.

The railway that keeps on going

If the EVs crept up gradually, the trains did something more dramatic: they opened doors to places I’d wanted to reach for years that simply had not been accessible in any sensible amount of time.

Jiuzhaigou, in Sichuan province, was the first. The only way in used to be a road journey of about 10 hours from Chengdu, through mountain passes, or a flight. The Huanglong-Jiuzhaigou line opened in 2024, making the journey to the legendary turquoise lakes from Chengdu East station less than two hours.

Yanan was next, and it carries its own piece of history. This is the town in the loess hills of Shaanxi province where Mao Zedong and the Communist Party regrouped after the Long March, governing from a network of cave dwellings for over a decade before taking the rest of the country. The American journalist Edgar Snow made the same journey in 1936, and it took him nearly two days by truck. The high-speed line that opened in 2025 does it in about an hour, which finally makes Yanan’s revolutionary sites, the caves, the museums – the whole “red tourism” itinerary – something you can see and do without needing the constitution of a 1930s war correspondent.

Then there was Xingping, in the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, and the cormorant fishermen I’d always wanted to get up close and personal with. I did it via a direct high-speed line from Guangzhou South to Guilin. The line’s Yangshuo stop, despite the name, is in Xingping itself, so I went straight from the train to the riverbank, to the exact scene I’d always wanted to capture.

This is a part of China’s rail network that doesn’t get talked about as much as the headline speeds: reaching into places previously cut off by geography rather than by lack of ambition. The whole system runs on the backbone of trunk lines, eight running broadly north to south and another eight running broadly east to west, with regional lines branching off the spine to feed smaller cities. The trains keep getting faster regardless; the CR450 has already hit 400km/h, making it the fastest on the planet.

The seat that puts business class to shame

China’s high-speed trains run four classes: second, first, a premium first on newer routes, and business, the one worth knowing about. On the newest Fuxing trains, business-class seats sit two and one across the aisle, with two metres of legroom, and each reclines fully flat. It is, in essence, a bed. You get a personal screen, a reading light, slippers and, on longer journeys, an attendant who treats the cabin the way a flight attendant might treat first class.

I have sat in first class on the Shinkansen in Japan and on the high-speed lines in Europe, and neither comes near a flatbed for the price. Japan gives you a wider seat and an admirably straight spine. Europe gives you a bit more elbow room and a quieter carriage. Neither lets you lie down, and the fare for trying is nothing like the modest premium business class commands here, where it runs at two to four times the price of second class, not the eye-watering sums you’d hand over to go flat on a flight.

Two systems, one habit of mind

What connects the trains and the cars isn’t just the technology, but the willingness to build the whole system at once. Decide where the chargers go before everyone owns an EV. Decide where the railway goes before the towns at the end of it have grown into the decision. Decide that business class ought to put everyone else’s first class to shame, and sort out the pricing later.

None of it announces itself. You only really notice when the sheer geographic cheek of the whole thing catches up with you all at once when you come back.

Lu-Ann Ong’s forthcoming book, Experience China: What Maps Don’t Tell, explores contemporary China through landscape, cuisine, history and memory.

item.title: [SCMP] Will Donald Trump’s China squeeze for summit leverage actually work?
item.description:
Washington’s recent wave of trade, tech and visa restrictions on China appears to be a deliberate push to build leverage ahead of the presidential summit in September, according to Chinese analysts.

However, they warn that such aggressive pressure tactics risk souring the political atmosphere ahead of the high-stakes meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.

The assessment comes as the two powers seek to establish a new framework of “constructive strategic stability”, in line with the agreement following the May Xi-Trump summit in Beijing.
item.content:encoded:
Washington’s recent wave of trade, tech and visa restrictions on China appears to be a deliberate push to build leverage ahead of the presidential summit in September, according to Chinese analysts.

However, they warn that such aggressive pressure tactics risk souring the political atmosphere ahead of the high-stakes meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.

The assessment comes as the two powers seek to establish a new framework of “constructive strategic stability”, in line with the agreement following the May Xi-Trump summit in Beijing.

On Thursday, Trump said plans were still on track for Xi’s visit to the White House on September 24, with AI expected to figure prominently in the talks.

Yet, underlying friction continues to build, driven by fresh US tech curbs and tariffs on major trading partners, including China.

Washington has moved to tighten exemptions for defence contractors procuring critical minerals from foreign adversaries. At the same time, officials have alleged that Chinese firms are illicitly using US artificial intelligence (AI) models to siphon intellectual property.

The US will also tighten restrictions on educational ties, by expanding a Pentagon blacklist barring more Chinese universities from receiving American military research funding.

In addition, US-bound foreign students and journalists, including those from China, face shorter visa durations.

The measures show that strategic stability “has not replaced strategic competition”, and that the geopolitical manoeuvring between the two will only deepen, according to Zhao Minghao, a professor at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies.

“Given the coming series of bilateral negotiations, the US also aims to use these restrictive measures as ‘bargaining chips’ to gain extra leverage against China,” Zhao said.

Beijing was likely to retaliate with countermeasures but “not to the extent” that it would cancel Xi’s planned US visit, he added.

In response to Trump’s remarks about Xi’s visit, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian on Friday referred to the “irreplaceable strategic guiding role” that head-of-state diplomacy has played in Beijing’s relationship with Washington.

“China is willing to work with the US to implement the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state in the field of artificial intelligence,” Lin said, adding that tariff wars and trade wars served no party’s interests.

According to Sun Chenghao, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, the latest US policies targeting China may not derail the coming meeting, but they would add tension to talks.

They would also complicate the pre-summit political atmosphere and narrow the room for domestic public opinion in both countries, Sun cautioned.

“On the other hand, it is precisely because of these growing frictions that the importance of high-level communication becomes even more pronounced.”

Past experience underscored the vital role of head-of-state diplomacy in establishing guard rails and managing risks, he added.

Sun argued that Washington’s roll-out of restrictive measures signalled a shifting strategic perception of China, driven by a growing consensus that technology, security and supply-chain issues demanded a much tougher approach.

“Before entering any formal negotiation phase, the US typically uses policy actions to strengthen its leverage, aiming to secure the upper hand in agenda-setting and rule-making,” he said.

Ma Zhaoxu, China’s foreign vice-minister, made a two-day trip to the US this week, in what was widely seen as the latest effort to pave the way for Xi’s anticipated visit to Washington in September.

The Chinese foreign ministry referred to the visit on Friday, confirming an earlier report by the South China Morning Post.

According to a statement from the Chinese embassy in Washington, Ma met key officials in charge of foreign affairs and defence policy regarding China, including Christopher Landau, the US deputy secretary of state, and Elbridge Colby, the US undersecretary of defence for policy.

Ma was also said to have exchanged views with members of both the US Senate and House of Representatives during his July 22-23 visit.

“The two sides had in-depth exchanges of views on implementing the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state and promoting the development of a constructive strategic stability relationship between China and the US,” the embassy said in a social media post.

Zhao suggested that Ma’s visit meant preparations for the next head-of-state summit were accelerating.

“If the meeting takes place in the US this September, the Trump administration will inevitably want to project a position of strength over China on American soil to showcase its leadership to US voters,” he said, calling such posturing “a subtle nuance inherent in head-of-state diplomacy”.

Sun observed that carrying on “dialogue while competing” had become a defining characteristic of current US-China relations.

“The core of this model is not about eliminating competition but rather establishing the necessary stabilising mechanisms within it,” he said.

He Weiwen, a senior fellow with the Centre for China and Globalisation (CCG), a Beijing-based think tank, said China and the US were engaging in both cooperation and competition and that this had become a new normal.

“Tariffs and technology curbs are consistent policies of this US administration and will not change, regardless of whether a leadership summit takes place,” said He, who previously worked as a commercial counsellor at the Chinese consulates in New York and San Francisco.

According to Sun, the vital question was whether the US measures primarily served the purpose of risk management or were gradually evolving into systemic containment.

The latter would only erode strategic mutual trust and make it more difficult for head-of-state summits to yield substantive results, he added.

He of the CCG noted that while the September summit was expected to stabilise overall relations and keep specific disputes from derailing broader ties, Taiwan remained a red line, whereas other points of contention were seen as manageable.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Senior American officials have previously suggested that Trump and Xi might meet as many as four times this year, including at November’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen and the Miami Group of 20 summit in December, apart from the reciprocal state visits.

item.title: [SCMP] Amid Hormuz woes, China tests Central Asian land corridors to bypass maritime chokepoints
item.description:
Beijing is doubling down on overland trade routes across Central Asia as continued disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region expose the vulnerability of global shipping chokepoints.

A new link to Afghanistan via Uzbekistan offers a practical example of this long-term diversification push. However, observers caution that security concerns and capacity constraints could make a meaningful shift away from sea freight difficult.

Officially launched in May with pilot shipments, the multi-modal freight corridor allows containers to be moved by rail from China through Kazakhstan into Uzbekistan, and then by road via Turkmenistan to Herat in western Afghanistan.
item.content:encoded:
Beijing is doubling down on overland trade routes across Central Asia as continued disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region expose the vulnerability of global shipping chokepoints.

A new link to Afghanistan via Uzbekistan offers a practical example of this long-term diversification push. However, observers caution that security concerns and capacity constraints could make a meaningful shift away from sea freight difficult.

Officially launched in May with pilot shipments, the multi-modal freight corridor allows containers to be moved by rail from China through Kazakhstan into Uzbekistan, and then by road via Turkmenistan to Herat in western Afghanistan.

According to media reports in Afghanistan and Uzbekistan, the 7,400km (4,600-mile) route cuts delivery times by up to two-thirds – taking 30 days instead of two to three months via traditional sea-and-land routes through Iran or Pakistan.

China and Afghanistan share a border only at the Wakhan corridor, a narrow, high-altitude strip.

The rugged terrain, a lack of paved infrastructure and security concerns in China’s western Xinjiang region severely limit direct trade via the corridor. As a result, Beijing relies on safer, established routes.

Goods bound for western Afghanistan earlier typically travelled by sea to Iran’s Bandar Abbas port or via Pakistan before overland trucking. Such journeys often took an average of 31 to 55 days.

Afghan officials have hailed the corridor as a more efficient, lower-cost pathway, citing reduced costs and improved cargo safety despite domestic instability.

They told TOLOnews, an independent Afghan news broadcaster, in May that the corridors were operating regularly and could transform the landlocked, mountainous country into a key regional transit hub connecting Central Asia with South Asia and Iran.

“The transportation of commercial goods through the two corridors, China-Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan-Afghanistan and China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan-Afghanistan, is ongoing regularly,” a spokesman for Afghanistan’s public works ministry was quoted as saying.

“Given its strategic location, Afghanistan can facilitate regional connectivity and link Central Asian countries with South Asia and Iran.”

Uzbekistan Railways subsidiary Uztemiryulkonteyner confirmed the pilot shipments in May, noting that containers were consolidated at the Bukhara logistics centre before being trucked onwards.

Nargiza Umarova at the University of World Economy and Diplomacy in Tashkent sees the corridor as part of a broader strategic vision linking two railways.

She noted that it was expected to connect with the proposed Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan (UAP) corridor and the imminent China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway project.

“It is important to understand that no transcontinental land corridor can compete with maritime transport routes in terms of cargo volume,” said Umarova, who heads the Centre for Strategic Connectivity at the university’s Institute for Advanced International Studies.

The corridor moves containers, not oil or gas, and China’s chokepoint problem is an energy problem

Jennifer Murtazashvili, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace

“At the same time, however, rail transport enables the diversification of foreign trade flows and significantly reduces delivery times.

“In light of the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, it also offers an opportunity to minimise the risks associated with crises in maritime shipping.”

She described Uzbekistan, which sees itself as a rising transit hub, as playing a “pivotal role” in these projects, reflecting Tashkent’s long-standing drive to diversify foreign trade flows and reduce logistics costs as a doubly landlocked country – a landlocked nation surrounded by other landlocked nations.

“Integrating these initiatives will not only take Uzbekistan to a qualitatively new level of development, but also benefit the entire Central Asian region, which will become a hub for intercontinental logistics,” she said.

Jennifer Murtazashvili, a non-resident scholar in the Asia Programme at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, offered a somewhat different assessment.

She described the corridor as “mostly a political signal, with modest regional trade value and almost no energy hedge”.

“The corridor moves containers, not oil or gas, and China’s chokepoint problem is an energy problem,” Murtazashvili said.

“You cannot truck the roughly 11 million imported barrels a day China burns across Afghanistan. So, this route does close to nothing for China’s sea-lane energy exposure.”

She added that while the new route mattered for regional trade in grain and consumer goods, “it’s trivial against maritime volumes”.

“What it does do is give Afghanistan and its neighbours an overland alternative to the old China-to-Bandar Abbas sea route,” she noted, while arguing that the corridor’s biggest challenge was not one single bottleneck but a chain of them.

Containers move by rail from China through Kazakhstan into Uzbekistan, then transfer to trucks through Turkmenistan to Herat.

“Each border is a separate customs regime and a separate place to extract rents,” she said, emphasising that overland transport was structurally more expensive than sea for goods that were not time-sensitive.

Murtazashvili stressed that Afghanistan’s risk lay less in “instability” in the abstract than in weak governance.

“The Taliban lack the administrative capacity, contract enforcement and security guarantees that make cross-border transit routine at scale,” she said, adding that “militant groups including ISKP pose a direct threat to infrastructure and personnel, with a documented pattern of attacks on Chinese targets”.

ISKP or Islamic State Khorasan (Province), also known as Isis-K, is a regional affiliate of Islamic State or Isis.

“Afghanistan can be a functioning link for modest regional trade. It can’t be a reliable partner for great-power logistics while it can’t govern or secure transit,” Murtazashvili cautioned.

“Hold this route as an option in a portfolio, don’t depend on it as a lifeline,” she said, adding that in a crisis, each state tended to act in its own interest.

Zhu Yongbiao, director of the Centre for Afghanistan Studies at Lanzhou University in China, said the Afghan corridor underscored Beijing’s diversification efforts, as the Hormuz crisis had exposed just how much of China’s energy supply and trade still depended on sea lanes vulnerable to conflict.

But he cautioned against overstating the strategic importance of the Afghanistan route.

The combined rail and road transport network had operated in various forms for years, beginning as a commercial initiative under the previous Afghan government rather than as a direct response to Hormuz tensions, Zhu noted.

“It has no direct link to the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.”

He also pointed to the corridor’s limited capacity and focus on containerised goods rather than bulk energy shipments such as oil.

Zhu argued that Afghanistan’s ambition to become a transit hub was undermined by severe infrastructure gaps, limited economic viability and sanctions by the United States and its allies including counterterrorism penalties targeting the Taliban and its funds.

“On the map Afghanistan appears to have potential, but in reality the conditions do not support it,” he said.

“Even without considering politics, sanctions or security, the problems are significant and feasibility is very low because the infrastructure and economic viability are weak, so the corridor is more of a supplement than a main artery.”

He also pointed to “core internal obstacles”: the Taliban government’s lack of broad international recognition, ongoing governance struggles and tense border clashes with neighbouring Pakistan.

“The main obstacles come from Afghanistan itself, not external factors. Without internal change and infrastructure improvement, the problem cannot be solved,” Zhu warned.

China has yet to officially recognise the Taliban government that took power in 2021, but Beijing maintains an embassy in Kabul, hosts Taliban leaders and engages in security talks as well as investment and economic cooperation.

Beijing has also considered utilising the ancient Wakhan Corridor as a potential direct link between Afghanistan and Xinjiang, underscoring its long‑term interest in cross‑border connectivity.

Despite these challenges, rail traffic between Afghanistan and Uzbekistan has grown sharply.

According to TOLOnews, railway officials in Uzbekistan said that January to May trade volume nearly doubled year-on-year, with more than 41,000 freight wagons moving 2.7 million tonnes of goods between the two countries.

The Hormuz crisis, triggered by US and Israeli strikes on Iran since February, has revived long-standing concerns in Beijing about the “Malacca dilemma”, shorthand for China’s dependence on maritime chokepoints such as the Strait of Malacca for oil and gas imports.

While maritime routes remain essential, Beijing has spent years building cross-border railways, port links and inland corridors to ensure no single chokepoint dominates its energy security.

While the Afghan corridor will not resolve China’s broader exposure to Gulf instability on the energy front, it forms part of Beijing’s wider effort to broaden supply and transport options, from the flagship China-Pakistan Economic Corridor to the Middle Corridor via Kazakhstan and Turkey, as well as proposed trans-Afghan links.

Zhu said the cross-border corridor projects fitted into Beijing’s wider Belt and Road Initiative, which he described as a resilient network designed to avoid reliance on single routes amid geopolitical turbulence.

Many alternative routes bypassing Afghanistan were already advancing, he noted, with Kabul at risk of being marginalised given its high investment costs.

“Afghanistan’s image as the ‘heart of Asia’ or ‘crossroads of Eurasia’ is more imagination than reality,” he said.

“If this situation continues, its role as a transit hub will decline further. Within [the] belt and road’s network, Afghanistan is at best an add-on, not a critical node.”

He contrasted Afghanistan’s limitations with the stronger potential of Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan to emerge as transport hubs, because of their superior infrastructure, governance and stability.

But Umarova was more optimistic.

She argued that despite the risk of instability in Afghanistan amid tensions along the Afghan-Pakistani border, the Taliban government had shown strong political will to “integrate the country into regional connectivity projects”.

She suggested that Pakistan, which has direct access to the Indian Ocean, should be part of a China-Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan transport corridor to “create alternative opportunities for China to access global markets by bypassing the Strait of Malacca and Hormuz”.

Its importance, she argued, went beyond immediate crises, such as the military conflict in the Middle East.

“The project is strategically founded and designed to ensure sustainable transport connectivity between the various poles of the Asian continent, with the active participation of Central Asian states and Afghanistan,” she said.

She said the planned Trans-Afghan Railway, also known as the Kabul Corridor, could provide the shortest land link between Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent, potentially handling up to 22 million tonnes of cargo a year and offering a route 1,200km shorter than the International North-South Transport Corridor through Iran.

The proposed line, first put forward by Uzbekistan in 2018, is intended as an alternative north-south transport and transit route. In Umarova’s view, it could eventually connect major economic centres in Europe, China, Russia and India.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s policy playbook took its EV sector from zero to hero – can other countries follow?
item.description:
China’s electric vehicle (EV) industry sits at the centre of numerous economic and geopolitical trends: consumer spending, environmental protection, trade policy, high-end manufacturing, technology and more. In this short series, we assess the current state of the sector within these broader contexts. Here, Yeon Woo Lee asks whether Beijing has written a blueprint for developing countries to kick-start their own contenders in the field.

Emerging markets once seemed like also-rans in the global car industry. In the days when petrol vehicles predominated, manufacturers required vast supplier networks and hard-won expertise in engines, transmissions and other core power train technologies to compete – two advantages among many for established, wealthier players.

But with a global shift towards electric engines and China’s consequent rise from automotive latecomer to EV powerhouse, that calculus has changed.
item.content:encoded:
China’s electric vehicle (EV) industry sits at the centre of numerous economic and geopolitical trends: consumer spending, environmental protection, trade policy, high-end manufacturing, technology and more. In this short series, we assess the current state of the sector within these broader contexts. Here, Yeon Woo Lee asks whether Beijing has written a blueprint for developing countries to kick-start their own contenders in the field.

Emerging markets once seemed like also-rans in the global car industry. In the days when petrol vehicles predominated, manufacturers required vast supplier networks and hard-won expertise in engines, transmissions and other core power train technologies to compete – two advantages among many for established, wealthier players.

But with a global shift towards electric engines and China’s consequent rise from automotive latecomer to EV powerhouse, that calculus has changed.

Many emerging-market governments have taken cues from China’s state-led playbook, using incentives to create demand while pushing companies to localise production and supply chains.

As the thinking goes, electrification can accelerate industrial catch-up and help them build domestic champions before global EV markets become more firmly dominated by a handful of large firms from a few early adopter countries.

“China’s rapid rise in the EV sector demonstrates that disruptive innovation can dismantle entrenched technology barriers – such as internal combustion engine – and unlock viable pathways to industrial upgrading,” said Claire Yuan, director at S&P Global Ratings. “Established international players could risk losing their competitiveness as local, state-backed national champions expand.”

Electrification has lowered some traditional barriers to entry by reducing the importance of engines and transmissions. At the same time, China’s vast EV supply chain has given aspiring carmakers a faster foothold by making key components easier to source.

But the same supply chain, though it has made entry easier, has also raised a difficult question: without full integration, how much value can these countries ultimately retain at home?

[VinFast] … would be an impressive example of a non-Chinese company applying the lessons from China

Centre for Strategic and International Studies

National champions take shape

Vietnam offers one of the clearest examples of a domestic EV industry built, at least partially, in China’s image, with policymakers leveraging state support to help transform a domestic firm into a national champion. At the centre is VinFast, founded in 2017 by Vingroup, one of the country’s largest private conglomerates.

According to state news agency Viet Nam News, by 2025 VinFast had become the country’s bestselling car brand, delivering 175,099 vehicles and nearly doubling the previous annual sales record set by foreign carmakers.

But its rise has not been driven solely by market forces. It has been underpinned by a strong government campaign to build a domestic EV industry, with Hanoi using policy support to localise production, strengthen supply chains and accelerate adoption. Vietnam has set a target for all road vehicles to be electric by 2050.

Incentives introduced under a July 2025 decree are among the strongest Vietnam has offered, according to Vietnam Plus, a website operated by the state-run Vietnam News Agency. The measures cover taxes, land use and rental fees. Foreign-invested companies seeking incentives are also required to include at least one Vietnamese company in their supply chains, a rule intended to deepen local industrial capacity.

The government has also helped to open another fast-growing market for VinFast: public transport. Vietnam wants taxis, buses and other vehicular forms of urban transport in major cities to shift to EVs by 2030, and VinFast has already secured a commanding position in that segment.

VinFast is now trying to turn its home-market momentum into a regional springboard. It launched electric taxi services in Indonesia in 2024 and the Philippines in 2025, while also building factories in India and Indonesia.

“There are some questions … but it [VinFast] does appear to have rapidly transformed the domestic four-wheeler market and, if successful, would be an impressive example of a non-Chinese company applying the lessons from China to succeed in technological leapfrogging,” the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a Washington-based think tank, wrote in an October report.

A short cut with long odds

But even with its proven track record, China’s model is not easy to emulate. Not every emerging economy has the industrial base or fiscal capacity to nurture a domestic EV champion. Smaller markets with limited automotive manufacturing bases, such as Nepal and Costa Rica, have largely relied on imports to electrify their roads, according to CSIS.

Building a domestic EV champion is slower and costlier than relying on imports or assembly, but if it works, electrification offers the chance to build domestic manufacturing capacity and move up the value chain.

“EV sales are where all the growth is happening. It’s pretty clear what the long-term bet is,” said Euan Graham, senior electricity and data analyst at energy think tank Ember. Global sales of petrol and diesel cars, he noted, had already peaked in 2017.

Turkey is among the countries trying to seize that opening, drawing on its manufacturing base that global carmakers have long used as a hub for exports to Europe.

To meet its target of putting 2 million EVs on the road by 2030, Ankara is offering a wide range of support, including tax breaks, charging infrastructure expansion and multibillion-dollar manufacturing incentives. It is also seeking to localise battery production, with a target of 80 gigawatt-hours of annual capacity by the end of the decade.

At the centre of the push is Togg, a domestic EV maker formed in 2018 by five major Turkish industrial groups – Anadolu Group, BMC, Kok Group, Turkcell and Zorlu Holding – together with the Union of Chambers and Commodity Exchanges of Turkey, a confederation of private-sector groups.

Togg became Turkey’s top-selling electric car brand last year, selling 39,020 units and ranking ahead of global rivals such as Tesla and BYD in the domestic market, according to Daily Sabah, a Turkish newspaper with links to the government.

India’s bet, meanwhile, is bigger and more protective, reflecting the scale of its domestic car market and the strength of its existing manufacturing base.

New Delhi has focused on production-linked incentive schemes for advanced batteries, automobiles and auto components, while the states of Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra have developed their own strategies to attract EV investment.

Those incentives are reinforced by high tariffs. India maintains some of the world’s highest duties on imported EVs, with rates reaching around 100 per cent for some models, giving domestic manufacturers additional room to scale up.

That protected and policy-backed market has helped local players take a commanding position. Tata Motors and Mahindra & Mahindra, along with JSW MG Motor – a joint venture established in 2023 between India’s JSW Group and China’s SAIC Motor – accounted for 87.3 per cent of the country’s passenger EV market in the 2025-26 financial year, according to the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations of India.

“Some domestic manufacturers have seen extreme success in some local markets,” Graham said. “The challenge they face now is being able to replicate this domestic success abroad, which would be key to scaling further.”

The dependence dilemma

Analysts say the policy logic is broadly similar across these countries. Like China, governments are using subsidies and tax incentives to create an early EV market before gradually pushing companies towards more local production and component sourcing.

The harder question is how much of the higher-value EV supply chain they can capture at home, particularly as their path into the industry increasingly runs through China.

Ryan Featherston, an associate fellow at CSIS’ Trustee Chair in Chinese Business and Economics, said the major uncertainty was whether emerging-market carmakers could move into higher-value parts of the EV supply chain, especially batteries, where Chinese firms remain the most competitive.

“I do think for countries that have that domestic market scale and industrial policy commitment, they have a shot at developing a real industrial base,” said Featherston, who wrote the CSIS report from October. “For many of those countries, though, that base is also going to come in part from investment from Chinese companies.”

That dependence is already visible. VinFast procures batteries from Chinese battery maker Contemporary Ampex Technology Ltd, commonly known as CATL, while Togg has teamed up with Farasis Energy to operate Siro, a battery joint venture. JSW MG Motor India is partly backed by China’s SAIC Motor, BYD supplies batteries for some Mahindra models and some Tata models rely on batteries from Chinese firm Gotion.

“Consequently, fully replicating China’s EV development model is difficult for most emerging countries in the short-run,” said Yuan of S&P Global Ratings.

That reliance creates a difficult trade-off. Chinese investment and technology can help emerging economies build EV capacity faster, but heavy dependence on foreign suppliers could limit how much value they ultimately capture at home.

The challenge is sharper for smaller markets. Limited domestic volumes may not be enough to justify the heavy R&D spending required for batteries, software and vehicle platforms.

Industrial policies that encourage too many domestic players also risk creating more capacity than local demand can absorb, said Michael Smitka, an emeritus professor of economics at Washington and Lee University who specialises in the global auto industry.

That could push some governments towards a more defensive approach. Yuan said some emerging economies may initially rely on imported components to launch domestic brands, then seek to protect those national champions through high import tariffs or local standards.

But the bigger test, the CSIS report said, is whether governments can turn Chinese investment into deeper local capacity by pushing firms to localise production, train local staff, support domestic suppliers and transfer some technology and manufacturing know-how.

Attracting non-Chinese investment would also be crucial to reducing both geopolitical and economic dependence on China, it added.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines’ Pax Silica AI hub plan slammed for mineral ‘plunder’
item.description:
On a 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) site north of Manila, Philippine and US officials are pitching a hi-tech hub as a global gateway to AI, semiconductors and critical minerals.

For critics, however, the proposed development – part of the US-backed global Pax Silica project – is concrete proof of another infrastructure push over contested land at the expense of local communities, threatening their livelihoods and scarce water supplies.

It is, they argue, a further example of ambitious investment pitches racing ahead of environmental safeguards and proper cost-benefit analysis.
item.content:encoded:
On a 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) site north of Manila, Philippine and US officials are pitching a hi-tech hub as a global gateway to AI, semiconductors and critical minerals.

For critics, however, the proposed development – part of the US-backed global Pax Silica project – is concrete proof of another infrastructure push over contested land at the expense of local communities, threatening their livelihoods and scarce water supplies.

It is, they argue, a further example of ambitious investment pitches racing ahead of environmental safeguards and proper cost-benefit analysis.

Manila is seeking to finalise a framework agreement with Washington for the hub within two to three months, according to Joshua Bingcang, president and CEO of the state-run Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA).

The BCDA is tasked with turning former US military bases into centres of economic growth, including the one in New Clark City near Capas, Tarlac province – about 100km (62 miles) north of Manila – where the hub is set to be located.

Pax Silica aims to secure critical supply chains for artificial intelligence, semiconductors and other strategic technologies. The Philippines and Singapore are the only Southeast Asian members of the coalition.

Bingcang said the hub would likely start operations within two years, attract an initial US$10 billion in investment and generate “hundreds of thousands of jobs”.

The hub forms part of the Luzon Economic Corridor, a US-Japan-Philippines project linking four cities on Luzon Island that is projected to generate US$100 billion for the local economy.

Bingcang confirmed that Manila and Washington were exchanging draft agreements and denied earlier reports that the hub would operate under US legal jurisdiction despite being sited on Philippine soil.

In a television interview on Wednesday, he said Washington was aiming to conclude the deal before US President Donald Trump’s potential visit to the Philippines to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in November and mark 80 years of US-Philippine ties.

The US State Department has described Pax Silica as an effort to build “a secure, resilient” technology supply chain, as Washington looks to reduce its reliance on Chinese suppliers, especially for critical technologies.

Opposition to the planned hub has grown, with critics expressing concerns about the continued marginalisation and displacement of indigenous communities and farmers, environmental degradation and resource exploitation.

IBON Foundation has challenged claims that the hub would accelerate industrial, saying in a social media post in May that the Philippines “doesn’t have a strategy for national industrialisation”.

“Pax Silica isn’t about industrialising the Philippines but about deeper integration into US-controlled semiconductor and AI supply chains,” the non-profit think tank said, adding that industrialisation required building “national productive power” through local industries, labour, science and technology.

On Tuesday, around 3,000 members of the indigenous Aeta community in Capas marched in protest against restrictions they said authorities had imposed on their lands, including limits on access and basic supplies, which they claimed were partly related to the hub.

“The single most dangerous thing about Pax Silica is what it adds to a crisis that was already exploding before the announcement was made,” said Cathleen De Guzman, national coordinator for the Kalikasan People’s Network for the Environment, a Philippines-based environmental campaign group.

De Guzman said the Aeta community had fought for decades to secure titles to its ancestral domains, with the government repeatedly declining to issue them.

“The absence of a paper document was used to erase the existence of a community that has lived there since before the Spanish arrived,” she said, adding that an estimated 20,000 indigenous people and 15,000 farmers were at risk of displacement from the New Clark City development.

She also raised concerns about the Sacobia watershed – the primary water source for areas across New Clark City – warning that the risk of it drying up had been flagged as far back as 2020.

This Week in Asia has contacted the BCDA for comment.

Middle ground?

The backlash has exposed gaps in transparency, timing and legal process, according to environmental analysts.

Paulo Burro, an environmental policy and government affairs consultant and managing partner of Climate Balanced Business Advisors, said land conversion and the displacement of farmers, fisherfolk and indigenous people remained the biggest concerns surrounding the Pax Silica hub.

“With the drive to consolidate the supply chain, there may be increased mineral demand … questions remain around its actual economic impact on displaced farmers and fisherfolk,” Burro said.

Jonas Marie Dumdum, an energy and sustainability researcher and consultant, said such concerns were understandable given the scale of the project, noting the likely demand for minerals such as nickel, cobalt and copper to supply the hub.

Companies at the hub would not only draw an estimated 5,000 megawatts from Luzon’s coal-dependent grid, but also be located near identified watersheds and northeast of Mount Pinatubo, he said, referring to the active volcano whose 1991 eruption caused hundreds of deaths.

“The real pressure points in Capas come down to three things: carbon emissions, water and waste,” Dumdum said.

Industries would draw on the same water systems used to irrigate farms in central Tarlac, while mineral processing would produce heavy-metal waste in an area vulnerable to both flooding and volcanic eruption, he said.

“These points raise a question not just about our climate commitments but about whether there’s enough power, fresh water, and enough space and capacity to treat e-wastes in the area.”

However, Burro said that compromise remained possible, provided the interests of businesses, environmental groups and local communities were all protected.

The question was “how the project gets built and who gets a say, not necessarily over whether it should exist at all”, he said.

Dumdum said the public should be informed about the sources of the hub’s water and power supply, as well as the waste treatment process for mineral extraction.

He added that there should be a proper assessment of the potential environmental impact and “real consent” from farming and indigenous communities before the finalisation of any deal.

De Guzman said she “outrightly rejects Pax Silica”, calling it “plunder” of the country’s critical minerals and energy sources, as well as an attack on national sovereignty and patrimony.

She also questioned the authorities’ commitment to community engagement, calling the process a “pattern of consultation theatre”.

“This unequal agreement that the Philippines has joined opens our lands and vulnerable sectors to further exploitation and displacement,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Tuscan, Korean and Cantonese: 3 chefs reimagine classic beef dishes in Hong Kong
item.description:
It’s the same animal. In a Tuscan kitchen, it’s carved tableside as a ritual. In a Korean kitchen, it’s sliced thin and gone in seconds. And in a Cantonese kitchen, it’s been braising since morning.

In Hong Kong, three chefs are bringing their love of beef from home, each cooking through the lens of a childhood tradition that shaped them long before they ever stepped into a professional kitchen. Here is how to eat beef well, because whether in Tuscany, Seoul, or Hong Kong, the rule is simple: when it comes to beef, do as the locals do.

Tuscan at Carna by Dario Cecchini
item.content:encoded:
It’s the same animal. In a Tuscan kitchen, it’s carved tableside as a ritual. In a Korean kitchen, it’s sliced thin and gone in seconds. And in a Cantonese kitchen, it’s been braising since morning.

In Hong Kong, three chefs are bringing their love of beef from home, each cooking through the lens of a childhood tradition that shaped them long before they ever stepped into a professional kitchen. Here is how to eat beef well, because whether in Tuscany, Seoul, or Hong Kong, the rule is simple: when it comes to beef, do as the locals do.

Tuscan at Carna by Dario Cecchini

Dario Cecchini is a proud Tuscan – and when an eighth-generation butcher from Panzano in Chianti tells you how to eat beef, you listen.

For Cecchini, the Bistecca alla Fiorentina is the centrepiece of Italian beef. The steak arrives whole, close to 2kg, still shimmering from the grill. It is 4cm thick, which allows the surface to develop a deep, mahogany crust while the inside stays rare and cool. What you get in a single bite is a series of contrasts – char and blood, fat and lean, smoke and minerality. Cecchini calls this “a conversation of textures”.

He brings that conversation to Mondrian Hong Kong, where his eponymous Carna by Dario Cecchini serves the same Bistecca by the same rule: never season the steak before it touches fire. Salt and Tuscan olive oil are applied only after cooking. Salt draws moisture to the surface, which then steams rather than sears, robbing the crust of its depth. But the rule runs deeper than food science. “You are saying to the steak, you are already complete,” Cecchini says. “I am only here to finish your essence.”

If you want a deeper cut, Cecchini recommends the spider steak. Known in Italian as ragnolino, it is a small, humble cut from the inner thigh. A lean and muscular cut, it is often overlooked in favour of more famous names. Grilled simply on the bone and dressed with extra virgin Tuscan olive oil and Cecchini’s own herb salt, Profumo del Chianti, it proves his philosophy better than any sermon could: no cut is tough if treated with care. It is only ever waiting for the right hands.

That philosophy traces back to cucina povera – the cooking of the poor – that has shaped Tuscan tradition for centuries. Cecchini’s grandmother made one of his favourite dishes from boiled beef knees – Tenerumi in Insalata. “Those memories shaped me,” he says. “It is knowledge passed down through generations, and what we are doing is keeping that conversation alive.”

On Carna’s menu, each muscle is named: the scamone, the costata, the cappello del prete. Diners can look at an illustration of the cow marked with numbers and pick the part they want to try. “It is an act of respect,” Cecchini says. “To the animal that gave its life, to the farmer who raised it, and to the guest, whom we trust to care about where their food comes from.”

Korean at Moo-Lah by Born and Bred

The grill is already hot. Thin slices of beef hit the metal and curl at the edges within seconds, smoke rising as chopsticks dart across the table. The meat goes from raw to perfect in the time it takes to grab a spoonful of rice. If Tuscany celebrates beef with stately reverence, this is the Korean rhythm, where speed matters.

For Jung Sang-won, co-founder of Born & Bred in Seoul and Moo-Lah in Hong Kong, the etiquette of the grill is one he learned young. He remembers eating tteok-galbi patties made from rib finger meat as a child: the meat’s aroma slowly grilling, the texture tender yet structured, and the way the fat caught the edge of the fire.

“For me, this memory is not just about food,” Jung says. “It was my first deep experience of understanding texture and flavour in beef.”

That memory now travels to Hong Kong, where Jung is developing a wonton inspired by tteok-galbi, using hand-chopped Hanwoo finger meat to intentionally preserve structure and bite.

Hanwoo, Korea’s native cattle, is at the centre of Jung’s kitchen. But it is more than just a breed of cow; it is “the result of farming environments, the philosophy of producers, and long-developed rearing practices”, the chef says.

Historically, cattle in Korea were not just livestock – they were partners in farming. Because of this, Korean beef culture developed around the idea of using the whole animal rather than focusing only on the premium cuts. The Korean saying, Il-dubaekmi, literally translates to “one cow, one hundred flavours”. While Western butchery divides a cow into about 10 primary cuts, Korean butchers can break a cow down into over 120 distinct parts.

Ask Jung to name one cut most non-Koreans may have never heard of, and his answer is immediate: jebichuri. Jebichuri (neck chain) comes from the area between the neck and chest, a heavily used muscle that develops a deep flavour and a distinctive chew. “Many people assume that highly marbled cuts define quality,” Jung says. “But once they experience jebichuri, they realise that the beef’s flavour is not defined only by fat content.”

Because it is lean, jebichuri demands a fast hand and tastes best when thinly sliced and quickly grilled over high heat, allowing the surface to caramelise fast while the inside stays juicy. It is the perfect expression of the Korean preference for quick cooking, tied to communal dining. Meat is shared at the table, cooked together and never eaten in isolation. “Korean food culture is deeply tied to rice,” Jung explains. “Thin slicing allows for the ideal balance of temperature and texture when eaten with rice.”

Cantonese at Duddell’s

The pot starts cooking long before service. Inside are beef brisket tendon and white radish, submerged and simmering; the liquid barely moving as the hours pass. You’ll know it’s ready when the meat yields and absorbs the sweetness of the radish. As much as the brisket is the star, time is the ingredient that cannot be rushed. And for chef Chan Yau-leung of Duddell’s, this patience is the foundation of his cooking.

Chan grew up in Hong Kong in the 1960s, in modest circumstances. Beef brisket and tendon (ngau gan lam) noodles were a rare luxury reserved for festivals or birthdays. He still remembers the weight of those bowls. “It left an indelible impression,” he says.

He holds ngau gan lam to an exceptionally high standard because he knows what it meant to him and others like him even before he stepped into a professional kitchen. The tendons must be thick and unctuous. The brisket must have a robust beef flavour and be soft and aromatic – elevated into what he calls the signature “radish brisket” profile that defines comfort in Cantonese cuisine.

The preparation demands patience, and the cut must be subjected to slow, gentle heat. This is where Chan sees home cooks go wrong. Cuts that require time, like brisket, are rushed, while delicate cuts that need a flash of heat, like rib-eye or Wagyu, are overcooked. “The key is to match the cooking time and method precisely to the cut’s characteristics,” he says.

Chan has honed this precision in the kitchen for more than four decades. At Duddell’s, his Spicy Mala Beef Shank is marinated, boiled for two to three hours, then infused again with Sichuan peppercorns and chilli for depth. He takes a different approach to the tender rib-eye, choosing to mince and steam it with 20-year-old tangerine peel for his steamed minced beef patty.

His own favourite cut is one that rarely appears in the spotlight: ngau lei sam (ox tongue heart). It is also the most challenging to cook properly, according to the chef. “The texture varies significantly throughout the muscle,” Chan says. “Some parts are soft while others are tough. It requires immense precision, care, and experience to handle correctly.” To honour it, he slowly simmers the tongue to infuse it with flavour, then isolates only the tenderest core, preparing it with port wine and vine tomatoes. Time does the rest.

item.title: [SCMP] Why and how the media industry can fit into Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan
item.description:
Mainstream media, particularly in Hong Kong, have historically been conservative in their research and development spending. Media executives prefer to shop for off-the-shelf solutions, treating technology as back-office support rather than a core growth engine.

This mode of operation now faces an existential challenge amid the explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI), large language models and Web3 technologies. Concurrently, these developments offer Hong Kong’s media industry fresh opportunities, particularly as such innovations have been identified as key components of China’s 15th five-year plan and, by extension, a focus of Hong Kong’s alignment with the national strategy.

One of the bottlenecks in AI development is the lack of high-quality, verified data that encompasses local culture and nuances. Professional journalism, in-depth reports and historical archives held by traditional media can be a gold mine for good model training.
item.content:encoded:
Mainstream media, particularly in Hong Kong, have historically been conservative in their research and development spending. Media executives prefer to shop for off-the-shelf solutions, treating technology as back-office support rather than a core growth engine.

This mode of operation now faces an existential challenge amid the explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI), large language models and Web3 technologies. Concurrently, these developments offer Hong Kong’s media industry fresh opportunities, particularly as such innovations have been identified as key components of China’s 15th five-year plan and, by extension, a focus of Hong Kong’s alignment with the national strategy.

One of the bottlenecks in AI development is the lack of high-quality, verified data that encompasses local culture and nuances. Professional journalism, in-depth reports and historical archives held by traditional media can be a gold mine for good model training.

International publishers have already pivoted to monetise these assets. News Corp recently signed a deal worth a reported US$250 million over five years with OpenAI. The Associated Press, Reuters and a growing list of publishers are building recurring revenue from content they already own.

Hong Kong has remained largely an idle observer. This passivity risks more than missed financial opportunities. It brings security and cultural concerns. As younger generations increasingly rely on AI models to synthesise information and understand the world, the data used to train these models becomes the new frontier of the global narrative war. If local media companies do not actively invest in processing, protecting and commercialising their data, the digital narrative of Hong Kong will be written by external models trained on unverified or biased sources.

Addressing this requires a fundamental shift from both the industry and the government. The Hong Kong government encourages AI adoption in traditional sectors through programmes such as the Enterprise Support Scheme (ESS) under the Innovation and Technology Fund (ITF). Yet as of March 2024, the ESS Assessment Panel had approved 220 projects out of 762 applications. The beneficiaries were almost exclusively deep-tech start-ups, biomedical firms, microelectronic companies and software-as-a-service developers. Not a single media outlet was among them.

Industry inertia is the main reason. Hong Kong media outlets traditionally invest in tech applications rather than genuine innovation, rarely designing proprietary tools with the intention of spinning them off as commercial software products for global markets. Consequently, media applications struggle to prove commercial product viability under strict innovation and technology (I&T) definitions.

However, there is also the issue of bureaucratic silos. For decades, Hong Kong’s media and creative industries have been isolated in a different administrative ecosystem from tech start-ups. Media is grouped with film, sports and entertainment under bureaus that prioritise artistic creativity, cultural impact and audience reach, while the ITF focuses on hard tech.

This division is outdated. Media operations – including speech-to-text, real-time multilingual translation, automated video generation, smart content recommendation and blockchain-based copyright protection – offer the most natural, high-density sandbox for developing and testing advanced AI technologies. With the right policy support, the media industry can branch out beyond the narrowly defined “culture industry” into the media-tech sector. Nurturing such a new industry would broaden professional horizons for local tech graduates, who currently face limited options.

For this transformation to occur, we must dismantle institutional barriers. We could consider classifying media-tech, generative AI content and digital language infrastructure as strategic technology industries. This reclassification would grant media organisations legal and administrative parity when applying for tech funding and resources, effectively moving them from the periphery of the cultural sector to the core of the I&T ecosystem.

For instance, Hong Kong currently offers a 300 per cent tax deduction for R&D expenditure, but media companies are excluded because content creation is not recognised as technical R&D. Policymakers should explicitly clarify that capital spent by media companies on developing proprietary software, algorithm engineering and data cleaning for AI training qualifies for these deductions.

Even more critically, the government must establish a modern legal and technical framework to protect local intellectual property from predatory mining. Hong Kong is updating its copyright laws by introducing a text and data mining exception into the Copyright Ordinance. While this amendment aims to allow AI developers to use copyrighted data for training without prior permission under specific conditions, it must include stringent safeguards, such as legal protections for paywalls and mandate clear opt-out mechanisms for local media outlets.

Because most traditional media companies lack the technical staff to build sophisticated digital walls against global AI scrapers, the government’s Digital Policy Office should step in. The DPO can help build and deploy practical shared infrastructure to explicitly signal to global web crawlers that Hong Kong media archives are protected by copyright.

This regulation is not an invitation for the media industry to become free riders. Rather, it corrects a massive market failure where small local content creators face global tech monopolies. In this struggle between David and Goliath, the government cannot be just a passive referee.

Only by establishing a regulated and fair market can the industry stand a chance of investing in and commercialising data for AI development. Traditional media cannot fund multimillion-dollar research on declining advertising revenues. They need structured government matching and equity investments for these changes to take place. We do not need to invent new funds; rather, we should loosen bureaucratic constraints to make existing ones accessible to the media sector. Over time, the government can champion locally developed media-tech by becoming the “first customer” that adopts tools such as public sentiment analysis and multilingual content creation.

By treating media-tech with the same financial and policy weight currently afforded to fintech or biotech, the Hong Kong government can convert a legacy industry into a vibrant node of new quality productive forces. This strategy would preserve local journalism while aggressively expanding Hong Kong’s digital cultural footprint under the 15th five-year plan.

In the age of AI, impactful storytelling requires technological leverage. For Hong Kong to cement its role as China’s international centre for technological and information innovation over the next decade, a vibrant media industry is critical.

item.title: [SCMP] A cloud above the clouds: US, China race to make space a computing platform
item.description:
In 1957, the Soviet Union kicked off the Cold War’s space race, shocking the world by sending Sputnik, the world’s first artificial satellite, into orbit.

Four years later, it did the same to cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, making him the first human in space. In 1969, the US provided another image that defined the era: Neil Armstrong leaving the Eagle lunar lander and planting the American flag on the moon, declaring it “one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.”

For the two superpowers, the space race was an ideological contest measured in firsts – with each milestone setting down a marker for technological know-how, national pride and a renewed commitment to push beyond the bounds of Earth.
item.content:encoded:
In 1957, the Soviet Union kicked off the Cold War’s space race, shocking the world by sending Sputnik, the world’s first artificial satellite, into orbit.

Four years later, it did the same to cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, making him the first human in space. In 1969, the US provided another image that defined the era: Neil Armstrong leaving the Eagle lunar lander and planting the American flag on the moon, declaring it “one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.”

For the two superpowers, the space race was an ideological contest measured in firsts – with each milestone setting down a marker for technological know-how, national pride and a renewed commitment to push beyond the bounds of Earth.

Half a century later, a new space race is taking shape, with China emerging as one of the leading actors.

However, this competition is about more than symbolic firsts. Countries are seeking to make the technological achievements necessary to occupy, operate and utilise space, creating a new layer of digital infrastructure through satellites, networks, sensors and computing systems.

SpaceX, the US tech giant gearing up for what is expected to be the world’s biggest initial public offering as early as next month, has become a major player in this contest, releasing plans for orbital data centres, an experimental technology that is nonetheless sending ripples through global supply chains by driving demand for base metals, chips, satellites and rockets.

China, nurturing its own commercial space sector, is racing to keep up. Industry insiders and analysts based in the country said space was the new battlefield for technological competition, and Beijing could not afford a strategic absence.

“Talking too much about ‘the first’ is meaningless in a truly innovative context,” said Wang Jian, an academician at the Chinese Academy of Engineering, adding he wanted the country to “send computing power and AI into space”.

Wang, a founder of Alibaba Cloud, helped build China’s cloud computing industry. He now leads a research institute backed by Zhejiang’s provincial government, known as Zhejiang Lab. Its flagship Three-Body Computing Constellation project aims to build a thousand-satellite network for space computing.

Calculating beyond the clouds

“Space computing refers to shifting computing capability into orbit,” said Lin Guangrong, constellation communications systems architect at Chinese satellite maker GalaxySpace. “[It lets] satellites and spacecraft perform sensing, processing and data transmission directly in space.”

The ultimate vision is “space-based primary computing” – data centres that float in a layer above the actual clouds – according to China’s Academy of Information and Communications Technology, a think tank affiliated with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.
