For decades, the aerospace industry operated under a standard procedure: sense in space, compute on Earth. Satellites were merely orbital cameras and mirrors, capturing raw data and waiting for a designated “downlink window” to beam it to a terrestrial ground station.

But a paradigm shift is under way, accelerated by rapid changes in the terrestrial economy and their attendant challenges.

On Earth, there are fears the boom in artificial intelligence data centres – described by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as “the largest infrastructure buildout in human history” – could run into crippling physical constraints such as land shortages, strained power grids and access to the water required for cooling.

“Current advances in AI are dependent on large terrestrial data centres,” wrote SpaceX CEO Elon Musk in a February memo announcing SpaceX’s acquisition of xAI. “In the long term, space-based AI is obviously the only way to scale.”

Tech leaders have begun to make the case for moving heavy AI workloads into orbit – where solar energy is abundant and the vacuum of space, in theory, would provide unlimited coolant – arguing it is the only sustainable way to ease the compounding infrastructure pressures on Earth’s ecosystems.

But more immediately, space computing would serve as a boon for data preservation – a wide-ranging benefit.

“As the number of satellites in orbit continues to grow alongside mission density, the volume of space data is rising rapidly,” Lin said.

Wang said about 90 per cent of remote-sensing satellite data was discarded in space because Earth-based networks could not handle the sheer volume of information.

That could result in delays and, sometimes, missed signals. Information about floods, wildfires, ship movements or cosmic ray bursts lasting only seconds could lose much of its value by requiring a downlink window before being analysed on Earth.

The race begins

China entered the space race relatively late. Its first satellite, Dongfanghong 1, lifted off from Jiuquan in 1970 and broadcast the revolutionary song “The East Is Red” from orbit.

“From the perspective of technological competition, China cannot afford a strategic absence,” said Mi Lei, founder of CAS Star, a venture capital firm backed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences whose portfolio spans low-Earth-orbit communications, launch companies and satellite makers.

“Space is too important. In the new round of technological competition, a country has to be good at everything.”

While China does not face the same severe electricity and land constraints limiting the US capacity for data centre construction, it wants a central role in the next race.

Its advantage lies in its ability to fully mobilise a centralised industrial system – uniting components, satellites, rockets, launch sites, measurement systems, applications and a manufacturing base – under state command, according to a recent report by a research institute affiliated with the information technology ministry.

That holistic ecosystem allows China to bypass some of the fragmented commercial inefficiencies that can plague Western tech deployment.

Chinese authorities have voiced their support for space-based computing, sending a clear signal for capital and industry players. At a news conference last month, an official from the ministry said China would “support forward-looking research into space computing technologies and promote the orderly development of the space-computing industry”.

In the blueprint for the latest five-year plan, which runs through 2030, the commercial space sector was listed as one of 10 new industries and growth areas China would nurture and develop, as Beijing for the first time included the goal of becoming a “space power” among its national “strong country” objectives.

Against that backdrop, new research labs and companies are emerging.

The Three-Body Computing Constellation, designed to solve space’s data problem in space with AI, successfully launched an initial batch of 12 computing satellites in May last year. It is aiming for 100 next year and is equipping each spacecraft with an onboard computing unit capable of delivering up to 744 trillion operations a second.

Zhejiang Lab said in February it had deployed 10 AI models in orbit, including a remote-sensing model, an astronomical time-domain model, and a Qwen large language model from Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post. Several of the models can be updated while in orbit.

In one recent experiment, satellites equipped with cosmic ray detectors used a space-based astronomical model to rapidly identify and classify gamma-ray bursts.

Zhejiang Lab also established in-orbit network links between six satellites this year, marking a significant step towards inter-satellite networking.

“The field is still in an early phase of exploration and technical validation,” said Lin of GalaxySpace.

The US’ head start

The most immediate hurdle facing China’s ambition is the infrastructure required to get orbiting computers into the sky efficiently – an area where the US holds a long-standing advantage.

Driven by tech titans with deep pockets, the American aerospace industry has made strides in high-frequency, low-cost reusable rockets.

SpaceX completed roughly 165 orbital launches last year, with that rapid-fire capability enabling the construction of Starlink – a fully functioning global broadband low-Earth-orbit network with over 10,000 satellites.

Musk’s company is now leveraging that dominance, seeking US regulatory approval for a constellation of up to 1 million solar-powered satellites engineered specifically as orbital data centres. Such a massive fleet would solidify America’s architectural dominance over the lower atmosphere.

China, however, has yet to master high-frequency, SpaceX-style reusable rocket technology.

While its Qianfan and Guowang megaconstellation plans are ambitious, each has only launched a few hundred satellites so far.

Compounding the hardware gap is the nature of the competition itself. Beijing is primarily relying on state-directed labs, targeted pilot programmes, and a still-maturing commercial space industry, while Washington’s space computing push is being propelled by an aggressive, cash-rich alliance of private AI and chip giants.

Google is advancing its Project Suncatcher, a moon-shot effort to link solar-powered satellites equipped with its proprietary Tensor Processing Units in an orbital AI cloud.

AI start-up Anthropic struck a deal with SpaceX this month to use the latter’s Colossus 1 data centre, while signalling interest in a broader partnership to develop gigawatt-scale AI computational processing power in orbit.

Nvidia, meanwhile, unveiled a Space-1 Vera Rubin module at its GTC conference in March, describing it as part of a new accelerated computing platform for space applications. The company has already placed an H100 graphics processing unit in orbit on a satellite launched by Starcloud, a start-up it backs.

Humbled by physics

Yet both sides must confront the laws of physics, which favour no superpower.

“To make space computing work at scale, onboard computing, inter-satellite links, space-ground integration and thermal management all have to move forward together,” Lin said.

High-power computing units generate massive amounts of heat, but cooling is an issue in such a brutal environment. While space is cold, it is also a vacuum – meaning there is no air for convection.

Instead, heat must be laboriously conducted through the structural body of the spacecraft and radiated away through large thermal panels, making high-power space computing a heavy, complicated and expensive thermodynamic challenge.

Then comes the power paradox. Running trillions of operations per second requires immense energy, forcing engineers to develop lightweight, foldable, radiation-resistant solar arrays that must constantly balance thermal design with spacecraft orientation.

It is a systems-level conundrum, and no current solar cell has presented a clear solution. Every material choice involves severe trade-offs between weight, flexibility, lifespan and radiation tolerance.

To combat these challenges, industry players like GalaxySpace have not only poured capital into mass production of synthetic aperture radar satellites, but also into complex pumped fluid-loop thermal management systems and advanced flexible solar arrays.

According to a paper written by Google researchers, the engineering hurdles also encompass high-bandwidth inter-satellite laser communications, radiation-hardened components and long-term hardware reliability in an environment hostile to delicate silicon.

Google’s researchers were not as positive as Musk, who frames orbital data centres as a near-term possibility. They said the cost of launching and operating a space-based data centre would not become economically comparable to terrestrial infrastructure until the mid-2030s, assuming launch prices fall below US$200 per kg.

To put that into perspective, SpaceX says its Falcon 9 can send up to 22,800kg (50,265 pounds) into low-Earth orbit, and with each launch reported to cost about US$74 million, that implies a full-capacity launch cost of roughly US$3,245 per kg.

item.title: [SCMP] Houthi blockade of Saudi trade threatens wider Middle East conflict
item.description:
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Tehran-allied Houthi movement edged closer to opening a new front in the Iran war overnight, after Riyadh bombed the port city of Hodeidah in retaliation for a Houthi missile strike on one of its ships in the Red Sea.

The exchange marks the latest escalation since the Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, imposed an embargo on Saudi shipping on Monday, disrupting maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects Asia to Europe via the Suez Canal.

A near-identical Houthi missile attack on an oil tanker owned by the National Shipping Company of Saudi Arabia on Thursday had already prompted threats of American military intervention from US President Donald Trump.
item.content:encoded:
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Tehran-allied Houthi movement edged closer to opening a new front in the Iran war overnight, after Riyadh bombed the port city of Hodeidah in retaliation for a Houthi missile strike on one of its ships in the Red Sea.

The exchange marks the latest escalation since the Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, imposed an embargo on Saudi shipping on Monday, disrupting maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects Asia to Europe via the Suez Canal.

A near-identical Houthi missile attack on an oil tanker owned by the National Shipping Company of Saudi Arabia on Thursday had already prompted threats of American military intervention from US President Donald Trump.

“If they do this again, the US will hold Iran responsible, in that the Houthis are a surrogate and/or proxy of Iran, and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The Houthis claimed a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday, after media the group controls accused Saudi Arabia of a “dangerous escalation” and said its actions “will not go unanswered”.

Pakistan, which shares a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia, warned it would “take all necessary measures, including lawful use of force”, should its own “maritime interests” come under threat.

Despite these warnings, the Houthis struck and lightly damaged a tanker operated by Saudi state-owned National Chemical Carriers on Friday, shortly after the group’s official spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam clarified that the blockade applied exclusively to Saudi shipping.

“There is no closure of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait as some promote,” he posted on social media, as several Asian-owned tankers loaded with Saudi crude oil and petrochemicals, which had previously been turned back by the Houthis, were belatedly allowed through to the Indian Ocean.

Houthi ground forces have also launched attacks on two fronts in southwest Yemen held by Saudi-backed government troops and factions supported by the United Arab Emirates.

Houthi brinkmanship

Observers describe the Houthi strikes on Saudi shipping as “brinkmanship” rather than a coordinated effort with Iran to choke off both Gulf states’ oil export routes to Asia – though they say that possibility cannot be ruled out.

For now, further escalation “is not inevitable”, according to Adam Baron, a policy analyst and fellow with the future security programme at Washington-based think tank New America.

“We’re certainly looking at a very tense moment,” he said. “This brinkmanship not only reflects a willingness to potentially use force, but a wider posture that creates greater risks of things spiralling into conflict.”

Political scientist Annelle Sheline, a former US State Department official and Middle East fellow at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, sees Trump as “the figure most likely to escalate”.

She said the Houthis “do not necessarily want a return to full-scale war” with the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen’s civil conflict in 2015 to prevent the government’s overthrow. A tenuous UN-brokered ceasefire has been in effect since April 2022.

Rather, Sheline said the Houthis “are trying to increase pressure on Riyadh” to lift the restrictions imposed on flights and shipping links with Iran, which has long supplied the group with weapons such as anti-ship ballistic missiles.

Both analysts agree that the Houthis are opportunistically exploiting the Hormuz crisis for their own advantage.

“The Houthis view Iran’s success against the US and Israel, and the renewed closure of the Strait of Hormuz, as an opportunity to press Saudi Arabia to lift restrictions on their territory,” Sheline said, adding that this explained their decision to welcome the Iranian commercial flight to Sanaa from Tehran on July 3, which carried a Houthi delegation to the funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Riyadh reportedly saw this flight as an attempt by the Houthis to re-establish logistical supply routes with Iran’s Revolutionary Guards. The group wants regular flights between Sanaa and Tehran and other airports, as well as unrestricted maritime traffic through the ports it controls.

When an Iranian airliner attempted to bring home the Houthi mourners on July 13, Sanaa airport was bombed to prevent it from landing. Yemen’s Saudi-led backed government formally claimed responsibility, but then Houthis blamed Riyadh.

‘Opening another front’

Baron said the current escalation in the Red Sea “broadly fits into a long-standing pattern of tensions rising as the Houthis aim to get further concessions on key issues”.

With hostilities between the US and Iran also mounting, “this is certainly an opportune time for the Houthis to join the battle by opening up another front”, he said.

Sheline believes the Houthis will likely impose a full closure of the Bab el-Mandeb if Trump “restarts an air war” against them. The US and Britain previously conducted air strikes on Houthi targets in retaliation for attacks on Red Sea shipping between 2024 and 2025.

Renewed fighting would pile further pressure on oil markets and disrupt imports of food and other essentials to Saudi Arabia via Red Sea ports, Sheline said.

With access to its Gulf port of Dammam largely cut off, Saudi Arabia is currently importing roughly 80 per cent of its food through Jeddah on the west coast.

Baron said both Riyadh and the UAE would “certainly prefer to avoid being sucked into a war” with the Houthis, particularly given that the Iran conflict “remains hot”.

Yet he warned that a Red Sea blockade “certainly constitutes a significant risk not just to their economic interests, but also national security”.

Should the US launch an air campaign against the Houthis, Sheline believes “Riyadh and Abu Dhabi may be willing to join a coalition against them”, in order to reopen the Bab el-Mandeb Strait sooner.

The looming threat of a wider conflict has already prompted tanker owners to begin re-routing cargoes from Saudi Arabia to Asian markets via the Suez Canal and Africa’s Cape of Good Hope, significantly increasing both delivery times and costs.

Saudi Aramco, the desert kingdom’s state oil giant, has meanwhile begun ramping up crude shipments via Egypt’s Mediterranean Sidi Kerir oil terminal, in a bid to reduce the vulnerability of its exports to Houthi attacks.

In the months since the US and Israel first attacked Iran on February 28, leading to Hormuz’s closure, much of the oil previously exported via Saudi Arabia’s Persian Gulf ports has been diverted through a pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.

Additional reporting by Agence-France Presse

item.title: [SCMP] South Korean unions use new labour rules to push envelope on bonus demands
item.description:
Barely four months into its implementation, South Korea’s new labour-friendly law is coming under growing scrutiny as workers’ demands for bonuses tied to a fixed percentage of corporate profits spread across the country.

If left unchecked, critics warn, the revised Trade Union and Labour Relations Adjustment Act – commonly known as the Yellow Envelope Act – could fuel labour disputes, create uncertainty for businesses and threaten an economy that is only beginning to recover.

At the heart of the controversy is whether calls for bonus adjustments and other such demands fall under the new act, which has expanded the scope of labour disputes beyond traditional issues such as wages, working hours, welfare and dismissals to include “business management decisions affecting working conditions”.
item.content:encoded:
Barely four months into its implementation, South Korea’s new labour-friendly law is coming under growing scrutiny as workers’ demands for bonuses tied to a fixed percentage of corporate profits spread across the country.

If left unchecked, critics warn, the revised Trade Union and Labour Relations Adjustment Act – commonly known as the Yellow Envelope Act – could fuel labour disputes, create uncertainty for businesses and threaten an economy that is only beginning to recover.

At the heart of the controversy is whether calls for bonus adjustments and other such demands fall under the new act, which has expanded the scope of labour disputes beyond traditional issues such as wages, working hours, welfare and dismissals to include “business management decisions affecting working conditions”.

That broader definition has emboldened some unions to make demands that would previously have been considered beyond their collective bargaining remit.

Samsung Electronics’ labour union, for example, has argued that the company’s planned 800 trillion won (US$545 billion) investment in a new semiconductor manufacturing complex in the southwestern city of Gwangju should require union approval because it could affect employees’ working conditions through relocation and reassignment.

The controversy over profit-linked bonuses began at SK Hynix, which agreed last year to remove its previous cap and allocate 10 per cent of annual operating profit to an employee bonus pool for the next decade.

Following the threat of strike action, Samsung Electronics reached a similar agreement in May, earmarking more than 10 per cent of the semiconductor division’s performance bonuses for a new 10-year programme paid entirely in company shares.

Those deals have encouraged unions at other major companies to seek similar arrangements.

Among them are Hyundai Motor, whose union is demanding bonuses equivalent to 30 per cent of net profit; HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, where workers are seeking 30 per cent of operating profit; retail conglomerate Shinsegae, where the demand is 15 per cent of operating profit; and telecoms operator LG Uplus, where workers are also seeking 30 per cent of operating profit.

In the latest dispute, workers at Leeno Korea, Busan’s largest listed company and a manufacturer of semiconductor testing components, walked off the job on Thursday.

The union is demanding that performance bonuses be fixed at 800 per cent of base salary and additional benefits equivalent to 15 per cent of the company’s operating profit be paid each year. Management has rejected the demands as financially unsustainable.

Blurred boundaries

Song Heon-jae, a business administration professor at the University of Seoul, warned of a potential crisis.

“A small number of highly profitable semiconductor companies may be able to afford such generous bonus schemes. But most Korean companies, many of which are struggling to remain competitive, simply cannot absorb demands for bonuses linked to a fixed percentage of operating profit,” he said.

The revised law has become a new source of conflict because it is unclear where the boundary should be drawn between legitimate management decisions and issues subject to collective bargaining, according to Song.

“Militant labour unionism appears to be making a comeback in South Korea,” he said.

Organised labour has gained influence under Employment and Labour Minister Kim Young-hoon, a former prominent activist who supports strengthening workers’ rights.

Against that backdrop, President Lee Jae Myung has sought to draw clearer boundaries.

“Is the issue of distributing a certain percentage of operating profit truly a subject for industrial dispute? I believe it is more likely that it is not,” Lee said at a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, warning that the scope of industrial disputes was expanding too broadly.

Citing Samsung Electronics’ labour union’s claim that the Gwangju complex should be subject to negotiation because the project could result in employee relocation, he said: “If we follow that logic, the exercise of management rights by any company would become subject to disputes.”

The president said that rather than leaving such questions entirely to the courts, the executive branch should clarify the law through enforcement decrees and administrative guidelines.

Labour organisations immediately rejected Lee’s interpretation, arguing that the expanded scope under the amended Yellow Envelope Act included business management decisions affecting working conditions.

The Federation of Korean Trade Unions warned that enforcement regulations or administrative guidelines would effectively reverse the legislature’s expansion of workers’ fundamental rights.

The Korean Confederation of Trade Unions likewise accused the government of attempting to undermine a law achieved through years of labour activism by limiting its practical application through administrative measures.

‘Serious hurdle’

Labour lawyer Kim Hye-rim also argued that Lee’s interpretation was inconsistent with lawmakers’ intent.

By explicitly adding “business management decisions affecting working conditions” to issues previously limited to the “determination of working conditions”, the legislature clearly intended to broaden the range of what could become the subject of industrial disputes, she said.

The opposition People Power Party accused Lee of contradicting legislation that his own administration had championed. “After forcing through the Yellow Envelope Act, the president is now interpreting the law in a way that suits his own interests, bringing about clashes with labour unions,” the party said.

To add to the uncertainty, the revised law also allows labour unions representing subcontractors to negotiate directly with major purchasing companies such as Samsung Electronics and Hyundai Motor, said Sejong University business management professor Kim Dae-jong.

“The new labour law poses a serious hurdle for the country’s economy,” he said.

South Korea’s outward foreign direct investment reached around US$37.7 billion in 2025, more than double the US$18 billion in foreign direct investment that entered the country on an implemented basis.

The professor said only about 44 per cent of university graduates secured employment, arguing that rigid labour regulations remained one of the factors discouraging investment and job creation.

The Ministry of Employment and Labour is now reviewing the revisions, with officials expected to clarify that demand for profit-linked bonuses is not a matter for industrial disputes.

That might become another source of conflict in itself because administrative interpretations carried less legal authority than the statute, experts said. As a result, differing interpretations by labour and management could trigger a wave of litigation.

“South Korea is going through an inevitable adjustment period as it searches for a new balance of power between organised labour and corporate management,” Song said.

“The government and the ruling Democratic Party should amend the Yellow Envelope Act to eliminate the legal ambiguities that are fuelling confusion and industrial disputes.”

item.title: [SCMP] As Laos’ methanol poisoning case begins, victims’ families, friends slam ‘cover-up’
item.description:
Almost two years after six travellers died and one survivor was left blind from suspected methanol-tainted drinks in Laos, the criminal case is finally moving forward, with charges filed against a distillery owner – as victims’ families continue to demand answers and stern punishment.

The distillery owner, whose products are thought to have caused the deaths, was charged last Friday with running an illegal business and selling harmful food products. He faces a jail term of three months to four years if convicted.

The families described the potential punishment as inadequate given the scale of the tragedy, having earlier called for manslaughter charges against both the distillery owner and the manager of the Nana Backpackers Hostel bar in the backpacker town of Vang Vieng, where the deaths occurred.
item.content:encoded:
Almost two years after six travellers died and one survivor was left blind from suspected methanol-tainted drinks in Laos, the criminal case is finally moving forward, with charges filed against a distillery owner – as victims’ families continue to demand answers and stern punishment.

The distillery owner, whose products are thought to have caused the deaths, was charged last Friday with running an illegal business and selling harmful food products. He faces a jail term of three months to four years if convicted.

The families described the potential punishment as inadequate given the scale of the tragedy, having earlier called for manslaughter charges against both the distillery owner and the manager of the Nana Backpackers Hostel bar in the backpacker town of Vang Vieng, where the deaths occurred.

Two Danish nationals, 20-year-old Anne-Sofie Orkild Coyman and 21-year-old Freja Vennervald Sorensen died after drinking suspected methanol-tainted alcohol at the hostel in November 2024.

Also killed were Australians Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, both 19; British lawyer Simone White, 28; and American national James Louis Hutson, 57.

Foreign media were barred from attending a press conference on July 17, at which Laotian authorities announced the charges.

That same day, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen expressed his dissatisfaction with the case.

“I am … deeply disappointed that the charges do not reflect the seriousness and scale of the tragedy that has affected so many families. We will now discuss next steps in the case together with the bereaved families and the other affected countries,” he said.

British podiatrist Bethany Clarke, who now lives in Australia and survived the methanol poisoning incident that killed White, her childhood friend, told This Week in Asia that she was frustrated with the investigation.

Clarke and White had spent the day of the incident tubing in Vang Vieng before attending a nightly happy hour at the hostel, where they were given six free shots of locally produced whisky and vodka.

“It is just a cover-up and the charges are not even for the right person,” Clarke said. “The owner of the hostel and the person managing the buying of the alcohol are responsible.”

Clarke said the vodka she and White drank appeared to come from locally made Tiger brand bottles.

“No other bar was affected, so how could it be a distillery issue?” she asked.

Not long after the deaths were reported, Australia’s foreign affairs department warned its citizens against drinking Tiger Vodka and Tiger Whisky made in Laos “due to serious safety concerns”.

According to Laotian state media, police said they could not determine responsibility for some of the deaths due to difficulties establishing evidence. Methanol was detected in blood samples from the two Australian victims, and local reports indicate excessive methanol was found in the Tiger Vodka they had consumed.

Warning on travel to Laos

Methanol, a toxic, colourless and odourless form of alcohol, causes poisoning when it is not properly removed from alcoholic products during production. Methanol poisoning is common across Southeast Asia, where illicit alcohol is often sold. A single shot glass full, or about 25ml, can be fatal.

Globally, around 40,000 people have died of suspected or confirmed methanol poisoning between February 2019 and last month, according to data from Medecins Sans Frontieres.

Laotian authorities have said the case will remain open for 15 years, with further charges possible should fresh evidence emerge, according to the Danish foreign ministry.

That assurance offered little comfort to Clarke, however.

“It is just dragging it on, and for what? No one is going to come forward. It is not good enough. There is no transparency and accountability,” she said.

Following news of the recent charges, Australia updated its advisory for travel to Laos: “We now advise exercising a high degree of caution due to crime, the risk of methanol poisoning and ongoing concerns around lack of transparency in the justice system.”

Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong said in a statement on the same day that she was “deeply frustrated and bitterly disappointed” by the charges.

Canberra had sent an envoy to Laos “to convey the Australian government’s objections and reinforce our expectations for an investigation that delivers justice for Holly, Bianca and the other victims of the methanol poisoning”, Wong said.

Laos’ ambassador to Canberra was also summoned for a meeting, she added.

Phil Robertson, director of Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates, said he was not surprised by the charges, which he believed were aimed at securing a quick conviction while limiting further scrutiny.

He questioned whether authorities were “cutting a deal with the distillery owner”, reflecting Vientiane’s desire to protect its tourism industry.

Local authorities were likely more concerned about the new Australian travel advisory than the legal proceedings themselves, Robertson said.

“From the Lao government perspective, this case has always been less about those who died and more about trying to repair the serious public relations damage,” he said.

Moving on

British national Calum Macdonald, 24, survived the poisoning incident but was left permanently blind after the methanol in the drinks he consumed attacked his optic nerves.

He had been drinking free shots at the hostel with Coyman and Sorensen, a day before White and Clarke did the same.

Macdonald told This Week in Asia that he had only learned, some months after returning to the UK, that Coyman and Sorensen had died.

“It was a very eerie feeling as their faces were some of the last I ever saw before I lost my sight. I feel lucky. If I had had one more drink, I might not be alive.”

Regarding the case, Macdonald said he did not wish for anyone to face criminal charges.

“I don’t think anyone did anything on purpose to hurt anyone. The hostel had also been operating for a long time and this had never happened before. It is difficult, but I don’t feel the need to see anyone punished or any particular charges,” he said.

He acknowledged that his views differed from those of the grieving families, however.

“I didn’t lose a child, or a brother or a sister. I understand the level of distress caused to the families and I support whatever justice they feel is necessary,” said Macdonald, who is studying to be a financial analyst while working in the investment sector.

“I am not angry or upset about it any more. I have accepted what happened to me and adapted in my own life.”

This Week in Asia has reached out to three law firms in Laos for comment on the case and the country’s legal system. One declined to comment, while the others did not respond.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘She’s blown it’: support frays for Japan PM Takaichi over controversial laws
item.description:
Public support for Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi appears to be fraying, with two new opinion polls suggesting voters are losing patience with a leader who won a sweeping mandate in February but has since spent political capital on conservative causes instead of tackling cost-of-living pressures.

Analysts said the problem was not simply that Takaichi’s honeymoon period was ending, but that she had used her commanding position to push through legislation dear to the most conservative elements of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party while making little visible progress on day-to-day issues affecting the public’s well-being – chiefly, rising prices.

“She was given an immense mandate with a two-thirds majority for her own party, so there should have been nothing to obstruct her policies and no need to extend the Diet session, which they have just done,” said Michael Cucek, a professor of Asian Studies at Temple University’s Tokyo campus.
item.content:encoded:
Public support for Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi appears to be fraying, with two new opinion polls suggesting voters are losing patience with a leader who won a sweeping mandate in February but has since spent political capital on conservative causes instead of tackling cost-of-living pressures.

Analysts said the problem was not simply that Takaichi’s honeymoon period was ending, but that she had used her commanding position to push through legislation dear to the most conservative elements of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party while making little visible progress on day-to-day issues affecting the public’s well-being – chiefly, rising prices.

“She was given an immense mandate with a two-thirds majority for her own party, so there should have been nothing to obstruct her policies and no need to extend the Diet session, which they have just done,” said Michael Cucek, a professor of Asian Studies at Temple University’s Tokyo campus.

According to Cucek, Takaichi has failed to get her “key policy ducks in a line”, her credibility has been “eaten away by her obsequiousness” to US President Donald Trump and she has focused on fringe issues that may have pleased the far-right but have done nothing to improve the lives of ordinary people.

“In short, she has blown it and I see these opinion polls as more of a performance review than a sign that Takaichi’s ‘honeymoon period’ has come to an end.”

Two pieces of legislation pushed through the Diet this month made it a crime to “desecrate” the national flag – a law that critics say violates the constitutional right to free speech – and a revision to the Imperial Household Law that solidifies the long-standing rule of only allowing a man to ascend the Chrysanthemum Throne.

By preserving this restriction, the law makes it impossible for 24-year-old Princess Aiko, the only child of Emperor Naruhito, to become empress. A Kyodo News poll in May showed that 83 per cent of Japanese favoured altering the law to allow an empress on the throne, with just 13.1 per cent opposed.

Cucek said it was notable that both opinion polls were conducted immediately after revisions to the imperial law were passed, reflecting the public’s disdain for the prime minister’s priorities.

A poll published in the Asahi newspaper on Tuesday showed Takaichi’s support slipping 7 percentage points in the last month and her disapproval rate rising to 35 per cent from 27 per cent.

A Mainichi survey released on Wednesday, meanwhile, showed her backing plunging 10 percentage points over the same period to 41 per cent – below the 50 per cent threshold for the first time since her election in October.

“People are very disappointed in her administration, especially in her economic policies,” said Toshimitsu Shigemura, a professor of politics at Tokyo’s Waseda University.

“The sense is that she has no economic policies and that means prices continue to rise and the yen continues to weaken. Instead, she has made the new imperial law the priority. People are unhappy that there was so little discussion in the Diet and that the public’s wishes were ignored.”

Shigemura said Japan’s business leaders were concerned about worsening relations with China and the impact that could have on trade, noting there were whispers of discontent within the LDP that would only grow louder if public support continued to decline.

He added that Taro Aso, the party’s deeply conservative vice-president who is widely regarded as its kingmaker, had achieved his personal aim of reinforcing the prohibition on a female emperor and might no longer feel such a close allegiance to Takaichi.

Hiromi Murakami, a political-science professor at Temple University, also sees the empress vote as driving the sudden downturn in Takaichi’s popularity.

“It has caused huge controversy and people are angry that there was such little debate and that their opinions on the matter were ignored. There have been many polls that show the public is in favour of having an empress, but this decision only makes the conservatives happy,” she said.

“At a time when people need help with prices that seem to be constantly rising … Takaichi instead put priority on a new law to make it illegal to damage the flag. People are asking why and there do not seem to be any answers,” Murakami added.

“People are pretty angry about these peculiar bills.”

Takaichi is a firm follower of former prime minister Shinzo Abe, according to Cucek, but has failed to learn from his mistakes.

Abe opened his first term in 2006 “with all guns blazing”, Cucek said, but immediately ran into a crisis in the national pension system when the now defunct Social Insurance Agency lost about 50 million pension records. Abe vowed to solve the issue immediately but could not keep his word as the pressure mounted and he resigned exactly one year after taking office, citing ill health.

When he returned for a second – far more successful – spell as prime minister in December 2012, Abe approached the task far more pragmatically, Cucek said. “Abe put all of his focus on staying in office to effect policy over the longer term.”

While prime minister, Abe mostly avoided visiting Tokyo’s controversial Yasukuni Shrine, – where Japan’s war dead, including convicted war criminals, are honoured – after a visit in 2013 drew an international backlash. He also failed to revise the pacifist constitution, even though it was a stated ambition and he had the votes in the Diet.

“Takaichi is constantly looking back at Abe, but she is making the mistakes he made in his first term,” Cucek said.

He warns the omens are not good for Takaichi, who recently admitted she gets by on less than three hours of sleep every night.

“She is trying to show how hard she is working, but that’s a stupid thing for a leader to do,” Cucek said. “I can only see her burning out and crashing. That’s unfortunate because this is Japan’s first female prime minister, but I expect more opinion polls in the coming weeks and months to replicate these two recent polls.”

item.title: [SCMP] US slaps fresh tariffs on China, 50-plus countries in latest wave
item.description:
The United States imposed late on Thursday a fresh wave of tariffs against 60 countries, including China, Japan, South Korea, India and European Union member states, hours before a temporary 10 per cent blanket levy was due to expire.

The tariffs, ranging from 10 to 12.5 per cent, are the outcome of a Section 301 investigation into forced labour, with Washington arguing that existing measures have failed to keep goods produced with forced labour out of supply chains.

“Today’s action will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere,” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement.
item.content:encoded:
The United States imposed late on Thursday a fresh wave of tariffs against 60 countries, including China, Japan, South Korea, India and European Union member states, hours before a temporary 10 per cent blanket levy was due to expire.

The tariffs, ranging from 10 to 12.5 per cent, are the outcome of a Section 301 investigation into forced labour, with Washington arguing that existing measures have failed to keep goods produced with forced labour out of supply chains.

“Today’s action will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere,” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement.

China faces a 12.5 per cent tariff rate, while Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and the European Union are subject to tariffs ranging from 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent. Countries like Canada, Mexico, India, Indonesia and the United Kingdom face 10 per cent tariffs on top of their other US import levies.

Experts say the forced labour allegations are a pretext for imposing tariffs as part of US President Donald Trump’s broader America-first trade agenda.

Another Section 301 investigation under the 1974 Trade Act is ongoing, focused on excess industrial capacity in 16 economies, including mainland China, Taiwan, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, the European Union and several Southeast Asian countries.

Thursday’s move represents one of the most sweeping tariff actions since “Liberation Day” in April 2025, when US President Donald Trump’s administration unveiled global tariffs targeting nearly every US trading partner, sparking market panic.

This time around, the new levies are unlikely to trigger a similar reaction, with the caveat that Trump’s repeated declarations and climbdowns have lost some of their shock value.

The USTR announcement comes after months of relative quiet and welcome respite for industries, marking a return to Trump’s favoured playbook.

“It’s the uncertainty, not the rate, that’s the real cost,” said Ashley Kalyn, an international trade consultant with consultancy Peacock Tariff Consulting.

“Every time one legal authority gets struck down, the administration pivots to another.”

The administration has used the forced breather to hone workarounds that would let the self-described “tariff man” once again wield import taxes at will, analysts said, allowing him to maximise leverage and retribution unencumbered by investigations or vetting.

The search for new tools became necessary after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump’s expansive levies under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) unconstitutional in February.

Thursday’s notification came hours before a sweeping 10 per cent tariff imposed under Section 122 – a levy introduced in February following the court’s ruling – was set to expire.

There has been a growing list of trade measures announced in recent days, including new charges that target imports from Brazil and Canada.

The administration imposed 25 per cent tariffs on roughly one-third of Brazilian imports, which took effect on Wednesday following a Section 301 investigation into alleged unfair trade practices.

Brazil was targeted with tariffs even though Washington has maintained a long-standing trade surplus with the country.

According to USTR figures, the US recorded a US$14.4 billion goods trade surplus with Brazil in 2025, up 112.8 per cent from 2024.

In a separate move on Monday, underscoring his bid to bypass restrictions or precedent, Trump invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods within 30 days, justified on the basis of Ottawa’s alleged “trade discrimination” against multiple US industries.

The obscure 1930 trade enforcement provision, passed at the height of Depression-era protectionism, has never been used before and, in theory, gives Trump broader, faster and less restricted authority to levy tariffs than almost any other trade statute on the books.

Earlier this month, China expressed “strong dissatisfaction” over the Section 301 investigations and warned of “necessary measures”.

“By once again abusing the Section 301 process and placing domestic law above international rules, the US is making a serious mistake,” the Chinese embassy in Washington said.

However, people familiar with the matter told the South China Morning Post that the additional tariffs were unlikely to disrupt negotiations or derail President Xi Jinping’s expected visit to the US in September.

China currently faces an effective tariff rate of just over 20 per cent, reflecting the temporary trade truce reached in November 2025, and the impact of the US Supreme Court’s ruling.

Washington is now seeking to reinstate the import levies struck down by the court through a combined tariff of around 20 to 25 per cent under its Section 301 investigations. The tariffs announced on Thursday represent one component of that broader package.

The latest tariffs were announced a day after Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations foreign ministers’ gathering in Manila.

After the talks, Rubio confirmed that discussions included the implementation of newly created trade and investment boards, adding that both sides were working to make them operational.

“I think that’s one of the potential concrete deliverables that we can have before September when that visit happens,” Rubio said.

The board of trade was a key outcome of Trump’s visit to China in May, with both sides agreeing to establish a tariff-free mechanism that would cover up to US$30 billion in non-sensitive goods from each country.

Meanwhile, those on the front lines are bracing for more uncertainty and upheaval.

“Companies can price around a known number,” said Kalyn. “They can’t plan around a rate that’s flipped four times in five months.

“Cash gets over-reserved, capital projects get delayed, and a lot of the manufacturing investment we hear about on paper still isn’t breaking ground.”

There are some industries that are reviving domestic manufacturing, including semiconductors, pharmaceuticals and steel, in line with Trump’s vision of a blue collar renaissance, she said. But overall factory employment has fallen by 72,000 jobs since Liberation Day.

“USTR has Section 301 investigations that could bring in a new tariff right behind it, so nobody’s celebrating,” Kalyn added.

“Smaller importers mostly can’t afford to reshore, so they’re diversifying suppliers and stockpiling instead of relocating.”

item.title: [SCMP] Trump’s manufacturing push meets reality as costs rise and investment stalls
item.description:
At Zion Foodtrucks in the US state of Colorado, American-made steel and aluminium are combined with globally sourced stoves, refrigerators, vents and titanium piping to transform everyday vehicles into mobile restaurants.

But instead of benefiting from Donald Trump’s push to revive US manufacturing, the company says it has been squeezed by higher costs and tougher competition.

Since taking office, the US president’s import taxes on steel and aluminium have hit 50 per cent tied to his “beautiful” tariffs; truck delivery prices have jumped US$1,000 on higher fuel prices caused by the Iran war he launched in February; and Mexican manufacturers with lower labour costs and less expensive Chinese steel are gobbling up market share.
item.content:encoded:
At Zion Foodtrucks in the US state of Colorado, American-made steel and aluminium are combined with globally sourced stoves, refrigerators, vents and titanium piping to transform everyday vehicles into mobile restaurants.

But instead of benefiting from Donald Trump’s push to revive US manufacturing, the company says it has been squeezed by higher costs and tougher competition.

Since taking office, the US president’s import taxes on steel and aluminium have hit 50 per cent tied to his “beautiful” tariffs; truck delivery prices have jumped US$1,000 on higher fuel prices caused by the Iran war he launched in February; and Mexican manufacturers with lower labour costs and less expensive Chinese steel are gobbling up market share.

“Our company business has definitely come down because of the war and the tariff situation,” said company owner Appu Jacob Varghese.

“Competitors have actually closed their doors. So if that was the objective, to expand American manufacturing, I don’t know if that has worked out.”

Trump re-entered office promising a blue-collar renaissance. But 18 months into his second term, the evidence is mixed, say executives, economists and logistics experts, as policy churn, market instability and structural weakness undercut US competitiveness, discourage investment and frustrate supply-chain reform.

“His Liberation Day policies were implemented on April 2 of 2025 and that’s 15 months ago” said Robert Lawrence, international trade and investment professor with Harvard University.

“We might expect to see some green shoots, and we might expect to see signs of a reversal in manufacturing. Output in manufacturing, and productivity in manufacturing, and all of those are disappointing.”

Trump’s factory revival faces reality check

Spending on factory construction fell 20 per cent and factory jobs declined by 80,000 between January 2025 and mid-2026, according to US government data; and manufacturing as a share of GDP narrowed from 9.8 per cent in 2024 to 9.4 per cent in 2025.

Trump has repeatedly discounted inconvenient data as “deep-state” lies, arguing that his tariff and “America first” policies have spurred a manufacturing boom that is bringing factory jobs “roaring back”.

Some US$17 trillion in new investments landed during his first eight months, he claimed, including US$600 billion from Apple, US$250 billion from Micron and US$30 billion from Broadcom. A separate White House investment tracker put the figure at US$10.6 trillion.

Critics, however, say his numbers do not compute.

“Donald Trump is living in a fantasy world,” said Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.

“If there is US$17 trillion somewhere, the government doesn’t know about it,” the California lawmaker added. “He’s either a liar, or he’s somehow stashed away money in some magical way.”

A number of sectors have seen robust activity, including AI data centres and defence contractors profiting from the war.

But many involve relatively few blue-collar jobs. Others, facing White House political pressure, have found ways to look cooperative without making commitments that could hurt their economic interests.

“I don’t think threats work,” said Amrita Bhasin, a manufacturing economist and chief executive at California-based Sotira, which tracks and resells excess factory inventory.

“It’s been really difficult for brands to bring manufacturing back to the US … Literally, you can’t manufacture half the items here.”

The fact that Trump is loose with his facts and mercurial with his policies is hardly news. But the potential cost is high, analysts said, at a time when the US is trying to counter Beijing’s growing economic leverage and well-reasoned, multi-year development strategy.

Instead, the US finds itself squandering resources on an unpopular war with a politically divided and financially stressed workforce, led by a reactive president battling record low polling numbers.

“China has a plan. They tell us what it is every five years. They tell us what the top 10 priorities are, and then they execute on it,” said Jeffrey Moon, founder of consultancy China Moon Strategies, formerly with the National Security Council.

“What is Trump’s economic priority? The opportunity cost really is America’s future.”

How companies are adapting to US policies

Amid often searing political pressure, companies have sought ways to avoid Trump’s ire, analysts said, many employing tactics honed during his first term.

These include repackaging long-standing investments, including some launched under former president Joe Biden, into eye-catching headlines; and signing non-binding “letters of intent”.

Others include front-loading imports to avoid empty shelves that invite political scrutiny; crafting deals premised on easily unwound tax breaks; and announcing multi-year timelines that provide flexibility or outlast the administration.

In 2016, air conditioner-maker Carrier promised to keep 1,100 jobs in Indiana only to quietly lay off more than 450, shift production to Mexico and use the tax breaks to automate.

The next year, Foxconn announced a US$10 billion liquid crystal display line in Wisconsin, promising 13,000 high-paying jobs that Trump called “the eighth wonder of the world”.

After Joe Biden was elected, the Taiwanese maker of Apple products cut its projected investment by 93 per cent after hiring just 1,450 workers and walked away from a huge, unused industrial park.

Why bringing production back is so difficult

Companies juggling global supply chains cite structural impediments and contradictory policies.

Despite his investment push, Trump’s distrust of clean energy and electric vehicles saw 38 major US clean-energy projects cancelled in 2025, totalling US$19.8 billion, according to labour-environmental partnership BlueGreen Alliance.

“Policies have been incredibly inconsistent,” said Lawrence, also a senior fellow with the Peterson Institute for International Economics. “And Trump just keeps changing his mind.”

Other frustrations, companies say, include a shortage of the manufacturing hubs, supplier networks and government incentives that China is adept at providing.

And the administration’s aggressive deportation policies have undercut hiring in construction, manufacturing and other sectors, as skilled craftsmen age out and AI data centres push up capital and electricity costs.

“It doesn’t make financial and logistical sense,” said Bhasin, who said some competitors ship goods to Dubai and back to dodge high US factory costs.

“Even if President Trump had the money to bring this back to the US, it would take years until the average manufacturer would even be able to produce in the US.”

Bringing manufacturing back to the US is far more complex than just comparing labour costs and tariffs, including supply chain concentration, interest rates and geopolitical risk.

“The calculation has become much more nuanced,” said Anthony Raphael Escoboza, managing member with Esco Global Strategies, which advises companies on reshoring factory production.

“Relocating production to the US is one path, but many companies are also evaluating allied and nearshore manufacturing locations.”

Supporters of Trump’s vision counter that major changes take time, even as companies in the domestic steel, fossil fuel, semiconductor and defence industries cite benefits from Trump’s “America first” policies.

Pure Choice Apparel, a small clothing manufacturer in Arizona, has seen more buyer interest since Trump’s higher tariffs narrowed importers’ advantage.

“Customers who were previously sourcing blank garments or finished goods overseas – especially from China – are asking us more often about domestic alternatives, and some are converting,” said company founder Shane Kelley.

“I won’t overstate it. Domestic production still carries real cost premiums. And not every customer can absorb them. But for the first time in years, ‘made in the USA’ is a genuine competitive point rather than just a marketing line.”

Pennsylvania-based defence contractor Intervala, meanwhile, recently reported a US$6 million advanced manufacturing investment.

But some question the entire goal of revitalising US manufacturing – rather than services and intellectual property where it has a natural advantage.

Too often, they add, arguments are shaped by rust-belt politics and nostalgia for an idealised America attractive to octogenarians like Trump and Biden.

“Both of them are kind of revivalists with restoration theories of American prosperity moulded by their experiences,” said Lawrence. “We don’t need a ministry of industry. We need a ministry of services.”

China still holds the structural advantage

For many, China is the model and competitive obsession – even as Beijing tries to foster its service and consumer economy.

“China has its own structural pressures,” said Selina Wei, a technical specialist at Guangdong-based Hongwang Holding Group.

“Competition is intense in sectors where capacity has grown faster than demand, and margins are tighter.”

Voracious price competition, mounting global trade tension, slowing growth and structural bottlenecks made worse by “zombie” state-owned factories are other problems vexing Beijing.

“Huge costs are incurred by the current set of policies,” said Loren Brandt, international trade and economics professor at the University of Toronto. “There are no easy solutions.”

For Zion’s Varghese, trained as a mechanical engineer, the food truck idea came when he saw a greasy, burned-out taco truck.

He had worked as a volunteer firefighter, and figured he could do better. In 2023, he acquired a bankrupt company that he turned around and named after his eldest daughter.

Modern food trucks were pioneered by Mexican vendors serving migrant workers at remote worksites, sometimes dubbed “roach coaches”, outfitted with makeshift kitchen equipment that went flying when vehicles stopped short.

As Mexico has continued to dominate low-end manufacturing, Zion and others have moved upscale.

His custom-made trucks, which take about six weeks to manufacture, dish out everything from Texas barbecue to hibachi to wood-fired pizza costing up to US$200,000, with proper warranties – and no flying griddles.

Rough industry estimates suggest the market was around US$4.5 billion with some 200 specialised manufacturers in 2024, declining to 160 makers collecting roughly the same revenue by 2026.

Once customers place their order, Varghese acquires used FedEx or other vehicles, mostly from a New Jersey dealer, delivered to his workshop outside Denver.

Skilled employees then set to work installing plumbing, gas lines, steel and aluminium counters, stoves, refrigerators, propane tanks, windows and even toilets.

Some jobs, especially for school districts, require complete made in America production.

“It’s such a challenge,” said Varghese. “Even the things you think are made in the US and sold by US companies are not made in the US.”

Having weathered two earlier failed ventures, the serial entrepreneur expects more promise and pitfalls ahead.

“It’s not like you see a slowing of demand. They want food trucks,” he said. “But the challenge will be there. I don’t see prices coming down, just increasing. The war, it affects things.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why PLA fighter jet sorties near Taiwan dropped to a 3-year low in the first half of 2026
item.description:
There is a change in the skies and waters around Taiwan.

In the first half of this year, the number of People’s Liberation Army (PLA) fighter jets detected near the island more than halved year on year to 1,334.

It was a three-year low and marked the lowest operational tempo since 2023, according to a tally by the South China Morning Post based on data from Taiwan’s defence ministry.
item.content:encoded:
There is a change in the skies and waters around Taiwan.

In the first half of this year, the number of People’s Liberation Army (PLA) fighter jets detected near the island more than halved year on year to 1,334.

It was a three-year low and marked the lowest operational tempo since 2023, according to a tally by the South China Morning Post based on data from Taiwan’s defence ministry.

At the same time, the number of days no PLA jets were detected by Taiwan hit a new high, and the PLA did not stage any large-scale drills around the island – a first since 2022.

It is a long way from August 2022, when then US House speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei and Beijing responded with live-fire drills around Taiwan.

Those drills set new norms, with mainland China sending fighter jets and later, vessels, near the island on an almost daily basis.

The number of air sorties rose to more than 5,400 in 2025, increasing pressure on the island and prompting some strategists to argue that the PLA would take over Taiwan in 2027, the deadline for the mainland military’s “centennial goals”.

Yet this year, with the deadline for the vaguely defined goals just a year away, Beijing’s military signalling near Taiwan appears to have shifted.

Why fewer PLA sorties?

Observers say that improvements in Beijing’s relations with the US, pending US arms sales to Taiwan and non-official engagements between Beijing and Taipei, could be among the key external factors behind the change.

Internal considerations by Beijing could also be at play, they argue, including a push to control military costs and a shifting focus for PLA exercises.

By the numbers

In the years following Pelosi’s visit, the PLA sent more planes and more vessels, which went closer to the island. They also experimented with more sophisticated collaboration between various units.

The aerial pressure culminated in 2025, when the PLA sent the most annual aircraft sorties near the island (5,461) and had the highest count of sorties crossing the median line (3,782) of the Taiwan Strait – the notional midpoint between the two sides.

But for the first six months of this year the number of PLA aircraft sorties around Taiwan dropped to less than half those counted in each 2025 half-year period: January-June (2,762) and July-December (2,699).

Of these, the number of aircraft crossing the unofficial median line – considered by Taiwan to be more dangerous – this year (810) was well down on the half-year periods in 2025 (1,984 and 1,798).

From January to June 30 this year, no PLA aircraft were detected on 38 days, much higher than the six days in the first half of last year and the eight in the second half.

And five out of the first six months this year saw the lowest monthly totals since 2023. The total aircraft recorded for March (162) was the lowest monthly figure since January 2023.

What role did Xi-Trump summit play?

Experts have largely attributed the dip in mainland military activity around Taiwan to the summit held in Beijing between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, where both sides touted agreements on strategic stability.

Despite continued tension between the world’s two biggest economies, the two sides are trying to stabilise ties, with subtle de-escalation signs coming from Beijing, Washington and Taipei.

“Following [Trump’s] meeting with Xi, there’s some sort of a leaders’ consensus on trying to turn down tensions, especially over Taiwan,” said Collin Koh, a senior fellow at the Institute of Defence and Strategic Studies with the Singapore-based S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS).

Media reports said Trump might delay or roll back arms sales to Taiwan, according to Koh.

“Then there’s no reason for Beijing not to reciprocate with obvious moves. And this is a very obvious move,” he said.

Shi Yinhong, a professor of international relations at Renmin University of China, also said Beijing had an eye on US arms sales.

“It seems that military operations around Taiwan have reduced dramatically and for numerous months, which could be explained by [the mainland] withholding any major reasons for [the] US and its related allies to increase military support to Taipei,” he said.

The first half of this year also coincided with outreach by Beijing to Taiwan’s main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). In April, Xi met KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun for the first such talks in nearly a decade. Beijing followed this by releasing a package of 10 measures to promote cross-strait exchanges in the economy.

Lyle Goldstein, director of the Asia programme at the Washington-based think tank Defence Priorities, said Beijing now saw that “Cheng’s discourse is having some effect in Taiwan politics, kind of opening the window to a wider debate of cross-strait relations”.

“I think they find this favourable and that could explain partially why tensions are lowering,” he said.

Reassessing the 2027 Davidson window

The US intelligence community is reversing its previous assessment of the so-called Davidson window, the idea that the mainland would attack Taiwan in 2027.

The Office of the Director of National Intelligence said in a report in March that “Chinese leaders do not currently plan to execute an invasion of Taiwan in 2027”, reversing course on predictions that have shaped US battleforce strategy for the past six years.

Following the Xi-Trump summit, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio sought to explain why military means were not the preferred way for Beijing to take Taiwan.

“What they would want is some vote or a referendum in Taiwan that agrees to fold in. I think that’s what they would prefer,” he said in an NBC interview in May.

A similar assessment was offered by Lloyd Austin, defence chief in the Joe Biden administration.

“I don’t think that President Xi wants to take Taiwan by force” and “there is probably less risk of escalation going forward here in the near term”, Austin said last month.

Goldstein argued that these were signs of change in Washington’s China policy debate.

“I do think the space for debating China policy is opening again. It’s been closed for a long time. It did seem that Washington was set on a very hard-nosed approach to China, but I do think eyes are open to a different possibility here,” he said.

The role of PLA drills

A shift in training focus for the PLA and calls to cut costs could also be behind the change, observers said.

Fu Qianshao, a retired PLA Air Force colonel, said the change in the PLA’s tempo was partly because it had already completed management and control around Taiwan, and that the training focus of the PLA had expanded towards the western Pacific Ocean.

“Adjustment has been made based on the current cross-strait situation, and more training now is in the far seas, not necessarily around the Taiwan Strait,” Fu said.

“This expanded scope [of the western Pacific] also covers the cross-strait area. It’s just that the diameter has been expanded. This, I think, is a key characteristic for the first half-year.”

Koh said the lower frequency could also be the result of practical reasons, such as the time required to maintain high-end equipment and deliver balanced training to military personnel.

Analysts also point to the impact of Beijing’s ongoing anti-corruption campaign on the military leadership, as well as its call to cut costs in the armed forces, as possible factors.

The campaign has led to the downfall of many of the most senior figures across the top PLA leadership and various forces and theatre commands, leaving only two members from the original seven-member Central Military Commission.

The process to fill the vacancies is continuing. After Beijing’s most recent ceremony to promote two full generals in July, the PLA has just six full generals in active duty, while normally it would have at least 20.

“Reshuffling of the armed forces’ chains of command necessarily requires a long time, along with the shrinkage of financial capability that would not cease in [the] short, or even much longer, term,” Renmin University’s Shi said.

Cost-cutting in the military is a theme that has reappeared many times in recent years. The 15th five-year plan endorsed by the national legislature in March calls for “building the armed forces through diligence and thrift”, and taking the path of “high efficiency, low cost and sustainability”.

The fragile de-escalation

Nevertheless, since taking office in May 2024, Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te has been seen by Beijing as highly provocative for his pro-independence stance.

He has sought to pass an unprecedented US$40 billion special defence budget to fund the US arms purchases. Although only around US$25 billion was approved, Lai is seeking to pursue the remainder through separate proposals.

Zhang Wensheng, deputy dean of the Graduate Institute for Taiwan Studies at Xiamen University, said that while the cross-strait military struggle would remain, “under the US pressure, I don’t think [Lai] will dare be too aggressive”.

Maritime activity around Taiwan

However, there are already signs of fresh tensions around the island.

Starting in June, the number of official mainland Chinese ships, which includes the coastguard and survey ships, jumped.

The number of these law enforcement vessels rose to 252 in the first half of this year, up by 89 per cent from July-December last year (133), and a 66 per cent jump compared with the six months before that (152).

The number of mainland law enforcement ships nearing Taiwan reached 111 in June – the most in a month since July 2024, when such ships started to be involved in daily PLA operations around the island.

That appeared in response to the Japan-Philippines maritime delineation talks which started in late May.

The talks could concern exclusive economic zones claimed by Beijing and Taipei, and Beijing has condemned them as breaching China’s maritime rights.

“[The Chinese coastguard] used to be seen as secondary only to the PLA, but now [the China Coast Guard] is taking on a more active role in the round-Taiwan-island patrols,” said Koh at the Institute of Defence and Strategic Studies in Singapore.

“I guess there is a desire to create a less militaristic impression. And so, using white hulls instead of grey hulls might actually be something that will feed that sort of strategic narrative,” he said, referring to the hull colours of CCG and naval warships.

Despite the ongoing tensions, observers say this trend of easing Chinese military activity could continue into the second half of the year.

But they warn that US midterm elections and the Taiwan local legislative elections, both in November, could affect the delicate de-escalation.

“Since the Xi-Trump meeting, we can see that mainland and the US are managing Taiwan together. And how does the US manage Taiwan? It is through arms sales,” said Lu Li-shih, a retired Taiwanese navy lieutenant commander.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Payback’: why China’s world-beating car industry faces plunging sales at home
item.description:
China’s electric vehicle (EV) industry sits at the centre of numerous economic and geopolitical trends: consumer spending, environmental protection, trade policy, high-end manufacturing, technology and more. In this short series, we assess the current state of the sector within these broader contexts. Here, Emma Ma examines the forces driving higher exports and lower domestic sales.

Wang Wenfei, a 30-year-old chef from central China’s Henan province, had long dreamed of buying a new car. So, when he received his annual bonus in February, he decided to splash out as a gift to himself after a decade of hard work at a restaurant in Shanghai.

“A comfortable new car that I can drive home to Henan for Chinese New Year was all I wanted,” he said, setting himself a budget of 100,000 yuan (US$14,700).
item.content:encoded:
China’s electric vehicle (EV) industry sits at the centre of numerous economic and geopolitical trends: consumer spending, environmental protection, trade policy, high-end manufacturing, technology and more. In this short series, we assess the current state of the sector within these broader contexts. Here, Emma Ma examines the forces driving higher exports and lower domestic sales.

Wang Wenfei, a 30-year-old chef from central China’s Henan province, had long dreamed of buying a new car. So, when he received his annual bonus in February, he decided to splash out as a gift to himself after a decade of hard work at a restaurant in Shanghai.

“A comfortable new car that I can drive home to Henan for Chinese New Year was all I wanted,” he said, setting himself a budget of 100,000 yuan (US$14,700).

However, just weeks later, Wang received an unpleasant surprise: the government had slashed its subsidy for new car purchases by 33 per cent to 10,000 yuan. Meanwhile, petrol prices were rising amid the war in the Middle East – and his employer had declined to give him a pay rise.

Reluctantly, he decided to put his dream on hold.

Wang is far from alone. China is now the world’s largest car exporter, but sales at home have hit the skids in recent months, as the government scales back its subsidy programme and consumers remain reluctant to spend amid a shaky job market and prolonged property downturn.

The trend is creating a headache for Chinese carmakers like BYD and Chery Automobile – pushing them to lean more heavily on overseas markets at a time of rising trade tensions – as well as complicating Beijing’s efforts to rebalance China’s economy towards domestic consumption.

The trade-in ‘payback’ effect

The subsidy change is a major reason behind the fall. China introduced a generous trade-in programme for new cars in 2024 as part of a drive to rev up the domestic economy, which offered buyers 15,000 yuan off any purchase.

The scheme proved hugely successful and was extended last year, when China invested a whopping 300 billion yuan (US$44 billion) to provide subsidies on an array of consumer goods to help the economy ride out a trade war with the United States.

But with China and the US reaching a trade truce and the trade-in programme showing signs of diminishing returns, Beijing trimmed its subsidies earlier this year. The total funding for the programme was reduced by 50 billion yuan, and discounts for new car purchases were adjusted downwards.

Previously, buyers received a flat 15,000 yuan subsidy on any new car regardless of price. Now, they receive a subsidy equivalent to 10 per cent of the purchase price, which is capped at 15,000 yuan. That means the subsidy for a 100,000 yuan petrol car – like the one Wang hoped to buy – has fallen by 5,000 yuan.

The reduction has had a direct impact on car sales, according to analysts. China was always going to experience a form of “payback” for the trade-in programme, as the subsidies effectively front-loaded future demand by convincing large numbers of consumers to replace their cars earlier than needed, Beijing-based research firm Gavekal Dragonomics said in a research report in late June.

Consumer sentiment is extremely weak, and we are pessimistic about the sales outlook this year

Steve Shi, Juchen Auto Trade

Now, with the subsidies scaled back, the payback effect has kicked in and may continue for some time, with Gavekal Dragonomics predicting that it could “depress retail sales growth” for “as long as two years”.

Sales of passenger vehicles in China fell 20.2 per cent year on year during the first half of 2026, data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) showed. The decline accelerated over the past two months, with sales tumbling more than 23 per cent in June – the second-steepest decline recorded so far this year.

Why consumers expect another price war

The outbreak of the Iran war has compounded the problem, with higher petrol prices making consumers less willing to invest in a car. Though China imposed some price controls, petrol prices on the mainland still climbed over 25 per cent between late February and early April, and remained elevated into July.

“The biggest drag on May and June’s weak sales performance was the collapse of consumers’ demand for petrol vehicles, a direct fallout from elevated pump prices,” said Cui Dongshu, secretary general of the CPCA.

The sales decline also has a self-reinforcing dynamic, as Chinese consumers widely expect carmakers to respond by slashing prices. China’s car industry has been gripped by vicious price wars for years, especially in the electric vehicle (EV) segment, where Beijing has repeatedly railed against “involutionary” competition, policymakers’ term for the race to the bottom in certain sectors.

Now, many buyers believe brands will soon be forced to cut their prices once again, and they are deliberately delaying purchases as a result.

“Consumers now have become less inclined to pay premiums for owning foreign-branded cars,” Cui said. “Instead, they widely expect petrol car prices to slide further.”

That was exactly what Wang had in mind. “The vehicle market is seeing a sales decline, and we bet carmakers will have to offer big discounts later this year to draw new buyers. I will not make a purchase decision unless prices appear to be attractive,” he said.

Wu Jinling, a Shanghai-based consumer, made a similar point. She is looking to buy an electric vehicle to replace her petrol car, but believes she might get a better deal later this year.

“Competition among new models will get fiercer in the coming months,” Wu said. “Price cuts can be expected, as all the car brands struggle to reduce their inventories.”

Juchen Auto Trade, a car showroom in Shanghai, is already feeling the pressure. “Most buyers appear to be budget-conscious and want us to offer steeper discounts,” said Steve Shi, a manager at the firm. “Consumer sentiment is extremely weak, and we are pessimistic about the sales outlook this year.”

The subsidies will shore up domestic entry-level auto consumption in the short term

Cui Dongshu, China Passenger Car Association

How Beijing aims to boost demand

The Chinese government has already rolled out several measures in an attempt to shore up the car market, including a fresh round of subsidies for vehicle purchases in rural areas.

The rural subsidy programme dates back to 2009, and since 2020 it has focused solely on supporting electric car purchases. According to figures from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers, the policy has helped generate more than 20 million EV sales in rural China over the past six years.

This year, the programme has expanded to cover 155 vehicle models, 31 more than last year. The subsidies also cover cars in a wider range of price brackets, applying to models costing from 30,000 yuan to 500,000 yuan, according to a report by Kaiyuan Securities released in late June.

“The subsidies will shore up domestic entry-level auto consumption in the short term,” said Cui of the CPCA. “This year’s subsidies also cover EV charging infrastructure construction across rural areas, which will eventually stimulate fresh demand for trading in old petrol cars for EVs.”

But he warned that any sales bounce would not match those seen over the previous few years.

Analysts have echoed that view. In late June, Goldman Sachs lowered its forecast for passenger vehicle sales on the Chinese mainland over the next five years, after demand turned out to be weaker than expected in the first five months of 2026.

The pivot to exports – and growing pushback

Sluggish demand at home is driving China’s carmakers to focus more on expanding their overseas sales.

China has rapidly emerged as a car export powerhouse over the past few years, driven by the breakout success of the country’s EV industry, and the trend accelerated further in May.
